A four-word run of KJV relative-clause boilerplate. 2 Chronicles 7:14 is the Solomonic promise to a people 'called by my name'; Jacob 1:2 is a colophon distinguishing one record from another. Nothing but the relative construction is shared.

'Partake of the goodness of God' has no KJV source. 'The goodness of God' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 52:1 and Romans 2:4, and neither is being drawn on: Psalm 52:1 taunts a mighty man, and Romans 2:4's goodness leads to repentance rather than being partaken of. Psalm 33:5's 'the goodness of the LORD' is a different phrase filling the earth. The partaking in Jacob 1:7 belongs to the Hebrews 3 argument catalogued at that verse ('partakers of the heavenly calling', 3:1; 'partakers of Christ', 3:14), not to any goodness verse.

The four-word run is real but the governing phrase is 'lest by any means', which occurs in exactly three KJV verses and all three are Pauline (1 Corinthians 8:9, 2 Corinthians 11:3, Galatians 2:2). 1 Kings 20:39 has 'if by any means he be missing' in a parable about a guarded prisoner. Superseded by the Hebrews 3:8 link at this verse, which carries the Pauline phrase in its provenance.

'Provoke him to anger' occurs in exactly six KJV verses and the wider formula ('provoked the LORD to anger', 'provoke me to anger') runs through Deuteronomy, Judges, Kings and Jeremiah in dozens of places. It is the standard Deuteronomistic idiom for apostasy and points at no particular verse. Deuteronomy 4:25's specific content — graven images made by a settled generation — is not in view at Jacob 1:8.

The shared string is four common words split across a clause boundary in the KJV: David's 'to be a king's son in law' is not 'to be a king'. The candidate is an artifact of the possessive. The real background of Jacob 1:9 is 2 Chronicles 6:5, whose 'man to be a ruler over' is a KJV singleton, plus the Samuel anointing formula of 1 Samuel 9:16 — both carried on the accepted link.

A tempting candidate, and worth the entry. 'Reign in his stead' in that exact form occurs in exactly one KJV verse — 2 Chronicles 1:8, Solomon on succeeding David — which looks like a singleton and which is thematically apt, since Jacob 1:15 goes on to David and Solomon. But the singleton is an accident of tense: 'reigned in his stead' occurs in exactly 63 KJV verses, the regnal formula of Genesis 36, Kings and Chronicles, and Jacob 1:11 is using the formula, not the one verse that happens to inflect it as an infinitive. Recorded here rather than as a link because no single source can be named; the phrase belongs in the Index Verborum.

Five words, and the sense is opposed at the point that matters. 1 Kings 12:31's clause is 'priests of the lowest of the people, which were not of the sons of Levi' — a negation about priestly descent, marking Jeroboam's illegitimacy. Jacob 1:13's is 'the people which were not Lamanites, were Nephites' — a definition of an ethnonym. The run ends exactly where the two sentences diverge.
Pure connective tissue; 'the reign of the' is how the KJV dates anything. 2 Chronicles 36:20 concerns the Babylonian deportation and shares no content word with the second Nephite king.

The strongest-looking candidate in the verse and it should be declined. 'With all diligence' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 4:23 — 'Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life' — and a KJV singleton is normally decisive evidence in this catalogue. But the singleton is adverbial boilerplate attached to an unrelated imperative: Proverbs guards an inward heart, Jacob teaches an outward people the word of God. Nothing else of Proverbs 4 is present, and the phrase is ordinary English of the period independent of the KJV. Filed as the model of a singleton that proves nothing.

Four words of connective negation. Paul's 'we would not be chargeable unto any of you' and Jacob's 'we would not be found spotless' share only the auxiliary construction, and the same run appears at Genesis 42:21. What is genuinely borrowed in Jacob's clause is 2 Peter 3:14's 'found … without spot', catalogued as a link.

The chapter's top machine candidate, and genuinely tempting: Proverbs 30:12 is the only KJV verse that sets purity against filthiness in one sentence — “a generation that are pure in their own eyes, and yet is not washed from their filthiness” — and purity against filthiness is exactly the opposition Jacob 3:1-3 is built on. It is declined because the shared four words break across incompatible constructions (Proverbs has pure in one's own EYES, Jacob pure in HEART) and because the real source of the phrase is a KJV singleton: “pure in heart” occurs once in the Bible, at Matthew 5:8, which is catalogued as a link at this verse. “Filthiness” is a fifteen-verse word and is in any case the Book of Mormon's own leading term in this passage rather than a borrowing.

“Possess the land” is Deuteronomic boilerplate, drawn here by both Isaiah 57:13 and Amos 2:10 at identical scores, which is itself the sign that no one verse is in view. The Book of Mormon's own formula is “the land of your inheritance”, used continuously from 1 Nephi onward, and the threat that an enemy will possess it is the standard covenant curse rather than a citation. Nothing distinctive is shared with either candidate.

A five-word run and the highest n-gram score at the verse, produced entirely by a relative clause of commandment-transmission that the KJV uses everywhere (compare Nehemiah 9:23, which the same stream returned at the same verse for the same reason). Psalm 78:5 is about a testimony established in Jacob — the patriarch — which is likely why it scored, and that is a coincidence of the speaker's name. The verse's real sources are Ezekiel 16:52 and 1 Samuel 24:17, both catalogued. Worth noting for the record that 1830 reads “our fathers” where 1920 prints “our father”, so the string the machine matched exists only in the first edition.

Scored 2.00 and is the closest the machine came to a real find at this verse, because the sense as well as the string is parallel: God sees a people's conduct and therefore “I will not destroy them, but I will grant them some deliverance”. Declined because “not destroy them” occurs in three KJV verses (2 Kings 13:23, 2 Chronicles 12:7, and by paraphrase Isaiah 65:8) and the relenting formula is common well beyond those, while the conditions could hardly be less alike — Rehoboam's princes humbling themselves before Shishak, against Lamanite monogamy. The argument of Jacob 3:5-6, obedience answered by mercy and a future blessing, is catalogued instead at 3:5 against Genesis 22:16-18.

A real curiosity rather than a link, and it deserves the space. Ezekiel 16 IS a source in this chapter — 16:52 supplies the KJV singleton behind “are more righteous than you” seven verses earlier — so a second contact seven verses further up the same chapter looks like corroboration. It is not. Ezekiel 16:45's sisters “lothed their husbands and their children”; Jacob 3:7's Lamanites love theirs. The polarity is exactly inverted, the shared words are three function-heavy ones, and the wording Jacob actually uses is Titus 2:4's, whose two halves (“love their husbands”, “love their children”) are each KJV singletons. Filed here because a reader who has just accepted the Ezekiel 16 link at 3:5 is precisely the reader who would accept this one.

Proposed by us, not by the machine, and rejected in order to state the point plainly rather than leave it implied. “Whiter than” occurs in exactly two KJV verses: Psalm 51:7 (“wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow”) and Lamentations 4:7 (the Nazarites “whiter than milk”). Psalm 51 is attractive because it is David's psalm after Bathsheba and this is a sermon on sexual sin, so a chastity sermon reaching for whiteness might be expected to reach there. But Jacob 3:8 completes the comparison with “than yours” and applies it to skin, and no KJV verse compares the complexions of two peoples. The right catalogue entry for the passage is what has a source and what does not: the venue clause “before the throne of God” has one (Revelation 7:15, and see the link at this verse), and the racial vocabulary of 3:5-9 has none. Handled as at 1 Nephi 12:23 — the language is the Book of Mormon's own and is not catalogued as scriptural.

exclusions.sharedText: which is the word of God
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and the second-highest score at the verse, and it means nothing: “the word of God” is among the commonest phrases in the KJV, and the relative that attaches it here is a relative clause, not a citation. Ephesians 6:17's referent is the sword of the Spirit; Jacob's is a commandment about how to speak of the Lamanites. The verse's identifying phrase is the singleton at its head, “commandment I give unto you” (John 13:34), which is catalogued.

“Hundredth part” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and a singleton is normally the strongest evidence this catalogue has — which is why the entry is worth writing. Nehemiah 5:11 is a rate of interest: the nobles are to restore “the hundredth part of the money, and of the corn, the wine, and the oil, that ye exact of them”. Jacob 3:13's hundredth part is a measure of how little of a record fits on a plate, and it is a Book of Mormon formula with its own life — Words of Mormon 1:5, Helaman 3:14, 3 Nephi 5:8, Ether 15:33 — introduced here at its first use. A rare phrase in an unrelated sense, and the model case for why frequency alone never decides.

A genuine KJV singleton — 'surely come to pass' occurs in exactly one verse — and therefore exactly the kind of candidate CONVENTIONS §5 says must be written up rather than passed over. It is still nothing. 1 Kings 13:32 is the man of God's oracle against the altar at Bethel and the high places of Samaria; Jacob 6:1 says that Zenos's allegory of the olive tree 'must surely come to pass'. Nothing is shared but a formula for the certainty of prophecy, and the singleton is an artifact of the KJV's preference for 'shall surely come to pass' over the commoner 'shall come to pass' (which it uses several hundred times). A rarity count is evidence about a phrase, not about a link, and this is the case that shows the difference.

Scored second in the verse at 2.00 and the sense is opposed at the subject. Isaiah 42:13 has the LORD himself going forth 'as a mighty man' to stir up jealousy and prevail against his enemies; Jacob 6:2 has 'the servants of the Lord' going forth in his power to nourish and prune. The shared four words are a possessive plus a verb of motion, and the agreement disappears the moment the next word is read: Isaiah's warrior against Jacob's gardeners. The verse's real borrowing is the ten-word run from Isaiah 11:11 that the same stream also found.

Recorded because the rarity is real and tempting. 'Prune' occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Leviticus 25:3, 25:4 and Isaiah 5:6 — and Leviticus 25:3-4 is the only place the KJV puts the verb next to a vineyard, which is what Jacob 6:2 does ('to nourish and prune his vineyard'). But Leviticus 25 is sabbath-year legislation about when a farmer may and may not work his land, with no eschatology, no servants and no house of Israel, and the collocation is what any English writer would produce who needed a verb for vineyards. The proximate model is Jacob 5, where the Lord of the vineyard prunes and digs and nourishes for seventy-seven verses; Isaiah 5:6's unpruned vineyard is recorded with the Isaiah 5:7 link at 6:3 as the KJV background that actually bears.

Five words, and the sixth decides against it. Matthew 8:12 casts the children of the kingdom out 'into outer darkness'; Jacob 6:3 casts the cursed out 'into their own place'. The completion is not Matthew's and the image is not Matthew's — darkness against a location. The phrase Jacob is using is his own book's: Zenos at Jacob 5:77 has the bad branches 'cast away into its own place', four verses before Jacob begins speaking, and the reader met it minutes ago. This is the within-a-book repeat that ADJUDICATING §4 says to adjudicate at first use and register here. If a Bible source is wanted for 'his own place' the KJV offers four verses, of which Acts 1:25 (Judas going 'to his own place') is the only judicial one; four occurrences will not identify a source.

exclusions.sharedText: stretched forth … hands … all the day … people
exclusions.reason: The obvious source and the wrong one, and saying so is the chapter's principal finding rather than a rejection. Isaiah 65:2 is the Old Testament verse behind Jacob 6:4's outstretched hands, but the Book of Mormon does not have Isaiah's English. Isaiah reads 'I have spread out my hands all the day unto a rebellious people'; Jacob reads 'he stretches forth his hands unto them, all the day long: and they are a stiffnecked, and a gainsaying people'. 'Stretched forth my hands' is a KJV singleton at Romans 10:21 and 'gainsaying people' is a KJV singleton at Romans 10:21; Isaiah has neither expression. The link is therefore filed at Romans 10:21 with mediation OT-via-NT, and Isaiah 65:2 is carried there as a composite. Note that tools/mediation-check.py could not resolve this pair, because the Book of Mormon shifts Paul's first person into the third and a word-level aligner then sees the Book of Mormon agreeing with neither; the rarity counts settle it without ambiguity.

The top-ranked machine candidate in the verse at 1.41, and it is a phrase, not a link. 'All the day long' occurs in thirteen KJV verses, eight of them in the Psalms, and Deuteronomy 28:32 uses it of parents whose eyes fail with longing for children sold into slavery. The five-word run only reaches six words because Jacob's pronoun 'them' happens to precede it as Deuteronomy's does. A textbook case of CONVENTIONS §9: rare-looking boilerplate outscoring the real source, which in this verse is Romans 10:21 and which the n-gram stream did not return at all, because the Book of Mormon's change of person breaks every contiguous window.

Four words spanning a clause boundary in both texts and joining nothing. Jacob's 'cleave unto God as he cleaveth unto you' ends one clause at 'God' and begins a comparison at 'as he'; Eliphaz's 'Can a man be profitable unto God, as he that is wise may be profitable unto himself' does the same at the same words, and the sense is a rhetorical denial that God gains anything from human righteousness — the opposite of the reciprocity Jacob is asserting. The verse's real source is Acts 11:23, the KJV's one verse joining purpose of heart to cleaving, which the n-gram stream did not rank.

exclusions.sharedText: to day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your heart(s)
exclusions.reason: The Psalm is the ultimate source and not the proximate one, and the whole of the case is a plural. 'Harden not your hearts' occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Hebrews 3:8, 3:15 and 4:7 — and in no Old Testament verse; Psalm 95:8 reads the singular, 'Harden not your heart'. Jacob 6:6 has the plural, so the twelve-word run is the epistle's rendering of the Psalm and not the Psalm. Among the three Hebrews verses, 4:7 is the one where the quotation from David terminates at 'hearts' with no 'as in the provocation' following, which is where Jacob's also stops; 3:8 and 3:15 both continue. Filed as a quotation at Hebrews 4:7 with Hebrews 3:15 and Psalm 95:7 as composites, mediation OT-via-NT. Note that tools/mediation-check.py returned no decisive divergence here: the KJV's versification splits the sentence between Psalm 95:7 and 95:8, so a comparison run against 95:7 never sees the singular that decides the question.

exclusions.sharedText: hewn down, and cast into the fire
exclusions.reason: Matthew 3:10, Matthew 7:19 and Luke 3:9 are the three KJV verses carrying this seven-word run, and the n-gram stream ranked all three identically at 1.12 because on the run alone they are indistinguishable. A second rarity breaks the tie. Jacob 6:7 also has 'bring forth evil fruit', which is a KJV singleton at Matthew 7:18 — the verse standing immediately before Matthew 7:19. Neither Matthew 3:10 nor Luke 3:9 has a neighbour supplying 'evil fruit'; both read 'bringeth not forth good fruit'. So the source is the Sermon on the Mount, not the Baptist's preaching, and the difference is substantive: Matthew 3:10 and Luke 3:9 threaten the Pharisees with an axe at the root, while Matthew 7:15-20 is teaching a congregation to recognise false prophets by their fruit, which is the subject Jacob 6:8 turns to in the next breath. Filed at Matthew 7:19 with 7:18 as composite; Luke 3:9 is excluded on the same reasoning.

exclusions.sharedText: the power of God and the
exclusions.reason: Top-ranked in the verse at 1.15 and it is a list joint. Jacob 6:8 is running a series — 'the good word of Christ, and the power of God, and the gift of the Holy Ghost' — so 'the power of God, and the' is the seam between two items and carries no content. 1 Corinthians 1:24 has the phrase inside a genuine christological claim ('Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God') that Jacob does not make. The verse's real borrowings are 1 Thessalonians 5:19, whose 'quench … the Spirit' is a KJV singleton, and Acts 2:38 / 10:45 for 'the gift of the Holy Ghost'; the phrase 'plan of redemption' that the sentence is actually arguing for occurs in no KJV verse at all.

A genuine rarity — 'hearts of the people' occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and therefore exactly the kind of candidate a careful reader accepts. The sense is opposed. At Ai the hearts of the people 'melted, and became as water' in defeat; Sherem 'did lead away many hearts' by persuasion. Joshua's idiom is courage failing, the Book of Mormon's is allegiance transferred, and nothing else in the two verses touches. A singleton is not by itself an argument.

'According to the power' occurs in three KJV verses and the construction 'according to the power of X' is ordinary KJV English. The apparent piquancy — Paul's 'according to the power of God' against Sherem's 'according to the power of the Devil' — is a coincidence of a common frame taking the two commonest objects, not an inversion of a source. 2 Timothy 1:8 is about suffering for the gospel and has nothing to do with eloquence or flattery.

exclusions.sharedText: I say unto you, that none of
exclusions.reason: Seven words, and the string 'I say unto you, that none of' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, so the n-gram stream ranked it first in the verse at 2.03. It is still boilerplate: 'I say unto you that' is the Book of Mormon's standard preface and 'none of' is the ordinary negative quantifier. Luke 14:24 is the close of the parable of the great supper and concerns bidden guests tasting a meal; the shared material stops at the join. The real source of Jacob 7:11 is John 5:39, adjudicated at this verse.

Tempting for the wrong verse. James 4:14 joins ignorance of the morrow to the brevity of life — 'what is your life? It is even a vapour' — and the chapter does return to the brevity of life at 7:26. But at 7:16 the shared string is only the connective 'on the morrow, for', and Sherem is not ignorant of his morrow; he is announcing it. Where the chapter does take up the figure, at 7:26, the image is a dream and the verb is 'passed away', which is Psalm 90:9's and Job 20:8's, not James's vapour. Recorded there as the declined alternative.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that on the morrow
exclusions.reason: The longest n-gram run in the chapter, nine words, and 'that on the morrow' occurs in exactly one KJV verse — which is precisely the trap. The run is the Book of Mormon's universal narrative connective plus a date. Numbers 17:8 is Aaron's rod budding in the tabernacle; the Book of Mormon verse is a crowd assembling to hear a dying man recant. There is no contact beyond the join. Covered in principle by the standing connective exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1 and recorded here only because the rarity score invites acceptance.

exclusions.sharedText: that he fell to the earth
exclusions.reason: The machine ranked this first in the verse on a seven-word run, but 2 Samuel 1:2's man falls to the earth and does obeisance to David — a deliberate act of homage, with his clothes rent and earth on his head. Sherem is struck down. The KJV's one instance of an involuntary collapse under divine power is Acts 9:4, 'and he fell to the earth', which occurs in exactly one KJV verse and which the surrounding narrative (nourished for many days, then confession) confirms. Adjudicated to Acts 9:4 at this verse.

exclusions.sharedText: and he gave up the ghost
exclusions.reason: 'Gave up the ghost' occurs in ten KJV verses, so the phrase cannot pick its own source; the stream chose Genesis 25:17 because 'and he gave up the ghost' with the conjunction occurs in exactly one KJV verse. But Genesis 25:17 is a genealogical formula for Ishmael dying old and full of days, gathered to his people. Sherem dies under judgment immediately after confessing that he lied unto God, which is the sequence of Acts 5:4-5. Adjudicated to Acts 5:5 at this verse.

'As he was about to' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which is why it scored 1.50 and led the verse — and it is pure temporal connective. Acts 20:3 is Paul changing his travel plans to avoid a Jewish ambush before sailing for Syria; the Book of Mormon has a man about to die. Neither the subject, the action, nor the setting touches. The verse's real contact is with Acts 5:11, adjudicated here.

'I make an end of' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the sense is opposed in the most consequential way. In Ezekiel 20:17 God does NOT make an end — 'neither did I make an end of them in the wilderness' — so the KJV's only instance of the phrase is a negation, and the object is a people spared destruction. Jacob makes an end of his writing. The colophon idiom is the Book of Mormon's own (compare 1 Nephi 9:5, Enos 1:26) and needs no biblical source.

The top-ranked candidate for the verse is four words of narrative hinge inside 'it came to pass, that I, Jacob'. Covered by the standing exclusion for KJV connective formulae; recorded here only because it was the chapter's highest-scoring machine proposal and a reader of the dossier will wonder why nothing came of it.

Four words of ordinary epistolary construction, and Paul's sentence runs the other way — he has written these things so that they should NOT be done for him. Jacob's 'for this intent have we written these things' has its purpose clause fulfilled, not disclaimed.
Four function words. The n-gram stream ranks it because the run is unbroken, which is precisely the failure mode CONVENTIONS §9 describes.

A real trap rather than noise, because both verses put a beloved son in a wilderness to be tested, and Jacob 4:5 is expressly building a typology between a father's sacrifice of his son and God's. But the shared words belong to different clauses on either side: Matthew has Jesus led up into the wilderness TO BE TEMPTED of the devil, and Jacob has Abraham in the wilderness, TO BE OBEDIENT unto the commands of God. The tester differs, the tested differs, and the infinitive that follows differs; the four-word run is an artifact of English word order. The typology Jacob is actually drawing is Hebrews 11:17's, catalogued as a link at this verse.

'Be obedient unto' is ordinary KJV idiom (compare Titus 2:9, 'Exhort servants to be obedient unto their own masters'), and Deuteronomy 8:20 is about the nations perishing for disobedience — the opposite pole of Jacob's sentence, which is about Abraham's obedience being accounted for righteousness.

Four function words, and Paul's 'even as it was told me' is about a shipwreck. The clause that matters in Jacob 4:5 is what follows those four words — 'accounted unto Abraham' — which is Galatians 3:6's and is catalogued as a link.
A five-word purpose clause of the commonest kind. Isaiah 41:23 is the LORD's taunt to the idols; nothing in Jacob's confession of weakness and grace touches it.

Five words, and a genuine KJV singleton — 'no man knoweth of his' occurs only at Deuteronomy 34:6 — which makes this the most tempting rejection in the chapter. It fails on the noun. Deuteronomy 34:6 is about the burial of Moses: 'no man knoweth of his SEPULCHRE unto this day', a fact about one grave in Moab. Jacob 4:8 is about the unknowability of God's ways, 'no man knoweth of his WAYS, save it be revealed unto him', which is a claim about God, not about a location. The sentence's real source stands two clauses earlier and supplies the whole thought: Romans 11:33, 'how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out', where 'how unsearchable' and 'the depth of the riches' are each KJV singletons. The Deuteronomy run is the accident of a very common four-word opening plus one preposition.

'Mysteries of God' is a KJV singleton at 1 Corinthians 4:1, which is why the stream ranks it, but Jacob does not have that phrase — he has 'the depths of the mysteries of Him', where the pronoun blocks the match and the governing noun is 'depths', which is Romans 11:33's. Paul's verse is about stewards of the mysteries, a claim about office; Jacob's is about their unsearchability.

'The world was made' is a KJV singleton at John 1:10, and the verse is about creation, so the proposal is not frivolous. But Jacob's four words are not a clause: 'if God, being able to speak, and the world was' is a conditional whose apodosis is the bare verb 'was', where John's runs 'the world was made by him, and the world knew him not'. The construction Jacob is imitating is Psalm 33:9's 'For he spake, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast' — speaking paired with commanding, which is exactly the inference the rest of his verse draws — with Hebrews 11:3 supplying the doctrine that the worlds were framed by the word. Both are catalogued as a link at this verse. Recorded at length because a Johannine reading of Jacob 4:9 is the kind of thing this catalogue will be asked about.

An appeal-to-the-audience formula. Paul's is about working with his own hands at Miletus; Jacob's introduces God's wisdom, justice and mercy. The verse's link is Psalm 145:9, on the singleton 'over all his works' in the same sentence.

Paul's 'so run, that ye may obtain' is about the prize in a footrace and the effort that wins it; Jacob's 'that ye may obtain a resurrection' is about what the atonement confers. The four words are identical and the theology is opposed at the point that matters — earning against receiving. The Pauline material genuinely present in this verse is 2 Corinthians 5:20, 1 Corinthians 15:20-23, Philippians 3:10, Colossians 1:27 and 1 Timothy 3:16, all catalogued.
Four words spanning a clause boundary in 1 Peter ('a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God'), where 'which is in' introduces a location and not, as in Jacob, an indwelling.

The KJV's formula is 'the first and the last' (Isaiah 44:6, Revelation 1:11, 1:17, 2:8, 22:13) and Jacob 4:16 reads 'the great, and the last, and the only sure foundation'. The substitution of 'great' for 'first' is deliberate and is the one word of the sentence that is Jacob's own; taking Revelation as the source would credit the borrowing with the very word it does not have. The verse's source is Isaiah 28:16, on the KJV singleton 'sure foundation', which Hardy also gives and which is catalogued as a link.

1 Peter 2:7 is the fifth New Testament quotation of Psalm 118:22 and shares 'is made the head of the corner' with Jacob 4:17, so it belongs among the candidates. It is displaced on the verb: 1 Peter reads 'the stone which the builders DISALLOWED', where Jacob 4:15 and 4:17 both read 'reject'. Acts 4:11, which Hardy also lists, is displaced the same way — it reads 'was SET AT NOUGHT of you builders'. Only Matthew 21:42, Mark 12:10 and Luke 20:17 give 'rejected', which is why the link at 4:17 names the Synoptic form specifically. Note that 1 Peter 2:6-8 is nevertheless the New Testament's fullest fusion of the three stone texts (Isaiah 28:16, Psalm 118:22, Isaiah 8:14), the same fusion Jacob performs across 4:15-17; it is recorded as a composite at 4:15 rather than as a source here.

exclusions.sharedText: unto you the word of God
exclusions.reason: The top-ranked machine candidate for this verse, and genuinely tempting: Hebrews 13:7 is about leaders 'which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God', which is exactly Jacob's situation as he comes up into the temple to 'declare unto you the word of God'. But the six-word run is the KJV's ordinary phrase for preaching and occurs across the New Testament, and the verse's real borrowing is elsewhere in the same sentence: 'magnify mine office' is a KJV singleton at Romans 11:13, and it is a claim about the speaker's office, which is what Hebrews 13:7 only made this candidate look like.

Jeremiah 44:9 rehearses the wickedness of fathers, kings and wives in a chapter about idolatry in Egypt; the four shared words are a possessive construction the KJV uses continuously. Nothing in Jacob 2:6 points at Jeremiah 44 in particular, and the verse's one distinctive string, 'before the presence of', points at Jude 1:24 instead.

Worth writing up because the thematic pull is real and misleading. Numbers 22:20 is God telling Balaam that he may go, 'but yet the word which I shall say unto thee, that shalt thou do' — a prophet constrained to speak only what he is given, which is precisely Jacob's plea at 2:9-11 that he speaks under 'the strict commandment which I have received from God'. The typological expectation is that a reluctant prophet under compulsion is being drawn as Balaam. The wording will not bear it: 'the word which I shall give thee' is the KJV's standard commissioning formula (Exodus 25:16, Jeremiah 1:7), Jacob's verb is 'give' where Balaam's is 'say', and no other element of the Balaam narrative appears anywhere in the chapter.

'Is a land of' is the KJV's standard formula for describing territory and appears in dozens of verses. Deuteronomy 11:11's subject is rain and topography; Jacob's is a land abounding in gold and silver. The four words carry nothing.

A five-word run shared with both Acts 3:22 and Acts 7:37, and the highest-scoring candidate at this verse — but the sense is opposed at the only point that matters. In Acts the phrase is Deuteronomy 18:15's messianic promise: God will raise up a prophet 'of your brethren, like unto me', where 'like unto' governs Moses and the whole weight of the clause is that one man will resemble one other man. Jacob 2:17 reads 'Think of your brethren, like unto yourselves', where 'brethren' means the poor of the congregation and 'like unto yourselves' is an appeal to common humanity against a claim of superiority. The word-run is an artifact of two different uses of 'like unto' colliding after the same two nouns. Note that the Deuteronomy-via-Acts pairing is a real and important link elsewhere in this catalogue (1 Nephi 22:20); it is not one here.

The run is an accident of 'ye' abutting 'for the kingdom of'; Matthew 3:2 is John's 'Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand', where 'for' is a conjunction and the kingdom is 'of heaven', not 'of God'. The verse's actual source is the seek-the-kingdom saying, Matthew 6:33 or Luke 12:31, catalogued as a link at this verse.

The highest-scoring candidate at this verse and the polarity is wrong. Paul's clause is 'the things which God hath prepared for them that love him' — the unseen, unimagined future reward. Jacob's is 'the things which God hath given you', the present wealth his hearers are proud of and are being rebuked for. The shared five words are a relative clause with a common verb; the two sentences are about opposite kinds of possession.

'Were it not that I' is a KJV conditional formula shared with Deuteronomy 32:27 and 2 Kings 3:14 alike, and 'I make an end of' (Ezekiel 20:17) is narrative boilerplate the Book of Mormon uses continuously. Neither Elisha's refusal to look at Jehoram nor Ezekiel's sparing of Israel in the wilderness has any contact with Jacob's transition from pride to unchastity.

exclusions.sharedText: people forth out of the land of
exclusions.reason: The longest machine run in the chapter (seven words) and a real echo, but of a formula rather than of this verse. 'Brought thy people forth out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand' is the KJV's standing exodus recital and stands in Daniel 9:15, Exodus 32:11, Deuteronomy 9:26 and elsewhere in nearly identical words, so Daniel has no claim to be the source. The verse's demonstrable borrowings are Exodus 6:6, whose 'stretched out arm' Jacob renders 'the power of mine arm' and whose 'rid you' he has already used at 2:16, and Jeremiah 23:5's 'righteous Branch'; both are catalogued as links here.

The expected source for a law of one wife, and it is not the source. Genesis 2:24 and its four New Testament quotations (Matthew 19:5, Mark 10:7-8, 1 Corinthians 6:16, Ephesians 5:31) were put through tools/mediation-check.py against Jacob 2:27, and the result is that the test cannot run: Jacob reproduces none of the wording the candidates share — no 'leave his father and his mother', no 'cleave', no 'one flesh', no 'twain' — so there is nothing at which the OT and NT forms could be shown to diverge. The finding is worth recording precisely because it is negative. The chapter that legislates monogamy does not argue it from the one-flesh text, and its actual English ('save it be one wife') belongs to the three Pastoral verses on the qualifications of bishops and deacons, catalogued as a link at this verse. A reader who assumes Genesis 2:24 stands behind Jacob 2:27 is importing a connection the text declines to make.

A five-word run with a high rarity score and no content. Joshua 1:5 promises that no man will be able to stand before Joshua; Jacob 2:27 forbids any man to have more than one wife. The shared string is a universal negative subject, and the continuation ('be able to stand' against 'among you have') diverges at the sixth word.

The top-scoring candidate at this verse on n-gram rarity (2.00) and entirely worthless: the five words are a prepositional chain, and Obadiah 1:13 is about Edom entering the gate of Jerusalem in the day of its calamity. The verse's real source is the doubled seeing-and-hearing formula of Exodus 3:7, which the machine stream cannot see because Jacob splits it across a clause boundary and substitutes his own nouns.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that the
exclusions.reason: Standing exclusion for the whole of Jacob 5. The allegory is built on a small set of refrains that recur dozens of times across seventy-seven verses: 'and it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard sayeth unto his servant', 'it grieveth me that I should lose this tree', 'lay it up against the season, unto mine own self', 'let us go down into the vineyard, that we may labor'. The n-gram stream ranks Joshua 1:1 ('and it came to pass after the death of Moses') first or near-first at eleven separate verses of this chapter on runs of six and seven words, all of them connective. Nothing in that class is adjudicated here; see the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5 and 2:1 for the same decision in the pilot.

Hardy's cross-reference apparatus files Isaiah 11:11 at this verse, and the recovery it announces — the Lord setting his hand 'again the second time to recover the remnant of his people' — is unquestionably the theology of the second grafting at Jacob 5:52-68. But there is no verbal contact at 5:2, whose only shared material is the vocative 'O house of Israel'. The wording Isaiah 11:11 answers to stands two chapters later at Jacob 6:2, 'in the day that he shall set his hand again the second time to recover his people', where the phrase 'the second time to recover' is a KJV singleton; that is where the link belongs and it is left for the adjudication of Jacob 6.

'I will liken thee, O House of Israel, like unto a tame olive tree' contains a genuine KJV singleton: 'I will liken' occurs in exactly one verse of the Authorized Version, Matthew 7:24, 'I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock'. The count is real and the temptation is real, but the sense is not shared at any level — Matthew's clause introduces a simile about obedience and building, Zenos's introduces an extended allegory about a tree — and the formula 'I will liken X unto Y' is ordinary English independent of any verse. A singleton that is a singleton only because the KJV happens to prefer 'whereunto shall I liken' elsewhere is a fact about the concordance, not evidence of dependence.

Hardy's apparatus files Isaiah 65:2 and Romans 10:21 at Jacob 5:4, which in our text reads only 'I will prune it, and dig about it, and nourish it'. There is no stretched-forth hand here. The sentence the two references answer to is at Jacob 5:47, 'I have stretched forth mine hand almost all the day long', and that is where the link is catalogued — with the mediation decided, since the Book of Mormon has Romans 10:21's 'stretched forth' and not Isaiah 65:2's 'spread out'. Recorded as an exclusion at 5:4 so that the Hardy row is accounted for at the verse where his apparatus places it.

Hardy's apparatus files Psalm 95:7-8 at this verse. Jacob 5:6 reads 'after many days, it began to put forth somewhat a little, young and tender branches; but behold, the main top thereof began to perish', and Psalm 95:7-8 reads 'To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your heart, as in the provocation'. There is no shared vocabulary, no shared figure, and no shared syntax; the only connection available is thematic — a people given time and failing to use it — which is the theme of the whole allegory and not of this verse. Recorded rather than passed over because it is a scholarship-stream row and every such row must end as a link or a reasoned exclusion.

'The nethermost part of my vineyard' is one of the chapter's structural terms — it recurs at 5:14, 5:19, 5:20, 5:38, 5:39 and 5:52 and carries the allegory's whole New World application — and 'nethermost' is a KJV singleton, at 1 Kings 6:6. But the singleton is architectural: it names the lowest of the three storeys of side chambers around Solomon's temple. Nothing in the Book of Mormon's use is spatial in that sense, nothing in 1 Kings is horticultural, and no other word of either context is shared. This is the model case for the register: an absolute rarity count that establishes only that the writer knew an English word the KJV happens to use once.

The n-gram stream ranks Genesis 1:4 first at both 5:17 and 5:20 on 'he beheld that it was good' against 'And God saw the light, that it was good'. The temptation is a real one, since the creation refrain is among the most recognisable formulas in the KJV and an allegory about a maker inspecting his work could plausibly reach for it. It is declined because the refrain in Genesis 1 is 'God saw that it was good' seven times over and the shared string is the four commonest words in it; the Book of Mormon's verb is 'beheld', which Genesis 1 never uses, and the object is fruit, not a completed act of creation. Nothing distinguishes this from ordinary approving English.

Jacob 5:21-25 turns on the quality of ground — 'the poorest spot in all the land of thy vineyard', 'this spot of ground was poorer than the first', 'this have I planted in a good spot of ground' — and the parable of the sower is the obvious KJV background for a planting whose outcome varies with the soil. It is declined because the sower's distinctions are wayside, stony places, thorns and good ground, and none of the first three appears here, while 'good ground' by itself is four words of common English. Jacob 5's variable is the owner's choice of site, not the seed's fortune, and the surprise of the passage is the opposite of Matthew 13's: here the poorest ground bears much fruit and the best ground fails.

'And it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard wept' is the emotional centre of the allegory and has no counterpart in any of its three sources — Isaiah 5's owner is angry, Luke 13's is impatient, Romans 11's does not appear as a character. Luke 19:41, where Jesus beholds the city and weeps over it two chapters before telling the parable of the wicked husbandmen, is the nearest KJV analogue and the sequence is suggestive. It is declined because 'wept' occurs in seventy-two KJV verses and nothing else is shared; the tear is recorded in the note at 5:41 as the Book of Mormon's own addition to Isaiah 5:4 rather than as a borrowing.

'Let us go to, and hew down the trees of the vineyard' uses an idiom the KJV has at Genesis 11:3, 11:4 and 11:7 ('Go to, let us make brick', 'Go to, let us build us a city', 'Go to, let us go down, and there confound their language') and at James 4:13 and 5:1. The Babel verses are the closest in form, and the third of them is even a divine 'let us go down'. Declined as an idiom rather than an allusion: the Book of Mormon uses 'go to' six times in this chapter (5:49, 5:52, 5:61, 5:62, 5:71) in every register, including the servant's speech, which is what an inherited interjection looks like and not what a Babel allusion would look like.

A five-word run of pure connective tissue — 'And this will I do, that the tree may not perish' against 'that will I do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son'. No content word is shared. Recorded only because the machine ranked it first at this verse.

'I will take of the branches of this tree' against 'I will take of the spirit which is upon thee'. Five connective words and a shared partitive construction; the subject of Numbers 11:17 is the distribution of Moses's spirit to the seventy elders and shares nothing else with the grafting instruction.

The n-gram stream ranks Revelation 1:11 highest at this verse on 'the first and the last', which is a real six-word agreement and a phrase Revelation makes into a divine title (1:11, 1:17, 2:8, 22:13). It is superseded. Jacob 5:63 reads 'begin at the last, that they may be first, and that the first may be last', which is Matthew 20:16's antithesis, not Revelation's self-designation; and the same verse's 'begin at the last' answers Matthew 20:8's 'beginning from the last unto the first', a KJV singleton from the parable that already supplied this chapter's name for God at 5:8. Revelation's phrase is a title for a person; the Book of Mormon's is an order of operations.

'They shall be one' occurs in exactly two KJV verses and Genesis 2:24 is one of them. It is superseded by Ezekiel 37:19, the other, where the phrase describes two separated portions of Israel — the stick of Joseph and the stick of Judah — made one in the Lord's hand. Genesis's 'one flesh' is a marriage formula and cannot carry the sense Jacob 5:67-68 needs, which is the reunification of branches that were divided and dispersed.

The machine proposes Jeremiah 38:23 at the allegory's last verse on 'to be burned with fire' — Zedekiah told that he shall cause Jerusalem to be burned with fire. The five-word run is real but the phrase is common KJV judgment language, and the verse it stands in has been reached by a different route: 5:77's controlling source is Matthew 13:47-50, whose 'gathered the good into vessels, but cast the bad away' supplies two singletons to the same sentence, and whose burning at 'the end of this world' (Matthew 13:40, 13:49) supplies the clause Jeremiah is being proposed for.

Hardy keys Isaiah 5:1-7 to Jacob 5:3, the verse that introduces the allegory — 'I will liken thee, O House of Israel, like unto a tame olive tree, which a man took and nourished in his vineyard'. That is the right place for a cross-reference to a whole chapter's governing image, and 5:3 itself reproduces no wording from it. The catalogue places the link where the verbal evidence is: Jacob 5:41 quotes Isaiah 5:4's 'what could have been done more', a KJV singleton, converting its passive to a first-person active. Recorded here so Hardy's row is discharged at his own verse and a reader who looks for it at 5:3 is sent to 5:41.

As with Isaiah 5:1-7 above: Hardy keys Paul's olive tree to the verse that introduces the allegory, and the catalogue places it at Jacob 5:7, where the branches are broken off and the wild are grafted in, with recurrenceRefs back to 1 Nephi 10:12, 10:14 and 15:13 where the Romans 11 claim was first argued. Note the limit the Jacob 5 pass registered and that the 1 Nephi rows did not: the KJV spells the verb 'graff' at all four places in Romans 11, and Jacob 5 spells it 'graft' twenty-two times and 'graff' never, in 1830 as in every later edition. The allegory is Paul's; the orthography is not.

A figural link stood here on the strength of Hardy's cross-reference to Genesis 22, argued as the obedience-conditioned Abrahamic promise transferred to the Lamanites. Its own whyNot named the condition that would withdraw it — “if the reference belongs with the Abraham-and-Isaac discussion at Jacob 4:5” — and on 2026-09-05 that condition was met: the study edition's running heads bound each page, and the note is on the page that carries Jacob 4:5, where Jacob names the offering of Isaac as a similitude of the Father and the Son. The row is cited there now. Nothing verbal ever connected Genesis 22 to Jacob 3:5, and with the reference gone there is no case left to make. The 1 Samuel 24 and Ezekiel 16 links at this verse stand on their own evidence and are untouched.

A genuine KJV singleton — 'spake many things unto them' occurs only at Matthew 13:3 — and therefore a real temptation, which is why it is registered rather than passed over. It is declined because the words are the Book of Mormon's own narrative frame rather than a borrowing: Nephi is introducing a speech, and Matthew is introducing the parable of the sower. Nothing in the two contexts touches, and the verse's actual borrowing is in the clause immediately after it, Mark 5:19's 'how great things the Lord'. A singleton that is pure reporting formula is still a formula.

'The mercies of God' is a KJV singleton, at Romans 12:1, and it stands verbatim in 2 Nephi 1:2 — which on rarity alone would make a strong row. It is declined on sense. Paul's phrase is the ground of an appeal ('I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice'): the mercies are what obligates the hearer. Lehi's phrase names an event — 'the mercies of God in sparing their lives, that they were not swallowed up in the sea' — and obligates nobody. The construction differs too: Paul's is instrumental, Lehi's is possessive. This is the register's standard case, a rare phrase that means something else, and it is filed at length because rarity is exactly the evidence that would otherwise have carried it.

Deuteronomy 11:8-12 is the standing scriptural background for every land-of-promise sentence in this book, and the machine's proposal is not absurd. But 'a land which the LORD thy God careth for' shares only its opening article and relative pronoun with 'a land which the Lord God hath covenanted with me', and the distinctive content of Deuteronomy 11:12 — the eyes of the LORD upon it from the beginning of the year to the end — is nowhere in 2 Nephi 1. The land-promise idiom is diffused across Genesis, Deuteronomy and Joshua and cannot be pinned to one verse here.

A six-word run, and the highest-ranked candidate the machine offered for this verse. 2 Kings 9:10 is the prophecy of Jezebel's death: 'the dogs shall eat Jezebel in the portion of Jezreel, and there shall be none to bury her.' The shared string is a negative-existential construction whose sense in the source is the denial of burial and in the Book of Mormon the promise of undisturbed tenure. The construction is what matched; the completing infinitive — 'bury' against 'molest' — is what decides it. The verse's own link is filed at Ezekiel 34:28.

exclusions.sharedText: from the creation of the world
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and a KJV singleton, which makes this the hardest exclusion in the chapter. Romans 1:20 reads 'For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made' — the phrase is adverbial there, modifying how long God's attributes have been perceptible, and the argument it serves is that the heathen are without excuse. 2 Nephi 1:10 has 'all men knowing the great and marvellous works of the Lord from the creation of the world', where the phrase names the content of a knowledge that was given rather than inferred, and the argument is that a people who received revelation are more culpable than one that did not. The two verses are making opposite arguments about the same words. Registered rather than accepted, but a reader who wanted to take it as an allusion would not be behaving unreasonably, and the verse's accepted link (Revelation 15:3) does not exclude it.

Tempting for a reason that has nothing to do with the phrase: Isaiah 29 is the chapter 2 Nephi 27 expands, so any contact with it in this book earns a second look, and 29:10's 'the LORD hath poured out upon you the spirit of deep sleep, and hath closed your eyes' is thematically apt for sons who will not wake. Declined because 'deep sleep' occurs in ten KJV verses and because the chapter's demonstrable source for the whole awake-and-arise complex is Isaiah 51:17-52:2, which supplies two singletons in the same sentence. The Isaiah 29 contact this verse's neighbour does have is at 1:23, 'out of obscurity', and it is filed there as a link.

The machine's best candidate for this verse. 'The judgments of the LORD are true and righteous altogether' shares four words, but Psalm 19:9 is praising the judgments as an object of delight and Lehi is enjoining them as a rule of conduct — 'remember to observe the statutes and the judgments'. The pairing with 'statutes' is what identifies the source, and it points to 1 Kings 2:3, two verses after the verse this chapter quotes verbatim at 1:14. Superseded, not merely weak.

A five-word run whose next word decides it. Job 20:22 reads 'In the fulness of his sufficiency he shall be in straits' — Zophar on the prosperity of the wicked, where the fulness belongs to the man and is about to fail him. 2 Nephi 1:17 has 'the fulness of his wrath', where the fulness belongs to God and is about to arrive. The genitive construction is all that matches, and it is one of the KJV's commonest. The verse's link is at Matthew 19:8.

exclusions.sharedText: by the sword, and by famine
exclusions.reason: Jeremiah pairs sword and famine, usually with pestilence, more than twenty times, and Jeremiah 16:4 has no better claim to the phrase than a dozen of its neighbours. The Book of Mormon's 'visited by sword, and by famine' is that stock pair and identifies no verse. What is not stock in 2 Nephi 1:18 is the clause about the devil's will and captivity, which is filed as a link to 2 Timothy 2:26.

Six words shared with 'If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love', and the temptation is real because the Book of Mormon's sentence is a conditional promise in the same syntax. It is declined because the verse announces its own source — 'and he hath said' — and what was said is 1 Nephi 2:20-21, where the catalogue placed 1 Kings 2:3. The apodosis is what separates them: John promises abiding in love, 1 Kings 2:3 promises prospering, and the Book of Mormon promises prospering in the land. Superseded by the OT-via-earlier-BoM row at this verse.

Registered only because the dossier ranked it second in the chapter. 'It must needs be that' is a KJV connective the Book of Mormon uses continuously, and Matthew 18:7's subject is the inevitability of offences. No content word is shared. Covered in principle by the standing exclusion filed at 1 Nephi 2:1.

The chapter's most instructive machine failure. A six-word run, top-ranked for the verse, and its source is Jehu's letter to the elders of Samaria: 'If ye be mine, and if ye will hearken unto my voice, take ye the heads of the men your master's sons.' The Book of Mormon clause is a father's condition for leaving a blessing to his sons; the KJV clause is a usurper's condition for the decapitation of seventy of them. The shared string is a conditional formula that occurs across Deuteronomy and Samuel and cannot identify a source; the accepted reading of 2 Nephi 1:28-29 is Genesis 27:36, filed at 1:29. Recorded at length because it is the kind of hit that looks strongest exactly where it is worth least (ADJUDICATING §4).

The dossier's top candidate for this verse. Lehi's “they unto whom he shall minister in the flesh” and Deuteronomy's “he shall minister in the name of the LORD his God” share a verb and an auxiliary. Deuteronomy 18:7 concerns a Levite's right to serve at the sanctuary; the Book of Mormon's subject is Christ's mortal ministry. The real link at this verse is Hebrews 13:8, which the n-gram stream ranked nowhere.

This is the identification every reader expects, and the KJV will not support it. Psalm 51:17 reads “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart” — broken spirit, contrite heart. The Book of Mormon reads “a broken heart and a contrite spirit”: the same two adjectives on the opposite two nouns. “Broken heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and it is Psalm 34:18, which also supplies “contrite spirit” in the second half of the same sentence, in Lehi's order. The link is written at Psalm 34:18. Psalm 51:17 is excluded not because it is unrelated — it is the same idiom and the same theology — but because it is not the verse whose words these are.

“No flesh should glory in his presence” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and Lehi's “no flesh that can dwell in the presence of God” shares its two distinctive terms. The sense is opposed. Paul's point is that God has chosen the foolish and weak so that no one may boast before him — a statement about human pride, in which flesh is standing in the presence and is merely forbidden to glory there. Lehi's point is that flesh cannot be in that presence at all. The nearer thought is Exodus 33:20, “there shall no man see me, and live,” which shares no wording. Recorded because the verbal overlap is genuine and a careful reader might take it.

One of the three KJV verses containing “make intercession,” and with Jeremiah 27:18 it accounts for two of them. In both, the phrase is “make intercession *to*” and the act is praying to God — Jeremiah is forbidden to do it in 7:16 and challenges the false prophets to do it in 27:18. Lehi's Messiah makes intercession *for* men, which is the priestly sense and occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 7:25. A rare phrase pointing at the opposite transaction.

exclusions.sharedText: for it must needs be that
exclusions.reason: The highest-scoring n-gram candidate anywhere in this chapter — rarity 3.00, a six-word run — and worthless. “For it must needs be that” is a KJV auxiliary construction; Matthew's sentence is “it must needs be that offences come,” a woe on the world, and Lehi's is “it must needs be, that there is an opposition in all things.” Nothing is shared but the modal. The construction recurs at 2:12 and 2:15 and drew the same candidate again. A standing instance of CONVENTIONS §9: rare boilerplate ranks high and means nothing.

“A thing of nought” occurs in four KJV verses and the 1830 text preserves the KJV's spelling against 1920's “naught,” so the idiom is plausibly scriptural rather than merely English. But the dossier's candidate is the wrong one of the four. Isaiah 29:21 is about men who “turn aside the just for a thing of nought” — who pervert judgment over a trifle — where the phrase means a triviality. Lehi's creation, had there been no opposition, would have been “created for a thing of nought”: an absolute nothingness, no purpose in the end of its creation. That sense is nearer Isaiah 41:12 (“as nothing, and as a thing of nought”), and it is not close enough there either to distinguish a KJV allusion from ordinary English usage, in which “a thing of naught” was current in 1830 independently of the Bible. No link written.

A six-word run and a real contact: Nehemiah 9:6's creation doxology supplies “the earth, and all things that.” But it continues “are therein,” and the Book of Mormon's 1830 text continues “in them is” — the KJV formula of Exodus 20:11 and Acts 4:24, with the singular verb the first edition preserves and 1920 corrected away. The link is written at Exodus 20:11 with Nehemiah 9:6 recorded as a composite; the phrase Lehi's verse actually reproduces is not Nehemiah's.

A ten-word longest run, the longest in the chapter, and it is the wrong bird. Daniel 2:38 reads “the beasts of the field and the fowls of the **heaven**”; Lehi reads “fowls of the **air**.” The pairing of beast-of-the-field with fowl-of-the-air occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 2:19, which is where the link is written. The sense is opposed as well: Daniel's animals are what Nebuchadnezzar has been given dominion over, Lehi's are what God created before man had anything to do with them. The trap CONVENTIONS §9 describes, in its clearest form — a long run, a high score, and one substituted noun that destroys it.

“The tree of life” occurs in six KJV verses, three in Genesis 2-3 and three in Revelation. The machine offered Revelation 22:14; the frame is Eden. Lehi's tree of life stands in opposition to the fruit Adam and Eve are about to be told not to eat, four verses before he quotes Genesis 3:4-5 and the expulsion of Genesis 3:23-24. The link is written at Genesis 2:9. Revelation's tree is in the New Jerusalem and is offered rather than guarded.

One of only two KJV verses containing “fallen from heaven,” which is what makes it worth an entry. In Job it is “the fire of God is fallen from heaven, and hath burned up the sheep” — a natural disaster in the messenger's report to Job, with no personal subject. Lehi's is an angel. The other of the two verses, Isaiah 14:12, is the link, written at 2:17.

A genuine five-word run: “they were driven out from Pharaoh's presence.” The passive-plus-preposition is identical and the referent is not — Moses and Aaron thrown out of an audience during the plagues. The verse Lehi is working is Genesis 3:23-24, which he reproduces for eight consecutive words in the same clause, and whose “from the garden of Eden” the 1830 text preserves against 1920's “of.” A run of the right length attached to the wrong expulsion.

“So is the will of God, that with well doing ye may put to silence the ignorance of foolish men.” The shared string is a connective. Note that the chapter does contain one real link of this shape, at v. 29, where “the will of the flesh” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “the will of God” occurs in dozens and identifies nothing.

Five words of subscription boilerplate closing the book of Leviticus. Lehi's “the commandments which the Lord God gave unto the children of men” is the same stock phrase with a universal recipient in place of Israel, which is the point he is making and not a borrowing.

“The garden of Eden” occurs in five KJV verses; three are Genesis 2-3 and two — Ezekiel 36:35 and Joel 2:3 — are similes for a restored or devoured landscape. Lehi's is the place Adam would have remained in, which is Genesis's. This verse's Eden is continuous with vv. 15, 18 and 19, all of which are keyed to Genesis 2-3, and it adds no wording of its own to adjudicate separately.

Four words of connective tissue from the lament over Babylon's merchandise (“all things which were dainty and goodly are departed from thee”). Lehi's clause is “all things which were created, must have remained in the same state.” No content word is shared.

Hardy cross-references Deuteronomy 30:19 at this verse, where Lehi writes “choose eternal life.” The verbal contact is one verse earlier: 2:27 has Moses' whole figure — a choice set before the hearer between two opposed pairs, “free to choose liberty and eternal life … or to choose captivity and death” — against Deuteronomy's “I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life.” “Choose life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The link is written at 2:27, which is right for a verbal reference; keying it at 2:28 is right for a study edition's chapter-level cross-reference. CONVENTIONS §6a. No drift in the parse: the printed apparatus and our extraction agree, and both are pointing at the same paragraph of Lehi's.

The chapter's highest-scoring candidate for this verse and pure connective tissue. Psalm 2:8 gives the heathen to the Son for an inheritance; 2 Nephi 3:2 consecrates a land to Joseph for his inheritance and his seed's. The five shared words are a preposition, a noun the two verses use in different senses, and two articles. No content word is distinctive.

exclusions.sharedText: of the Lord which he made
exclusions.reason: A six-word run of covenant boilerplate. 'The covenant of the LORD, which he made with our fathers' is the standard KJV formula and occurs in this shape across Deuteronomy, Kings, Chronicles and Jeremiah; Solomon's dedication prayer has no other contact with Lehi's genealogy of Joseph. The Egypt in 1 Kings 8:21 is the exodus from it and in 2 Nephi 3:4 the captivity into it, which is the reverse motion.

Five words of connective tissue that the Book of Mormon uses continuously. 2 Timothy 3:7 concerns women ever learning and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth; 2 Nephi 3:7 brings Joseph's seed to the knowledge of the covenants. Covered in principle by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5 and listed here only because it was the machine's second-ranked candidate for the verse.

'Highly esteemed among' is a KJV singleton at Luke 16:15, and 2 Nephi 3:7 reads 'he shall be esteemed highly among the fruit of thy loins', which is the same three words with the adverb moved. It is nevertheless rejected, because Luke 16:15 is the one verse in the Bible that makes being highly esteemed a disqualification: 'that which is highly esteemed among men is abomination in the sight of God'. The Book of Mormon uses the phrase as unqualified praise of the choice seer, and the source's whole force is condemnation. A rare-phrase match whose sense is exactly inverted is the register's model case; note that 3:24 then reaches for Luke 1:15's 'great in the sight of God', which is the construction Luke 16:15 opposes to human esteem.

Also ranked first for 3:18, where the run reaches six words ('give unto him that'). It is a formula of divine promise with no distinctive content: Revelation 21:6 gives the water of life freely to him that is athirst, and 2 Nephi 3:8 and 3:18 give a commandment and a writing. Nothing of the Alpha and Omega context comes across, and the Book of Mormon uses 'I will give unto him' as ordinary future speech throughout.

A stock eschatological formula occurring in fourteen KJV verses. Ezekiel 38:16 is the Gog oracle and has nothing to do with the writings of Judah and Joseph. Listed because the true source of this verse is two chapters earlier in the same book, Ezekiel 37:16-19, and a reader working from the machine list would be pointed at the wrong end of Ezekiel.

The second Gog candidate in two verses, and the same objection. 'In that day when my people of Israel dwelleth safely' and 'in that day when my work shall commence among all my people' share a temporal formula and the word 'my'. The verse's real borrowing is Hebrews 11:34's 'out of weakness were made strong', a KJV singleton the n-gram stream could not rank because the Book of Mormon reverses the number of the verb.

'They that seek to destroy him, shall be confounded' looks like the KJV lament formula, and Psalm 40:14 is the closest single verse ('let them be ashamed and confounded together that seek after my soul to destroy it'). It is excluded because the formula is distributed rather than located: Psalm 35:4, 40:14, 70:2, 71:13 and 83:17 all pair confounding with those who seek the speaker's hurt, and the exact string 'seek to destroy him' occurs in no KJV verse. No one of these verses can be identified as the source, and choosing among them would be arbitrary.

The machine's top-ranked candidate for the verse at rarity 2.00, and the sense is opposed. Lamentations 1:21 is Zion wishing her enemies reduced to her own condition - 'thou wilt bring the day that thou hast called, and they shall be like unto me' - a curse. 2 Nephi 3:15 has Joseph promise that the seer 'shall be like unto me', a blessing and an inheritance. The five-word run is an artifact of a very common English construction; the real sources of this verse are Luke 1:59 and Genesis 48:6, which are linked.

exclusions.sharedText: and I will give power unto
exclusions.reason: The chapter's highest-scoring machine candidate overall (rarity 2.02, a six-word run) and superseded. Revelation 11:3 gives power unto the two witnesses to prophesy in sackcloth; 2 Nephi 3:17 gives power unto a Moses figure 'in a rod', and the rest of the verse is Exodus 4 throughout - the rod of 4:17, the impeded speech of 4:10, the spokesman of 4:16, which is a KJV singleton. The shared run stops one word before the word that decides the source. See the link at 3:17 to Exodus 4:16. Revelation 2:26's 'to him will I give power', ranked first at 3:11, is excluded on the same ground.

A four-word run of an unusual but empty construction. Exodus 14:17 is the hardening of the Egyptians' hearts at the Red Sea and shares no content word with the appointment of a spokesman. The chapter does draw on Exodus 4 heavily at 3:17, which makes this candidate more tempting than it deserves to be; the resemblance is to Exodus's cadence, not to this verse.

'From the dust' is a KJV singleton, and it is Isaiah 52:2's 'Shake thyself from the dust; arise, and sit down, O Jerusalem'. 2 Nephi 3:20 reads 'And they shall cry from the dust', which matches the singleton exactly and means something else: Isaiah's dust is what a captive shakes off in rising, and the Book of Mormon's is what a buried record speaks out of. The source of the image is Isaiah 29:4, the KJV's one instance of speech coming out of the dust, which is linked at 3:19. Worth recording because the false candidate is the rarer string, and because 2 Nephi 8:25 transcribes Isaiah 52:2 in full a few chapters later, where a reader will meet the phrase in its own sense.

'Their words shall proceed forth out of my mouth' looks like Isaiah 55:11's 'my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth', and 'goeth forth out of my mouth' is a KJV singleton. It is excluded because the Book of Mormon does not have that string: it has 'proceed forth', where Isaiah has 'goeth forth', and 'out of my mouth' by itself occurs in five KJV verses spread across Psalms, Isaiah and Revelation. Deuteronomy 8:3 and Matthew 4:4's 'proceedeth out of the mouth of God' supply the verb but not the possessive. With the distinctive verb absent, no single source can be named, and the clause is left unlinked rather than assigned to the nearest of several.

Ranked first for the verse at rarity 2.00, with a five-word run, and the sixth word reverses it: Luke 12:26 reads 'do that thing which is least', 2 Nephi 3:24 'do that thing which is great in the sight of God'. Luke's clause is an a fortiori about anxiety over small things; the Book of Mormon's is a superlative of achievement. The trap ADJUDICATING section 4 names - the window closing one word early - in its cleanest form. The verse's actual New Testament contact is Luke 1:15's 'great in the sight', which is linked.

Ranked first by the n-gram stream at 4:3, 4:5 and 4:9 on the same five-word run. Lehi is addressing a mixed company of grandchildren and has no other way to say so; Genesis 31:28 is Laban complaining that Jacob stole away without letting him kiss his children goodbye. No contact beyond the phrase, and the phrase is unavoidable.

Tempting because “give ear to my words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and Lehi says “give ear unto my words”. But Psalm 5:1 is a petition addressed upward — Give ear to my words, O LORD, consider my meditation — and Lehi is addressing children downward, which is the Deuteronomy 32:1 posture, not the Psalm's. Neither source is close enough to name: “give ear” with “words” is standard KJV summons-language across Deuteronomy, Job, Psalms and Isaiah, and the singleton count reflects the KJV's preference for “the words of my mouth” rather than any distinctiveness in Psalm 5.

Covenant boilerplate. The conditional-obedience formula is the KJV's standard Deuteronomic construction and appears in dozens of verses; nothing in 1 Kings 9:6 (turning to serve other gods) is present at 2 Nephi 4:4. The verse's one identifiable borrowing is Leviticus 22:3's “cut off from my presence”; see the accepted link.

The five-word run is the accident of a shared conditional. John 15:10's apodosis is abiding in love, not prospering in a land, and the Book of Mormon's covenant formula is established four books earlier at 1 Nephi 2:20 without any Johannine element.

A genuine KJV singleton — “leave a blessing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and therefore exactly the kind of count that can carry a bad link. But Joel 2:14's subject is God, who may repent and leave a blessing BEHIND HIM in the form of a meat offering and a drink offering restored to the temple; Lehi's subject is a dying man leaving a blessing UPON his grandchildren. The idiom is ordinary English for a deathbed bequest and needs no source. The real borrowing in the verse is Proverbs 22:6, which occupies its whole second half.

The stream's only proposal for this verse. In Matthew the thing taken from you is the kingdom of God and the taking is the judgment; in 2 Nephi 4:6 the thing taken is a curse and the taking is the mercy. The senses are opposed and the shared run is a passive construction with no distinctive vocabulary in it.

Connective narrative. Abraham speaking to the sons of Heth about a burying place has no contact with Lehi speaking to the sons of Ishmael, beyond a construction the KJV uses whenever anyone addresses a named lineage.

“Died, and was buried” occurs in exactly 8 KJV verses and is the chronicler’s standard closing formula (Judges alone has three). With the pronoun attached the count collapses to one — 2 Chronicles 35:24 is the only KJV verse reading “he died, and was buried”, which is exactly 2 Nephi 4:12’s wording — and that is precisely the trap this register exists for: the singleton is an artifact of the other seven verses naming their subject (Rachel, Jair, Elon, Abdon), not a mark of distinctiveness. Josiah’s death by arrows at Megiddo has no contact with Lehi’s. The verse does carry a link, but it is a figural one to the whole shape of Genesis 49 rather than to any verse’s wording; see the accepted link.

Pure connective tissue spanning a clause boundary in both texts. The candidate is a good illustration of CONVENTIONS §9: the n-gram stream is a recall floor and a rare-looking run of function words is worth nothing.

A five-word run and the highest-scoring candidate for the verse, but Matthew 13:3's “many things” are parables and the clause introduces the sower. 2 Nephi 4:14 is a bibliographic aside about which of Nephi's two sets of plates hold which sayings. The Book of Mormon uses “spake many things unto them” at 2 Nephi 1:1 as well, in the same narrative sense; it is the book's own formula.

The obvious background for “my soul delighteth in the Scriptures; and my heart pondereth them”, and it will not bear weight. Psalm 1:2 has delight and meditation and the law; 2 Nephi 4:15-16 has delight and pondering and the scriptures, and shares not one phrase with it — the KJV never says “delighteth in the scriptures”, and its verb here is meditate, not ponder. This is the chapter's central discipline: psalm-idiom is not a psalm. The two identifiable sources at these verses are Romans 15:4 and Luke 2:19, both KJV singletons, and both are accepted.

“He hath confounded mine enemies, unto the causing of them to quake before me” sits inside the Lamentations 3 anaphora of 4:20-25 and reads like a Psalm, which is why it is registered here rather than passed over. But it matches no Psalm in particular: the KJV's confounding of enemies is spread across Psalm 35:4, 40:14, 70:2, 71:13, 83:17 and Jeremiah, and “quake” occurs in 22 KJV verses, almost all of them of the earth or the mountains rather than of persons. No source is identifiable and none is claimed.

“Visions of the night” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Job 4:13 and Genesis 46:2, and 2 Nephi 4:23 reads “visions in the night time” — a different preposition and a different noun, and “in the night time” occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses. Genesis 46:2 is the more resonant of the two (God speaking to Israel in the visions of the night as he goes down into Egypt, which is where this chapter began at 4:1), and that resonance is exactly why it is filed here rather than linked. The verse's accepted link is Psalm 40:1's “heard my cry”, which is a singleton and does not need the night half to stand.

“Upon the wings of his spirit” invites Psalm 18:10's “he did fly upon the wings of the wind”, and “wings of the wind” occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses (2 Samuel 22:11, Psalm 18:10, Psalm 104:3). But the noun is changed, and the sentence's identifiable sources are elsewhere: the exceeding high mountain is Matthew 4:8's KJV singleton and the being carried away in the spirit is Revelation's. The wings are the Psalter's idiom generally, and the Book of Mormon's substitution of spirit for wind is what makes them unattributable to any one verse.

“My soul linger in the valley of sorrow” pulls hard toward Psalm 23:4, where “the valley of the shadow” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and toward Psalm 84:6's valley of Baca. Neither reads “valley of sorrow”, which is in no KJV verse at all. Note also that the verse's most conspicuous word, “condescension”, is not in the KJV: “his condescension” occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses, and the word appears nowhere in the King James Bible. The verse is written in scriptural cadence out of non-scriptural vocabulary, which is worth recording as the counter-example to the rest of the chapter.

Four function words across a clause boundary; Micah 3:11 is an oracle against venal priests. Jeremiah 31:7's “and say, O LORD” is the same accident. The verse's two real sources are Isaiah 12:1 and Psalm 89:26, both accepted, and both were also in the stream's list — which is the stream working correctly, buried in noise.

The verse a reader will expect, and the wrong one. Psalm 51:17 reads “a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart”; 2 Nephi 4:32 reads “my heart is broken and my spirit is contrite”. The adjectives are swapped. Psalm 34:18 — “them that are of a broken heart … such as be of a contrite spirit” — has the Book of Mormon's assignment exactly, and “broken heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which is Psalm 34:18. The link is therefore filed at Psalm 34:18, and the difference is not cosmetic: Psalm 51 makes the broken heart a sacrifice offered, Psalm 34 makes it the condition God draws near to, and 2 Nephi 4:32 uses it as a ground of confidence in a petition. Later Book of Mormon occurrences of the pair (3 Nephi 9:20, 12:19, Moroni 6:2) should be checked against this distinction rather than assumed to follow Psalm 51.

“Wilt thou not place a stumbling block in my way?” is close to Romans 14:13's “put a stumblingblock … in his brother's way”, and closer still in sense to Leviticus 19:14. But “stumblingblock” occurs in exactly 13 KJV verses and is one of the KJV's standard moral nouns; no single verse is identifiable, and the three clauses on either side of this one each rest on a KJV singleton (Isaiah 61:10, 1 Corinthians 10:13, Hosea 2:6), which is what a borrowed clause looks like in this verse and what this clause does not look like.

exclusions.sharedText: he that putteth his trust in
exclusions.reason: Isaiah 57:13 and Proverbs 28:25 both carry the six-word run “he that putteth his trust in”, and Psalm 73:28 the shorter “put my trust in”. They supply the Book of Mormon's formula but not its content: in all three the trust is in the LORD and the outcome is blessing, whereas 2 Nephi 4:34 curses the man who trusts in man. The source is Jeremiah 17:5, from which the verse takes “maketh flesh his arm” verbatim — a KJV singleton — with the curse reworded into the commoner idiom. Proverbs 28:25 is retained in the accepted link's composite as the donor of the wording; Isaiah 57:13 and Psalm 73:28 are discharged here.

The stream's top proposal for the verse and a near miss: Psalm 63:4 lifts up hands, 2 Nephi 4:35 lifts up a voice, and “lift up my voice” occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses. The verse's identifiable borrowings are James 1:5 and James 4:3, neither of which the stream saw.

exclusions.sharedText: seek my life / take away my life
exclusions.reason: The obvious candidate, and it loses on word order. 1 Kings 19:10 and 19:14 read “they seek my life, to take it away”, and the Elijah setting is inviting for a chapter in which a prophet flees into the wilderness from those who want him dead; 1 Kings 19:4 even has “take away my life” exactly, of Elijah asking to die. But the Book of Mormon's clause is “seek to take away my life”, which is Psalm 31:13's “they devised to take away my life” — the KJV's only occurrence of that order — and it is a conspiracy verse, which 5:2-4 is and 1 Kings 19 is not. The link is at 5:2 to the Psalm. Recorded also because tools/mediation-check.py, run on 1 Kings 19:10 against its New Testament quotation at Romans 11:3, returns a decisive verdict for Romans on the ground that the Book of Mormon lacks the contiguous string “to take it away”. That verdict is an artifact of contiguous matching: the Book of Mormon has all four of those words, reordered, and Romans 11:3 has none of them. Neither candidate wins; a third verse does.

exclusions.sharedText: all things according to the law
exclusions.reason: Top of the machine ranking for this verse, and not worthless: “all things according to the law” is a KJV singleton and Luke 2:39 reads “the law of the Lord” where the Book of Mormon reads “the law of Moses”. It is carried into the 5:10 link as a composite rather than dismissed. What it cannot do is account for the verse, whose three-noun list and appeal to the law of Moses and immediate promise of prospering are all 1 Kings 2:3's.

A genuine trap and worth registering. “Of gold, and of silver” is a KJV singleton, and its verse gives the same six-material catalogue this one gives — “the gods of gold, and of silver, of brass, of iron, of wood, and of stone” — in a comparable polysyndeton. But Daniel 5:4 is Belshazzar's feast, the materials are the substance of idols rather than of workmanship, and nothing else in 2 Nephi 5:15-16 touches Daniel. The catalogue's list belongs with Exodus 31:4-5, where the identical metals are what a sanctuary craftsman is filled with the spirit of God to work in, and where the Book of Mormon's five-word run “work in all manner of” is the KJV's only occurrence.
