The verse a reader would expect behind a temple built by a founder who works metals: Huram sent to Solomon, “skilful to work in gold, and in silver, in brass, in iron, in stone, and in timber … also to grave any manner of graving.” The materials overlap almost completely and not one phrase does — 2 Chronicles has no “work in all manner of”, no “after the manner of”, and its polysyndeton drops the repeated preposition after the second item, where both Exodus 31:4 and the Book of Mormon keep it. 1 Chronicles 29:2's “all manner of precious stones … in abundance” is the closest KJV wording to 5:16's “so many precious things” and shares nothing distinctive either. Registered so that the absence is on record: the temple movement of this chapter has real KJV wording behind it, and it is the tabernacle's, not the temple's.

“Cut off” in the Levitical sense is excision from the people for a named offence, and the KJV uses the formula dozens of times; Leviticus 20:17 scored on it here only because the pronoun and number happen to match. The Book of Mormon's phrase is completed by “from the presence of the Lord”, which is Genesis 4:16's and is linked as such.

The reading every reader of this verse arrives at, and the catalogue declines it at the level of wording while granting everything else. The Cain frame is genuinely in the chapter — it was argued at 1 Nephi 2:21 and reaches 5:20 through that verse, and the sequence here is Genesis 4's in order: a brother's murderous anger, a curse, a going out from the presence of the LORD, and a mark by which the cursed are afterwards known. But Genesis 4:15 shares not one word with 2 Nephi 5:21. Its mark is set to protect Cain from being killed, not to make him unenticing; the KJV's noun is “mark” and the Book of Mormon's is “skin”; and no KJV verse anywhere joins blackness of skin to a divine curse. What the chapter takes from Genesis 4 it takes at 5:20 and takes verbally; what it does at 5:21 it does without the KJV.

The one KJV verse in which the colour of skin is the subject of a theological argument, and it argues the opposite of this one. “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil” makes skin the emblem of what cannot be altered, precisely in order to say that the moral condition is the thing at issue and is as fixed. 2 Nephi 5:21 has God altering skin as the sign of a moral condition. No wording is shared beyond the noun. Registered because the search for a KJV background to “a skin of blackness” ends here or nowhere, and it ends nowhere.

A type-scene pulling hard toward a link the wording will not bear, and it deserves saying why. Numbers 12 is the KJV's one story in which elder siblings challenge a younger brother's sole authority — “Hath the LORD indeed spoken only by Moses? hath he not spoken also by us?” — and are punished by a change in the skin of one of them. That is the plot of 2 Nephi 5:3 and 5:21 in two verses of Numbers. But the punishment runs the other way (Miriam “became leprous, white as snow”, where the Book of Mormon's curse is a darkening), it falls on the sibling who spoke and not on a posterity, it is lifted after seven days, and not a word of Numbers 12 appears in 2 Nephi 5. Compare CONVENTIONS §5's Exodus 2:2 entry: a typological expectation is not evidence.

“An idle” is a KJV singleton only because the KJV normally writes “idle” without an article, and Proverbs 19:15's “an idle soul shall suffer hunger” is a proverb about individual sloth, not a description of a people. Two words, one of them a determiner. The verse's real KJV content is the pairing of mischief with subtilty, which is Acts 13:10's and is linked there.

The natural candidate for a consecration of brothers to the priesthood, and it cannot be narrowed. “Consecrate” occurs in twenty-eight KJV verses and “the priest's office” in twenty-three, most of them in the same handful of Exodus and Leviticus chapters, and “priests and teachers” occurs in none. There is no phrase here to attach to a verse. Worth registering for a second reason: 2 Nephi 5:26 consecrates Jacob and Joseph, who are Nephi's brothers and not Levites, four verses after 5:10 says the people keep the law of Moses in all things. The KJV's only warrant for a non-Levitical consecration is Judges 17:5 and 1 Kings 12:31, both of them narrated as offences, and the Book of Mormon borrows nothing from either. The departure is silent, and it is not made with the KJV's words.

Top-ranked by the machine for this verse on a four-word run. Isaiah 32:13 is a judgment oracle — thorns and briers coming up on the land — with no relation to a consecration of priests. Connective agreement of the kind CONVENTIONS §5 says may be passed over; recorded only because it heads the dossier's list here and a reader consulting it would meet it first.

“Good in my sight” occurs in two KJV verses, 1 Samuel 29:6 and 29:9, both of them Achish the Philistine assuring David of his standing. The Book of Mormon's “many things upon them which are good in my sight” is God's own approval of a record, and the idiom is ordinary biblical English (“right in the sight of the LORD”, “evil in the sight of the LORD”) that the KJV distributes across the whole canon. No link.

A five-word run of pure connective tissue joining a purpose clause to its subject. Paul is warning the Corinthians not to be puffed up over their teachers; Jacob is saying he speaks Isaiah's words so his hearers may glorify God. The only content word shared is 'sakes', and 'for your sakes' is ordinary KJV English. Nothing in 6:4 has any further contact with 1 Corinthians 4.

'Of the house of' is one of the commonest constructions in the KJV and 'the house of Israel' alone runs to well over a hundred verses. 1 Corinthians 1:11's house is Chloe's household in Corinth. There is no candidate here, and the phrase is covered in principle by the standing formulaic exclusions.

A textbook case of CONVENTIONS §9: rare boilerplate scoring high. The run is four words of subordinating conjunction and pronoun, and it scored 2.00 only because 'because that ye' is an uncommon way for the KJV to say 'because you'. Numbers 11:20 is quail coming out of Israel's nostrils; 6:5 is Isaiah's words being likened to the house of Israel. There is no shared content word at all. Note that the 1830's 'because that ye are of the House of Israel' is itself the reason for the match, and 1920 deleted the 'that' — so in the modern text this candidate does not exist.

The four words match and the subject matter is genuinely adjacent — both verses concern whether exiles from Jerusalem will return to Judah — which is what makes this worth registering rather than passing over. But the sense is exactly opposed. Jeremiah 44:14 is a denial: of the remnant gone down to Egypt, 'none... shall escape or remain, that they should return into the land of Judah... for none shall return but such as shall escape.' Jacob's clause is an affirmation, that the Lord 'hath shewn unto me that they should return again'. A parallel that reverses its source's polarity and shares no distinctive vocabulary is not a link; the return Jacob has in view is 2 Chronicles 36:22-23, which the rest of the paragraph is walking through (see the 6:10 link).

The n-gram stream's highest-ranked candidate for the verse, and it is the wrong one. John 19:6 is the crowd's shout before Pilate — 'Crucify him, crucify him' — so the four-word run is an artifact of a doubled imperative, and the sense is a demand rather than a prediction. Jacob's clause is a prediction, and it pairs scourging with crucifixion; that pairing occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 20:19 ('to mock, and to scourge, and to crucify him'), where the syntax is also future. The link is filed there, with Mark 10:34 and Luke 18:33 as composite for the distributed pronoun.

Four words, three of which are the preposition, article and conjunction. Philemon 1:16 concerns Onesimus as a brother 'both in the flesh, and in the Lord'. The real contact in 6:9 is the KJV singleton 'manifest in the flesh' (1 Timothy 3:16), where the link is filed; this candidate is the tail of that phrase running into the next clause.

A genuine KJV singleton and therefore a real temptation: 'hardened their hearts' occurs in exactly one verse, 1 Samuel 6:6, where the Philistine priests ask why Israel should harden its heart 'as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts'. Jacob has the phrase exactly. It is nonetheless not the source, because he has a second and rarer phrase in the same clause — 'stiffened their necks' — and 'stiffened' is a King James hapax, occurring only at 2 Chronicles 36:13, which happens to be the one verse in the Bible that puts stiffening the neck and hardening the heart in a single sentence. A source that accounts for both phrases displaces one that accounts for the commoner of them, and 2 Chronicles 36 also accounts for the captivity and return of 6:8-9. Recorded here because the singleton would otherwise look decisive to anyone who checked only the first phrase.

Five words of connective tissue; 'come upon them' alone is in more than thirty KJV verses. Jeremiah 46:21 concerns Egypt's hired men fleeing like fatted bullocks. This was the only candidate the machine offered for 6:10, which is the chapter's strongest verse — a clean illustration of the n-gram stream being a recall floor and not a ranking (CONVENTIONS §9).

The phrase is Pastoral-Epistles idiom and appears in three verses in that shape (2 Timothy 3:7, 1 Timothy 2:4, Hebrews 10:26), always followed by 'the truth'. Jacob's object is different — 'the knowledge of their Redeemer' — and the construction is too widely distributed to point at any one of them. Registered rather than passed over because 2 Timothy 3:7 headed the machine list for this verse.

Five words, and both verses concern the fate of a punished people, so the candidate deserves an answer. But Isaiah 24:22's gathering is an imprisonment — 'they shall be gathered together, as prisoners are gathered in the pit, and shall be shut up in the prison' — and Jacob's is the opposite, a merciful regathering 'to the lands of their inheritance' after scattering. The whole force of the phrase is reversed by its object, and 'gathered together' is common KJV usage.

'Driven to and fro' is a KJV singleton, which is normally the strongest evidence this catalogue can produce, and it is being declined anyway. Job 13:25 is Job's protest at being pursued by God: 'Wilt thou break a leaf driven to and fro? and wilt thou pursue the dry stubble?' The image is of a man too slight to be worth God's attention. Jacob's clause is about the scattering of a nation — 'after they are driven to and fro... they shall be scattered, and smitten, and hated' — a corporate judgment, not a complaint of divine over-attention, and 'to and fro' with a verb of driving is unremarkable English for aimless movement. The singleton is a fact about KJV word-frequency, not evidence of dependence, and this entry exists so that the count is on record where a later reader will find it.

A partial exclusion, filed for clarity rather than to reject the verse outright. 'The dust of their feet' — with the third-person possessive Jacob uses — occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:51, and Luke's context is suggestive: Paul and Barnabas shake the dust off against those who rejected them and turn to the Gentiles, which is the sequence of Jacob's own paragraph. But the governing verb decides it. Jacob's is 'lick up the dust', which is a KJV singleton at Isaiah 49:23 — the verse he quoted six verses earlier and is here glossing. The link is therefore filed at Isaiah 49:23 with Acts 13:51 recorded as composite, since the pronoun Jacob substitutes is the one Acts has.

exclusions.sharedText: the mighty shall be taken away
exclusions.reason: Six consecutive words, which is a long run and would be persuasive in isolation. It is an artifact of the window closing one word early on either side (ADJUDICATING §4). Job 34:20 says 'the mighty shall be taken away without hand' — the mighty are the ones removed, by death. Isaiah 49:25, which Jacob is quoting verbatim here, says 'the captives OF the mighty shall be taken away' — the mighty are the captors, and it is their prisoners who are removed. The genitive inverts the whole sentence. Displaced by Isaiah 49:25, which accounts for twenty-five consecutive words of the verse.

Tempting because the next verse ends with 'the Mighty One of Jacob', and Psalm 132:5 has 'an habitation for the mighty God of Jacob' — apparently the same title, and with the same preposition Jacob uses. But the two halves come from different places and neither is the Psalm's. 'The Mighty One of Jacob' at 6:18 is Isaiah 49:26's own phrase, standing where the KJV verse being quoted puts it, and the KJV has it in exactly two verses (Isaiah 49:26, 60:16) — the Psalm's 'the mighty God of Jacob' is a third and distinct formula. The interpolated 'the Mighty God' at 6:17 is absolute, with no 'of Jacob' attached, which is Isaiah 9:6's and Isaiah 10:21's usage, and both of those Isaiah chapters are transcribed later in this same book. The link records Isaiah 9:6 and 10:21 as composite; the Psalm is superseded.

The machine's top proposal for the verse, and it is a coincidence of connective phrasing. Daniel 8:12 concerns the host given against the daily sacrifice in the little-horn vision; 2 Nephi 9:6 concerns the fall of Adam. 'By reason of' is KJV connective tissue and 'transgression' is one of the commonest theological nouns in the corpus. The real borrowing in this verse is Romans 5:12, which the n-gram stream did not propose at all — a clean instance of CONVENTIONS §9: contiguous windows rank rare boilerplate above the true source.

Five words, and the noun that follows them is what matters. Numbers 12:14 shuts Miriam out from the camp for seven days as a leprosy quarantine; 2 Nephi 9:9 shuts the damned out from the presence of God for ever. The shared string breaks exactly where the sense begins, which is the trap ADJUDICATING §4 names — the window closes one word early. The verse's real sources are 2 Corinthians 11:14 and John 8:44, both linked.

exclusions.sharedText: the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel
exclusions.reason: A standing exclusion for this chapter and, so far as the machine stream is concerned, for Jacob's whole discourse. 'The Holy One of Israel' is Isaiah's signature title — it occurs some two dozen times in Isaiah — and Jacob uses it fourteen times in 2 Nephi 9 alone (9:11, 9:12, 9:15, 9:18 twice, 9:19, 9:23, 9:24, 9:25, 9:26, 9:40, 9:41, 9:51). It is his adopted formula for God, not a fresh borrowing at each occurrence, and it will match Isaiah 30:15, 41:14, 43:3, 49:7 and a dozen others indifferently. The n-gram stream proposes it at 9:20 and 9:24; it is passed over in silence everywhere else in the chapter. The same applies to 'for the Lord God hath spoken it' (Isaiah 21:17, 22:25, 25:8 and others), which the stream flags at 9:24.

One of only three KJV verses containing 'living soul', so it will surface on any rarity search behind 2 Nephi 9:13's 'they are living souls'. But Revelation 16:3 is the second vial poured on the sea, where 'every living soul died in the sea' — the phrase there means a marine creature and the verb is death. Jacob's living souls are resurrected men who cannot die again. The sense is not merely different, it is opposite. The link at this verse is to 1 Corinthians 15:45, with Genesis 2:7 behind it.

A five-word run spanning a clause boundary in both texts, and the agreement is grammatical rather than lexical: 'his angels' followed by a plural future. Matthew 13:41 has the Son of man sending forth his angels to gather; 2 Nephi 9:16 has the devil's angels going away into fire. The angels belong to opposite parties. Matthew 25:41, where the angels are the devil's and the fire is everlasting, is the source and is linked.

Five words of the commonest possible construction — a relative pronoun, a perfect tense of 'believe', and a preposition. Titus 3:8 is about maintaining good works; the phrase there is 'they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works', and the run is broken by the object. Nothing distinctive is shared. The verse's real sources are Hebrews 12:2 and Matthew 25:34.

The stream proposes Revelation 21:8 at 9:19 and again at 9:26 because both share 'fire and brimstone which is'. But Revelation 21:8's lake 'burneth with fire and brimstone' and is glossed as 'the second death', while Jacob's is 'a lake of fire and brimstone, which is endless torment' — the genitive construction and the torment are Revelation 20:10's and 14:11's, which are linked at 9:16 where the phrase first enters. 9:19 and 9:26 are Jacob repeating his own formula within one chapter (ADJUDICATING §4), and are registered as recurrences on that link rather than given rows of their own.

'For the LORD God of Israel hath spoken it' is a prophetic subscript formula, not a source. It stands at Isaiah 21:17, 22:25, 24:3, 25:8 and elsewhere, and Jacob uses his own version of it four times in this chapter. See the standing exclusion at 9:11. The borrowings in 9:24 are Mark 16:16 and Matthew 10:22, with John 1:12 on Frederick's reading.

A true match to a KJV singleton, and the stream is right that the phrase is here — but it is the same phrase Jacob used two verses earlier at 9:34, of the liar rather than the whoremonger, inside one continuous series of woes. A narrator who has adopted a formula is not borrowing afresh each time he uses it within a single chapter (ADJUDICATING §4). The link is adjudicated at 9:34, where the phrase first enters, and 9:36 is carried there in recurrenceRefs.

Recorded because it is the tempting one in this chapter and because declining it is a judgment a reader may want to reverse. 2 Nephi 9:41 adds to Matthew's strait gate a detail Matthew has not got: 'the keeper of the gate is the Holy One of Israel: and he employeth no servant there'. John 10 is the KJV's one passage about a gatekeeper and a fold — 'to him the porter openeth' (10:3), 'I am the door of the sheep' (10:7) — and it is hard to read Jacob's explicit denial of a servant without hearing it as an answer to John's porter. But there is no verbal contact whatever: the KJV says porter and door, never keeper and gate, and the words Jacob does share with John here ('open', 'sheep' is absent, 'there is none other way') come from Matthew 7 and Acts 4:12 respectively. A figural link built on a resemblance this unanchored would be manufacturing evidence for a hunch. The hunch is recorded here instead, with the condition that would withdraw the objection: any KJV passage pairing a gate with a keeper would change the judgment, and there is none.

The dust-shaking of Acts 13:51 (and Matthew 10:14, Mark 6:11, Luke 9:5) is the gesture a reader is likeliest to reach for behind 'I take off my garments, and I shake them before you'. It is the wrong one: those passages shake dust from the feet, and Jacob shakes garments. The KJV has exactly one verse where a preacher shakes his clothing and disclaims his hearers' blood in the same breath — Acts 18:6 — and the blood is the decisive half of Jacob's sentence ('am rid of your blood'). The link is filed there, with Acts 20:26 as a composite.

Pure connective tissue. Ezekiel 47:21 divides the land among the tribes; 2 Nephi 9:47 asks whether the preacher should speak plainly. The five words are a preposition, a pronoun and a comparative particle, and they carry no content in either place. Covered in principle by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

Five words, of which four are function words and one is a noun Jacob uses eleven times in this chapter. Isaiah 45:13 concerns Cyrus raised up in righteousness to build the city; 2 Nephi 9:49 concerns Jacob's own delight in righteousness and his praise of God's name. There is no shared subject, image or argument, only the accident that both sentences turn from a prepositional phrase to a first-person future.

Four words, and the KJV verse is the lying prophet of Bethel: 'an angel spake unto me by the word of the LORD... But he lied unto him.' 2 Nephi 10:3's parenthesis is the angel of 2 Nephi 6:9 telling Jacob the Messiah's name. The one KJV verse where an angel speaks to a man in these words is the one where the claim is false, which makes the string match actively misleading rather than merely empty.

A standing exclusion for this chapter. 'They which are' is the 1830 text's ordinary relative construction — the 1920 edition rewrote it to 'those who are' at 10:3, 10:16 twice, 10:19, 10:21 and 10:22 — and it will match any KJV verse using the same relative. Romans 9:8, Mark 12:43 ('all they which have', proposed at 10:22) and Luke 8:10 are all instances of this and none is a borrowing. The same applies to 'it must needs be' (Matthew 18:7) and 'and now, behold, the Lord' (Joshua 14:10).

The machine's run stops one word short of the noun that matters. Leviticus 26:36 has 'in the lands of their ENEMIES' — the curse of exile; 2 Nephi 10:7 has 'unto the lands of their INHERITANCE' — the promise of return. 'Lands of their inheritance' is in no KJV verse at all, which is why the window closes early (ADJUDICATING 4). Malachi 4:1 ('the day cometh that'), Exodus 10:6 and Galatians 1:16 are proposed at the same verse on connective strings and are covered by the standing exclusion at 10:3.

The top-ranked candidate for the verse and it is a coincidence of five common words. Luke 1:15 is Gabriel on John the Baptist, 'he shall be great in the sight of the Lord'; 2 Nephi 10:8 is 'the nations of the Gentiles shall be great in the eyes of me'. Luke 1:15 is a real source elsewhere in this book (2 Nephi 3:24, on being filled with the Spirit from the womb), which makes the false positive here worth registering rather than passing over. The verse's actual sources are Isaiah 11:11-12, which the n-gram stream did not propose at all.

A genuine four-word run whose sense is exactly opposed. Luke 22:25: 'The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and they that exercise authority upon them are called benefactors' — a warning against Gentile rule. 2 Nephi 10:9: 'the kings of the Gentiles shall be nursing fathers unto them' — a promise that Gentile rule will nurse Israel. The verse's source is Isaiah 49:23, where the phrase 'nursing fathers' and 'nursing mothers' are both KJV singletons; 'kings of the Gentiles' is Jacob's own gloss on Isaiah's unspecified 'kings', not a borrowing from Luke.

Five words, and the fifth diverges: Psalm 41:2 has 'blessed upon the EARTH' of the man who considers the poor; 2 Nephi 10:10 has 'blessed upon the LAND', the land being the subject of the whole passage. The construction is ordinary KJV blessing-formula English and points at no particular verse.

Five words of pure land-promise boilerplate. Numbers 32:22 is the Reubenites' conditional possession of Gilead; 2 Nephi 10:11 is the land of liberty. Nothing after the shared string agrees. The theological warrant behind 10:11-14 is 1 Samuel 8, which is linked at 10:11, and 'land of liberty' is in no KJV verse.

Proposed at both 10:15 and 10:17, which is a sign it has caught Jacob's own repeated clause ('that I will do unto them while they are in the flesh') rather than a source. Ezekiel 7:27 has 'I will do unto them after their way', a judgment formula; the Book of Mormon's clause is a promise about timing. Common connective phrasing in both.

The string is real but the source is not. Numbers 5:3 puts male and female lepers out of the camp; it has no bond and free and no Jew and Gentile. 2 Nephi 10:16 gives all three pairs in the order of Galatians 3:28, where 'male nor female' is a KJV singleton and 'bond nor free' occurs in only two verses. The link is written at Galatians 3:28, with 1 Corinthians 12:13 recorded as the source of the substituted first pair.

Five words of comparison boilerplate. Lamentations 1:21 says the enemies 'shall be like unto me' in ruin; 2 Nephi 10:18 says the Gentiles 'shall be like unto a father' to Lehi's seed. Opposite valence, no other contact.

exclusions.sharedText: upon the isles of the sea
exclusions.reason: The longest run the machine found in the chapter — six words, and 'isles of the sea' occurs in only two KJV verses — but Esther 10:1 is the extent of Ahasuerus's tribute, 'upon the land, and upon the isles of the sea', with no covenant content whatever. The other of the two is Isaiah 24:15, 'glorify ye the LORD... in the isles of the sea', which is where the link is written, with Isaiah 49:1's 'Listen, O isles' as a composite because Jacob had transcribed Isaiah 49 four chapters earlier. Note the crux recorded there: the verse Jacob is actually expounding, Isaiah 11:11, reads 'islands of the sea' in the KJV and in the Book of Mormon's own transcription at 2 Nephi 21:11 — so the plural he builds an argument on is not the plural his source gives him.

exclusions.sharedText: the house of Israel according to
exclusions.reason: Six words, and every one of them is a fixed KJV collocation. 'The house of Israel' occurs well over a hundred times and 'according to' is connective. Ezekiel 45:8 is about the division of the land among the tribes; 2 Nephi 10:22 is about branches led away 'according to his will and pleasure'. The verse's source is Romans 11:17-20, on 'broken off', which the n-gram stream missed.

Registered because the rarity is startling and the sense is absurd. 'Cheer up' is a KJV singleton, and the one verse is the newlywed's exemption from military service: 'he shall be free at home one year, and shall cheer up his wife which he hath taken.' 2 Nephi 10:23's 'Therefore cheer up your hearts' has nothing to do with it, and the idiom had passed into ordinary nineteenth-century English by any route. The model case for CONVENTIONS 5's warning that a rarity count is evidence about a phrase, not about a link.

Five words, and the fifth is the hinge. Titus 2:11 is 'the grace of God that BRINGETH SALVATION hath appeared to all men' — grace appearing; 2 Nephi 10:24 is 'the grace of God that YE ARE SAVED' — grace saving. The saving formula is Ephesians 2:8's, 'by grace are ye saved', a KJV singleton in that exact form, and the link is written there. Titus 2:11 remains the machine's best guess for the chapter and is worth recording as a near miss.

A five-word run across the most theologically loaded word in the verse, and it is a coincidence. 2 Samuel 21:3 is David asking the Gibeonites what blood-price will make atonement for Saul's slaughter of them; 2 Nephi 10:25 is a benediction about deliverance from everlasting death 'by the power of the atonement'. The English 'make the atonement, that ye may' and 'the atonement, that ye may' are the same words doing unrelated work. The verse's sources are Philippians 3:10 and 2 Peter 1:3-11.

A standing exclusion for this chapter. Nephi's editorial formula 'only these things have I caused to be written' is his own, and it will match any KJV causative. Jeremiah 13:11 has 'so have I caused to cleave unto me the whole house of Israel'. Exodus 24:12 ('which I have written'), Psalm 102:18 ('be written for the') and 2 Corinthians 4:18 ('for the things which') are proposed at the same verse on the same kind of connective tissue and are covered here.

A five-word run and a complete accident of English. Job 4:8 is Eliphaz beginning a proverb — 'Even as I have seen, they that plow iniquity, and sow wickedness, reap the same' — where the clause governs what follows. 2 Nephi 11:2 has 'he verily saw my Redeemer, even as I have seen him', where it governs what precedes and the object is a person. The stream proposes the same string again at 11:3. Nephi's seeing-language belongs with Job 19:25-26, which is linked at 2 Nephi 9:4 in Jacob's sermon, not with Job 4.

The highest-ranked candidate in the chapter, and it is a speech-introduction formula. 2 Corinthians 6:16 quotes Leviticus 26:12 on God dwelling among his people; 2 Nephi 11:3 quotes the law of witnesses. Hebrews 13:5 ('hath said, I will never leave thee') is the same shape and the same non-event. The verse's real sources are Deuteronomy 19:15 and its New Testament citations, which the stream did propose in part — 2 Chronicles 29:15 and Hosea 6:5 both matched on 'by the words of', which is Nephi's phrase for the three witnesses, but neither KJV verse has anything to do with witnesses.

Four words of relative-clause filler. Matthew 13:35 has 'things which have been kept secret from the foundation of the world'; 2 Nephi 11:4 has 'all things which have been given of God from the beginning of the world'. The near-agreement of the two temporal phrases is worth noting and does not survive inspection: 'from the foundation of the world' and 'from the beginning of the world' are both common KJV formulas (the latter in Isaiah 64:4, Matthew 24:21, Acts 15:18 and Ephesians 3:9), and neither points at a source. Revelation 18:14, Ephesians 6:6 and 2 Samuel 6:12 are proposed at the same verse on strings of the same kind.

Five words, and the sense is unrelated in both directions. Daniel 2:28 is 'But there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets' — an answer to the Chaldeans who could not recover the king's dream; 1 Samuel 17:46, proposed alongside it, is David telling Goliath 'that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel'. Both assert God's existence against a rival claim of power. 2 Nephi 11:7 asserts it as the conclusion of a chained reductio — 'For if there be no Christ, there be no God... But there is a God, and he is Christ' — and the form of that argument, not the assertion, is what is borrowed; the link is written at 1 Corinthians 15:13.

Five words across a phrase that is doing nothing in the KJV verse. Job 20:22 is Zophar on the wicked man: 'In the fulness of his sufficiency he shall be in straits.' Romans 15:29, proposed with it, has 'in the fulness of the blessing of the gospel of Christ'. 2 Nephi 11:7's 'he cometh in the fulness of his own time' is the temporal sense, which in the KJV is Galatians 4:4's 'the fulness of the time' — a singleton, adjudicated at 2 Nephi 2:3 and recorded here as a composite rather than a second row.

exclusions.sharedText: which are of the house of
exclusions.reason: A six-word run, and the longest match the machine found for this verse, but the houses are unrelated: Paul's is the household of Chloe, whose members reported the Corinthian factions; Nephi's is the House of Israel. The formula 'which are of the house of' is a KJV commonplace of genealogy and household.

Achish vouching for David to the Philistine lords. No content word is shared beyond the auxiliary and the pronoun, and the n-gram score of 1.50 is an artifact of the phrase's low frequency rather than its distinctiveness — the trap CONVENTIONS §9 names.

A five-word run of connective tissue spanning a clause boundary. John 15:27's subject is apostolic witness 'from the beginning'; Nephi's is the plainness that has been with him 'from the time that I came out from Jerusalem'. The shared words are a temporal preposition and a pronoun.
Pure connective. Nephi's verse repeats 'the things of the Jews' four times in one sentence, which is what raised the score; Paul is discussing priestly maintenance from the temple.

A genuine KJV singleton — “for the space of three” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and it is the wrong one. Acts 19:8 continues 'months', of Paul disputing in the Ephesian synagogue; Nephi continues 'days', of Christ in the sepulchre. This is the trap ADJUDICATING §4 names as the window closing one word early, and it is worth the register entry precisely because the rarity count is real and would tempt an adjudicator who did not read the whole verse. The link at this verse is to Mark 9:31, which supplies the frame with the interval attached.

'Rise from the dead' is common in the gospels, and Mark 12:25's subject is the marital status of the resurrected, not a passion prediction. Superseded by the Mark 9:31 row at the same verse, which shares the whole temporal frame and not just the verb.

exclusions.sharedText: came to pass that after the
exclusions.reason: Narrative boilerplate of the kind covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1. The Chronicler's verse is the siege of Rabbah.

Connective. The coincidence is faintly interesting — Exodus 32:34 is the aftermath of the golden calf and this chapter draws twice on that complex (Exodus 33:5 at 25:28, Exodus 17:6 here) — but nothing in the shared words points at it, and the phrase is a KJV commonplace.

Five words of connective tissue. 1 John 2:18's subject is the many antichrists as evidence that it is the last time; the link at this verse is to Ephesians 2:8, which supplies the clause the connective introduces.

A tempting one, and it should be recorded as declined rather than passed over. “the deadness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 4:19, and 2 Nephi 25:27 uses the noun twice in a single sentence — 'the deadness of the law', 'by knowing the deadnes of the law' (1830 spelling). But Romans 4:19's deadness is Sarah's womb, a physical incapacity that Abraham's faith overlooks, and Romans 4 is not arguing that the law is dead; it is arguing that Abraham was justified before the law existed. Nothing but the bare noun is shared, and the noun is an ordinary English abstraction from a common adjective. The Pauline material this verse is actually working with is 2 Corinthians 3, which is catalogued as a link at the same verse.

Connective, and the same string already excluded at 25:20. Ezekiel's oracle concerns the delay of prophecy, which is thematically adjacent to Nephi's insistence that his words will stand — but the four shared words are a KJV commonplace and carry none of that.

'The Holy One of Israel' occurs in 31 KJV verses, 25 of them in Isaiah, and it is 2 Nephi's habitual title for Christ — the book has already transcribed a dozen of those Isaiah verses at chapters 12-24, including Isaiah 12:6 at 2 Nephi 22:6. No single occurrence can be identified as the source of Nephi's use, and the machine's selection of Isaiah 12:6 is arbitrary among 31. Recorded here once as a standing note for the title throughout 2 Nephi 25-33.

Tempting because Deuteronomy 18:15-19 is the prophet-like-Moses oracle that 1 Nephi 22:20 quotes and that this corpus uses repeatedly, and because 26:1 is about words Christ will speak that 'shall be the law which ye shall do'. But the shared string is a relative clause of pure connective tissue, and Deuteronomy 18:19's subject is the requiring of obedience from those who will not hearken, not the giving of a new law. If Deuteronomy 18 is in view here it has left no verbal trace; the adjudicated link for that oracle sits at 1 Nephi 22:20.

Malachi 4 is genuinely in view in this chapter, but at 26:4 and 26:6 (v. 1) and 26:9 (v. 2), not here. Malachi 4:3's treading down of the wicked as ashes shares only a connective run with 26:3, whose sources are Genesis 4:10 and the Abel-to-Zacharias tradition of Matthew 23:35 and Luke 11:50-51.

Nephi's 'whirlwinds shall carry them away' and Isaiah 41:16's 'the wind shall carry them away, and the whirlwind shall scatter them' share the idiom and split the two winds differently. The image of chaff or stubble taken by a whirlwind is distributed across Isaiah 17:13, 40:24, 41:16 and Job 21:18, and no one of them can be identified as the source. Recorded because the verse's neighbours do borrow from Isaiah and a reader may expect this clause to as well.

The sense is opposed. Psalm 71:20 is a promise of rescue — 'shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth' — and 26:5 has the depths of the earth swallowing the killers of the prophets. The nearer image is Korah at Numbers 16:32, where the earth opens her mouth and swallows them up, and that is recorded as composite on the Hosea 10:8 row.

'Anger kindled against' is one of the KJV's commonest formulas of judgment — eleven verses have 'the anger of the LORD was kindled' alone. Deuteronomy 31:17 has 'my anger shall be kindled against them in that day', which matches Nephi's tense; but the link at this verse is to Isaiah 5:25, whose participial 'the anger of the LORD kindled' is a KJV singleton and which Hardy cross-references here alongside the stubble.
Four words of the same formula, from the episode of Miriam's leprosy. Superseded by the Isaiah 5:25 row at this verse.

A real rarity pointed at the wrong verse, and worth the entry. 2 Kings 10:30 is the Lord's reward to Jehu — 'thy children of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel' — a dynastic promise with no bearing on Nephi's four generations of righteousness before destruction. The formula Nephi is using is the Decalogue's 'unto the third and fourth generation' (Exodus 20:5, Numbers 14:18, Deuteronomy 5:9), which he inverts from a reach of punishment into a span of reprieve, and which is catalogued as a link at this verse. Note that Exodus 20 returns at 26:32.
Connective. Qoheleth's subject is the prosperity of sinners; Nephi's is the certainty of a foreseen destruction. The link at this verse is to Isaiah 52:3.

A six-word run and a real one: John 20:31 is the Fourth Gospel's statement of purpose, 'that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God', and 26:12 twice says that Jews and Gentiles must be convinced 'that Jesus is the Christ'. But the clause is the New Testament's standard confession and appears at Acts 9:22, 17:3, 18:5, 18:28 and 1 John 5:1; the distinctive word in Nephi's sentence is 'very', which points at Acts 9:22 and John 7:26, and the link is filed there. Recorded here because a reader who knows Frederick's work on Johannine language in the Book of Mormon might expect John 20:31 to be claimed at this verse, and this catalogue declines to claim it.

'It must needs be' is one of the Book of Mormon's own commonest connectives and appears throughout 2 Nephi 25-30. Matthew 18:7's subject is offences. Covered in principle by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.
'By the power of God' is a KJV commonplace. The link at this verse is to Revelation 14:6's fourfold list of nations, kindreds, tongues and peoples.
Narrative boilerplate; Saul's relief of Jabesh-gilead. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1.

Hardy cross-references Isaiah 29:3-5 at 26:14, which introduces the prophecy ('But behold I prophesy unto you concerning the last days') without quoting anything. The wording begins in the next verse and runs through three: Isaiah 29:3's camp, siege and forts at 26:15, Isaiah 29:4's voice out of the ground at 26:16, and Isaiah 29:5's chaff and instant at 26:18. CONVENTIONS §6a: the links sit where the wording is and this entry sends the reader from his verse to all three. This is not drift in our extraction — his reference is a chapter-level pointer placed at the head of a passage, which is what a study edition's apparatus is for.
Connective. Paul is delivering the institution of the supper; Nephi is asserting that the Lord God worketh not in darkness — a clause whose real relative is John 3:19, catalogued at 26:10.

Five words of formula. Isaiah 50:4 is the servant's tongue of the learned, and this book transcribes it at 2 Nephi 7:4 — which makes the match worth naming and rejecting rather than passing over, since a reader may suspect the transcription is being reused. It is not: 26:30's source is 1 Corinthians 13.

Connective, though Job 34:28's 'cry of the poor' is thematically adjacent to 26:20's grinding upon the face of the poor. The shared words carry none of that, and the invitation formula in 26:33 is Matthew 11:28's.

Recorded as a deliberate absence rather than a rejected candidate, because it is the most informative fact about this chapter's relation to its source. 2 Nephi 27 is an expansion of Isaiah 29 and it begins at Isaiah 29:6. Isaiah 29:3-5 were used in the previous chapter at 2 Nephi 26:15-18. Isaiah 29:1-2 — 'Woe to Ariel, to Ariel, the city where David dwelt! add ye year to year; let them kill sacrifices. Yet I will distress Ariel …' — are used nowhere in the Book of Mormon, and they are the only two verses of the oracle that name its subject and tie it to Jerusalem and the temple cult. In their place 27:1 supplies a wholly non-biblical frame: 'in the last days, or in the days of the Gentiles'. The oracle's geography is removed and its addressee replaced, and at 27:3 the surviving occurrence of Ariel is itself replaced by Zion. A reader collating the two chapters will look for Isaiah 29:1-2 and should be told that the omission is systematic.

Isaiah 30:30 has 'the flame of a devouring fire' with the indefinite article; Isaiah 29:6 has 'the flame of devouring fire' without it, which is the Book of Mormon's form, and 29:6 supplies the whole of the rest of the verse. Recorded because Isaiah 30 is a neighbouring oracle with a similar storm-theophany and a reader might reasonably wonder whether both are in play. On the evidence only 29:6 is.

Deuteronomy 19:15 is the origin of the law of witnesses and the obvious place to key 27:12's three witnesses. The verbal link is at 27:14 and it is to the New Testament form of the law, not Deuteronomy's: 27:14 has 'in the mouth of' (Matthew 18:16, 2 Corinthians 13:1) rather than Deuteronomy's 'at the mouth of', and establishes a 'word' rather than Deuteronomy's 'matter'. Recorded so that a reader who expects Deuteronomy at the witnesses verse is sent to the mediation argument two verses on.

exclusions.sharedText: speak as if it were from the dead
exclusions.reason: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 29:4 at 27:13, and the reference is right about the book and wrong about the verse for this catalogue's purpose. 27:13 says only that 'the words of the faithful should speak as if it were from the dead', which paraphrases Isaiah's ghost-voice without reproducing a phrase of it. The verbal link to Isaiah 29:4 — speaking out of the ground, speech low out of the dust, a voice as of one that hath a familiar spirit, a whisper out of the dust — is at 2 Nephi 26:16, where all four clauses stand in Isaiah's order and where the catalogue files it (CONVENTIONS §6a). This is not drift in our extraction: 27:13 genuinely alludes to the same verse, and a study edition is right to point a reader there. The register sends him to 26:16 for the wording.

Revelation 5:1-5 is the Bible's other great sealed book — written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals, with none in heaven or earth worthy to open it until the Lion of Judah prevails — and it is the passage a reader of 2 Nephi 27 is most likely to think of. It is declined here because there is no verbal contact at all: the Book of Mormon's book is sealed by God's power and reserved to his own due time, not opened by a worthy one, and none of Revelation's distinctive vocabulary (loose the seals, prevailed to open, worthy) appears. The conceptual row filed at this verse is to Daniel 12:4 and 12:9 instead, on the ground that Daniel supplies the sealing, the withholding and the appointed time together — but that row is graded moderate and carries a whyNot, and Revelation 5 remains the strongest alternative to it.

A seven-word run, and the longest non-Isaiah-29 match in the chapter. Isaiah 32:15 has the wilderness becoming a fruitful field and the fruitful field 'counted for a forest'; 2 Nephi 27:28 has Lebanon turned into a fruitful field and the fruitful field 'esteemed as a forest', which is Isaiah 29:17's wording exactly, together with 'a very little while' which Isaiah 32 lacks. The shared run is the phrase the two Isaiah verses share with each other.

The n-gram stream's top candidate for the verse and pure connective tissue: a relative pronoun, an auxiliary and a participle. Revelation 1:19 is John's commission to write what he has seen; 28:2 is about the worth of a book to a remnant of Israel. Nothing beyond the five function words is shared, and 'the things which' is among the commonest openings in the KJV.

exclusions.sharedText: for it shall come to pass in that day
exclusions.reason: A nine-word run and worth nothing, which is CONVENTIONS §9 in one line — the longest run in the chapter is its emptiest. 'It shall come to pass in that day' is the KJV's standard prophetic formula and Jeremiah 30:8 goes on to break a yoke off Israel's neck, which has no contact with churches contending over the Lord's name. The real link at 28:3 is Isaiah 44:5, which the same stream ranked below this.

exclusions.sharedText: he is not a God of
exclusions.reason: A genuinely tempting match and exactly inverted. Luke 20:38 is Jesus proving the resurrection from the burning bush: 'For he is not a God of the dead, but of the living.' 28:6 is a false teacher's syllogism: 'for this day he is not a God of miracles: he hath done his work.' The five shared words are identical and the argument they carry is opposite — Luke's clause is a denial made in order to affirm, and Nephi's is a denial made in order to deny. The Book of Mormon's own source for the formula is nearer to hand and is not Luke: 2 Nephi 27:23, four chapters earlier and in the Lord's own voice, reads 'I am God; and I am a God of miracles', which 28:6 contradicts word for word. Registered rather than passed over because the shared run is long, the vocabulary is content-bearing, and only reading both whole verses shows the reversal.

exclusions.sharedText: to eat, and to drink, and to be merry
exclusions.reason: Hardy cross-references Ecclesiastes 8:15 here alongside Isaiah 22:13, Luke 12:19 and 1 Corinthians 15:32, and for a study edition tracing the sentiment that is right. For a verbal catalogue it is superseded. Ecclesiastes 8:15 has infinitives — 'to eat, and to drink, and to be merry' — where 28:7 has Luke 12:19's imperatives, 'eat, drink, and be merry', and the KJV's only occurrence of that string is Luke's. Ecclesiastes also lacks the second half of the sentence entirely; it commends mirth as a good under the sun rather than as a consequence of tomorrow's death. The links are filed at Luke 12:19 and 1 Corinthians 15:32.

Considered and declined. 'Dig a pit for thy neighbor' looks like a proverb and there are three KJV verses that dig one — Psalm 57:6, Jeremiah 18:20 and 18:22, all in the perfect ('they have digged a pit') and all about enemies plotting against the speaker, not about a neighbour. Proverbs 26:27's 'Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein' is the closest in sense but shares only the verb and its object, and its point is the digger's own downfall, which 28:8 does not make. The clause is more likely a free formation on Exodus 21:33's law of the open pit than a borrowing from any of them, and no rarity count supports a link.

Hardy cross-references Isaiah 2:12-14 at this verse, and this is the shape the 2 Nephi brief warns about rather than drift: Isaiah 2 is transcribed in this same book at 2 Nephi 12, so the reader is being sent from Nephi's exposition to Nephi's own transcription of the text he is expounding. The verbal contact will not carry a link. The one distinctive phrase in Isaiah 2:12, 'proud and lofty', is a KJV singleton and does not appear at 28:12; what appears is 'lifted up', which occurs in 137 KJV verses, and 'puffed up', which is Pauline (six verses, five of them in 1 Corinthians) and not Isaiah's at all. The thematic relation is real — pride brought low is Isaiah 2's subject and 28:12-15's — and it is discharged here rather than manufactured into a figural link. A reader wanting Isaiah 2:12-14 in this book should be sent to 2 Nephi 12:12-14, where it is collated verse by verse.

The 1830's 'wo, wo, wo be unto them' is the KJV's only threefold woe in form, Revelation 8:13's 'Woe, woe, woe, to the inhabiters of the earth', and the resemblance is sharpened by 28:16 going on to speak of the Lord visiting 'the inhabitants of the earth'. It is registered rather than linked because the shared material is one interjection repeated, which is a rhetorical figure available to anyone writing a woe-oracle, and because Revelation 8:13's woes are three specific coming trumpets rather than an intensifier. The real borrowing in 28:15 is Luke 10:15's 'thrust down to hell', which is where the link sits.

'A thing of nought' occurs in Jeremiah 14:14 and in Isaiah 29:21, and the n-gram stream offered both. Isaiah wins outright: 28:16 reproduces nine consecutive words of Isaiah 29:21 — 'turn aside the just for a thing of nought' — where Jeremiah shares only the four-word phrase, embedded in a sentence about prophets who prophesy lies in the LORD's name. The chapter has also been quoting Isaiah 29 since verse 9. The link is filed at Isaiah 29:21.

The n-gram stream's only candidate for the verse and the wrong one. Job 12:5's 'him that is at ease' is the comfortable man whose thought despises the lamp of one ready to slip — a proverb about contempt, not about complacency, and Job's clause is the subject of the scorn rather than its object. 28:24 is a woe pronounced on the man at ease, and the words 'at ease in Zion' occur in exactly one KJV verse, Amos 6:1, which supplies the woe-formula as well as the ease. The link is filed there.

exclusions.sharedText: the power of God and the
exclusions.reason: 'The power of God' occurs in thirteen KJV verses and the six-word run here is that phrase plus a conjunction and an article. 1 Corinthians 1:24 makes Christ the power of God to the called; 28:26 denies the power of God and the gift of the Holy Ghost together. The genuine New Testament contact in this verse is 'the gift of the Holy Ghost', confined to Acts 2:38 and 10:45, and the link is filed at the first of those.

Hardy cross-references Isaiah 29:13 here, correctly — 'hearkeneth unto the precepts of men' is the KJV singleton 'taught by the precept of men' in Nephi's own idiom. The link is filed at 28:14, the phrase's first occurrence in this chapter, where the evidence for the mediation is: the KJV has a singular 'precept' and this book's own transcription of the verse at 2 Nephi 27:25 has the plural 'precepts', which is what 28:14, 28:26 and 28:31 all read. ADJUDICATING §4 governs the repeat — within one book a phrase is adjudicated at first use — and this entry sends the reader from Hardy's verse to ours.

exclusions.sharedText: cursed is he that putteth his trust in man, or maketh flesh his arm
exclusions.reason: Hardy cross-references Jeremiah 17:5 here and the quotation is real — 'maketh flesh his arm' occurs in exactly one KJV verse and is reproduced exactly. But it is not a fresh borrowing. 2 Nephi 4:34, in this same book and in the same narrator's voice, already reads 'cursed is he that putteth his trust in man, or maketh flesh his arm' word for word, and the link is adjudicated there with its full argument: Jeremiah's two singletons ('trusteth in man', 'maketh flesh his arm') fused with 2 Chronicles 32:8's 'arm of flesh', and Jeremiah 17:7's blessing performed in the verse before the curse is quoted. ADJUDICATING §4 governs: within one book, later occurrences are the narrator using his own formula, adjudicated at first use and registered here. What 28:31 adds is not Jeremiah's — 'or shall hearken unto the precepts of men' is Isaiah 29:13's clause again, in the plural form this chapter uses throughout, and it belongs with the link at 28:14.

exclusions.sharedText: he that putteth his trust in
exclusions.reason: Proverbs 28:25 and Isaiah 57:13 were the n-gram stream's two candidates, both for the six-word run 'he that putteth his trust in'. That formula is the KJV's own commonest way of saying it, and in both proposed verses the trust is placed in the LORD and the outcome is blessing — the opposite polarity to Nephi's curse. Their real relevance is that they supply the idiom into which Jeremiah 17:5's 'cursed be the man that trusteth in man' has been reworded, which is recorded in the note at 2 Nephi 4:34 where that verse is adjudicated.

Five words of prophetic boilerplate — a prepositional phrase and the KJV's commonest attribution formula. Jeremiah 31:32 concerns the broken Sinai covenant; 28:32 is a woe on the Gentiles with an offer of mercy. Covered in principle by the standing formulaic exclusions and listed only because it was the sole candidate the stream returned for the chapter's last verse, which is worth knowing when reading the Isaiah 65:2 echo filed there on manual evidence alone.

Registered as a deliberate negative finding, because this is the most quoted verse in the chapter and the temptation is to catalogue it. 'A Bible, a Bible, we have got a Bible, and there cannot be any more Bible' quotes nothing. The word 'Bible' does not occur in the King James Version at all — not once, in either Testament — so the sentence that gives 2 Nephi 29 its popular name has no biblical source and cannot have one. Nor is the surrounding rhetoric borrowed: the trebled noun, the possessive boast and the inference drawn from it are the Book of Mormon's own composition. What IS borrowed in this chapter arrives on either side of verse 3 — Isaiah 29:14 and Isaiah 11:11 at verse 1, Isaiah 5:26 and 49:22 at verse 2, Luke 24:25 at verse 4 — so the chapter's centre is precisely the point at which it stops quoting. Worth stating plainly: a reader who assumes the famous line must be scriptural in origin is wrong, and the exclusion register is where that is recorded.

exclusions.sharedText: I will contend with him that contendeth with thee
exclusions.reason: The stream reached for Isaiah 49's promise that the Lord will save the children of those who oppress Zion, which is thematically close to 'I will return all these things upon your own heads' and shares no wording with it. Isaiah 49 is quoted at length elsewhere in this book (Jacob at 2 Nephi 6:6-7, 2 Nephi 6:16-18), which makes the association natural and still does not make it verbal. The link at 29:5 is filed at Joel 3:7, whose 'upon your own head' is one of the KJV's three.

'The isles of the sea' occurs in exactly two KJV verses and Esther 10:1 is the other one — Ahasuerus laying tribute on the land and on the isles of the sea. It is excluded on sense, not on rarity: Esther's isles are a revenue district and 29:7's are a place where the Lord remembers a people. Isaiah 24:15's isles, where the name of the LORD God of Israel is glorified, are the only KJV isles that could be meant, and Hardy cross-references that verse here. Recorded because a phrase confined to two verses will always draw the machine to both, and the register should say why one was taken.

The divine self-identification formula, which the KJV uses dozens of times and Leviticus alone uses as a refrain through the whole Holiness Code. Five words of it are shared with 29:7 and nothing else is; Leviticus 19:2 commands holiness, 29:7 asserts that God created all men. Covered in principle by the standing formulaic exclusions.

exclusions.sharedText: at the mouth of two witnesses… shall the matter be established
exclusions.reason: This was the obvious source to reach for and it is the wrong one to file the link at. The two-witness rule is Deuteronomy's — 17:6 and 19:15 — and it is unquestionably the law 29:8 is reasoning from. But the KJV's Deuteronomy says 'at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established', with no 'testimony' anywhere in it, while 29:8 says 'the testimony of two nations' twice. 'The testimony of two' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 8:17, where Christ cites the same law against the Pharisees in an argument about whether one witness can establish anything. The link is filed at John 8:17 with the Deuteronomy verses as composite, and the mediation is recorded as OT-via-NT on that evidence.

exclusions.sharedText: the same yesterday, to-day, and forever
exclusions.reason: Adjudicated at 2 Nephi 27:23, where the formula first enters this book, and recorded there in recurrenceRefs. “yesterday, and to day, and for ever” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; by 29:9 Nephi is using his own settled formula — the corpus has already printed it without Hebrews' second conjunction at 1 Nephi 10:18 and at 27:23 — so this is not a fresh borrowing (ADJUDICATING §4). What IS particular to 29:9 belongs on the record even so: Hebrews 13:8 is a statement about a person, and 29:9 makes it a statement about a practice, the premise for saying revelation has not stopped — “because that I have spoken one word, ye need not suppose that I cannot speak another.” That inverts the verse's usual devotional use, and Hebrews' own next verse warns against being “carried about with divers and strange doctrines”, so the sentence used here to argue for more scripture sits, in its source, beside a caution against novelty. Collapsed by the dispatching session, which the chapter-29 pass could not do itself: it wrote the link and flagged it, because chapter 27 was being adjudicated in parallel and an exclusion pointing at an adjudication that might not exist is worse than a link that might be redundant.

Acts 17:31 — 'he hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness' — shares four words with 29:11's 'I will judge the world' and is a real candidate, since Paul on the Areopagus is also arguing to Gentiles about a God who is not confined to one nation. It is superseded rather than dismissed. 29:11 judges the world specifically 'out of the books which shall be written… according to that which is written', which is Revelation 20:12's assize: 'the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Acts has the judgment and Revelation has the books, and the books are what the verse is about.

exclusions.sharedText: every man according to their works
exclusions.reason: Not a rejection but a redirection: Revelation 20:13 is genuinely present at 29:11 and is recorded as composite on the Revelation 20:12 link rather than as a link of its own, because 20:12 supplies the books and 20:13 only the measure. Note also that Revelation 20:13's 'judged every man according to their works' has already been adjudicated in this book at 2 Nephi 28:23, where the same pair of Revelation verses is used for the judgment of the damned; ADJUDICATING §4's rule about repeats within a book is why it is not argued again here.

'Everlasting covenant' occurs in fifteen KJV verses and Genesis 9:16's is the rainbow given to Noah and every living creature — the opposite of the particular covenant 29:14 invokes, which is with Abraham and his seed. The stream ranked it twice for the chapter. The link is filed at Genesis 17:7, on substance rather than on wording, and its `kjvSpecific` is set to 'no' for exactly the reason this exclusion gives: the covenant vocabulary here is too widely distributed to identify any English version, let alone any one verse.

A four-word run consisting of the KJV's commonest noun phrase. Numbers 25:11 is Phinehas turning away wrath; 29:14 is the house of Israel gathered home. Covered by the standing formulaic exclusions and listed only because the stream returned it among the chapter's top candidates, which is a useful measure of how little the machine had to offer for a chapter whose real borrowings are almost all in verses 1, 2 and 11.

exclusions.sharedText: of the Lord: and as many
exclusions.reason: A six-word run straddling a clause boundary, made of an attribution formula and a quantifier. The association is tempting for a better reason than the wording — Acts 13:46-48 is Paul turning from the Jews to the Gentiles, which is 30:2's subject exactly — but Acts's 'as many as were ordained to eternal life believed' is a statement about election and 30:2's 'as many of the Gentiles as will repent' is a statement about condition. Nothing verbal survives the comparison. Registered rather than passed over because the thematic pull is real and a careful reader might accept it on that pull alone.

'The Holy One of Israel' is the Book of Mormon's standing title for Christ and occurs in some thirty KJV verses, most of them in Isaiah. Isaiah 12:6 is one of them and is also transcribed in this book at 2 Nephi 22:6, which is why the stream ranked it; neither fact makes it the source of an epithet the record uses continuously. Covered by the standing formulaic exclusions.

exclusions.sharedText: and the things that I have given them shall pass
exclusions.reason: The stream's top candidate for the verse and pure connective tissue. Jeremiah 8:13 is the surely-consuming of Judah's vine and fig tree; 30:3 is a book coming forth to the Gentiles and being carried to a remnant. No content word is shared, and the run consists of a relative clause and an auxiliary. The two other candidates for this verse, Ezekiel 12:28 and Exodus 32:34, are of the same kind and are covered by the same reasoning.

'From the hand of' is one of the KJV's commonest prepositional formulae and it is doing nothing here beyond joining a blessing to its giver. Psalm 106:10 saves Israel from the hand of him that hated them. The two other candidates the stream returned for this verse, 1 Samuel 6:9 and Job 2:10, are the same kind of match on 'the hand of God' and are covered here. The real borrowing at 30:6 is Acts 9:18's falling scales, which no stream proposed.

exclusions.sharedText: it came to pass that the Lord
exclusions.reason: The narrative formula, covered by the standing exclusion filed at 1 Nephi 2:1. Listed only because it was the sole candidate the stream returned for a verse whose actual source is Revelation 14:6, identified manually — a clean illustration of CONVENTIONS §9: the machine offered boilerplate and missed a four-item list matching one of Revelation's seven orderings exactly.

exclusions.sharedText: with the fruit of his mouth
exclusions.reason: The stream's second candidate for a verse whose first candidate scored 22.71 and is right. Proverbs 18:20's 'A man's belly shall be satisfied with the fruit of his mouth' shares a construction with Isaiah 11:4's 'with the rod of his mouth' and nothing else; the sense — being fed by one's own speech — is unrelated to smiting the earth. Registered because the phrase looks distinctive in isolation and is not.

exclusions.sharedText: the lion shall eat straw like the
exclusions.reason: The most instructive exclusion in the chapter. Isaiah 65:25 is the same vision by the same prophet — 'The wolf and the lamb shall feed together, and the lion shall eat straw like the bullock… They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain' — and it is exactly what a writer working from memory would be expected to conflate with Isaiah 11:6-9. The Book of Mormon does not conflate them. 30:13 reads 'straw like the ox', which is Isaiah 11:7's word, where 65:25 has 'bullock'; and it keeps the cow, the bear and their young ones lying down together, which 65:25 drops entirely. The stream ranked 65:25 here and again at 30:15, and it is excluded at both on the readings rather than on rank. That the two Book of Mormon witnesses to Isaiah 11 both avoid the parallel oracle is part of the collation result argued at 30:9.

exclusions.sharedText: as the waters cover the sea
exclusions.reason: 'As the waters cover the sea' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 11:9 and Habakkuk 2:14, and Habakkuk is excluded on the clause it governs. Habakkuk reads 'the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD'; Isaiah 11:9 and 2 Nephi 30:15 both read 'the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD' — 'full' not 'filled', and no 'glory of'. Two divergences in one clause, both going the same way. Registered because Habakkuk 2:14 is the more familiar form of the sentence in devotional English and is the version a reader is likelier to have by heart.

exclusions.sharedText: shall be made manifest… it shall be revealed
exclusions.reason: A genuine two-phrase overlap and still the wrong source. 1 Corinthians 3:13 has both 'shall be made manifest' and 'it shall be revealed', which is why the stream reached it, but its subject is every man's work tried by fire on the day of judgment, and it lacks the word the Book of Mormon's clause turns on: 'secret'. 'Nothing is secret' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 8:17, and Luke pairs 'secret' with 'made manifest' exactly as 30:17 does — where Mark 4:22 crosses the terms and Matthew 10:26 uses neither. The link is filed at Luke 8:17 with Ephesians 5:11-13 as composite for the works of darkness.

exclusions.sharedText: in the light, and there is
exclusions.reason: Six words of which five are function words, spanning a clause boundary in both texts. 1 John 2:10 is about abiding in the light without occasion of stumbling; 30:17's 'in the light' belongs to works of darkness being made manifest, which is Ephesians 5:13's antithesis and not John's. A textbook case of a contiguous window closing across a seam.

Five words of which four are auxiliary and preposition. Daniel 11:43 gives the king of the north power over the treasures of gold and silver of Egypt; 30:18 takes power away from Satan over the hearts of men. Only the construction is shared, and it is a common one. The verse's real source is Revelation 20:3, whose 'deceive the nations no more' occurs in exactly one KJV verse and which supplies the bounded term that 30:18 keeps while declining to say how long it is.

Hardy's apparatus cross-references all four baptism accounts at this verse — Matthew 3:16, Mark 1:10, Luke 3:22, John 1:32 — which is the right thing for a study edition to do and leaves the catalogue's question unanswered. The wording answers it. 'The Holy Ghost descended' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 3:22; Matthew 3:16 reads 'the Spirit of God descending', Mark 1:10 'the Spirit like a dove descending', John 1:32 'the Spirit descending from heaven'. All three name the agent as Spirit, not Holy Ghost, and Matthew and Mark both place the participle before the dove where the Book of Mormon and Luke place it after the noun. Matthew 3:16 is additionally excluded on its own account: its distinctive material — the heavens opened unto him, the lighting upon him — is entirely absent here, though Matthew 3:14-15 IS the source at 31:5. The link is at Luke 3:22. Mark 1:10 and John 1:32 are excluded on the same evidence and are not given separate entries.

A six-word run and a Deuteronomic commonplace: 'keep the commandments of the LORD' recurs through Deuteronomy, Joshua, Kings and Chronicles, and 'keep the commandments' is used some sixty times in the KJV. 2 Nephi 31:10 has 'keep the commandments of the Father', which is the Johannine rather than the Deuteronomic object and belongs with John 15:10. The verse's link is to John 21:22, on the singleton 'follow thou me'.

exclusions.sharedText: what ye have seen me do
exclusions.reason: The machine's top-scoring candidate for the verse at rarity 2.00, and the model case of the trap ADJUDICATING §4 names. Judges 9:48 is Abimelech on mount Zalmon, cutting a bough with an axe and laying it on his shoulder, telling his men 'What ye have seen me do, make haste, and do as I have done' — after which they burn a thousand men and women alive in the tower of Shechem. 2 Nephi 31:12 is the Son of God saying 'follow me, and do the things which ye have seen me do'. The five-word run is exact and the referent could hardly be more opposed: an imitation that leads to a massacre against an imitation that leads to salvation. There is also no reason to think the Book of Mormon knows Judges 9 — nothing else in 2 Nephi touches it — whereas the imitation-of-Christ language of the verse is fully accounted for by John 13:15 and by the chapter's own 'he having set the example before them' at 31:9.

Proposed at both 31:13 and 31:14 at rarity 1.50, and it is the window closing one word early. Exodus 14:24 has the LORD looking through 'the pillar of fire and of the cloud'; 2 Nephi 31:13 has 'the baptism of fire and of the Holy Ghost'. The shared string is a preposition, a noun, a conjunction and an article, and the word that decides the sense is the one on the far side of the window in each case — cloud there, Holy Ghost here. The real background of the phrase is Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16, both of which the Book of Mormon inverts (Holy Ghost first, then fire, in the KJV; fire first here), and that inversion is registered on the 1 Corinthians 13:1 link at this verse rather than given a row of its own, because it holds at 31:13, 31:14 and 31:17 alike and is Nephi's settled form rather than a fresh borrowing at each occurrence.

exclusions.sharedText: unto the Holy One of Israel
exclusions.reason: A standing exclusion for this chapter, carrying forward the one filed at 2 Nephi 9:11. 'The Holy One of Israel' is Isaiah's signature title and Nephi's adopted name for God; it will match Isaiah 31:1, 30:15, 41:14, 43:3, 49:7 and a dozen others indifferently, and the choice among them is arbitrary. The machine proposes Isaiah 31:1 here only because that verse happens to carry the preposition as well. Passed over in silence wherever else it occurs in chapters 31-33.

exclusions.sharedText: I have told you that I
exclusions.reason: Six words at rarity 2.14, and every one of them is grammar. John 18:8 is Jesus in Gethsemane — 'I have told you that I am he: if therefore ye seek me, let these go their way' — and the run breaks at exactly the point where the sense would begin, on 'am he' against the Book of Mormon's 'have seen'. Nothing in 2 Nephi 31 is doing anything with the arrest narrative. The verse's substance is Acts 2:38, registered as a recurrence on the link at 31:11, together with the Matthew 7 gate at 31:9.

Real content words, too widely distributed to point anywhere. 'Received the Holy Ghost' appears at Acts 8:17, 10:47, 19:2 and in substance at 2:38, and 2 Nephi 31 has been talking about receiving the Holy Ghost since 31:12. Acts 10:47 is proposed rather than any of the others only because it shares the perfect tense. If any Acts verse stands behind 31:18 it is 2:38, which is linked at 31:11 and which this verse is recapitulating along with Matthew 7:14 — the recapitulation is why the verse has no link of its own.

Covered in principle by the standing formulaic exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5 and noted here only because the machine proposes it twice in these three chapters (31:19 and 32:9). 'Behold, I say unto you' is one of the Book of Mormon's commonest discourse markers and one of the KJV's; the harvest saying of John 4:35 has no other contact with either verse.

exclusions.sharedText: speak with the tongue of angels
exclusions.reason: Not a rejection of the source but of a second row for it. 'With the tongues of men and of angels' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 13:1, and that is unquestionably where the tongue of angels comes from — but the borrowing was made at 2 Nephi 31:13 and repeated at 31:14, and 32:2-3 are Nephi quoting himself, explicitly: 'Do ye not remember that I said unto you...' A reader who meets the phrase four times in two chapters of one sitting is meeting one borrowing, and ADJUDICATING §4 adjudicates it at first use. The link is at 31:13 and this verse is registered there in recurrenceRefs, along with 32:3.

The stream's top candidate for the chapter's most famous sentence, and it is four words of preposition and article. 2 Chronicles 32:8 has the people of Judah resting themselves 'upon the words of Hezekiah king of Judah'; 2 Nephi 32:3 has 'feast upon the words of Christ'. The verb is what makes Nephi's sentence and it is not shared. Nor is there any biblical source for the feasting: 'feast upon' in this sense occurs nowhere in the KJV, and the nearest scriptural images — Jeremiah 15:16's eating of the words, Ezekiel 3:1-3's scroll, Amos 8:11's famine of hearing the words of the LORD — share the metaphor of consuming scripture but not one word of the phrasing. This is recorded at length because 32:3 is the verse a reader is most likely to expect a link at, and the honest answer is that the most quoted sentence in the chapter appears to be Nephi's own.

exclusions.sharedText: again I say unto you, that if ye
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run and the longest in the chapter, which is exactly why it is worth an entry: length alone decides nothing (ADJUDICATING §4). Every word is discourse frame — an adverb, a speech formula, a conjunction, a pronoun — and the two verses diverge at the first content word, Matthew's 'shall agree on earth' against Nephi's 'will enter in by the way'. Galatians 5:2 is proposed at the same verse for the same reason and fails the same way. The verse's real source is John 16:13, on the 1830 'shew'.

Four words in which the only content word is 'flesh', a term the KJV uses several hundred times. Philemon 1:16 concerns Onesimus as a brother beloved both in the flesh and in the Lord; 2 Nephi 32:6 concerns Christ manifesting himself in the flesh. The Leviticus 13:3 and Leviticus 14:8 candidates at the same verse are of the same kind and are covered here rather than separately. Where 32:6 does have a source it is Deuteronomy 8:1, which the stream did not rank at all.

Rarity 2.00 and the top candidate for the verse, produced by a clause boundary falling in the same place in two unrelated sentences. Matthew 10:17 is 'beware of men: for they will deliver you up to the councils' — a warning about persecution. 2 Nephi 32:7 is 'the stiff-neckedness of men: for they will not search knowledge' — a lament about incuriosity. The shared string spans the colon in both and the agreement is punctuational rather than lexical. Nothing in 32:7 is about persecution and nothing in Matthew 10 is about knowledge.

exclusions.sharedText: the Father in the name of
exclusions.reason: Proposed here and again at 33:12 at rarity 2.02, and it is the commonest liturgical construction in the New Testament: Ephesians 5:20, John 14:13, 15:16, 16:23, 16:26, Colossians 3:17 and others all address the Father in a name. Ephesians 5:20 is about giving thanks and has no other contact with either verse. Where the construction does carry a source in this chapter it is John 16:23 — 'ask the Father in my name' occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and that is registered as a composite on the Luke 18:1 link rather than given a row here.

'In the first place' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Numbers 10:14, which makes it the kind of candidate a rarity search will always surface and a reader might well accept. It should not be. Numbers 10:14 is a marching order — the standard of the camp of Judah went in the first place, meaning first in the column — where the phrase is spatial and describes a position in a line. Nephi's 'save in the first place ye shall pray unto the Father' is temporal and means before anything else. The KJV singleton and the Book of Mormon idiom are homographs, not the same phrase, and the second is ordinary English of the 1820s needing no source at all. The model case of CONVENTIONS §5's wrong-sense category, and a warning that an absolute rarity is evidence only once the sense has been checked.

exclusions.sharedText: not mighty in speaking / I am not eloquent
exclusions.reason: The typological expectation is strong and the wording will not bear it, which is the shape of the Exodus 2:2 'goodly' entry from the pilot. 'Neither am I mighty in writing, like unto speaking' invites Moses' protest at the bush — 'I am not eloquent ... I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue' — and Nephi is a figure the book elsewhere assimilates to Moses at length (1 Nephi 17). But the terms are opposed in the one place it matters: Moses' deficiency is in SPEAKING and Nephi's is in WRITING, with speaking named as the thing he does well. The KJV supplies no phrase here. 2 Corinthians 10:10 is the closer conceptual parallel — Paul's letters weighty, his bodily presence weak — and it too is inverted, since Paul is strong on the page and weak in person and Nephi is the reverse. Neither is written as a link; the exclusion records that both were considered and that the inversion in each case is total.

'A thing of nought' occurs in exactly four KJV verses (Isaiah 29:21, Isaiah 41:12, Jeremiah 14:14, Amos 6:13), and Isaiah 29:21 is the one a reader will reach for, because 2 Nephi 27 is an expansion of Isaiah 29 and reproduces that very clause at 27:32. But that is the point: the phrase is already inside this book, at 27:32 and again at 28:16, before it reaches 33:2. By the time Nephi writes his colophon it is his own idiom, and ADJUDICATING §4 adjudicates a repeat within a book at first use. No link is written here; 27:32 and 28:16 hold it.

Proposed at 33:4 and again at 33:5, and it is four words of relative clause. Exodus 24:12 has the LORD promising Moses tables of stone 'and a law, and commandments which I have written'; the antecedent is the Decalogue and the writer is God. In 33:4 and 33:5 the antecedent is Nephi's book and the writer is Nephi. There is a genuine and much better link two words away in 33:3, where 'what I have written' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 19:22, and that is where the row sits. Recorded because a reader who notices Exodus 24:12 should be told the catalogue preferred the Johannine singleton and why.

Four words and the sense is inverted by the negative that precedes them. Jeremiah 10:5 is about idols — 'they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good' — a mockery of wooden gods who can do nothing at all. 2 Nephi 33:4 is about scripture: 'it persuadeth them to do good'. The subject in Jeremiah is incapable by nature and the subject in Nephi is efficacious; the shared string is the residue of a negated clause meeting an affirmative one. The Isaiah 44:7 candidate at the same verse ('people and the things') is of the same order and is covered here.

The window closes exactly one word early, in both directions. Leviticus 4:3 reads 'do sin according to the sin of the people'; 2 Nephi 33:5 reads 'it speaketh harsh against sin, according to the plainness of the truth'. In Leviticus the string is a single grammatical unit; in Nephi a clause boundary falls inside it, between 'sin' and 'according'. The 1830 'harsh' where 1920 reads 'harshly' is noted here rather than on a link, since the verse has none — the adverbless construction is the first edition's and is one of a series of such regularizations 1920 made across these three chapters.

exclusions.sharedText: enter into the narrow gate, and walk in the straight path
exclusions.reason: The Matthew 7:13-14 gate is unquestionably behind this verse, with the same transposition of the adjectives that runs through chapter 31 — narrow gate and straight path, where the KJV has a strait gate and a narrow way. No link is written here because the borrowing was adjudicated at 2 Nephi 31:9, where the transposition is argued in full, and 33:9 is registered there in recurrenceRefs. A reader who arrives at 33:9 expecting the Sermon on the Mount is sent to 31:9. The 1 Kings 22:30 ('and enter into the') and Ecclesiastes 11:9 ('and walk in the') candidates that the machine proposed for this verse are connective noise and are not given entries.

Five words at rarity 1.50 and every one of them structural. John 10:21 is the crowd's verdict on Jesus — 'These are not the words of him that hath a devil' — and 2 Nephi 33:11 is 'And if they are not the words of Christ, judge ye'. The construction is a negated copula with a genitive of source, which any two texts arguing about whose words something is will produce independently.
