There is a faint thematic rhyme (both verses ask whether words come from God or from a devil, and 33:5 has just invoked 'the spirit of the Devil'), and it is not enough: no distinctive vocabulary is shared and John 10:21 is a bystanders' aside, not a formula. The verse's link is Matthew 24:30, on 'with power and great glory'.

Four words, three of them function words, and the nouns that follow diverge completely: 1 Corinthians 5:5 has the spirit saved 'in the day of the Lord Jesus' after a man is delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh; 2 Nephi 33:12 has 'many of us, if not all, may be saved in his kingdom'. Saving and salvation are among the commonest words in both corpora. The Ephesians 5:20 candidate at the same verse is covered by the entry filed at 2 Nephi 32:9.

exclusions.sharedText: which are of the house of
exclusions.reason: Six words, the chapter's longest machine run, and it is a genitive formula that the KJV uses of any household or lineage — the house of Chloe here, the house of Israel there. 1 Corinthians 1:11 concerns contentions reported to Paul by Chloe's people and has no contact with a farewell to the house of Israel. This is the clean illustration of ADJUDICATING §4's first trap in these three chapters: the longest run in the dossier for chapter 33 is worth nothing, while the verse's real finding — 'the voice of one crying', in the New Testament's form and not Isaiah's — the stream did not propose at all. The 2 Timothy 1:15 and 1 Corinthians 3:1 candidates at the same verse are of the same kind.

Four words of which one is a content word. 'The goodness of the LORD' and 'the goodness of God' are distributed across Psalms, Romans and the prophets; Psalm 33:5 is proposed only because it is the highest-scoring of many. 2 Nephi 33:14's 'partake of the goodness of God' has the distinctive verb, and 'partake' does not appear in Psalm 33:5 or in any of the alternatives.

Written up because it is the verse a reader will propose for the last four words Nephi writes. 'I must obey' has the ring of scripture and Acts 5:29 — 'We ought to obey God rather than men' — is the passage that ring comes from. But the sentence shares one word with it, the modal is different (must, not ought), the contrast with human authority that gives Acts 5:29 its whole force is absent, and the object of Nephi's obedience is a specific command to write rather than a general principle. There is no KJV source for 'I must obey'. The catalogue's judgment is that the last clause of the Book of Nephi is his own, and that is worth recording as a finding rather than leaving as a silence.

exclusions.sharedText: hath dried the sea … made the depths of the sea a way
exclusions.reason: This verse is a word-for-word transcription of Isaiah 51:10, and its wording is that verse's. Hardy's cross-reference points at what ISAIAH is alluding to — the crossing of the Red Sea, which Isaiah 51:10 recalls as the drying of the great deep — which is a fact about the Hebrew prophet's sources, not about the Book of Mormon's. Registered rather than linked, because a catalogue of dependence that let a source's own allusions in through the transcription would end by crediting the Book of Mormon with every text Isaiah ever echoed.

Hardy cross-references Isaiah 11:11 here, and the verse will not carry it — which is worth the register entry, because the mismatch is the interesting part. Jacob builds an exegesis on a plural: “as it sayeth ISLES, there must needs be more than this”. But Isaiah 11:11 reads “the ISLANDS of the sea” in the KJV, and so does this book's own transcription of that verse at 2 Nephi 21:11 — the word he expounds is not in the text he is expounding. “Isles of the sea” is Isaiah 24:15's phrase, and the link at this verse is to 24:15 on those words. What Hardy is pointing at is the doctrine of the gathering from the isles, which is Isaiah 11:11's subject; what Jacob quotes is Isaiah 24:15's wording. Flagged for Wilson: whether the catalogue should record a case where a writer's argument turns on a word his cited source does not use is a question about scope, not about this row.

exclusions.sharedText: as his rod was upon the sea
exclusions.reason: This verse is a word-for-word transcription of Isaiah 10:26, and its wording is that verse's. Hardy's cross-reference points at what ISAIAH is alluding to — Moses' rod stretched over the sea — which is a fact about the Hebrew prophet's sources, not about the Book of Mormon's. Registered rather than linked, because a catalogue of dependence that let a source's own allusions in through the transcription would end by crediting the Book of Mormon with every text Isaiah ever echoed.

exclusions.sharedText: the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb
exclusions.reason: This verse is a word-for-word transcription of Isaiah 10:26, and its wording is that verse's. Hardy's cross-reference points at what ISAIAH is alluding to — Gideon's defeat of Midian and the death of Oreb at the rock — which is a fact about the Hebrew prophet's sources, not about the Book of Mormon's. Registered rather than linked, because a catalogue of dependence that let a source's own allusions in through the transcription would end by crediting the Book of Mormon with every text Isaiah ever echoed.

exclusions.sharedText: the day that cometh shall burn them up
exclusions.reason: Hardy keys Malachi 4:1 to both 26:4 and 26:6, and the wording is at 26:4 — “all they that are proud, and that do wickedly, the day that cometh shall burn them up”, which is Malachi's sentence almost entire. 26:6 has the visitation and the destructions but none of Malachi's words. The link is at 26:4 and cites him there (CONVENTIONS §6a: the link goes where the wording is, and the register sends the reader from his verse to ours).

Hardy's apparatus cross-references all four baptism accounts at this verse — Matthew 3:16, Mark 1:10, Luke 3:22, John 1:32 — which is the right thing for a study edition to do and leaves the catalogue's question unanswered. The wording answers it. 'The Holy Ghost descended' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 3:22; Matthew 3:16 reads 'the Spirit of God descending', Mark 1:10 'the Spirit like a dove descending', John 1:32 'the Spirit descending from heaven'. All three name the agent as Spirit, not Holy Ghost, and Matthew and Mark both place the participle before the dove where the Book of Mormon and Luke place it after the noun. Matthew 3:16 is additionally excluded on its own account: its distinctive material — the heavens opened unto him, the lighting upon him — is entirely absent here, though Matthew 3:14-15 IS the source at 31:5. The link is at Luke 3:22. Mark 1:10 and John 1:32 are excluded on the same evidence and are not given separate entries.

The n-gram stream’s second candidate here, on a four-word run whose content words belong to the temple-authority dispute. The whole phrase Mosiah 29:2 is using is “the voice of the people came”, and “voice of the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 8:7, which is the accepted link at this verse and the passage the entire chapter is rewriting. Matthew supplies the connective and nothing else.

exclusions.sharedText: gone up to the land of
exclusions.reason: Top-ranked machine candidate for the verse (rarity 1.08) and pure connective geography. Ezekiel 38:11 is Gog’s boast about invading unwalled villages; Mosiah 29:3 reports that Aaron has gone to the land of Nephi to preach. No content word is shared.

A real four-word run and a genuinely tempting one, because both sentences turn on a right that somebody lacks. The senses are unrelated: Hebrews 13:10 denies tabernacle-servers the right to eat of the Christian altar, a cultic-boundary claim; Mosiah 29:8 denies the community the right to put a rival claimant to death. The English construction is doing all the work.

The highest-scoring candidate at this verse (rarity 1.50) and the kind of match CONVENTIONS §9 warns about: rare boilerplate, ranked first, worthless. 2 Samuel 18:3 is David’s troops telling him to stay out of the battle against Absalom. The verse’s actual borrowing is four words later — “should be judged of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 4:3 — and that is where the link sits.

Proposed at 29:16 and again at 29:24. “It is not expedient” is one of the Book of Mormon’s standing formulae and the KJV’s ordinary way of saying a thing should not be done; Paul’s use of it concerns whether to boast about visions. Covered here for both verses so that the register does not carry it twice.

The stretched-out arm of the Exodus formula is the obvious biblical background for “extending the arm of mercy towards them”, and it is the wrong one. The arm-of-mercy phrase is a Book of Mormon formula with its own history: Jacob 6:5 (“while his arm of mercy is extended towards you”), then Mosiah 16:12, then Alma 5:33 and 3 Nephi 9:14. By ADJUDICATING §4 the repeat inside Mosiah is the author’s own idiom, not a fresh borrowing, and the adjudication belongs at Jacob 6:5. What is borrowed in this sentence is the clause that follows it — Proverbs 30:5’s “them that put their trust in him”, a KJV singleton — and that is the accepted link here.

A temporal connective the Book of Mormon uses continuously. John 16:2 concerns synagogue expulsion and killing; the shared words carry no signal. The 1830 “cometh” (1920 “comes”) is KJV register rather than evidence of this verse.

The single highest-scoring machine candidate in the chapter (rarity 2.00) and a clean example of the n-gram stream ranking boilerplate first. Deuteronomy 11:22 is a conditional about keeping commandments and cleaving to the LORD. The borrowing in this clause is the phrase the run stops one word short of: “ye do in the fear of the” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 19:9, Jehoshaphat’s charge to the judges he had set in the land, which is the accepted link and the passage standing behind 29:12 and 29:42 as well.

“The sins of many” in Hebrews 9:28 is Christ bearing them once for all — substitutionary and singular. Mosiah 29:31 says the sins of many people were caused by their kings and are charged back to the kings’ heads, which is the opposite movement: the chapter is arguing that no one may bear another’s account. The verse’s real source is Ezekiel 11:21 at 29:30, with Ezekiel 18:20 behind it.

Worth recording because the rarity is real and would tempt anyone counting: “shedding of blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 9:22, “without shedding of blood is no remission.” The sense is not merely different but opposed. Hebrews makes blood-shedding the condition of forgiveness; Mosiah 29:40 praises the king who “had not delighted in the shedding of blood”, and the chapter’s other uses (29:7, 29:21) treat it as the cost of dynastic politics. Nothing else in the verse touches Hebrews 9, and the phrase is the natural English for the thing. A singleton rejected on sense, per CONVENTIONS §5.

exclusions.sharedText: granted unto his people that they
exclusions.reason: Rarity 2.00, and connective tissue in both texts. 1 Chronicles 23:25 is David’s reason for retiring the Levites’ carrying duties. Where this verse does borrow is the vocabulary of royal extraction: “exacted” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, 2 Kings 15:20 and 23:35, both of kings taking money of their people, and that is recorded in the accepted link at 29:40.

Four words spanning a clause boundary in both texts; Acts 21:28 is the mob’s charge against Paul in the temple. The 1830’s “this they done” (1920 “did”) is a dialect past participle and has no bearing on any source.

The four-word run is a KJV singleton, which is why it ranked, but the rarity is an artifact of King James idiom rather than a signal: the KJV normally writes 'of king Ahasuerus' and only once expands the possessive into a relative clause. Esther 1:9 is Vashti's feast for the women in the royal house; Mosiah 1:1 is a summary of political peace. Nothing else of Esther 1 is present, and the 1830 'which' becomes 'who' in 1920, which is the ordinary relative-pronoun modernization and not a variant bearing on any source.

A five-word run of naming formula. Genesis 26:18 is Isaac re-digging Abraham's wells and calling them by the names his father had used — the names are of wells, the point is inherited ownership, and the verb has an indirect object the Book of Mormon does not have. Mosiah 1:2 simply lists three sons. Naming-by-the-father is too widely distributed in the KJV to be traced to this verse.

See the fuller entry at Mosiah 1:16. 1 Kings 7:36's 'plates' are the flat faces of the ledges of Solomon's laver bases, and what is 'graved' on them is cherubim, lions and palm trees — decoration, not text. Mosiah 1:3's plates carry records and commandments. The two senses of 'plate' happen to share a preposition.

“which have been kept” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, so the machine was right to rank it, but the KJV's participle governs 'secret' — things kept secret from the foundation of the world, which the speaker of parables is about to utter. Mosiah 1:5's participle governs 'and preserved by the hand of God', and the whole point of the sentence is that the things were NOT kept from anyone: they were kept so they could be read. The senses are opposed. The real source of this verse's argument is Isaiah 1:9, catalogued at the link.

A KJV singleton that is a genuine coincidence and an instructive one. Judges 20:16 counts seven hundred left-handed slingers 'among all this people' — and the people it is counting are the tribe of BENJAMIN, at the battle of Gibeah. The verse is therefore about a body of chosen men within Benjamin, which is close enough to king Benjamin's proclamation to his people that a careful reader might have taken it. It should not be taken: the shared string is a partitive adverbial phrase with no content, the KJV's context is a civil war and a marksmanship statistic, and the coincidence rests entirely on a personal name shared with a tribe the Book of Mormon never mentions.

Typology pulls hard here and the wording will not bear it. 'If he had not extended his arm in the preservation of our fathers' is the Exodus redemption formula in sense — a divine arm interposed to save a people from a stronger one — but the KJV's phrase is 'a stretched out arm' (Exodus 6:6, and some fifteen further verses in Deuteronomy, Kings and Jeremiah), never 'extended'. “extended” occurs in exactly two KJV verses and both are Ezra's 'extended mercy' before the kings of Persia, which is a different idiom with a different object. The Book of Mormon has the Exodus idea in nineteenth-century English rather than in King James English, which is a fact worth recording precisely because it is the opposite of what this catalogue usually finds.

The model case for this category in Mosiah. “plates of brass” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the Book of Mormon's most important physical object is named in a phrase the King James Bible uses once — and that verse is an inventory of Solomon's ten movable lavers: 'every base had four brasen wheels, and plates of brass'. They are sheets of bronze bolted to a wheeled stand. Nothing is written on them, they are not a record, and 1 Kings 7 has no interest in them beyond the specification. The coincidence is worth naming in the register rather than in the catalogue, because a reader who finds the singleton on their own will otherwise assume we missed it.

exclusions.sharedText: (dwelling in temporary shelters at a festal assembly)
exclusions.reason: The standing scholarly reading of Mosiah 2:5-6 is that Benjamin's assembly is a Feast of Tabernacles, and Leviticus 23:42 is the verse that would have to carry it: 'Ye shall dwell in booths seven days.' The wording will not do it. Leviticus has booths (Hebrew sukkot), which the KJV distinguishes throughout from tents; it has seven days, which Mosiah does not; and it has no orientation, where the Book of Mormon's whole point is that the doors faced the temple. The phrase the verse actually reproduces is 'pitched their tents', a KJV singleton at Numbers 9:17, and the arrangement is Numbers 2:2's camp about the tabernacle — both catalogued at the link. Filed here so that a reader who expects the Tabernacles reading can see that it was considered and on what grounds it was declined; the festal reading may still be right about the occasion, but it is not where the sentence came from.

Isaiah 6:10's ear-and-heart pairing, quoted at Matthew 13:15 and Acts 28:27, stands behind any English sentence of this shape, and this verse looked like a mediation case. It is not decidable as one: tools/mediation-check.py on Mosiah 2:9 against Isaiah 6:10 and Matthew 13:15 reports NO decisive divergence — the two candidates differ at every point except the ones the Book of Mormon reproduces, so the verse cannot settle its own mediation. It is excluded rather than recorded as 'uncertain' because the sense is also wrong: Isaiah's clause is a judicial hardening ('lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and convert, and be healed'), where Benjamin is inviting an audience to open what Isaiah's God shuts. The source of the verse's audience-qualification is Nehemiah 8:2-3, where 'hear with understanding' and 'were attentive' are both KJV singletons; see the link.

A five-word run, and Acts 7 is a source this corpus genuinely uses — 1 Nephi 2:22 and 3:29 both take 'ruler' from Acts 7:27 rather than from Exodus 2:14, and 1 Nephi draws on Stephen's speech at six places. But Acts 7:35's question is a hostile one ('Who made thee a ruler and a judge over us?') and its second noun is 'judge', where Benjamin's is 'king'. The verse's ruler-language was adjudicated one chapter earlier at Mosiah 1:10, where 'a ruler over' is a KJV singleton at 2 Chronicles 6:5 and the accompanying naming and temple material comes with it. Superseded by that link.

exclusions.sharedText: if ye would keep his commandments, ye should prosper in the land
exclusions.reason: The prosperity conditional recurs three times in these two chapters (1:7, 2:22, 2:31) and the machine proposes a fresh Deuteronomic source each time. It has one adjudication, at Mosiah 1:7, where the route is argued as OT-via-earlier-BoM: by Mosiah the formula is the Book of Mormon's own covenant refrain, established at 1 Nephi 2:20 out of 1 Kings 2:3 and Joshua 1:7 and already inherited at 2 Nephi 1:20. ADJUDICATING §4 governs — a repeat within a book is the speaker using his own formula, not a fresh borrowing. Recorded here and at 2:31 in recurrenceRefs on the 1:7 link. Note also what 2:22 adds and no Deuteronomic verse has: 'he never doth vary from that which he hath said', which is the Book of Mormon's own gloss turning a conditional promise into a statement about divine constancy.

A six-word run, and “the man that doeth this” occurs in exactly two KJV verses — Malachi 2:12, where the LORD cuts such a man off out of the tabernacles of Jacob, and Isaiah 56:2, where such a man is blessed. The phrase is therefore a neutral pointer that takes its charge entirely from what precedes it, and in both KJV verses that antecedent is specific (marrying the daughter of a strange god; keeping the sabbath), where Benjamin's is the general apostasy of 2:36. Nothing else of Malachi 2 or Isaiah 56 is present. The verse's real borrowings are Acts 13:10's 'enemy of all righteousness' and the Acts temple formula, both catalogued at the link.

One of the two KJV verses containing the phrase, and the machine ranked it alongside Revelation 14:12. It is the wrong one. Revelation 12:17 is the dragon making war with the remnant of the woman's seed; nothing else in it touches Mosiah 2:41. Revelation 14:12 is the one that stands immediately after the smoke of torment ascending for ever and ever — which this chapter has just used at 2:38 — and it makes the same contrast, endurance against endlessness, that Benjamin makes across 2:38-41. Superseded by the link at this verse.

The top-ranked candidate for the verse, and it is pure connective boilerplate — a speech-introduction formula the Book of Mormon uses continuously. Genesis 26:2 is the LORD appearing to Isaac and telling him not to go down to Egypt. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5, and recorded here only because the machine put it above Luke 2:10, which is the verse the sentence actually comes from.

exclusions.sharedText: the lame walk ... the lepers are cleansed ... the deaf hear ... the dead are raised
exclusions.reason: Hardy's apparatus cross-references Matthew 11:5 and Luke 7:22 together at this verse, which is right for a study edition and too coarse for a verbal catalogue: the two gospels give the same answer to John's disciples in nearly the same words, and they differ at exactly one point that the Book of Mormon reproduces. Matthew 11:5 opens 'The blind receive their sight'; Luke 7:22 has 'the blind see'. Mosiah 3:5 has 'the blind to receive their sight', and “receive their sight” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. tools/mediation-check.py on Mosiah 3:5 against the pair returns one decisive point, for Matthew. Luke is therefore excluded rather than carried as a composite; the link sits at Matthew 11:5 and cites Hardy for the cross-reference.

'Cast out devils' is one of the commonest phrases in the synoptic gospels and appears in a dozen KJV verses across Matthew, Mark and Luke; no one of them can be identified as the source of Mosiah 3:6, and the Book of Mormon's gloss — 'or the evil spirits which dwelleth in the hearts of the children of men' — is not from any of them. Recorded so the register shows that the exorcism clause in the miracle list was considered and left unattached, unlike the healing clauses of 3:5, which come from Matthew 11:5.

'He hath a devil' is said of Jesus at John 7:20, 8:48, 8:52 and 10:20, and of John the Baptist at Matthew 11:18 and Luke 7:33 — six KJV verses, all making the same charge in the same words, with nothing to choose between them. The Book of Mormon's 'shall say that he hath a Devil' is the charge in general, not any one occurrence of it. The verse's identifiable sources are John 1:11 and the synoptic passion prediction, both catalogued at the link; this phrase is real KJV contact that cannot be keyed to a verse.

“stiffnecked” occurs in nine KJV verses, six of them of Israel at Sinai and in Deuteronomy, and the phrase 'a stiffnecked people' in five. Nothing distinguishes Exodus 33:3 from Exodus 32:9, 33:5, 34:9, Deuteronomy 9:6 or 9:13, and the Book of Mormon supplies no further wording from any of them. The clause it does draw on in this verse — the law given as a response to that stiffneckedness — is Galatians 3:19's 'it was added because of transgressions', carried as a composite on the Hebrews 10:1 link at 3:15.

Ephesians 4:22-24 makes the same exhortation as Colossians 3:9-12 and is the passage more often quoted for it, so it is the natural rival here. The wording decides for Colossians: “put off the old man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Colossians 3:9, because Ephesians 4:22 separates the verb from its object ('put off concerning the former conversation the old man'). More decisively, the rest of Mosiah 3:19 follows Colossians and not Ephesians — 'becometh a saint' answers Colossians 3:12's 'as the elect of God, holy', and the virtue list reproduces Colossians 3:12's meekness, humbleness and longsuffering in order, where Ephesians 4:24 has only 'righteousness and true holiness'. Superseded by the Colossians 3:9 link.

exclusions.sharedText: drunk damnation to their own souls
exclusions.reason: The third occurrence of the phrase in Benjamin's sermon, after 2:33 and 3:18. Adjudicated at first use: “drinketh damnation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the argument for 1 Corinthians 11:29 as its source — a covenant meal taken unworthily by an assembled congregation — is made at Mosiah 2:33. ADJUDICATING §4 governs repeats within a book; recorded in recurrenceRefs there and here, not as three links.

exclusions.sharedText: smoke rose up for ever and ever
exclusions.reason: The Apocalypse says a smoke goes up for ever twice, and only one of the two is about persons. Revelation 19:3 is the hallelujah over the fall of Babylon — 'and her smoke rose up for ever and ever' — a burning city, in the past tense, and the verse two lines before the 'Lord God omnipotent reigneth' that this chapter takes at 3:5. Revelation 14:11 has the present-tense 'ascendeth up', and its smoke is 'the smoke of THEIR TORMENT', which is what Mosiah 3:27 is describing. Excluded on tense and on subject, and named here because its neighbour at 19:6 is a source in this same chapter, which makes it a plausible mis-assignment.

exclusions.sharedText: the multitude, and behold ... fallen to the earth
exclusions.reason: The machine's best-scoring candidate in the chapter and a real temptation: 2 Chronicles 20:24 has a leader looking toward a multitude, and bodies fallen to the earth, in one sentence, and the 1830 text's 'they had fell to the earth' makes the run longer than the modern text does. It is declined on sense, and the sense could hardly be more opposed. Jehoshaphat's watchman looks out on the corpses of an annihilated invading army — 'they were dead bodies fallen to the earth, and none escaped'. Benjamin looks out on his own people prostrate in the fear of the Lord and about to be forgiven. One verse is a battlefield after a massacre and the other is a congregation at the moment of conversion, and the only thing they share is the posture of bodies on the ground. This is the register's standard case and it is filed at length because the n-gram score would otherwise have carried it: a rare five-word run means nothing when the two contexts are enemies.

The publican's prayer is the KJV's model of a self-abasing cry for mercy, and Mosiah 4:2's multitude crying 'O have mercy' from the ground, after 'they had viewed themselves in their own carnal state', is the same gesture. It is not catalogued because the wording will not carry it: Luke 18:13 reads 'God be merciful to me a sinner', which shares no phrase with the Book of Mormon's cry, and the verse's actual borrowings — Exodus 24:3, Acts 15:9, Acts 26:18 — are all elsewhere in the sentence. A typological expectation was pulling toward a link the wording will not bear.

Ephesians 1:4 is a reasonable proposal — election before the foundation of the world is the doctrinal neighbourhood Mosiah 4:6 is standing in. It is superseded. 'Foundation of the world' occurs in six KJV verses and the discriminating word here is not 'foundation' but 'prepared', which appears with the phrase in exactly one verse, Matthew 25:34. Ephesians 1:4 reads 'chosen us in him before the foundation of the world', not prepared from it, and the preposition matters. The link is written at Mosiah 4:6 to Matthew 25:34, which is also the pericope this sermon returns to at 4:26 and 5:9-10.

A four-word run whose fifth word decides everything, which is the trap the pilot named at 2 Timothy 2:4. Deuteronomy 8:3 continues 'that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD' — a statement that revelation sustains life. Mosiah 4:9 continues 'that man doth not comprehend all the things which the Lord can comprehend' — a statement that revelation exceeds understanding. The two clauses share a subject and a negation and nothing else, and the verse's real borrowing is four words earlier, at Hebrews 11:6's 'believe that he is'.

Genuinely tempting, and registered for that reason. 'Have tasted of the' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 6:4, and Mosiah 4:11's 'have tasted of his love' sits inside a list of the same kind of past graces Hebrews is enumerating: enlightenment, the heavenly gift, partaking of the Holy Ghost. The two passages then go in opposite directions and the opposition is the point of each. Hebrews 6:4-6 is the KJV's hardest saying about apostasy — those who have tasted and fallen away cannot be renewed to repentance. Mosiah 4:11-12 is a promise that those who have tasted and remember will 'always retain a remission of your sins'. Benjamin's whole paragraph is about retaining what Hebrews says cannot be recovered, and to catalogue a borrowing here would be to make the Book of Mormon quote the one verse its argument contradicts. A shared idiom for religious experience is not a source.

Colossians 3:10's 'renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him' shares both a creation formula and the word 'knowledge' with Mosiah 4:12's 'grow in the knowledge of the glory of Him that created you', which makes it a better proposal than most of the stream's output. It is declined because 'him that created' is the KJV's ordinary circumlocution for God and because the distinctive content of Colossians 3:10 — the new man, the image, the putting on — is absent from Mosiah 4. The verse's borrowings are 2 Peter 3:18's 'grow in ... the knowledge' and 2 Corinthians 4:6's 'the knowledge of the glory', and both are registered as a composite link at this verse.

exclusions.sharedText: for silver, and for gold, and for all
exclusions.reason: 'For silver and for gold' is a KJV singleton, at 2 Chronicles 32:27, and the run continues into Mosiah's 'and for all the riches', so on rarity alone this is one of the better machine proposals in the chapter. It is declined because the two lists do the opposite work. Hezekiah's is an inventory of a king's treasuries, offered as evidence that God had prospered him. Benjamin's is a list of things nobody in the room owns — 'Do we not all depend upon the same being, even God, for all the substance which we have' — offered as evidence that every hearer is a beggar. The KJV's enumerative 'for X, and for Y' is a general accounting idiom, and where it appears in a sentence denying ownership it cannot be pointing at the sentence that asserts it.

Genesis 31:16 is Rachel and Leah agreeing that Laban's wealth has passed to them. The shared four words are a relative clause with no content term in common beyond 'riches', and the Book of Mormon's clause ends 'which we have of every kind' where Genesis's ends 'which God hath taken from our father'. Registered rather than passed over only because the score put it in the top fifty.

Pure connective tissue. 'The thing which thou hast' is a relative frame the KJV uses constantly, and Deuteronomy 1:14's subject — the people approving Moses's plan to appoint judges — touches nothing in Benjamin's rebuke of a man who withholds alms. Registered only because the run scored 2.00.

exclusions.sharedText: the hungry ... the naked ... the poor
exclusions.reason: Isaiah 58:6-7 is the Old Testament's own catalogue of the works of mercy and the obvious candidate for a Hebrew-Bible-era sermon on almsgiving; a reader who expects the Book of Mormon's chronology to hold would put the link here. The mediation test declines it. Isaiah 58:7 has bread for the hungry, the poor brought home, and the naked covered; it has no sick person and nobody visits anyone. Mosiah 4:26 has 'visiting the sick', which enters the KJV only at Matthew 25:36, and it clothes the naked rather than covering him, which is Matthew's verb and not Isaiah's. The link is written at Mosiah 4:26 to Matthew 25:35-36. Isaiah 58 remains the background of the whole paragraph and is named here so a reader is sent to it.

exclusions.sharedText: all these things are done in
exclusions.reason: The chapter's longest n-gram run against any single verse, and worthless, which is the pilot's finding about the stream restated. Mark 4:11 ends 'all these things are done in parables'; Mosiah 4:27 ends 'are done in wisdom and order'. The words that carry the Book of Mormon's sentence are 'in order', and the KJV instructs that things be done in order in exactly one verse, 1 Corinthians 14:40, where the phrase is 'decently and in order'. The link is written there. Read the candidate's whole verse before trusting its run length.

The borrowing is real and it is adjudicated at Mosiah 4:2, where the phrase first enters this assembly. 'With one voice' occurs in two KJV verses and only Exodus 24:3 is a covenant ratification, which is what makes it worth having; but Mosiah 5:2's use is the same narrator using his own formula eight verses later, not a fresh contact with Exodus. Registered here so that a reader who meets the phrase at 5:2 — where it is followed by 'we believe all the words which thou hast spoken unto us', the answering half of Exodus 24:3's 'All the words which the LORD hath said will we do' — is sent to the link at 4:2 rather than shown nothing.

A five-word run and an exact opposition. Jeremiah 44:16 is the people of Judah in Egypt refusing the prophet: 'As for the word that thou hast spoken unto us in the name of the LORD, we will not hearken unto thee.' Mosiah 5:2 is a people accepting one: 'we believe all the words which thou hast spoken unto us.' The shared clause is the formula for reporting a prophet's speech back to him, and the KJV supplies it to a refusal and the Book of Mormon to an assent. Filed at length because the run is long enough to tempt and because the register's best entries are the ones where a real string match points the wrong way.

'That which is to come' is connective English for the future and the Book of Mormon uses it constantly, including at 4:11 in the previous chapter. Revelation 1:4's 'him which is, and which was, and which is to come' is a divine title, not a temporal adverbial, and 1 Timothy 4:8's is the life to come as against the present one. Neither is in view in 'great views of that which is to come'.

exclusions.sharedText: make a covenant with our God
exclusions.reason: The chapter's highest-scoring machine candidate, at 3.00, and a fair one: Ezra 10:3 is a covenant made with God by an assembled people, which is exactly the scene. It is declined because 'a covenant with our God' is the KJV's ordinary phrase for the transaction and because Ezra's covenant is to put away foreign wives, a subject with no counterpart anywhere in Benjamin's sermon. Where the wording is the standard idiom for the act being performed, the parallel is a description of the act and not evidence of a source. The verse's real borrowing is in its second half, at Revelation 14:10-11.

exclusions.sharedText: take heed that ye do not
exclusions.reason: 'Take heed that ye do not' is a KJV singleton at Matthew 6:1, which makes this the kind of candidate that ought to be argued rather than dropped — and the context is more tempting still, since Matthew 6:1 governs the almsgiving instruction that Mosiah 4:16-26 has just been rewriting. It is declined on the continuation. Matthew's clause completes as 'do not your alms before men, to be seen of them'; Benjamin's completes as 'do not transgress, that the name be not blotted out of your hearts'. The one is a warning against performing righteousness publicly, the other a warning against breaking covenant, and nothing in Mosiah 5 is about display. This is the window closing one word early, in its purest form: the six shared words are an imperative frame the KJV happens to use once, and the seventh word is where the two verses part.

Jeremiah 31:33 is the obvious candidate for anything written in a heart, and its New Testament quotation at Hebrews 8:10 makes this look like a mediation question worth running. It was run and it decided nothing: the two forms differ at 'law in their inward parts' against 'laws into their mind', and Mosiah 5:12 reproduces neither. The reason is that Mosiah is not writing the law in the heart at all. What is written is a NAME — 'retain the name written always in your hearts' — and the KJV writes a name on a person in exactly one place, Revelation 14:1, where it is written in the forehead. The link is placed there, with 2 Corinthians 3:3 for the writing surface. Jeremiah 31 remains the passage a reader should have in mind and is registered so that they do.

A typological expectation pulling toward a link the wording will not bear. Benjamin's illustration is a legal casus about a stray animal, and the KJV has exactly one cluster of statutes on stray animals — Exodus 23:4-5 and Deuteronomy 22:1-4 — so a reader trained on the Covenant Code will reach for it, especially since Mosiah 4:28 has just borrowed Exodus 22:14 verbatim. It does not hold. The statutes require the finder to bring the animal back to its owner; Benjamin's man drives it away and casts it out, and approves of doing so. The shared vocabulary is one word, 'ass', which the KJV uses ninety times. The verse's expulsion language is Matthew 22:13's and the link is written there. Job 24:3's 'they drive away the ass of the fatherless' shares two more words and is likewise declined: in Job the driving away is the crime, and in Mosiah it is the right response of an honest man to an animal he does not know.

'In heaven and in earth' scored highest of the six candidates the machine returned for this verse, and four of them share the same run — Daniel 6:27, Philippians 2:10, Psalm 135:6, Matthew 28:18. That is the definition of a formula: a phrase distributed widely enough that its presence identifies nothing. The verse's borrowings are elsewhere in it, at 1 Corinthians 15:58, Revelation 19:6 and Ephesians 1:13/3:9, and the creation doxology is the Book of Mormon's own, used already at Mosiah 4:9.

The title is adjudicated at Mosiah 3:5, where it first enters the sermon in the angel's own words; 5:15 is the same speaker (Benjamin) using his own now-established title at the sermon's close, one of five recurrences (3:5, 3:17, 3:18, 3:21, 5:2) tracked there. Registered here, rather than left silent, because 5:15 happens to reproduce the exact three-word Revelation 19:6 sequence 'Lord God Omnipotent' most precisely of all six occurrences — a reader who notices that should be sent to 3:5, not shown nothing.

The chapter's highest-scoring machine candidate and a poor one. 'Entered into a covenant with' is the KJV's ordinary way of saying that a covenant was made — 2 Chronicles 15:12, Jeremiah 34:10, Ezekiel 16:8 — and Mosiah 6:1-2 says it twice because that is what the chapter is about. Ezekiel 16:8's covenant is a marriage, made by God with a foundling Jerusalem whose nakedness he covers; nothing in Benjamin's roll-taking answers to it. The distinctive act at Mosiah 6:1 is the recording of names, and the link is written to Nehemiah 9:38, the KJV's one covenant ratified that way.

'The name of Christ' occurs in exactly two KJV verses and both were proposed. 1 Peter 4:14 is declined in favour of 2 Timothy 2:19 on the strength of what surrounds the phrase rather than the phrase itself. Peter's verse is about being reproached FOR the name; Mosiah 6:2 is about taking the name UPON oneself, which is 2 Timothy's 'nameth the name of Christ'. Decisively, 2 Timothy 2:19 also contains a seal and the clause 'them that are his', both of which stand in Mosiah 5:15's 'may seal you his' four verses earlier. One KJV verse accounts for three Book of Mormon phrases; the other accounts for none.

exclusions.sharedText: to be a ruler and a
exclusions.reason: The longest run the machine found in this chapter, six words, and a textbook instance of the window closing one word early. Acts 7:35 completes as 'a ruler and a judge' and then 'a ruler and a deliverer'; Mosiah 6:3 completes as 'a ruler and a king'. Stephen's sentence is about Moses being refused by his people, and its whole point is that Moses was not made a king. The KJV pairs ruler with king in one verse only, 1 Kings 1:35, where David installs Solomon, and the link is written there. Registered at length because the run length would otherwise have carried it, and because Acts 7:35's rejected-deliverer typology is genuinely at home elsewhere in the Book of Mormon — just not here, in a peaceful succession.

'In his father's stead' is the Deuteronomistic regnal formula and the KJV uses it of Jehoahaz (2 Kings 23:30, 2 Chronicles 36:1) and of the anointed priest (Leviticus 16:32) among others; a phrase spread across the whole of Kings and Chronicles cannot identify a source. What is not formulaic is the infinitive: 'to reign in his stead' occurs once in the KJV, at 2 Chronicles 1:8, in Solomon's mouth, and that is where the link is written. The distinction is worth registering because the two look identical in a concordance.

'In the thirtieth year' is a date formula, and Ezekiel 1:1's is a date — the year of his call by the river Chebar, not anyone's age. Mosiah 6:4's is an age: 'in the thirtieth year of his age'. The KJV verse that gives a king an age of thirty at his accession is 2 Samuel 5:4, David's, and the link is written there. Registered because a shared four-word run in a chronological notice is exactly the kind of match a reader skims past and a machine scores.

A five-word run against a verse that matters elsewhere in this corpus — Acts 3:22 is the Deuteronomy 18 prophet-like-Moses text, and the mediation between its form and Deuteronomy's is one of the pilot's principal results at 1 Nephi 22:20. It has no business here. Mosiah 6:6's clause is 'did keep his commandments in all things whatsoever he commanded him'; Acts 3:22's is 'him shall ye hear in all things whatsoever he shall say unto you'. The shared words are a universal-quantifier frame with no content, the verbs differ, and Mosiah 6:6 is a regnal evaluation with no prophet in it. A rare-looking run against an important verse is still a formula.

A genuine two-verse rarity and the better half of a real question. 'His judgments and his statutes' occurs in Deuteronomy 8:11 and Nehemiah 10:29 and nowhere else, and the machine ranked them within a hundredth of each other. Nehemiah wins on three grounds: it supplies 'walk' and 'observe', which are two of Mosiah 6:6's three verbs and are absent from Deuteronomy 8:11; it is a positive oath rather than a warning ('Beware that thou forget not'); and its setting is a covenant sealed by a written list of names, which is what Mosiah 6:1 has just described. Deuteronomy 8:11 remains the background idiom and is registered so a reader is sent to it.

'The space of three years' is a duration, shared with Acts 20:31 and James 5:17 because three years is a common length of time and the KJV has one way of saying it. James's three years are Elijah's drought and Acts's are Paul's Ephesian ministry; Mosiah's are a period without contention. Registered only because two candidates scored on the same run and a reader might wonder why neither is a link.

The chapter's top-ranked candidate at verse 1 and a five-word run, but the run ends one word early in the way ADJUDICATING §4 warns about: Acts 19:8 reads 'for the space of three months' and Mosiah 7:1 'for the space of three years'. 'For the space of' is a KJV time formula used of everything from three days to seven years, and Paul disputing in the synagogue at Ephesus has nothing to do with a king enjoying continual peace. Nothing in the surrounding verse touches Acts 19.

Scored highest in the verse (rarity 1.50) on the strength of a five-word run, and the run is 'and they stood before the' — where Daniel's next word is 'image' and the Book of Mormon's is 'king'. Standing before a monarch is the commonest posture in the KJV's court narratives; the phrase carries no signal. The verse does have a link, and it is at 'their bands were loosed' (Acts 16:26), which the machine ranked below this.

'Brought before the king' occurs in five KJV verses across Esther, Daniel and 1 Samuel, all of them court narrative. Esther 9:11 is a body count delivered to Ahasuerus and has no other contact with Mosiah 7:8. Recorded rather than passed over in silence because it is the kind of four-word match that looks like evidence when the surrounding verse genuinely does depend on a New Testament prison scene, and it is worth saying which half of the verse is borrowed and which is not.

A genuine temptation, considered and declined. 'Bowed himself before the king' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Samuel 24:20 (Araunah) and 1 Kings 1:23 (Nathan), and 1 Kings 1:23 is attractive because it is a prophet coming in before a king, bowing, and then delivering a speech that changes a succession — which is what Ammon does. But five words of court protocol are the whole of the contact: the Book of Mormon has no 'with his face to the ground', no Bathsheba, no succession, and Ammon's speech is a self-identification, not an oracle. With two candidate verses and no way to choose between them on wording, and no metalepsis that survives the choice, this is a resemblance rather than a dependence. 2 Samuel 24:20 is excluded on the same evidence and is not given a separate entry.

'Be in subjection to' is 1 Peter's wifely-submission formula ('be in subjection to your own husbands') and Mosiah 7:18's political one ('no longer be in subjection to our enemies'). The KJV uses the phrase for household order and for the subjection of creatures to Christ; the Book of Mormon uses it for military occupation and a tax. The verse's real borrowing is Luke 21:28's 'lift up your heads', which the n-gram stream did not rank at all because the agreement is split across the clause boundary that CONVENTIONS §9 describes.

Hardy's apparatus cross-references Exodus 14:21-22 and Exodus 16:35 at this verse. The first is right and is cited on the Red Sea link; the second is where the manna narrative is, which is the right cross-reference for a study edition and the wrong one for a verbal catalogue. Exodus 16:35 reads 'the children of Israel did eat manna forty years' — Israel is the subject, the verb is 'eat', and God does not appear in the clause. Mosiah 7:19 has God as subject and 'fed' as the verb, which is Deuteronomy 8:3's construction and a KJV singleton: 'fed thee with manna'. The link is at Deuteronomy 8:3. This is a case of CONVENTIONS §6a's second bullet, not a mis-keyed row: the running head and verse are right, the reference is simply chapter-level.

'Put your trust in' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 4:5 ('put your trust in the LORD') and Judges 9:15 (the bramble's 'put your trust in my shadow'), which is rare enough to be worth checking and not rare enough to be worth keeping. Neither verse has any other contact with Mosiah 7:19, whose sentence is an exodus creed; the imperative plural is simply how English renders the commonest exhortation in the Psalter, and 'trust in the LORD' in one form or another runs through dozens of verses. Judges 9:15 is excluded on the same evidence. The phrase recurs at 7:33 and is passed over there in silence.

The machine's proposal for 'their doings shall be as a stumbling block before them', and a real candidate: Ezekiel 3:20's 'I lay a stumbling-block before him' is, as the KJV prints it with the hyphen, the only verse in the Bible with that string, and Ezekiel 14:3's 'the stumblingblock of their iniquity' is the closest thematic match anywhere. It is displaced because it explains one clause and Jeremiah 18:15 explains three. Jeremiah 18:15 is the only KJV verse with 'stumble in their ways', pairing the two nouns the Book of Mormon actually pairs; Jeremiah 18:17 then supplies both the day-of formula in the first half of Mosiah 7:29 and the east wind at 7:31. A source that accounts for a passage is preferred to one that accounts for a phrase in it. Ezekiel 14:3 is excluded on the same evidence and is not given a separate entry.

The top-ranked candidate at the chapter's last verse, on a six-word run, and the sense is inverted. Daniel 11:16 is the king of the north who 'shall do according to his own will, and none shall stand before him' — the phrase names an unaccountable human tyrant, and Mosiah 7:33 uses it of God's freedom to deliver ('he will, according to his own will and pleasure, deliver you out of bondage'). 'His own will' occurs in five KJV verses, of which Hebrews 2:4 and James 1:18 do have God as the subject, and the second half of the Book of Mormon's phrase points at Ephesians 1:5's 'according to the good pleasure of his will' — a KJV singleton. But four words with a possessive pronoun are not enough to choose among those three, and the verse's substantive borrowings are at Acts 11:23 and 1 Chronicles 28:9. Recorded here so the register says why the highest-scoring machine candidate in the verse was not taken.

exclusions.sharedText: he spake many things unto them
exclusions.reason: The chapter's highest-scoring candidate (rarity 3.00, a six-word run) and worth nothing. 'He spake many things unto them' is the KJV's own narrative connective for a discourse being summarized rather than reported — Matthew 13:3 uses it to introduce the parables, and Mosiah 8:1 uses it to explain why Limhi's sermon is not given in full ('only a few of them have I written in this book'). Both writers needed the same sentence for the same reason, which is what makes the run long and what makes it empty. Covered in principle by the standing formulaic exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5; recorded here because six words at rarity 3.00 will tempt anyone reading the dossier top-down.

Esther 4:7 is Mordecai telling Hatach 'all that had happened unto him' and the sum Haman promised to pay; Mosiah 8:2 is Ammon rehearsing to a multitude all that had happened to their brethren. Five words of the most ordinary reporting formula in either book, and no other contact whatever. Recorded because it ranks second in the chapter.

A tempting candidate because Exodus 3:18's 'three days' journey into the wilderness' is a phrase this catalogue has had reason to check before, and because Mosiah 8:7 is about a deliverance from bondage and an appeal to brethren. But 'journey into the wilderness' occurs in five KJV verses — Exodus 3:18, Exodus 8:27, Deuteronomy 1:40, Deuteronomy 2:1 and 1 Kings 19:4 — and Mosiah 8:7 has neither the three days nor the sacrifice that make Exodus 3:18 distinctive. The forty-three men are looking for Zarahemla, not going out to worship. No source is identifiable and none is needed.

Mark 3:5 is Jesus 'being grieved for the hardness of their hearts' and Mosiah 8:7 is Limhi 'being grieved for the afflictions of my people'. The four shared words end exactly where the sense changes: Mark's grief is at his hearers' obduracy, Limhi's at his people's suffering. ADJUDICATING §4's window-closes-one-word-early case, and worth noting because the corpus does elsewhere borrow Mark 3:5's actual phrase — 'hardness of their hearts' — with its pronoun correct, so the presence of the first four words here is not evidence that the same borrowing is happening.

'The hosts of Israel' is a KJV singleton, which is normally the strongest evidence this catalogue has, and it is worthless here. 1 Kings 2:5 is David's deathbed instruction to Solomon about Joab, who murdered 'the two captains of the hosts of Israel'; the phrase is a military office, and its rarity is an accident of the KJV translating a plural where it elsewhere translates a singular ('the host of Israel'). Mosiah 8:8 uses it as a measure of population — a people 'as numerous as the hosts of Israel' — which is the Book of Mormon's own idiom and not a quotation. A singleton in the wrong sense is still the wrong sense.

Joel 2:17 is the priests' prayer that God not give his heritage to reproach, 'that the heathen should rule over them'. Mosiah 8:20's 'neither do they desire that she should rule over them' has wisdom as the ruler and the people as those who refuse to be ruled — the pronoun 'she' is the whole point of the clause and Joel has no antecedent for it. The subject of Joel's verb is a foreign occupier and the subject of the Book of Mormon's is personified Wisdom, so the two clauses agree in five words and in nothing else. The link at this verse is to Proverbs 1-9, where the feminine pronoun for wisdom belongs.

'Beasts of the forest' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 104:20 (where they creep forth at nightfall) and Micah 5:8 (where a lion among them is a figure for the remnant of Jacob). Neither has a flock, a shepherd, or a scattering, and neither is about devouring anything. The verse's real sources are Ezekiel 34:5, which supplies the sequence of shepherdlessness, scattering and beasts, and Isaiah 56:9, which supplies the forest — 'all ye beasts in the forest', with 'in' rather than 'of'. Micah 5:8 is excluded on the same evidence and is not given a separate entry.

The top candidate at verse 1, and a near miss that is worth recording precisely because a genuine Galatians 2 link sits three verses of the same passage away. Galatians 2:14 reads 'when I saw that they walked not uprightly'; Mosiah 9:1 reads 'when I saw that which was good among them'. Five words of the commonest narrative transition in first-person prose, and the two clauses go opposite ways — Paul saw something wrong and confronted it, Zeniff saw something good and spared it. The real borrowing from this chapter of Galatians is at 2:4, and it is at Mosiah 9:12.

'Journey into the wilderness' occurs in five KJV verses and none of them is identifiable here; Deuteronomy 2:1's is Israel turning back toward the Red Sea after the failure at Kadesh. The same phrase was proposed and excluded at Mosiah 8:7 on the same grounds. What Mosiah 9:3 does borrow from the Deuteronomic account of that episode is the going up to possess, which is catalogued at Numbers 13:30 with Deuteronomy 1:21.

'Till the ground' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 2:5 and Genesis 3:23, both in the Eden narrative, and the phrase is tempting because Mosiah 9:9 is a founding-a-settlement verse and Genesis 3:23 is the sentence that sends man out to work the earth. But nothing else in Mosiah 9:9 touches Genesis 3 — the verse is a seed list ending in multiplying and prospering — and 'till the ground' is simply the KJV's English for farming, with 'tiller of the ground' (Genesis 4:2) and 'tilled' elsewhere. Recorded because the Eden reading is available and this catalogue should say that it was considered and refused.

The chapter's highest-scoring candidate by a distance (rarity 3.00, a six-word run) and the clearest wrong-sense case in this batch. “wheat and of barley” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 41:8 — ten men begging Ishmael for their lives by offering him hidden stores of wheat, barley, oil and honey, in the massacre at Mizpah. Mosiah 9:9 is a list of what a colony planted: 'seeds of corn, and of wheat, and of barley, and with neas, and with sheum'. The shared run is a commodity list, the KJV's most mechanical kind of sentence, and the two lists diverge at the two crops nobody can identify. A KJV singleton in a commodity list is an artifact of the KJV's habit of repeating 'and of' before each item, not evidence of anything.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that after we had
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run, the longest in the chapter, and empty. 'And it came to pass that after we had' is the Book of Mormon's standard narrative hinge and the KJV's; Acts 21:1 is Paul's party sailing from Miletus to Coos. Covered by the standing formulaic exclusion filed at 1 Nephi 2:1 and recorded here only because ADJUDICATING §4's first trap is exactly this — the longest run in a chapter is almost always the emptiest, and this chapter proves it twice over, here and at Jeremiah 41:8.

exclusions.sharedText: delivered out of the hand of our enemies
exclusions.reason: Considered seriously and declined on a pronoun-and-number check of the kind ADJUDICATING §4 reserves for the adjudicator. Luke 1:74 — the Benedictus — reads 'delivered out of the hand of our enemies', singular hand; Mosiah 9:17 reads 'out of the hands of our enemies', plural, as does Judges 8:34 ('out of the hands of all their enemies') and several others. 'Out of the hands of' occurs in three KJV verses and 'out of the hand of' in dozens, so the plural does not isolate a source either. Zacharias's canticle would have made an attractive metalepsis here — deliverance from enemies in order to serve without fear — and there is no wording to hang it on.

exclusions.sharedText: the Lord that he would deliver
exclusions.reason: Ranked first in the verse at rarity 2.07 on a six-word run, and the sense is not merely different but hostile. Psalm 22:8 is the mockery of the crucified: 'He trusted on the LORD that he would deliver him: let him deliver him, seeing he delighted in him' — words the Gospels put in the mouths of the chief priests at Matthew 27:43. Mosiah 9:17 is a sincere prayer: 'did cry mightily to the Lord, that he would deliver us out of the hands of our enemies.' The run is an accident of the KJV's syntax for petition, which is the same whether the petition is meant or jeered. The verse's real sources are Psalm 71:16 and Jonah 3:8.

1 Samuel 25:33 is David blessing Abigail for keeping him 'from avenging myself with mine own hand'; Mosiah 9:19 is Zeniff saying he helped bury the dead 'with mine own hands'. Four words, and the resemblance is a coincidence of the reflexive: David's is a hand that did not kill, Zeniff's a pair of hands that buried. 'With mine own hands' is in no KJV verse at all in the plural. The verse's link is to Acts 8:2 and rests on 'great lamentation'.

'Weapons of war' occurs in nine KJV verses (Deuteronomy 1:41, Judges 18:11/16/17, 1 Samuel 21:8, 2 Samuel 1:27, Ecclesiastes 9:18, Jeremiah 21:4, Ezekiel 32:27) with no distinctive setting shared by any of them. It is the King James phrase for the thing, not a borrowing from a verse. A standing exclusion for the chapter: 10:1's 'weapons of war made, of every kind' points at no particular verse. The same applies to the connective matches the machine returned at 10:13 (1 Chronicles 10:14, Psalm 135:3, 'of the Lord therefore he'), 10:14 (Numbers 4:49, 'of the Lord they were') and 10:15 (Judges 14:9, 'that he had taken the'; Joshua 4:2, 'of the people out of'), all of which are covered by the standing formulaic exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5 and are listed here only so the chapter's candidate list can be reconciled.

exclusions.sharedText: his son began to reign in his stead
exclusions.reason: 'His son reigned in his stead' occurs in forty-one KJV verses — the Deuteronomistic succession formula, and unusable on its own as evidence of dependence on any one of them. The Book of Mormon's fused form, 'began to reign in his stead', is in no KJV verse at all: it welds 'began to reign' (1 Kings 15:25 and its kind) to 'in his stead'. The regnal frame IS being borrowed here, but the place to argue it is Mosiah 11:1, where the same succession formula is followed immediately by a regnal evaluation ('he did not walk in the ways of his father') that has a traceable KJV source. The link is filed there; this verse sends the reader to it.

The machine's top-ranked candidate for the verse (rarity 3.00, a six-word run) and the model of a match that is real as a string and empty as a link. Genesis 3:7 is the moment Adam and Eve know they are naked and cover themselves; the nakedness is discovered, shameful, and immediately clothed. Mosiah 10:8's Lamanites are naked on purpose — shaven-headed, stripped for battle, and girded with the one garment the sentence does name. The KJV clause is about acquiring shame; the Book of Mormon clause is about a military appearance calculated to terrify. Nothing in the Eden context construes anything in Zeniff's, and the real borrowing in this verse is four words further on (Matthew 3:4, 'a leathern girdle about').

Mark 14:48 is Gethsemane — 'Are ye come out, as against a thief, with swords and with staves to take me?' — and the shared run is the repeated preposition of a weapons list, which Mosiah 10:8 uses six times over. Isaiah 7:24's 'with arrows and with bows' (also proposed here) is the same artifact with the pair reversed. Both are the n-gram stream counting a list's punctuation. Listed rather than passed over because a reader who noticed that the Gethsemane arrest party and the Lamanite host are described with the same words might think something was there; nothing is.

Exodus 10:11 has Moses and Aaron 'driven out from Pharaoh's presence' during the plague negotiations; Mosiah 10:12 has the Lamanite tradition that its fathers 'were driven out of the land of Jerusalem'. The four words are the ordinary KJV passive for expulsion and neither passage lends anything to the other. Worth an entry only because Mosiah 10-12 does draw on Exodus repeatedly (34:4 at 10:16, 5:2 at 11:27, 20:2-4 at 12:34-36), which makes an accidental Exodus hit here more tempting than it would otherwise be.

Proposed at both 10:15 and 10:16, and it has a genuine rarity claim behind it: 'wroth with him' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Samuel 29:4 and 2 Kings 13:19. But the collocation is unmarked English — 'wroth' plus a personal object — and the Book of Mormon uses it four times in five verses (10:14 twice, 10:15, 10:16) as the refrain of the Lamanite grievance list, which is a house formula, not four borrowings. The KJV verse is the Philistine lords refusing David a place in their line of battle, and it construes nothing. This is the pilot's lesson about the n-gram stream in miniature: a low count is not the same as a distinctive phrase.

The trap the pilot named at 1 Nephi 3 with Samson's fetters of brass, and here it lands on the phrase the whole project is named after. 1 Kings 7:36's plates are the flat bronze panels of the ledges of Solomon's temple lavers, engraved with cherubim, lions and palm trees; 'the plates of brass' in Mosiah 10:16 are a written record. The KJV never uses 'plates' of a document. The match is four words of prepositional tissue attached to a homograph, and the verse's actual borrowing is the eight-word run from Exodus 34:4 that follows it.

exclusions.sharedText: slew them with a great slaughter
exclusions.reason: 'With a great slaughter' occurs in eight KJV verses (Joshua 10:10, Judges 15:8, 1 Samuel 6:19, 19:8, 23:5, 1 Kings 20:21, 2 Chronicles 13:17, 28:5), five of them with 'slew' or 'smote' in front of it. It is the King James Bible's standing idiom for a decisive victory and points at no source. Recorded because 2 Chronicles 13:17 in particular — Abijah's victory over a numerically superior Israel after a speech about which side has the Lord — is close enough in narrative shape to Mosiah 10:19-20 that a reader might take the phrase as a marker of it. The shape may well be borrowed; the words are not evidence that it was.

exclusions.sharedText: if he turn from his sin
exclusions.reason: A standing exclusion for the chapter. The machine's five-word runs here and at 11:7 (Daniel 5:10), 11:13 (2 Samuel 19:9), 11:15 (Deuteronomy 25:19), 11:19 (Deuteronomy 28:20), 11:20 (Jeremiah 14:10), 11:21 (Judges 2:14, 'into the hands of their enemies'), 11:26 (Job 42:7, 1 Samuel 29:4, Exodus 4:24) and 11:29 (1 Chronicles 10:13) are all connective tissue of the kind the pilot filed at 1 Nephi 1:5 and 2:1 — 'and it came to pass', 'into the hands of', 'the words which', 'that which was' — and none of them shares a content word that construes. Judges 2:14 deserves a sentence of its own: 'delivered them into the hands of their enemies' is the Judges cycle's own formula and Mosiah 11:21 is unmistakably working in that cycle, but the phrase occurs across the historical books too widely to identify Judges 2:14 in particular, and the verse's real source is the covenant sanction quoted at 11:22.

'Pure gold' occurs in thirty-nine KJV verses, twenty of them in the tabernacle and temple specifications of Exodus 25-37 and 1 Kings 6-10. The Book of Mormon is certainly writing Noah's temple works in the register of those chapters — 'fine work within the walls of the temple, of fine wood, and of copper, and of brass' — and the register is worth naming, but the phrase itself cannot pick out 1 Kings 6:21 or any other single verse. The high priests' gilded seat and the breastwork built so the priests can rest their arms while they lie are the Book of Mormon's own furniture; no KJV verse supplies them.

Considered and declined. Babel is the obvious typological reach for a proud king's very high tower, and 'whose top may reach' is a KJV singleton (Genesis 11:4), but the Book of Mormon shares not one word of it: Noah's tower is high so that he can 'stand upon the top thereof and overlook the land of Shilom', which is surveillance, not ascent to heaven, and the text never says he made himself a name. The verse's tower belongs instead to the vineyard figure assembled across 11:12-15 and linked at 11:15 (Isaiah 5:2 / Matthew 21:33), where the KJV puts a tower and a winepress in a vineyard and does so in only three verses. Filed so that a reader who expects Babel here is told why it is absent.

NOT a rejection — a placement note, filed because the phrase is one of the strongest KJV singletons in the chapter and its absence from the link list at 11:14 would look like an oversight. 'Riotous living' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 15:13, and 'with harlots' in three, one of which is Luke 15:30 in the same parable; Mosiah 11:14 has both in one sentence ('he spent his time in riotous living with his wives and his concubines; and so did also his priests spend their time with harlots'). See the link at 11:14 for the argument. This entry exists to record that the two Lucan phrases were tested together and that Proverbs 29:3's 'keepeth company with harlots spendeth his substance' — also a singleton, and the wisdom-literature source of the same idea — was weighed as the alternative and folded into the link rather than rejected.

The unit of fifty entered this catalogue at 1 Nephi 3:31 and 4:1, where Laman's 'he can command fifty' was argued against 2 Kings 1:9's captain of fifty with his fifty. Mosiah 11:19's boast — 'their fifty could stand against thousands of the Lamanites' — is the same arithmetic in a different mouth, but the KJV captain-of-fifty story contributes nothing to it: there is no captain, no hill, no fire. The number here is doing covenant arithmetic, not Elijah's, and the link is written to Leviticus 26:8 accordingly. Recorded so that a reader coming from 1 Nephi is not left to assume the earlier source was overlooked.

Tempting, and it fails the test. 'Who is Abinadi, that I and my people should be judged of him?' has the shape of the rejection of Moses — 'Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?' (Exodus 2:14), 'Who made thee a ruler and a judge over us?' (Acts 7:27) — which is a pairing this catalogue has already decided twice, at 1 Nephi 2:22 and 3:29, in the New Testament's favour on the single word 'ruler'. Here `mediation-check.py` reports no decisive divergence, and by eye there is nothing to decide: the Book of Mormon has neither 'prince' nor 'ruler' nor 'made thee', only the verb 'judged'. What the verse does reproduce is the second half of Pharaoh's refusal, 'who is the Lord, that' (Exodus 5:2), and that is where the link is filed. A reader who wants Moses's rejection here should note that the sentence reaches for Pharaoh instead — a later moment in the same story, and a worse one.

A standing exclusion for the chapter. 'The space of two years' is a date, and Acts 19:10's two years are Paul's stay in the school of Tyrannus. The same applies to the connective runs the machine returned at 12:1 (1 Chronicles 20:1, 'pass that after the'), 12:4 and 12:5 (Numbers 33:56, 'it shall come to pass that I'), 12:11 (Job 11:17, 'thou shalt be as the'), 12:30 (Ezekiel 47:22, 'and it shall come to pass that ye shall') and 12:32 (Luke 16:11): every one is the boilerplate covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5, and none shares a content word that construes. Psalm 8:8 at 12:2 deserves a half-sentence more, because it is nearly interesting: the KJV's birds are 'the fowl of the air' and the Book of Mormon's are 'the vultures of the air', so the machine has matched the one part of that clause that is not the Book of Mormon's own choice. The link at 12:2 goes to Jeremiah 15:3.

Abinadi's most memorable image has no King James source, and it is worth saying so plainly. 'The life of king Noah shall be valued even as a garment in a hot furnace' — repeated by the accusers at 12:10 as 'a garment in a furnace of fire' — puts together two KJV elements that the KJV never puts together. 'As a garment' occurs in four verses, of which Isaiah 50:9's 'they all shall wax old as a garment; the moth shall eat them up' is the only prophetic threat and the only KJV singleton in the group; 'furnace of fire' occurs in exactly two, Matthew 13:42 and 13:50, the parable's furnace of wailing and gnashing of teeth. Neither has a garment in a furnace. The image is the Book of Mormon's own, and it is a good one — a garment does not burn slowly, and the point is that Noah's life is worth what a garment is worth once it is in the fire. Recorded so that a reader who goes looking for the KJV verse behind it is told there is none.

exclusions.sharedText: the feet of him that bringeth good tidings that publisheth peace
exclusions.reason: Nahum 1:15 shares eleven continuous words with Mosiah 12:21 and scored 3.83 in the machine stream, second only to Isaiah 52:7 itself — and it is superseded, cleanly. 'Publisheth peace' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 52:7 and Nahum 1:15, and the second half of the Book of Mormon verse settles which: Nahum has no mountains at the front ('Behold upon the mountains' comes first, not 'How beautiful upon the mountains'), no 'good tidings of good', no 'publisheth salvation' and no 'saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth'. The quotation runs on for another seventeen words that only Isaiah has, and then continues through three more verses of Isaiah 52. Filed because a reader who checks the phrase alone will find two verses and should be told why one of them is not the answer.

The mediation test, and the Book of Mormon fails it in the Old Testament's favour — which is worth recording, because the pilot's principal result was sixteen places where it does the opposite. `mediation-check.py` returns three decisive points for Isaiah 52:7: the Book of Mormon has 'bringeth good tidings, that publisheth' where Romans has 'preach the gospel of', 'that bringeth good' where Romans has 'and bring glad', and nothing at all corresponding to Romans's 'as it is written'. It also keeps Isaiah's 'upon the mountains' and Isaiah's singular 'him', both of which Romans drops. This is a counter-example to the OT-via-NT pattern of 1 Nephi 22:20 and its kind, and it belongs in the register rather than only in the link's note so that the negative results are as countable as the positive ones.

exclusions.sharedText: for the Lord hath comforted his people
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run, and the wrong Isaiah. Isaiah 49:13 ('break forth into singing, O mountains: for the LORD hath comforted his people, and will have mercy upon his afflicted') shares the comfort clause with Isaiah 52:9 and nothing else. Mosiah 12:23 has 'Break forth into JOY; sing together ye waste places of Jerusalem', which is 52:9 exactly, including the KJV singleton 'waste places of Jerusalem', and it sits inside a four-verse continuous transcription of Isaiah 52:7-10. Note that 1 Nephi 21 is Isaiah 49 transcribed in full, so the machine's proposal is a hit on a passage this corpus really does quote elsewhere — which makes it the kind of candidate that would be easy to accept and is still wrong here.

exclusions.sharedText: all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God
exclusions.reason: Psalm 98:3 has 'all the ends of the earth HAVE SEEN the salvation of our God' — the same clause in the perfect tense, and Isaiah 52:10 has it in the future, which is the Book of Mormon's tense. The verse is superseded by the block it stands in: 12:24 also reproduces 'made bare his holy arm', a KJV singleton belonging to Isaiah 52:10 and absent from the psalm. Recorded because the psalm is a genuine parallel and because a six-word run in a verse that is otherwise verbatim Isaiah is exactly where an unwary apparatus would put a second source.

Close, and it does not land. Leviticus 27:34 — 'These are the commandments, which the LORD commanded Moses for the children of Israel in mount Sinai' — is the KJV's nearest sentence to Mosiah 12:33's 'the commandments which the Lord delivered unto Moses in the mount of Sinai', and Leviticus 26:46 says nearly the same thing. But the Book of Mormon's own form is 'in THE MOUNT OF Sinai', which occurs in no KJV verse at all; the King James Bible always says 'in mount Sinai' (seven verses) or 'unto mount Sinai'. The verse is introducing the Decalogue quotation that follows at 12:34-36, and the introduction is the Book of Mormon's phrasing, not a borrowing. Filed rather than passed over because a reader who expects the frame to be quoted as tightly as the commandments should be told that it is not.

exclusions.sharedText: brought them forth out of the land of Egypt out of the house of
exclusions.reason: An eleven-word run, and it is superseded by a twenty-one-word one. Jeremiah 34:13 has 'in the day that I brought them forth out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of BONDMEN'; Mosiah 12:34 has 'which have brought THEE out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of BONDAGE', which is Exodus 20:2 word for word from first syllable to last. The last noun decides it, and so does the pronoun. Worth an entry because Jeremiah 34 is thematically apt — it is the oracle about Judah reneging on the release of slaves, and the whole Abinadi cycle is heading into bondage — so the temptation to accept it as a composite is real. Compare also Deuteronomy 5:6 at the same verse, and Deuteronomy 5:8 at 12:36: the Decalogue's second recension is a live candidate throughout the block and loses on wording at every point where the two recensions differ (see the links at 12:34-36).

“He spake with power and authority from God.” The collocation occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 9:1 (the twelve given power and authority over devils) and Luke 20:20 (the governor's power and authority, to which the spies hope to deliver Jesus). Both are nouns of delegated jurisdiction, and Luke 20:20 is even a trial setting — but the Book of Mormon's phrase is adverbial, describing how a man spoke, and neither Lucan verse is about speech. The nearest thing in the KJV to what Mosiah 13:6 says is Luke 4:32, “his word was with power”, which shares only one word. Excluded as a resemblance in vocabulary without a verse behind it.

exclusions.sharedText: thou shalt not make ... any graven image, or any likeness
exclusions.reason: Ranked second by the n-gram stream on a run of eight. Deuteronomy 5:8 is excluded by a single decisive reading, returned by tools/mediation-check.py: Deuteronomy has “waters beneath the earth” where Exodus 20:4 and Mosiah 13:12 both read “water under the earth”. Exodus's “make unto thee” against Deuteronomy's “make thee” is a second point in the same direction. The link is at Exodus 20:4.

exclusions.sharedText: thou shalt not bow down thyself unto them, nor serve them
exclusions.reason: Ranked FIRST by the n-gram stream at this verse, above Exodus 20:5, and on a genuine ground: Mosiah 13:13 reads “bow down thyself unto them”, which is Deuteronomy 5:9's preposition, where Exodus 20:5 has “to them”. This is the only point in the entire Mosiah 13 Decalogue where Deuteronomy is the closer text, and it is one word against six decisive readings for Exodus elsewhere in the recital (13:12, 13:16, 13:17, 13:18, 13:20, 13:24). Excluded as the source, recorded here rather than suppressed, and argued in the note at the accepted Exodus 20:5 link — a Decalogue reproduced from a reading Bible or from memory will not be uniform, and the exception is worth more to a reader than a tidy claim.

exclusions.sharedText: visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation
exclusions.reason: A real eleven-word run, and worthless as evidence of a source. The visitation formula is one of the KJV's set pieces and recurs at Exodus 20:5, Exodus 34:7, Numbers 14:18, Deuteronomy 5:9 and Jeremiah 32:18. Numbers 14:18 is excluded because it has none of the surrounding commandment — no bowing down, no jealous God, no “of them that hate me” — and because Mosiah 13:13 is the middle of a continuous recital of Exodus 20.

exclusions.sharedText: and shewing mercy unto thousands of them that love me, and keep my commandments
exclusions.reason: Tied with Exodus 20:6 by the n-gram stream, necessarily: the two verses are word-for-word identical in the KJV and the verse cannot decide its own mediation. Assigned to Exodus by the recital it belongs to, which is decisively Exodus's at six other verses. Recorded so that the register does not appear to have decided something it could not.

exclusions.sharedText: thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain
exclusions.reason: The longest single run in the chapter, twenty-seven words, and it matches Deuteronomy 5:11 exactly as well as Exodus 20:7 — the two differ only in punctuation. Undecidable on internal evidence and assigned to Exodus with the rest of the recital. The register entry exists because a reader checking this verse alone would be entitled to think the question open; it is, and the answer comes from the six verses around it.

exclusions.sharedText: six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work
exclusions.reason: Looks identical to Exodus 20:9 and is not. Deuteronomy 5:13 reads “Six days thou shalt labour”; Exodus 20:9 and Mosiah 13:17 read “Six days shalt thou labour”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse. A one-word inversion, invisible to a reader and decisive on a count — and it was missed on this catalogue's first pass through the verse, which is the argument for running tools/kjv-rarity.py on wording that looks too ordinary to check.

exclusions.sharedText: nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates
exclusions.reason: Excluded by two decisive readings from tools/mediation-check.py. Deuteronomy 5:14 inserts “nor thine ox, nor thine ass, nor any of” before the cattle and appends “that thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou”; Mosiah 13:18 has neither, and follows Exodus 20:10's shorter household list exactly. The link is at Exodus 20:10.

exclusions.sharedText: and the sea, and all that in them is
exclusions.reason: A thirteen-word run and a good example of ADJUDICATING §4's trap. Acts 4:24 is the apostles' prayer after the arrest of Peter and John and its creation formula is doxological, not legislative; it has no sabbath, no six days, no blessing and no hallowing. The shared string is the KJV's standard merism for the created order. Mosiah 13:19 is the fourth commandment's rationale, verbatim from Exodus 20:11.

exclusions.sharedText: for in six days the Lord made heaven and earth
exclusions.reason: Shares the creation clause and nothing else. Exodus 31:17 continues “and on the seventh day he rested, and was refreshed”, which Mosiah 13:19 does not have — indeed 13:19's one substantive departure from its source is the omission of Exodus 20:11's rest clause. The verse that supplies the blessing and hallowing of the sabbath, which is where Mosiah 13:19 ends, is Exodus 20:11 alone.

exclusions.sharedText: honour thy father and thy mother
exclusions.reason: Excluded by two decisive readings. Deuteronomy 5:16 inserts “as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee” after the commandment and expands the promise to “thy days may be prolonged, and that it may go well with thee”; Mosiah 13:20 has neither and reads “long upon the land”, which is Exodus 20:12's.

exclusions.sharedText: thou shalt not commit adultery, thou shalt not steal
