exclusions.reason: Ranked first by the n-gram stream on a nine-word run, and excluded on sequence. Matthew 19:18 gives the commandment Mosiah 13:21 renders “Thou shalt not kill” as “Thou shalt do no murder”, which is Matthew's peculiar wording and is not in the Book of Mormon; and Matthew's list is a Gospel dialogue, not a recital. The run is long only because Mosiah's 1879 versification happened to put Exodus 20:14 and 20:15 in one verse. The links are at Exodus 20:14-15.

exclusions.sharedText: thou shalt not commit adultery, thou shalt not steal
exclusions.reason: Excluded on order. Romans 13:9 runs adultery, kill, steal; Mosiah 13:21-22 runs kill, adultery, steal, which is Exodus 20:13-15's order and not Paul's. Romans also drops the commandments into an argument about love of neighbour and abbreviates the tenth to “Thou shalt not covet”, where Mosiah 13:24 gives Exodus 20:17 entire. A long shared string across a verse boundary that both texts inherit from the same source is not evidence that one depends on the other.

exclusions.sharedText: thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour
exclusions.reason: Deuteronomy 5:20 reads “vain witness” where Exodus 20:16 and Mosiah 13:23 read “false witness”. A single word, and the mediation tool does not count it decisive because the rest of the verse is identical; it is nevertheless a small point in Exodus's favour and is recorded here for the reader who checks this verse on its own.

exclusions.sharedText: thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house
exclusions.reason: The tenth commandment is where the two versions of the Decalogue differ most, and Mosiah 13:24 sides with Exodus at every point: house before wife (Deuteronomy reverses them), no second imperative “Neither shalt thou desire”, no “his field”, and “nor” three times where Deuteronomy has “or”. tools/mediation-check.py returns three decisive readings, the largest count in the chapter.

exclusions.sharedText: and now I say unto you
exclusions.reason: Six words of pure connective tissue, and one of the Book of Mormon's commonest sentence openings. Gamaliel's counsel to leave the apostles alone has no contact with Abinadi's account of why the law was given. Covered in principle by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

Ranked by the n-gram stream on a five-word run, and a genuine trap because this catalogue has already accepted the other half of the same Johannine saying: 1 Nephi 4:13 borrows John 11:50's calculus — one man should die, and the whole nation perish not — to justify the killing of Laban, and John 18:14 is John repeating it. But “expedient” is doing an entirely different job in Mosiah 13. Abinadi uses it three times in three verses (13:27, 13:28, 13:29) in its legal-temporal sense, of what a law it is currently advisable to keep, with no calculus of lives anywhere in view. The word is the same and the argument is unrelated; excluded as wrong-sense, with the register pointing a reader to 1 Nephi 4:13 for where the saying does bear.

exclusions.sharedText: because of the hardness of ... hearts
exclusions.reason: The pronoun decides it. Matthew 19:8 and Mark 10:5 read “the hardness of your hearts”, spoken by Jesus to his hearers; Mark 3:5 reads “the hardness of their hearts”, a narrator's description of a third party, and occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Abinadi is describing the fathers at Sinai, not the priests in front of him, so the third-person form is the grammatically correct one and the Book of Mormon has it. ADJUDICATING §4 flags this pair specifically because tools/mediation-check.py ignores single common words and cannot catch it.

“The resurrection of the dead” occurs in eleven KJV verses, five of them in 1 Corinthians 15, and a reader looking for a source at Mosiah 13:35 will reach for Paul. Nothing else in the verse is Pauline: the sentence's other half is Isaiah 53:7's “oppressed and afflicted”, a KJV singleton, and what follows in chapter 14 is Isaiah 53 entire. The phrase is standard New Testament doctrinal vocabulary and points at no verse in particular.

exclusions.sharedText: God himself shall come down among the children of men
exclusions.reason: The same sentence Abinadi has already used at 13:34, where it is argued as a borrowing from Philippians 2:7 (“took upon him the form of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse). Mosiah 15:1 is the resumption of the same speech two chapters later and is the speaker repeating his own thesis, not a fresh borrowing; ADJUDICATING §4 gives the repeat to recurrenceRefs, which is where it is recorded. 15:1 drops the Pauline half — there is no “form of man” here — and keeps only the descent, which is the part that has become Abinadi's own formula.

exclusions.sharedText: the flesh to the ... will of
exclusions.reason: A four-word run across a clause boundary in both texts, and the words are function words. 1 Peter 4:2 is about no longer living to the lusts of men; Mosiah 15:2 is about the incarnate Son's will. Nothing but “the flesh” and “the will of” is shared, and both are unavoidable in any sentence about either subject. The verse's real source is Luke 1:35, with John 5:30 behind “the will of the Father”; see the accepted link.

“Christ the power of God” is a title; “conceived by the power of God” is a causal claim about a birth. The phrase occurs in more than a dozen KJV verses and identifies no source. The verse Mosiah 15:3 is actually working from is Luke 1:35, the KJV's one verse deriving the title Son of God from a conception by divine power, whose “the power of the Highest” is the phrase Mosiah 15:3 varies.

A reader will reach for Hebrews 4:15 at “suffereth temptation, and yieldeth not to the temptation”, and the doctrine is the same — one tempted in all points, yet without sin. But nothing is reproduced: Hebrews has “was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin”, with no “suffer” and no “yield”. Recorded rather than accepted because the resemblance is real and entirely conceptual. The verse's verbal borrowing is at its other end, Matthew 20:19's mocking and scourging; see the accepted link.

exclusions.sharedText: and now I say unto you
exclusions.reason: Connective boilerplate, proposed by the n-gram stream at 15:10 and again at 15:28. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5; Gamaliel's counsel has no contact with either verse.

A genuine mediation candidate, tested and not decided. “Who shall declare his generation” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 53:8 and Acts 8:33, and Acts is the more suggestive of the two: Philip reads Isaiah 53 aloud to a man who asks of whom the prophet speaks, which is the situation of Mosiah 15:10 almost exactly. But tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive point, because Mosiah 15:10 quotes only the four words the two verses share and none of the clauses where they differ. Excluded as the source in favour of Isaiah 53:8 by way of Mosiah 14:8, which the chapter's other two departures (15:6, 15:12) establish as the route; the Acts resonance is recorded in the accepted link's significance field, where it belongs.

exclusions.sharedText: all the Holy Prophets ... ever since the world began
exclusions.reason: The Lucan formula, already adjudicated at Mosiah 13:33 where it enters Abinadi's speech alongside Acts 3:22's Moses. 15:13 is the same speaker reusing his own phrase twenty verses later, within one book and one sitting, which ADJUDICATING §4 assigns to recurrenceRefs rather than to a second link. The recurrence is recorded on the 13:33 row. Note that 15:13's application is new — there the prophets warrant a claim about the Messiah, here they are the Messiah's seed — but the wording is not.
Five words of narrative connective. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

exclusions.sharedText: the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace
exclusions.reason: Ranked second by the n-gram stream on a nine-word run, and a real candidate: Nahum 1:15 is the Old Testament's double of Isaiah 52:7 and shares its central clause word for word. Excluded by one decisive reading — Nahum begins “Behold upon the mountains the feet of him”, where Isaiah 52:7 and every one of Mosiah 15:15-18 begins “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet”. Nahum also lacks “that publisheth salvation” and “Thy God reigneth”, both of which Mosiah 15:14 has.

exclusions.sharedText: how beautiful are the feet of them that preach
exclusions.reason: Not proposed by any machine stream and the first place a reader would look, since Romans 10:15 is the New Testament's quotation of Isaiah 52:7 and this catalogue's usual finding at a doubly-attested text is that the Book of Mormon has the New Testament's form (1 Nephi 22:20, 1 Nephi 4:13). Here it does not. tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points for Isaiah: Romans's introductory clause “And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written” is absent, and Romans reads “bring glad tidings of good things” where Isaiah and Mosiah read “bringeth good tidings”. Romans also drops “upon the mountains”, which all five of Mosiah 15:14-18 keep, and substitutes “them that preach the gospel of peace” for Isaiah's participles. A clean direct-OT result, and worth the register entry precisely because the expected answer was the other one.

The KJV singleton is adjudicated at 15:24, where the phrase first appears in its full form. 15:26 is the negative of the same clause — “these are they that have no part in the first resurrection” — two verses later in one speech, and is recorded in the accepted link's recurrenceRefs.

exclusions.sharedText: and now I say unto you
exclusions.reason: Connective boilerplate; see the entry at 15:10 and the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5. The verse's actual source is Revelation 14:6, whose four-term formula for the nations occurs in exactly one KJV verse.

Five words, and the sense is opposed in the way that matters: 2 Chronicles 5:13 is temple singers with trumpets and cymbals at the dedication, Mosiah 15:29 is watchmen on a wall seeing the Lord bring again Zion. The shared string is the KJV's ordinary phrase for making a loud noise. The verse is a transcription of Isaiah 52:8, whose “see eye to eye” and “bring again Zion” are each KJV singletons.

Worth more than the usual note, because Mosiah 15:29 departs from its source at exactly this point. Isaiah 52:8, which the verse otherwise reproduces for twenty-two words, reads “Thy watchmen shall lift up the voice”; Mosiah reads “their voice”, which is Isaiah 24:14's and Isaiah 42:11's form. The candidate is nevertheless excluded: Isaiah 24:14 has no watchmen, no Zion and no seeing eye to eye, and shares nothing else with the verse. The right description is that the Book of Mormon has substituted the commoner KJV idiom for the rarer one inside a transcription — the same kind of small regularization as “a sheep before the shearer” for “her shearers” at 15:6.

exclusions.sharedText: for the Lord hath comforted his people
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run, and Isaiah 49:13 genuinely contains it — the clause is one Isaiah uses twice. But Mosiah 15:30 reproduces the whole of Isaiah 52:9, twenty-two words with no departure at all, including “ye waste places of Jerusalem”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “he hath redeemed Jerusalem”, which Isaiah 49:13 does not have. A shared clause inside a verbatim transcription of another verse is not a candidate.

The New Testament's approach to the same sentence, quoted from Isaiah 40:5 rather than 52:10, and the other mediation candidate a reader might reach for. Luke 3:6 reads “all flesh shall see the salvation of God” — no arm, no nations, no ends of the earth, and “God” without the possessive. Mosiah 15:31 has Isaiah 52:10's twenty-nine words entire. Excluded, and recorded alongside the Romans 10:15 entry at 15:18: this chapter twice had a New Testament form of an Isaiah verse available and twice took the Old Testament one.

exclusions.sharedText: all the ends of the earth ... the salvation of our God
exclusions.reason: “The salvation of our God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and Psalm 98:3 is the other. It is excluded on tense and on the missing first half: the psalm reads “all the ends of the earth have seen”, where Isaiah 52:10 and Mosiah 15:31 read “shall see”, and the psalm has nothing corresponding to “The Lord hath made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations”, which is a KJV singleton and is the first two-thirds of Mosiah 15:31.

exclusions.sharedText: shall see the salvation of the Lord
exclusions.reason: Hardy's apparatus cross-references Isaiah 52:8 and 52:10 at this verse, and both references are sound as chapter-level pointers: Abinadi has just transcribed Isaiah 52:8-10 as Mosiah 15:29-31, and 16:1 restates it. The verbal link belongs elsewhere in both cases. Isaiah 52:10's own wording is at Mosiah 15:31, verbatim for twenty-nine words, and that is where the link sits. What 16:1 actually has is “all shall see the salvation of the Lord” — and Isaiah 52:10 reads “the salvation of our God”, not “of the Lord”. The phrase Mosiah 16:1 uses occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 14:13 and 2 Chronicles 20:17, and the catalogue puts the link there (CONVENTIONS §6a: our reading governs, and the link goes where the wording is). The register sends a reader from 16:1 to Mosiah 15:31 for Hardy's Isaiah and to the Exodus 14:13 row for the wording.

“See eye to eye” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and the borrowing is real, but it was adjudicated twelve verses earlier: Mosiah 15:29 transcribes Isaiah 52:8 whole. 16:1 is the same speaker reusing a phrase he has just recited, within one speech, which ADJUDICATING §4 assigns to recurrenceRefs. It is recorded on the accepted link at 16:1, where the phrase now sits inside a compound built from Revelation 14:6 and Romans 14:11.
Four words of ordinary prophetic connective, used twice in this chapter and constantly in the corpus. No contact with John 16:4's subject.

A five-word narrative connective. John 18:1 is Jesus crossing the Cedron to Gethsemane; Mosiah 16:1 is Abinadi resuming after a pause. The Book of Mormon uses “after … had spoken these words” dozens of times as a paragraph marker. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

A real five-word run, and worth an entry because the gesture looks meaningful. It is not distinctive: the KJV has men and God stretching forth a hand throughout, and Matthew 12:49's gesture is toward the disciples to identify them as his family, which has no counterpart at Mosiah 16:1. The gesture there is a peroration's, and the verse's borrowings are in what he says, not what he does.

exclusions.sharedText: of the Lord, therefore the Lord
exclusions.reason: Six words that are three formulas end to end. 1 Kings 13:26 is the disobedient prophet killed by a lion; Mosiah 16:2 is the wicked not redeemed. The run exists because both sentences name the Lord twice in quick succession.

Four function words. Matthew 24:14's clause is “and then shall the end come”, a statement about the completion of the gospel's preaching; Mosiah 16:2's is “and then shall the wicked be cast out”. The shared string carries nothing.

Four words, and “cause” means different things in the two verses — Proverbs 31:8 has a legal cause to be pleaded, Mosiah 16:3 has a cause in the sense of an origin. The verse's sources are Revelation 12:9, 2 Corinthians 11:3, James 3:15 and Genesis 3:5; see the four accepted links.

A tempting four-word run, because Matthew 1:21 is the naming of Jesus — “he shall save his people from their sins” — and Mosiah 16:4 reads “God redeemed his people from their lost and fallen state”. The shared words are a possessive, a preposition and a possessive; the verbs differ (save/redeem) and so do the objects (sins / a lost and fallen state), and the Book of Mormon's phrase “lost and fallen state” has no KJV source at all. Excluded as a resemblance of syntax with no shared content word.

The same five-word run and the same yoke. Ezekiel 34:27 is the restoration of Israel to safety in their land; the bands broken are their servitude's. See the entry at Leviticus 26:13 for the full reason and for what “the bands of death” actually is.

The best exclusion in this chapter, because the string is a genuine five-word run and the KJV means something else by it every time. “Bands” in the King James Old Testament are the bands of a yoke — Leviticus 26:13's “I have broken the bands of your yoke, and made you go upright”, Ezekiel 34:27's identical phrase, Psalm 2:3's “let us break their bands asunder”. The KJV never speaks of the bands of death. That phrase is the Book of Mormon's own, coined in this speech (Mosiah 15:8, 15:9, 15:23, 16:7) and standard in the corpus thereafter, and it is one of the places where the text is manifestly composing rather than borrowing. The verse's actual New Testament source is 1 Corinthians 15:55, whose grave and victory and death and sting Mosiah 16:7 keeps in the KJV's own pairings; see the accepted link.
Four function words. Job 12:14's clause is “there can be no opening”, of a man God has shut up; Mosiah 16:9's is “there can be no more death”, whose source is the KJV singleton at Revelation 21:4.

Four words of a disjunctive formula. Ben-hadad's servants are guessing whether the Samaritans came out for peace or war. The construction at Mosiah 16:10 is Ecclesiastes 12:14's — “whether it be good, or whether it be evil”, which occurs in exactly two KJV verses and only there of a judgment — and it is recorded as a composite on the accepted Revelation 20:12 link.

Five words, of which the operative one is “brought”. Ezekiel 21:7's idiom is “it shall be brought to pass”; Mosiah 16:10's is “shall be brought to stand before the bar of God”, a different construction with a different object. The verse's sources are 1 Corinthians 15:53 and Revelation 20:12.

Four words spanning a clause boundary in both texts. Ezekiel is showing Israel the pattern of the house that they may be ashamed; Mosiah 16:12 is describing men warned of their iniquities who would not depart from them.
Four words of connective phrasing. Hosea's idols are made according to the craftsmen's own understanding; Mosiah's wicked go according to their own carnal wills. No content word is shared.

Ranked first by the n-gram stream and verbally the nearest thing in the KJV: Judges 2:17 reads “and yet they would not hearken unto their judges”, and Mosiah 16:12 reads “and yet they would not depart from them”. The exclusion is made with the reason stated openly, because it is a judgment a reader may fairly reverse. The formula “and ye/they would not” occurs in five KJV verses and identifies no source on its own; what the catalogue has proposed instead is a scene rather than a string — arms extended twice and twice refused, which is Matthew 23:37's lament over Jerusalem and nowhere else in the Bible. If the scene is declined, Judges 2:17 does not become the source; the verse simply has none, since its distinctive phrase, “the arms of mercy”, is in no KJV verse. See the whyNot on the accepted link.

Four words, and the sense is inverted. Psalm 37:17's arms are the wicked's and they are broken; Mosiah 16:12's are mercy's and they are extended. The collocation “arms of mercy” occurs in no KJV verse and is one of the Book of Mormon's own coinages.

exclusions.sharedText: a shadow of those things which are to come
exclusions.reason: The KJV singleton “shadow of things to come” was adjudicated at Mosiah 13:10, where Abinadi first applies it — to his own execution — and it recurs at 13:31 and here. 16:14 is the same speaker's closing instruction to the priests, “if ye teach the law of Moses, also teach that it is a shadow of those things which are to come”, and it is his own formula by now rather than a fresh borrowing. Recorded on the 13:10 row's recurrenceRefs. Note that 16:14 is the one place he attaches the shadow to the law itself rather than to an event, which is Colossians 2:17's own referent — so the chapter ends by putting the borrowed phrase back where Paul had it.
Four function words. Mark 6:15 is the crowd guessing at Jesus's identity. Nothing is shared but the construction.

The machine's top candidate for the verse, and a genuine KJV singleton: 'come out from among them' stands in 2 Corinthians 6:17 and nowhere else. The sense is opposed at every point. Paul's is an imperative to the faithful to separate themselves voluntarily from the unclean — 'come out ... and be ye separate ... and I will receive you' — and the movement is the believer's own. Mosiah 17:3 is passive and forced: 'the king ... caused that Alma should be cast out from among them, and sent his servants after him, that they might slay him.' What Paul offers as a blessing to be chosen, Noah imposes as a sentence of exile with assassins behind it. The Book of Mormon's verb is 'cast out', which is not Paul's, and the four shared words are the only contact. A careful reader could be tempted, because Alma's expulsion does in fact begin a separated church three verses of narrative later — but that is the reader's typology, not the text's borrowing, and accepting it would put a Pauline blessing in a murder order's mouth.

'Cast him into prison' is the KJV's ordinary English for imprisonment and Matthew 18:30 is the unforgiving servant's parable, which has nothing in common with Abinadi's arrest beyond the act. The phrase does carry a faint pull toward Revelation 2:10 — 'the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried ... be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life' — which would sit well with a martyr who says at 17:10 that he 'will suffer even until death'. That reading is declined here rather than catalogued: 'unto death' is not 'until death', the intervening five verses are trial diction and not apocalyptic, and the case for the chapter's New Testament debts rests on the singletons at 17:1, 17:7, 17:11 and 17:19, which do not need this one. Recorded so that a reader who thinks of Revelation 2:10 can see it was considered.

exclusions.sharedText: saith unto him, I say unto you
exclusions.reason: Both the 1830 'Abinadi saith unto him' and the following 'I say unto you' are speech formulae the Book of Mormon uses hundreds of times, and the gospels thousands. The 1830 present tense 'saith' — changed to 'said' in 1920, and flagged as a variant here — is a real observation about the first edition's KJV register and is worth noting on that account, but it points at the KJV's narrative style in general and not at Matthew 18:22 or Luke 7:9 in particular. No exclusion is needed for the dozens of other verses in this chapter that share such formulae; this one is written because the variant makes it look more significant than it is.

exclusions.sharedText: and it will come to pass
exclusions.reason: The chapter's highest-scoring candidate by n-gram rarity (2.50) and worthless, which is the pilot's finding about the stream restated (CONVENTIONS §9). 'And it will come to pass' is rare in the KJV only because the KJV prefers 'shall'; it is not rare as English and it is pure connective tissue. 2 Samuel 17:9 is Hushai's counsel about Absalom hiding in a pit and shares no content word with a threat of disease for iniquity. Logged rather than passed over in silence because the score is high enough that an adjudicator working down a ranked list would stop at it.

'On every hand' is a KJV singleton and it is worth recording why it cannot be the source. Its one occurrence is anatomical: the Philistine giant of Gath 'had on every hand six fingers, and on every foot six toes'. Mosiah 17:17's 'ye shall be smitten on every hand' uses 'hand' in the wholly unrelated adverbial sense of side or direction. This is the pilot's rare-word-wrong-sense trap exactly (ADJUDICATING §4, Samson's brass fetters), and the singleton count is what makes it dangerous rather than what makes it evidence. The genuine KJV background for the verse is the flock-and-beasts language of the scattering oracles — Ezekiel 34:5, 'they were scattered, because there is no shepherd: and they became meat to all the beasts of the field' — which the Book of Mormon reaches by sense and not by any phrase long enough to catalogue.

exclusions.sharedText: and never able to come to the knowledge of the
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and the chapter's second-highest n-gram score, drawn purely by 'come to the knowledge of the' — 2 Timothy 3:7's silly women 'ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth', against Mosiah's 'that it might not come to the knowledge of the king'. The object is the whole sentence: Paul's is truth and Alma's is a hostile monarch, and 'come to the knowledge of' is a Book of Mormon formula that appears in the same chapter twice more (18:30, 18:31) with three different objects. Logged because the run is long enough to look like evidence and the same candidate returns at 18:31.

exclusions.sharedText: in the day time from the
exclusions.reason: Six words shared, and the sense is inverted at the preposition. Isaiah 4:6's tabernacle is 'for a shadow in the day time from the heat' — shelter from the sun, in a vision of Zion covered by cloud and fire; Mosiah 18:5's Alma 'did hide himself in the day-time, from the searches of the king' — concealment from a manhunt. What Isaiah's day-time refuge protects against is weather and what Alma's protects against is soldiers, and the two texts share the string only because both need to name a time of day and a thing to be sheltered from. Worth an entry because Isaiah 4:5-6's thicket-and-covering imagery is thematically close enough that a reader running on typology could accept it, and the 1830 hyphenation 'day-time' makes the match look more deliberate than it is.

Pure narrative connective; the five words carry no content and the two verses have nothing else in common. Passed over here rather than argued because the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1 covers its kind, and recorded only because the score (2.00) put it at the head of the verse's candidate list. The real KJV background of Mosiah 18:11 — 'they clapped their hands for joy' — is the acclamation formula of 2 Kings 11:12 and Psalm 47:1, which the machine did not propose and which is too widely distributed to catalogue.

Luke 20:20's spies watch Jesus so as to 'deliver him unto the power and authority of the governor', and the five-word run is real. It is superseded: the verse's borrowing is Acts 2:47's 'added to the church', a KJV singleton reproduced four words deep and carrying the whole clause, and 'the power and authority of God' is the Book of Mormon's own standing formula for priesthood rather than a borrowing from Luke's Roman jurisdiction. The link is at Acts 2:47. Recorded because the Lukan trial vocabulary is genuinely thick in these two chapters (Luke 23:2 at Mosiah 17:12, Luke 23:5 at Mosiah 18:33), which makes a third Lukan candidate here more tempting than it deserves — and that thickness is exactly the condition under which a false positive slips through.

Revelation 14:6's angel with the everlasting gospel 'to preach unto them that dwell on the earth' is a verse the Latter-day Saint tradition has strong reasons to look for, which is precisely why it should not be accepted on four words of connective tissue. The verse's real source is in the same clause and is not in doubt: 'the things pertaining to the kingdom of God' is an eight-word KJV singleton from Acts 1:3. The link is there.

exclusions.sharedText: that they should gather themselves together
exclusions.reason: A six-word run at rarity 3.00, the highest score in the second half of the chapter, and it will not bear a link. 'Gather themselves together' stands in the KJV for armies, mourners, locusts and returning exiles alike; Ezra 10:7's proclamation summons the children of the captivity to Jerusalem to put away foreign wives, which has nothing to do with a weekly assembly for worship. The genuine background of Mosiah 18:25 is the sabbath-assembly language of Leviticus 23:3 ('an holy convocation') and the apostolic 'first day of the week' of Acts 20:7 and 1 Corinthians 16:2 — neither of which shares a phrase with the verse, which is why 18:25 gets no link at all despite being the chapter's most institutionally significant sentence.

The four words are pure narrative connective and would ordinarily be passed over in silence. This entry exists because the verse behind them is not neutral: Judges 1:6 is Adonibezek fleeing and being caught, and Judges 1:7 — his 'as I have done, so God hath requited me' — is catalogued as an echo at Mosiah 17:15, where Abinadi pronounces the same retributive formula over his judges. So a reader could reasonably propose that Mosiah 19:6's pursuit of the fleeing king completes an Adonibezek pattern begun two chapters earlier. It is declined. The pursuit here is verbally indistinguishable from any other in the KJV, and the chapter's tyrant-at-the-tower material has a much better source in Judges 9 (see the link at Mosiah 19:5), where the tower, the fire and the name Gideon all sit together. Recorded so that the Adonibezek reading is visible as considered rather than missed.

'Charmed' is a KJV singleton and it is a trap. Its one occurrence is Jeremiah 8:17's cockatrices 'which will not be charmed' — snake-charming, the technical sense, in an oracle of judgment. Mosiah 19:14's 'they were charmed with the beauty of their women' is the modern figurative sense of being enchanted by an attractive person, which the King James Bible does not have anywhere. This is the strongest available illustration in these three chapters of why a rarity count is evidence only after the sense has been checked: the count could not be better and the link could not be worse. The machine did not propose it, which is worth recording too — the trap here is one a human running kjv-rarity.py down a wordlist would walk into and the n-gram stream would not.

Nehemiah 9:24's Israel possessing Canaan against Mosiah 19:15's Nephites being granted their land back under tribute — the shared string is four words of connective around the word 'land', and the situations are opposed at the point that matters: Nehemiah's is conquest, Mosiah's is capitulation. The KJV material actually behind Mosiah 19:15 is the tribute vocabulary of 2 Kings 17:3-4 and 23:33-35, where a vassal king pays a conqueror a fixed levy and a puppet is installed — which is the whole of Limhi's situation at 19:26 — but it shares no phrase with the verse and is therefore recorded here rather than catalogued as a link.

Five words of legal boilerplate. Judges 20:13's demand that Gibeah surrender the children of Belial has a superficial pull, since Mosiah 19:21's crowd is likewise demanding the surrender of a guilty party and is likewise refused by their flight — but 'put them to death' is among the KJV's commonest formulae and the two situations share nothing else. Logged rather than passed over because the Judges background of this chapter is genuinely thick (Judges 9 at 19:5 and 19:20), and a further Judges candidate arriving in that neighbourhood is more tempting than its evidence warrants.

exclusions.sharedText: told him of all that had happened
exclusions.reason: The chapter's joint-highest machine score (2.00) and a five-word run: Esther 4:7's 'And Mordecai told him of all that had happened unto him' against Mosiah 19:22's 'the men of Gideon told them of all that had happened to their wives and their children'. It is reported speech, the commonest narrative filler in either book. The entry matters because Esther 4:16 IS accepted twelve verses earlier at Mosiah 19:12, and this candidate would make that row look like part of a sustained Esther borrowing when it is not: 19:12's case rests on a formula of choice with no verbal contact at all, and stacking a boilerplate match from the same chapter of Esther onto it would be exactly the false corroboration CONVENTIONS §0 exists to prevent. The two are independent and the second is rejected.

The machine's top proposal for the verse, on a four-word run. 2 Chronicles 20:22 is Jehoshaphat's singers going out before the army — 'when they began to sing and to praise, the LORD set ambushments' — and the run breaks at the word that matters, since the Book of Mormon's next verb is 'dance' and the KJV's is 'praise'. The verse's real background is Judges 21:21, where 'to dance' is used absolutely of a festival at which women are seized, one of only two KJV verses with the infinitive in that form; the link is filed at 20:1. Worth registering rather than passing over because the Chronicles verse does contain an ambush laid against people who are singing, which is exactly this chapter's situation and exactly what would tempt a reader who had not checked the fifth word.

'Go up to the land of' is the KJV's ordinary idiom of invasion and return and is spread across Genesis, Numbers, Joshua, Kings and the prophets; the five-word run is a function of the construction, not of Ezekiel. Nothing distinctive of Ezekiel 38 — the unwalled villages, Gog, the spoil — is present at Mosiah 20:7, which reports only that the Lamanite army went up to the land of Nephi. Registered because the rarity score put it first for the verse and because Gog's assembly against a people 'dwelling safely' is close enough in outline to catch a careless eye.

'They fought like lions for their prey' invites a lion-and-prey source, and the KJV has two good ones: Isaiah 5:29, where an invading army's roaring is 'like a lion … they shall roar, and lay hold of the prey, and shall carry it away safe', which is a battle simile of exactly this kind; and Psalm 17:12, 'like as a lion that is greedy of his prey, and as it were a young lion lurking in secret places', which is additionally tempting because 'secret places' has just appeared at 20:5. Neither is taken. There is no run of words: the Book of Mormon has 'like lions for their prey' and neither KJV verse has that collocation, 'his prey' occurring in four verses and 'like a lion' in eight, with no overlap between the two lists at any phrase this verse uses. The lion-for-prey simile is common property of Hebrew and English alike, and the verse's companion figure, 'like dragons did they fight', has no KJV warrant at all — the KJV's dragons are desert scavengers and sea monsters, never a model of courage — which is itself evidence that the similes here are the writer's own and not quarried.

exclusions.sharedText: fight ... your wives ... your sons and your daughters
exclusions.reason: A close call, registered because it was nearly written as a link. Nehemiah 4:14 is the KJV's one battle-exhortation that names the household as the thing being fought for — 'fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses' — and its situation matches Mosiah 20:11 unusually well: defenders who are outnumbered, taken by surprise, and told they will be delivered because the fight is for their own. Esther 9:16's 'stood for their lives', a KJV singleton, sits equally close to 'they fought for their lives'. It is declined because there is no run: Nehemiah has 'your', Mosiah 'their', and the longest shared sequence is two words. Fighting for one's wives and children is not a scriptural idiom but a universal one, and a verse that could as easily be pointed at Esther as at Nehemiah is pointing at neither.

A five-word run from the rescue of Lot, and pure narrative connective tissue on both sides. The same is true of 1 Samuel 17:57's 'and brought him before' at 20:13, proposed by the same stream. Bringing a man before a ruler is one of the KJV's most-used sentences and CONVENTIONS §5's standing exclusion covers the class; both are registered here once, together, because a rarity-ranked list will keep offering them in a chapter where a captive is brought before a king three times in four verses.

exclusions.sharedText: said unto the king, I pray thee
exclusions.reason: The longest n-gram run offered anywhere in the chapter — seven words, and it scored highest — and it is worth nothing. 'Said unto the king, I pray thee' is the KJV's standard way of introducing a petition to a monarch and the stream returns 2 Samuel 13:6 and 15:7 with identical scores precisely because neither is a source. This is CONVENTIONS §9's point in miniature: the run is long, the two candidates are Amnon feigning illness to get Tamar into his room and Absalom asking leave to go to Hebron, and neither has anything to do with an officer interceding for a people. The verse's real borrowing, Acts 7:60, produces a shorter run and was invisible to the stream.

exclusions.sharedText: it is better that ... than that
exclusions.reason: 'It is better that' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and only Genesis 29:19 completes it with the comparative — 'It is better that I give her to thee, than that I should give her to another man' — which makes it the closest match in the KJV to Mosiah 20:22's frame taken as a frame. It has an additional and misleading attraction in this chapter, since Laban is speaking about the disposal of a daughter and this chapter is about daughters carried off. It is superseded on the completing clause. Mosiah reads 'than that we should', which is a KJV singleton belonging to Exodus 14:12, and Exodus supplies not just the words but the terms of the comparison — servitude weighed against death — where Genesis compares two suitors. The link is filed at Exodus 14:12.

The register's standard case, and a sharp one, because the rarity is real: 'shedding of blood' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 9:22, and Mosiah 20:22 ends 'let us put a stop to the shedding of so much blood'. On rarity alone this would be a strong row. It is declined on sense, and the senses are not merely different but opposite in function. Hebrews means sacrificial blood, and means that there must be shedding of it: 'without shedding of blood is no remission' — the shedding is the condition of forgiveness. Mosiah means blood shed in battle, and means that there must be less of it: the clause is a proposal to stop. The insertion of 'so much' is the tell, since it quantifies what Hebrews treats as a categorical requirement. A phrase that a source makes necessary and a borrower makes regrettable is not a borrowing.

exclusions.sharedText: swear unto me ... oath ... covenant between two peoples
exclusions.reason: Genesis 21:22-32 is the best structural parallel in the KJV to the settlement at Mosiah 20:23-26: two rulers, a grievance about something violently taken by one side's servants, the accused ruler's plea that he had heard nothing of it, an oath sworn between the peoples, and both parties returning to their own land in peace. It is not filed as a link here because the wording will not carry it. 'Swear unto me' is in six KJV verses; 'with an oath' is in nine; the one genuinely rare string in the Genesis passage, 'neither yet heard I of it', is a singleton the Book of Mormon does not reproduce. The Genesis 21 material is registered where it does have verbal contact — as a composite at 20:16, where 'hath done this thing' is one of only three KJV occurrences and Abimelech's ignorance is Limhi's — and a reader who wants the Beersheba parallel should be sent there rather than given a second row for it.

'Dumb ass' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is 2 Peter 2:16, where Balaam's beast speaks with man's voice and forbids the madness of the prophet. Mosiah 21:3 has the Lamanites 'drive them as they would a dumb ass'. On rarity this looks decisive and it is not, because the two texts want opposite things from the animal. Peter's ass is dumb and then is not: the whole point of the sentence is that it spoke, and that a brute rebuked a prophet. The Book of Mormon wants a beast of burden that can be driven and cannot answer, which is the ordinary sense of the adjective and the reason the phrase is available at all. The register keeps this because 2 Peter has already supplied genuine borrowings elsewhere in the volume — 'mist of darkness' at 2 Peter 2:17 is one of the pilot's strongest rows — so a reader who has seen that will be inclined to take this one too.

exclusions.sharedText: none to help ... they cried unto the LORD in their trouble
exclusions.reason: Psalm 107:10-14 is the closest rival to Psalm 106 as the chapter's spine and was considered at length. It has a people 'bound in affliction and iron' because 'they rebelled against the words of God' — which Mosiah 21:4 says outright of Abinadi's words — then 'there was none to help', against Mosiah 21:5's 'there was no way that they could deliver themselves out of their hands', and then the crying and the saving. It is superseded on the wording. Psalm 107's refrain, 'they cried unto the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them out of their distresses', occurs four times and shares nothing with Mosiah's sentence but the idea; 'none to help' is in four KJV verses and Mosiah reproduces none of them. Psalm 106:43-46, by contrast, supplies two KJV singletons, the hinge adverb 'nevertheless', and the peculiar outcome — captors made to pity — that Mosiah 21:15 actually reports. The link is filed at Psalm 106:44.

This chapter is Exodus-shaped throughout — burdens, taskmasters in all but name, a people crying to God — so the murmuring at 21:6 pulls hard toward Exodus 16 and Numbers 14, where murmuring against the leader is the wilderness generation's characteristic sin. Two things decline it. The KJV's idiom is invariably 'murmur against' (six verses, Exodus 16:7-8, Numbers 14:27, 14:36, 16:11, 17:5); Mosiah 21:6 reads 'murmur with the king', a preposition in no KJV verse at all, which is the wrong direction of evidence for a borrowing. And 'murmur' is by this point the Book of Mormon's own established word for the same behaviour, running from 1 Nephi 2:11 onward, so its appearance here is the narrator's vocabulary rather than a fresh reach for a source. The Exodus frame of the chapter is real and is registered where it has words attached, at 21:3 and 21:15.

'Exceeding great joy' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 2:10, where the wise men see the star. Mosiah 21:24 has Limhi 'filled with exceeding great joy' on finding that his prisoners are brethren from Zarahemla, and the situational fit is not bad — a long search ended, strangers who turn out to be the sign one was waiting for. It is declined here because this is not the phrase's first use in the volume. It stands at 1 Nephi 8:12, of Lehi tasting the fruit of the tree, and recurs eleven times across the book; by Mosiah 21 it is the narrator's stock expression for joy and not a reach for Matthew. CONVENTIONS §4's rule is to adjudicate at first use, which puts the question in 1 Nephi 8 — where, as it happens, the catalogue currently carries no row for it. That is worth someone's attention: a KJV singleton is being used eleven times by this book and has not been adjudicated anywhere.

'Engraven' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 3:7 — 'the ministration of death, written and engraven in stones' — and Mosiah 21:27 reports a record 'of the people whose bones they had found', 'engraven on plates of ore'. The temptation is considerable, because the chapter has just borrowed Ezekiel's valley of dry bones at 21:26 and Paul's one use of the word calls the engraven thing a ministration of death; a record of the dead, engraven, found in a land of bones, would be a metalepsis worth having. It is declined on frequency inside the Book of Mormon rather than inside the KJV. 'Engraven' appears thirty times in the volume, from 1 Nephi 3:3 onward, and is simply this book's word for what is done to plates. A term the narrator uses in every plates-passage he writes cannot be evidence of a reach for Paul in this one.

Ammon declines to baptize, 'considering himself an unworthy servant', and the KJV's servant of that self-description is the one at Luke 17:10 who says 'We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do' — the right sentiment in the right mouth for this verse. The adjective is what declines it. 'Unprofitable servant' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 17:10 and Matthew 25:30; 'unworthy' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 13:46 and 1 Corinthians 6:2, and neither has a servant in it. If the Book of Mormon were following the KJV here it had a ready-made phrase and did not use it. The row is registered because the near-miss is itself evidence: a writer steeped in the KJV's servant-language reached for a word the KJV does not use in that collocation, which is a small argument against borrowing at this verse and worth being able to point at.

exclusions.sharedText: deliver them out of the hand
exclusions.reason: The chapter closes on 'all the study of Ammon and his people, and king Limhi and his people, was to deliver themselves out of the hands of the Lamanites, and from bondage', and 'deliver them out of the hand' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 3:8, where the LORD comes down to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Egyptians. The verse is doing real work in this chapter and its neighbours — the burdens, the taskmasters, the cry heard — but the sentence at 21:36 will not carry it. Mosiah has the plural 'hands', which belongs to a different KJV idiom ('delivered them out of the hands of', three verses, Judges 8:34, 1 Samuel 7:14 and 14:48), and it has the reflexive: these people intend to deliver themselves, which is the opposite of what Exodus 3:8 says and is the theological problem Mosiah 22 exists to resolve. The Exodus material is registered where it has verbal contact, as a composite at 21:15, and the deliverance itself is adjudicated in chapter 22.

'The voice of the people' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 8:7, where the LORD tells Samuel to hearken to it because in asking for a king the people 'have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me'. Mosiah 22:1 has Limhi and Ammon gather the people 'that they might have the voice of the people concerning the matter', which is a genuine and pointed use of a singleton — a people under a king being asked their voice about whether to leave. It is not adjudicated here because it is not the phrase's first appearance in this book. The link stands at Mosiah 7:9, and the phrase then becomes the constitutional vocabulary of Mosiah 29, where the catalogue already carries a row at 29:2. CONVENTIONS §4: within a book, a phrase the narrator has adopted is adjudicated at first use and later occurrences are registered, not re-argued.

'Unprofitable servant' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 25:30 and Luke 17:10, and Gideon's 'if thou hast not found me to be an unprofitable servant' reproduces it exactly. The link is nevertheless filed at Mosiah 2:21, where King Benjamin's 'ye would be unprofitable servants' is the phrase's first use in the book and where the catalogue already cites Luke 17:10. What is worth registering rather than passing over is what Gideon does with it, because it runs the source backwards. Luke's servants call themselves unprofitable after doing everything commanded; Gideon negates the term to claim a record of service and then asks for a hearing on the strength of it. Read alongside Mosiah 21:33, where Ammon calls himself an 'unworthy servant' — a word the KJV never joins to 'servant' — the two verses together show the book holding the KJV's phrase and a non-KJV substitute for it eleven verses apart, which is a small but real piece of evidence about how deliberately the borrowing is done.

exclusions.sharedText: gold ... silver ... carried out at the departure
exclusions.reason: The typological expectation is the whole temptation here. The chapter is an exodus by night, and the KJV's exodus by night has the departing people carrying out 'jewels of silver, and jewels of gold' obtained from their oppressors, so a reader arriving at 'they had taken all their gold, and silver, and their precious things, which they could carry' will supply Exodus 12:35-36 without being asked. The wording will not bear it: 'jewels of silver, and jewels of gold' is Exodus's phrase and Mosiah has neither noun in that form, and 'gold and silver and' is in ten KJV verses spread from Exodus to Revelation. The sense is opposed as well, which is the more interesting objection. Israel's gold is spoil taken from the Egyptians; Limhi's is the people's own property, carried out at cost and limited by what they could carry. The chapter's Exodus material is real and is registered where it has words attached, at 22:8.

'Pursued after' occurs in twenty-two KJV verses and Exodus 14:8-9 is the most famous of them — Pharaoh pursuing after the children of Israel and overtaking them encamping by the sea — which makes it the obvious proposal for a chapter that has just staged an exodus. It is superseded. Exodus's pursuit ends in an overtaking and then a drowning, and Mosiah's ends in the pursuers losing the trail and being 'lost in the wilderness', with no divine intervention reported at all. The pursuit that Mosiah 22:15-16 is shaped against is 2 Kings 25:5, where 'the army of the Chaldees pursued after the king, and overtook him in the plains of Jericho' — a KJV singleton, and the account whose other four beats this chapter has already reproduced. The link is filed at 22:11. Exodus 14 remains the background of the chapter's genre and is not the source of its sentences.

The five-word run is real and the wilderness setting is shared, but Exodus 16:35's clause is 'until they came to a land inhabited' — the end of the manna, the end of the wandering. Mosiah 23:4 is the beginning of a wandering, and the land it reaches is uninhabited: 'a very beautiful and pleasant land; a land of pure water.' The Exodus typology the chapter really carries is at 24:9 and 24:13, from Exodus 1 and 6, and it runs the other way.

Four words of narrative connective. Ezra 5:2 is the resumption of work on the temple by named leaders under prophetic encouragement; Mosiah 23:5 is a colony putting up houses and tilling ground, with the 1830 text's own '&c.' marking how little the writer cared to specify. No shared content.

The chapter's highest-scoring candidate at this verse and worth naming because the score is entirely speech-tag boilerplate. The 1830 reading 'saith' (1920 'said') is what raises the run to five words; the KJV uses the historic present of Jesus constantly, and John 6:20's content — 'It is I; be not afraid', on the water — has nothing to do with Alma refusing a crown. The verse's real borrowings are Romans 14:5 and 2 Corinthians 12:1; see the accepted link.

exclusions.sharedText: walk in his ways ... keep his commandments
exclusions.reason: Considered because 23:14's test for a teacher — 'a man of God, walking in his ways and keeping his commandments' — reads like a quotation. It is not from any one verse: walking in God's ways paired with keeping his commandments is the standard Deuteronomic doublet (Deuteronomy 8:6; 10:12; 26:17; 1 Kings 2:3; 8:58; 8:61) and the Book of Mormon uses it from 1 Nephi onward. Nothing selects a source.

Genuinely tempting, and rejected on a single point. Judges 18:28-29 is a migrating people who build a city and name it — 'they called the name of the city Dan, after the name of Dan their father' — which is the shape of Mosiah 23:19-20, a migrating people who name a land and then a city Helam. But the Danite naming is eponymous and the point of the Judges passage is the tribe stamping its ancestor's name on stolen ground, whereas Helam is not an ancestor and the Book of Mormon never explains the name. Take away the eponym and only four words of the commonest narrative English remain.

A clean four-word match in opposed senses. In Psalm 35:15 the gathering is hostile and the psalmist is its object — 'the abjects gathered themselves together against me' — while at Mosiah 23:26 the brethren of Alma gather into the city of Helam for refuge from an approaching army. The phrase is also common: it stands in more than a dozen KJV verses on both sides of the same distinction.

exclusions.sharedText: it came to pass that the Lord
exclusions.reason: Covered in principle by the standing exclusion filed at 1 Nephi 2:1 and noted here only because the seven-word run is the longest in the chapter and will draw a reader's eye. 'And it came to pass that the Lord' is the Book of Mormon's default sentence opening; its length here carries no signal whatever.

Exodus 18:20 supplies the wording — 'shalt shew them the way wherein they must walk' is the KJV's phrase and the 1830 spelling 'shew' preserves it — but not the sense: Jethro is telling Moses to teach ordinances, not to guide a column through a wilderness. The scene the two verses belong to is Judges 1:24-25, and the link is filed at 23:37 where the promise is broken, which is the finding. A reader arriving here should go there.

Leviticus 26:37 is a curse — Israel shall 'have no power to stand before your enemies' — and Mosiah 23:39 is a constitutional limit on a puppet king, who 'should have no power to do any thing contrary to the will of the king of the Lamanites'. The shared four words are an auxiliary verb and a preposition.

exclusions.sharedText: and his brethren that they should
exclusions.reason: The chapter's top-scoring candidate, and it is a six-word run of pure connective. Judges 9:41 is Zebul expelling Gaal from Shechem; Mosiah 24:1 is a king appointing teachers over conquered lands. The same run drew the machine at Mosiah 23:33 as well, which is what a connective string does.

Considered because 24:5's 'nevertheless they knew not God' is a striking flat statement about a whole people and the KJV has a standing idiom for it. But the idiom is distributed — Judges 2:10, Galatians 4:8, 1 Thessalonians 4:5, 2 Thessalonians 1:8, 1 John 3:1 — and no single verse is closer than the rest. Nothing else in Mosiah 24:5 is Pauline; the sentence goes on to the law of Moses and the words of Abinadi, which are the book's own.

In 2 Kings 13:19 the man of God is wroth with a king for striking the ground too few times, a rebuke inside a prophetic sign-act. At Mosiah 24:9 Amulon is wroth with Alma because Alma believed Abinadi and he did not. The four-word run is the KJV's ordinary way of saying anger and appears in dozens of verses; the verse's real source is Exodus 1:11, and the link is filed there.

Acts 12:19 is close in situation as well as words — Herod examines the keepers who let Peter out and commands that they should be put to death — and Acts 12 is genuinely present in this chapter, at 24:14 where 'know of a surety' is Peter's phrase after that same escape. But the death penalty here falls on the prisoners for praying, not on the guards for failing, and the decree-against-prayer belongs to Daniel 6:7. The link is filed at 24:11 to Daniel and the Acts 12 contact is recorded at 24:14, which is where it bears.

Daniel 2:30 is about Nebuchadnezzar coming to know the thoughts of his own heart through an interpreted dream; Mosiah 24:12 is about God knowing the thoughts of other people's hearts without being told them, which is the point of a prayer that is not spoken aloud. The two uses are nearly opposite and the shared string is four common words. The verse's sources are 1 Samuel 1:13 and 1:15; see the accepted link.

Tempting on the wording — Numbers 7:9 is one of very few KJV verses putting a load on shoulders that must be borne — but the sense is the reverse of Mosiah 24:14's. The Kohathites bear the sanctuary on their shoulders as a privilege, and are given no wagons precisely because the burden is holy. Alma's people carry a burden imposed by a slave-master, and the promise is that they will stop feeling it. The relief-from-a-shoulder verses are Psalm 81:6 and Isaiah 10:27, and the link is filed to the first.

The model case for this category in the chapter. 'Made light' is a KJV singleton at Matthew 22:5 and the string matches Mosiah 24:15's 'the burdens which was laid upon Alma and his brethren, were made light' exactly — but in Matthew the phrase is idiomatic contempt, 'they made light of it, and went their ways', of guests ignoring a wedding invitation. In Mosiah it is literal: a weight is reduced. Same two words, no relation whatever.

A genuine four-word run and the only other KJV verse promising a deliverance for the following day: 'to morrow I will deliver them into thine hand.' But Judges 20:28 delivers an enemy INTO Israel's hand for slaughter, and Mosiah 24:16 delivers a people OUT of bondage. Jeremiah 15:21's 'I will deliver thee out of' is the KJV's only match for the construction the Book of Mormon actually has, and the 1830 'thee' is what secures it; the link is filed there.

Deliverance boilerplate. Judges 8:34 is Israel forgetting the LORD 'who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side', and the run is the KJV's standard formula, which the Book of Mormon has used since 1 Nephi. Mosiah 24:21's substance — thanks poured out in a named valley for burdens eased — has no contact with Gideon's chapter.

Four words of narrative hinge, matched against a verse about the men of Gath being smitten with emerods. Listed only because it is the sole candidate the machine offered for the chapter's closing verse, which is a reminder that a ranked list with nothing in it still returns something.

Four words of assembly boilerplate, matched against Jacob telling shepherds it is too early to water the flocks. 'Gathered together' is among the Book of Mormon's commonest phrases and is used four times in this chapter's first four verses alone; the same run drew the machine at 23:26 and 25:4.

Noah going into the ark against Mulek's company coming into the wilderness. Four function words. Listed because the machine offered six candidates on this string at this verse and a reader of the raw list should know that none of them was considered.

Considered because 'shed many tears of sorrow' in a paragraph of alternating grief and joy invites the eschatological promise that God shall wipe away all tears. But 'tears of sorrow' stands in no KJV verse, Revelation 21:4 has neither of the Book of Mormon's constructions, and the verse's grief is for brethren slain by Lamanites, not for a world passed away. No wording, no link.

The same KJV singleton the machine ranked first at Mosiah 24:22, and this is its second occurrence in two chapters. Adjudicated at first use: the link is filed at 24:22, where the thanksgiving follows the deliverance directly, and this verse records the people of Zarahemla repeating the reaction on hearing about it. A reader arriving here should go to 24:22, including for the reason the row is thin.

Both Matthew 5:9 ('they shall be called the children of God') and Romans 9:26 ('there shall they be called the children of God') give a five-word run, and both are about a name conferred rather than inherited, which is the verse's subject. But the Book of Mormon's noun is Nephi, not God, and the passage about adopting another man's name into his people is Isaiah 44:5. The link is filed there; these two are the sound of a common relative clause.

A clean four-word match in a wholly opposed setting. Matthew 28:12 is the chief priests assembling with the elders to buy the soldiers' silence about the empty tomb; Mosiah 25:15 is a congregation assembled in bodies to be preached to. The machine flagged 'assembled' and 'large' as rare words, which they are — 'they gave LARGE money unto the soldiers' against 'assembled together in LARGE bodies'. Two rare words, no relation.

John 21:7 and 21:12 use the clause of recognising the risen Jesus on the shore; Mosiah 25:16 uses it of attributing a rescue to the right agent — 'that they should remember that it was the Lord that did deliver them.' The five shared words are a subject clause, and the Johannine sense, recognition of a person, is absent.

The machine's proposal is one verse short. 1 Corinthians 12:19 is a rhetorical question against uniformity — 'if they were all one member, where were the body?' — which argues the opposite of Mosiah 25:22. The verse the Book of Mormon is transposing is 12:20, 'now are they many members, yet but one body', the KJV's only 'yet but one body' and the affirmative form of the figure. The link is filed there.

'Take upon them the name of Christ' is a covenant formula this book has already established: it is spoken by king Benjamin at Mosiah 5:8 ('take upon you the name of Christ'), and CONVENTIONS practice is to adjudicate a formula at its first use within a book and record later occurrences as recurrence. The KJV's two 'the name of Christ' verses (2 Timothy 2:19; 1 Peter 4:14) are about naming and reproach, not about taking a name in covenant, and neither is a plausible source for either occurrence. A reader should go to Mosiah 5:8.

Numbers 11:29 is a KJV singleton for 'put his spirit upon them' and its context — Moses wishing all the Lord's people were prophets, in a chapter about the seventy elders — is genuinely close to a verse about churches multiplying under appointed teachers. But the Book of Mormon's verb is 'pour out', not 'put', and 'pour out my spirit upon' is a singleton of its own at Joel 2:28. The link is filed there, and the mediation against Acts 2:17 is the finding; see the note.

exclusions.sharedText: accused of their brethren / the accuser of our brethren
exclusions.reason: Tempting, because 'the accuser of our brethren' occurs in exactly one KJV verse and Mosiah 26:11 says the accused were 'accused of their brethren' — in 1830 usage, by their brethren. The temptation is doubled by the metalepsis that would follow: a church discipline system described in the diction the KJV reserves for the office of Satan. But the contact is one content word (brethren) plus a shared root, in opposite grammatical roles, and 'brethren' is the Book of Mormon's ordinary word for fellow members. Revelation 12:10's accuser accuses before God day and night; Mosiah's brethren testify once, in a hearing, and are believed. Recorded here because a careful reader might well take it, and because the reading it would license is attractive enough to be dangerous.

Ranked first at 26:13 on a five-word run that spans a clause boundary in both texts. Numbers 21:14 is a citation of the Book of the Wars of the LORD; Mosiah 26:13 is Alma asking God what to do. No content word is shared beyond the divine title.

A genuine competitor, not noise: 'poured out my soul' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and Hannah's distressed private prayer at a sanctuary, overheard and answered by a priest, matches Alma's situation better than Isaiah 53 does. It loses on grammar — Mosiah 26:14 has the third person, 'he had poured out his soul', which is Isaiah 53:12's form, not Hannah's — and on neighbourhood, since Isaiah 53 is transcribed into this same book at Mosiah 14 by the prophet named one verse later at 26:15. Retained as a composite on the accepted link rather than discarded.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass ... the word of the Lord came to him saying
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run built entirely from the KJV's standard prophetic-word formula plus the Book of Mormon's standard narrative connective. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5. Listed once here because the n-gram stream ranked it top at this verse and the real source of 26:14 lies elsewhere (see the Isaiah 53:12 link).

A five-word run from a KJV singleton — 'in my name shall they' occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and therefore exactly the kind of candidate the rarity heuristic is built to promote. It is nevertheless nothing. Mark 16:17's next word is 'cast out devils', and the verse is a list of signs following belief; Mosiah 26:18's next words are 'be called', and the verse is about a people who bear a name. The shared string is the frame 'in my name shall they', which any sentence of that shape produces, and the singleton status reflects the KJV's general preference for 'in my name' with a following infinitive rather than any distinctiveness in Mark. This is the trap ADJUDICATING.md §4 names as the window closing one word early, and it is worth the register entry because the rarity count here is as high as the count behind several accepted links.

exclusions.sharedText: shall know that I am the Lord their God
exclusions.reason: A nine-word run, the longest in the chapter after Matthew 25:41, and still not evidence. The recognition formula 'ye shall know that I am the LORD' and its variants run to scores of occurrences across Exodus and Ezekiel and are the KJV's standard way of stating the purpose of a divine act. Nothing else in Exodus 29:46 — the tabernacle, the dwelling among them, the bringing out of Egypt — appears at Mosiah 26:26, whose second clause turns instead to 'I am their Redeemer'. Length without distinctiveness (CONVENTIONS §9).
Four words of connective tissue. Numbers 10:30 is Hobab declining to travel with Israel; the run does not even fall on a shared clause.
The KJV's commonest speech-introduction, and the Book of Mormon's. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

'In all diligence' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which by this catalogue's usual standard would make it strong evidence. But 2 Corinthians 8:7 is a list of graces in which the Corinthians already abound, cited to shame them into finishing a collection for Jerusalem; diligence there is one item in a series, not a manner of walking. Mosiah 26:38's 'walking in all diligence' uses it adverbially, in a list of ministerial labours. Real singleton, no argument: the phrase is the sort of ordinary Jacobean adverbial that happens to have got into print once.

'The word of God' is among the KJV's most frequent phrases and 'teaching the word of God' is its unmarked verbal form. Also proposed at this verse from Acts 13:5 and 1 Corinthians 10:32 on the same and adjacent runs; all three are the same non-finding.

The 1830 'fellow-laborers' is a rare enough word to look promising — the KJV has 'fellowlabourer' or 'fellowlabourers' in four verses, all Pauline — and Philippians 4:3 is the most tempting of them, since it names fellowlabourers 'whose names are in the book of life' and Mosiah 26:36, two verses earlier, has names blotted out. But that pairing is an artifact of proximity in our text, not in Paul's; the word is a bare occupational noun that Mosiah uses without any of Philippians' setting, and the book-of-life argument is already carried at 26:36 by Revelation 3:5, where it belongs.

exclusions.sharedText: on the east and on the west
exclusions.reason: The chapter's top-ranked candidate, on a seven-word run that is nothing but a compass. Joshua 11:3 is a list of Canaanite peoples; Mosiah 27:6 is a note about population spreading. The KJV has no other way to say the four directions, and neither does the Book of Mormon.
Five words of hedging connective — Mosiah 27:11 uses 'as it were' twice in one verse to qualify the cloud and the voice of thunder. Isaiah 5:18's cart rope has no other contact.

Ranked at both 27:14 and 27:36 on a six-word run, and it is the wrong one of the phrase's three KJV homes. 2 Timothy 3:7 describes women 'ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth' — people who do not arrive. Mosiah 27:14 is about a man being brought there in answer to prayer, which is 1 Timothy 2:4's sense exactly, and 1 Timothy 2:1-4 is besides the KJV's defence of the intercessory prayer the angel has come to vindicate. The link is filed at 27:14 against 1 Timothy 2:4.

'Power and authority' occurs in exactly two KJV verses and the ranked one is the wrong one. Luke 20:20's power and authority belongs to the Roman governor, to whom the spies hope to deliver Jesus; Mosiah 27:14's belongs to God, of which the angel has come to convince Alma. Luke 9:1, the other occurrence, is the better sense-match — Christ giving the twelve power and authority over devils, which suits a chapter about an angel's demonstration against 'the enemy of God' (27:9) — but two ordinary nouns joined by 'and' will not carry a link at any confidence, and neither Lukan verse shares anything else with Mosiah 27:14.

exclusions.sharedText: how great things ... hath done for
exclusions.reason: A serious competitor and the one a reader of this catalogue would expect, because the same idiom was adjudicated to Mark 5:19 at 1 Nephi 7:11, where the 1830 'how great things the Lord hath done for us' is Mark verbatim and 1920's 'what' is in no KJV verse. Here it loses on the run itself. Mosiah 27:16 reads 'remember how great things he hath done for them', and 'how great things he hath done for' occurs in exactly one KJV verse — 1 Samuel 12:24 — which matches all seven words, while Mark 5:19 has 'the Lord' inside the run. 1 Samuel 12 also supplies the content Mosiah 27:16 supplies, a recital of deliverance from bondage. Recorded as an alternative on the accepted link rather than discarded, because the 1 Nephi precedent makes it a live reading.

Tempting for its situation rather than its words: Luke 7:15 is the widow of Nain's son, who 'was dead' and 'sat up, and began to speak', and Mosiah 27:23 has a man who has lain two days and two nights unable to move or open his mouth, who 'stood up and began to speak unto them'. A raising is genuinely what the scene depicts and the chapter says so at 27:19-20. But 'began to speak' occurs in six KJV verses and carries no mark of any of them, and the specific verb Mosiah uses for rising is not Luke's. The Acts 13:3 link filed at this verse rests on a phrase with two occurrences and a matching narrative position; this one has neither.

Correctly identified by the machine but keyed near the wrong verse in the ranked list. 'Without God in the world' occurs in exactly one KJV verse and the Book of Mormon has it at 27:31, not 27:29, where the link is filed.

exclusions.sharedText: teaching and preaching the word of the Lord
exclusions.reason: The KJV's standard summary of missionary activity, and the Book of Mormon's. Also proposed at Mosiah 26:38 from Acts 13:5 and 18:11 on the same run; all are the same non-finding, and no content distinguishes Acts 15:35 from the others.

The second appearance of the phrase in this chapter and the same mis-ranking; see the entry at 27:14. Within this book the phrase is adjudicated once, at 27:14, and 27:36 is recorded there in recurrenceRefs.

exclusions.sharedText: go up to the land of
exclusions.reason: Six words of geography, proposed again at 28:5. 'Go up to the land of Nephi' is the fixed Book of Mormon expression for this journey and occurs many times in Mosiah; Ezekiel 38:11's Gog going up to the land of unwalled villages has no other contact.
Narrative connective. Also proposed at 28:20 on the same run. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

Ranked first at 28:1 on a five-word run of pure petition boilerplate. Luke 1:74 is the Benedictus — 'that he would grant unto us, that we being delivered out of the hand of our enemies' — and shares nothing with a request for royal leave to travel. The genuine link at this verse is to Acts 9:2, on a shorter run with a matching situation.

The third appearance in this batch of a mis-ranked candidate on this phrase; see the entries at Mosiah 27:14 and 27:36. Note that Mosiah 28:2 does not in fact read 'knowledge of the truth' but 'the knowledge of the Lord their God', so the run is shorter than the ranking implies.

'The LORD their God' is among the KJV's commonest divine designations and Mosiah 28:2 uses it three times in one verse. Also proposed here from 2 Kings 17:14 and Exodus 29:46 on the same run; the last of these was excluded at Mosiah 26:26 for the same reason.

Genuinely tempting, and worth the entry for the thread it seems to belong to. 'Vilest' occurs in exactly one KJV verse in this sense, Psalm 12:8, 'when the vilest men are exalted' — and Psalm 12 is also the KJV's flattery psalm, 'with flattering lips and with a double heart do they speak', which would tie 28:4 back to the flattering words of Mosiah 26:6 and the 'much flattery' of 27:8. The thread does not hold. Psalm 12:8's vilest men are the wicked in power, and Mosiah 28:4's are penitents describing what they used to be; the superlative is one any writer forms from an ordinary adjective; and 26:6's 'flattering words' is a KJV singleton belonging to 1 Thessalonians 2:5, not to Psalm 12's 'flattering lips', which is a different noun. Recorded because a reader tracing the flattery vocabulary across these three chapters would very reasonably arrive here.

A five-word run that straddles a clause boundary in both texts: John 6:54's 'hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day' against Mosiah's 'they shall have eternal life; and I will deliver thy sons'. The shared words are the noun phrase plus a connective and a pronoun. The Johannine link at this verse is to John 17:20, on the believing-through-another's-word idiom.

Worth considering because Galatians 1:13 is an established source in this batch — it stands behind Mosiah 27:10 and, with 1:14, behind Mosiah 26:1 — so a third contact would be a real pattern rather than a coincidence. It is not one. 'Beyond measure' occurs in three KJV verses, two of them in Mark of crowds astonished at a miracle, and it is an ordinary intensifier in all three. Mosiah 28:12's 'desirous beyond measure, to know concerning those people which had been destroyed' is a curiosity, and Galatians 1:13's is a persecution. Nothing but the intensifier is shared.

Ranked at 28:13 by the machine but the run belongs at 28:17. Acts 11:19's 'they which were scattered abroad upon the persecution that arose about Stephen' uses 'upon' causally — scattered because of the persecution — and Mosiah 28:17 uses it spatially, scattered upon the face of the earth. The preposition is doing opposite work in the two verses, and the completing phrase is Genesis 11:9's, where the link is filed.
Connective tissue spanning a clause boundary. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

'According to the spirit' occurs in five KJV verses and is Alma's habitual formula of self-authorization in this chapter (7:5, 7:16, 7:26). Romans 1:4's 'according to the spirit of holiness' is a Christological predicate about the resurrection; Alma's is an epistemic hedge about his own confidence. Nothing but the prepositional phrase is shared.

exclusions.sharedText: I say unto you there be
exclusions.reason: A six-word run made entirely of the KJV's commonest speech formula plus an existential 'there be'. Matthew 16:28 promises that some standing there will not taste death; Alma 7:7 says there are many things to come. Covered in principle by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

exclusions.sharedText: I do not say that he
exclusions.reason: The string match is exact and the sense is opposed. John's 'I do not say that he shall pray for it' withholds intercession for the sin unto death; Alma's 'I do not say that he will come among us at the time of his dwelling in his mortal tabernacle' withholds a prediction about the Messiah's itinerary. The shared words are a negated verb of speech and a pronoun, and the two verses have no other contact of any kind.

Ranked first at this verse and superseded. Luke 17:21 has 'the kingdom of God is within you'; Alma 7:9 has 'the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand', which is Matthew's idiom and Matthew's clause, and the verse's other half is Matthew 3:3. The link is filed at Alma 7:9 on Matthew 3:2-3. Matthew 26:45, also proposed here on 'at hand and the son of', fails the same way: its 'hour' is at hand, not its kingdom, and the run spans a clause boundary.

Hardy's apparatus cross-references Matthew 1:18 and Luke 1:35 at Alma 7:10. Matthew 1:18 — 'she was found with child of the Holy Ghost' — is thematically apt and shares no distinctive wording with Alma's clause; every word Alma reproduces comes from Luke 1:31 and 1:35 ('overshadow', 'conceive', 'bring forth a son'). The link is filed at Alma 7:10 on Luke, with Luke 1:35 as composite. Registered rather than passed over because Hardy's row is real and a reader should be told where it went.

'Loose the bands' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Job 38:31 (of Orion) and Isaiah 58:6 (of wickedness), and 'bands of death' occurs in none. The Book of Mormon's 'bands of death' is its own formula, already worked through at Mosiah 15:8, 15:23 and 16:7 where the surrounding Pauline resurrection language is what carries those links. Nothing at Alma 7:12 reaches back to Job or Isaiah, and the verse's real borrowing is Hebrews 2:18, filed there.

'According to the flesh' occurs in fifteen KJV verses and is Paul's standing antithesis to 'according to the spirit'. Alma 7:12-13 uses it three times in two verses, of the incarnation, where Paul uses it of his own vacillation over a travel plan. Widely distributed content words pointing at no one verse.

'According to the power of' occurs across the Pauline corpus (Ephesians 3:7, 3:20, Colossians 1:29, 2 Timothy 1:8 among others). Alma's 'according to the power of his deliverance' has no KJV counterpart for its object, which is the only content-bearing word in the phrase.

A real contributor to the verse but not its source. Alma 7:14 reads 'if ye are not born again, ye cannot inherit the Kingdom of Heaven', which fuses John 3:3's 'cannot see the kingdom of God' with Paul's verb and Matthew's 'kingdom of heaven'; no single KJV verse has the sentence. The verse's link is filed at Alma 7:14 on John 1:29, where three KJV singletons stand in one clause, and the John 3 material is argued there.

The top machine candidate at 7:15 and connective. 'Made a covenant with him to give the land' (Nehemiah, of Abraham) and 'enter into a covenant with him to keep his commandments' (Alma, of a baptizand) share a preposition string and no argument. The verse's actual borrowing, Hebrews 12:1's 'lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us', was invisible to the n-gram stream because Alma redistributes its two objects onto one noun; the link is filed at Alma 7:15.
Connective tissue. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

exclusions.sharedText: I said unto you from the beginning
exclusions.reason: 'I said unto you from the beginning' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the run in Alma 7:18 is exact and eight words long, so the count alone would carry a link. It is excluded on thematic coherence, which is the criterion that separates it from the structurally identical row accepted at Alma 7:22. John 8:25 is Jesus answering the question 'Who art thou?' — a Christological self-identification, in a hostile temple dispute, whose whole force is the identity of the speaker. Alma 7:18 is a preacher reminding a congregation what he opened with. Every word of the run is a function word or a weak verb of speech, so the rarity is a rarity of ordering and nothing in the two contexts suggests the ordering was borrowed. The John 16:6 row at 7:22 was kept because both settings are farewell addresses; this one has no such support.

The patriarchal triad occurs in some two dozen KJV verses and cannot point at 2 Kings 13:23 specifically. What is rare at Alma 7:25 is 'sit down with Abraham', a KJV singleton at Matthew 8:11, and 'which have been since the world began', a KJV singleton at Luke 1:70. Both are filed as the link at Alma 7:25.
Connective tissue spanning a clause boundary. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

Connective.
