Alma 7:27's blessing — 'may the peace of God rest upon you, and upon your houses and lands, and upon your flocks and herds' — is a Hebraic anaphora of a common preposition, and the one phrase in it with any KJV distinctiveness, 'the peace of God' (Philippians 4:7, Colossians 3:15), is a two-verse phrase with no other contact. Not enough to catalogue at any confidence.

Ranked first on the verse and the sense is opposed. Matthew 25:6's cry at midnight announces the bridegroom and summons the wise virgins out to meet him; Alma 16:1's 'cry of war heard throughout the land' announces a Lamanite army already inside the borders. Both are shouts that end a long quiet, which is what makes the match tempting, but the KJV verse is an arrival hoped for and the Book of Mormon's is an arrival feared, and 'there was a cry' is four words of narrative English with no distinctive shape.

Top-ranked here and again at 16:6, in both cases because 'borders of the land' is a five-word run. It is geography, not allusion: Exodus 16:35 is the end of the manna at the borders of Canaan and Alma 16:2 is a raiding column crossing into the borders of Ammonihah. Mark 7:24's 'into the borders of' is the same non-finding. Covered in principle by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1.

exclusions.sharedText: those which had been carried away
exclusions.reason: The machine's best candidate on this verse, at rarity 1.64 with a six-word run, and it is the right deportation seen from the wrong end — Ezra 2:1 lists the returning exiles, Alma 16:4 the Nephites setting out to fetch theirs. The link is filed at Jeremiah 39:9, whose 'carried away captive into' is a KJV singleton and is the string Alma actually reproduces. Ezra shares only the periphrasis 'those which had been carried away', which the KJV uses of the captivity generally.

A typological expectation the wording will not bear, and worth recording because it is a strong one. Ammonihah is a great city whose people boasted 'God could not destroy [it], because of its greatness' and which was left desolate in a single day — which is the shape of Isaiah 47:8-9, where Babylon says 'I am, and none else beside me' and is told 'these two things shall come to thee in a moment in one day', and of Revelation 18:7-19, where the city that said 'I sit a queen' is 'in one hour made desolate'. But 'in one day' occurs in thirteen KJV verses and nothing else is shared: Alma has no boast in direct speech, no queen, no widowhood, no merchants. The Babylon-of-the-prophets reading of Ammonihah is available to any reader and is not evidence of dependence on either passage. 'Left desolate' occurs in no KJV verse; the KJV's nearest, 'your house is left unto you desolate' (Matthew 23:38, Luke 13:35), is about a temple and not a city and shares only the participle.
A four-word run spanning a clause boundary, joining Athaliah's murdered princes to the slain of the profession of Nehor. Connective tissue; covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

exclusions.sharedText: in all the region round about
exclusions.reason: Worth raising because the contact is real and the setting fits: Luke 4:14-15 has a preacher's fame go out 'through all the region round about' and then has him teaching in their synagogues, which is the order of Alma 16:13-15 reversed. 'Region round about' occurs in five KJV verses, all of them Gospel notices of a preacher's reach (Matthew 3:5, Mark 1:28, Mark 6:55, Luke 4:14, Luke 7:17), so no single verse is identifiable as the source. It also enters Alma one chapter earlier, at 15:14, which is where its first use in this book falls to be adjudicated; a reader sent from here should look there and at Luke 4:14-15.

A tempting count that means nothing here. 'On all the face of' is a KJV singleton — it occurs in exactly one verse, Acts 17:26 — but it occurs in twenty-nine verses of the 1830 Book of Mormon, from 1 Nephi 10:12 to Moroni 9:19, and is one of the book's most worn narrative formulas. Where a phrase is rare in the KJV and common in the Book of Mormon, the rarity count is evidence about the Book of Mormon's own diction and not about a source. The link at this verse is Joel 2:28's outpouring, which is what the sentence is actually built on.

exclusions.sharedText: enter into the rest of the Lord
exclusions.reason: The verse's closing clause, 'that they might enter into the rest of the Lord their God', is a standing Book of Mormon formula rather than a fresh borrowing here. Its mediation was settled at Jacob 1:7, where the KJV's psalm and the KJV's epistle differ and the Book of Mormon has the epistle's third person at every point ('enter into his rest', a KJV singleton at Hebrews 3:18, against Psalm 95:11's 'into my rest'); within Alma the phrase is the argument of chapters 12-13 and falls to be adjudicated there. tools/mediation-check.py returns Psalm 95:11 as 'decisive' on this verse, which is a false positive of the kind CONVENTIONS §4 warns about: the tool is registering the absence of Hebrews' trailing clause 'but to them that believed not', and an absence is not a reading. The links at 16:17 are Luke 8:13, John 15:1 and Romans 11.

exclusions.sharedText: also the resurrection of the dead
exclusions.reason: Ranked second on the verse with a six-word run, and the run is a doctrinal commonplace. 'Resurrection of the dead' occurs in eleven KJV verses across Matthew, Acts, 1 Corinthians, Philippians and Hebrews; the preceding 'also' is Paul's connective and Alma's alike. Nothing in Alma 16:19 answers to 1 Corinthians 15's argument from the first and second Adam. The verse's real sources are the two singletons in its first half, Revelation 1:1 and Philippians 2:16.

'Judgment seat' occurs in ten KJV verses (Matthew 27:19, John 19:13, five times in Acts, Romans 14:10, 2 Corinthians 5:10, James 2:6) and is the ordinary English for a magistrate's bench. It is also, from Mosiah 29 onward, the standing name of the Nephite chief office and appears dozens of times; a Pilate allusion would have to be argued from something other than the phrase, and Alma 1:2 supplies nothing — the man before the bench is the accused, not the judge, and the trial ends in a conviction rather than a hand-washing.

Four words spanning a clause boundary in both texts. Joel's imperative is addressed to the land and its reason is agricultural restoration; the borrowing at 1:4 is 'lift up their heads and rejoice', whose source is adjudicated at this verse as Luke 21:28.

A four-word narrative connective, and the verse behind it is Elisha mocked by the children of Bethel — a prophet insulted on a road, not a false teacher meeting a true one. The only thing the two share is a man walking. Recorded because the n-gram stream ranked it and because the Elisha cycle does supply real links elsewhere in this corpus (2 Kings 2:8 at 1 Nephi 4:2 and 17:26), which makes a stray Elisha proposal more tempting than it should be.

“The church of God” occurs in exactly 8 KJV verses, all Pauline, and is the Book of Mormon's ordinary term for the Nephite church from Mosiah 25 onward. Nothing in 1 Corinthians 10:32's argument about giving no offence to Jews or Gentiles is in view. The same candidate is ranked again at 1:19 and is excluded there for the same reason.

exclusions.sharedText: Now the name of the man was
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run, and the longest in the chapter, which is exactly the trap ADJUDICATING §4 names: it is the KJV's standing formula for introducing a named character (1 Samuel 25:3, Ruth 1:2, and the same construction with 'woman' and 'city' elsewhere). Tempting here because Nabal is a rich churl who despises a man asking for support, which is close to Alma 1's subject — but the man being introduced is Gideon, the victim, not the offender, and the formula is doing nothing but introducing him. Ruth 1:2 shares the same run and is excluded with it.

The KJV's idiom is 'stricken in years' (Genesis 18:11, Joshua 13:1, Joshua 23:1, Luke 1:7, with 'well stricken' in three of them) and the 1830 reads 'stricken with many years', which occurs in no KJV verse. The 1920 does not repair it. One shared participle, and the KJV's preposition is not the Book of Mormon's; the aged-priest resonance of Luke 1 has nothing else to rest on. The verse's real borrowing is adjudicated as Matthew 26:51.

The run is four words and it is a genuine legal collocation, which is why it ranked; but Ezekiel 35:5 is an oracle against Mount Seir for handing Israel over 'by the force of the sword in the time of their calamity'. It is a national indictment of a foreign people, not a homicide verdict, and it supplies no part of Alma's reasoning about blood coming upon the judges. The sentence's precedent is adjudicated at this verse as 2 Samuel 4:11.

Four words of pure connective tissue. Romans 4:21 concerns Abraham's confidence in the promise; Alma 1:15 concerns Nehor's confession on the scaffold. 1 Chronicles 28:21's 'of God and there' is excluded with it.

Connective boilerplate introducing a negative purpose clause, scoring 2.00 on rarity because the exact five-word sequence is uncommon and carrying no content word at all. Jeremiah's subject is the covenant of day and night.

“The word of God” occurs in exactly 45 KJV verses and four times in this one Book of Mormon verse. 1 Samuel 4:13's 'of God and when the' is the same non-finding with a clause boundary through it. The verse's proposed borrowing is adjudicated here as Matthew 10:24.

The collocation is a fixed KJV pair — “poor and needy” occurs in exactly 17 KJV verses — and Psalm 35:10 has no other contact with Alma 1:27. One caution for the record: the definite-article form “poor and the needy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 35:10, and Alma 1:27 has the article ('to the poor, and the needy'). The article is not doing enough work to carry a link on its own, and Psalm 35 is a plea for deliverance from personal enemies rather than a passage about almsgiving. The verse's care for the poor, the needy, the sick and the afflicted, and its refusal of costly apparel, are adjudicated at Alma 1:22 (Isaiah 58:6-7, the fast God chooses) and at Alma 1:30 (James 2:15-16). A reader arriving at 1:27 should be sent to both.

exclusions.sharedText: and of gold and of silver and of precious things
exclusions.reason: The gold, silver and precious things of this verse, together with its flocks and herds and its 'exceeding rich', are adjudicated at Alma 1:6 as one borrowing from 2 Chronicles 32:26-29, where they sit within four verses of the KJV singleton 'the pride of his heart'. 2 Chronicles 21:3 (Jehoshaphat's gifts to his sons) and Daniel 11:43 (the king of the north's plunder of Egypt) share the commodity list and nothing else, and neither has the pride that makes the Hezekiah page relevant. The silk and fine twined linen of the same verse carry their own low-confidence link to Exodus 26:1.

The five-word run is exact and the verse is the only KJV place where writing-adjacent decoration sits on a temple wall — cherubims and palm trees 'made, and on the wall of the temple'. But Ezekiel 41 is a measured architectural vision with no writing, no interpreter and no message, and Alma 10:2's point is that the writing needed reading. The link at this verse is Daniel 5:5, the KJV's one wall that has to be interpreted.

Ranked above Daniel 5:5 by the n-gram stream because 5:2 happens to contain the string 'the temple which was'. The right verse of the right chapter is 5:5, where the hand writes upon the wall, and 5:25-28, where the writing is interpreted; 5:2's temple is the one whose vessels are being drunk from in Babylon. The link is filed at Alma 10:2 against Daniel 5:5 with 5:25 composited.

The strongest n-gram in the verse — a six-word run, and the chapter's top-ranked candidate. It is nonetheless the wrong verse. Isaiah 11:2's subject is 'the spirit of the LORD' resting upon the messianic shoot, and the resting is permanent endowment; Alma 10:7's is 'the blessing of the Lord' resting upon a house that has taken in a prophet, which is the domestic reward of 2 Kings 4 and Genesis 39:5's 'the blessing of the LORD was upon all that he had'. Nothing messianic is in view and the grammatical subject differs. A good illustration of CONVENTIONS §9: the n-gram stream ranks by string rarity and cannot see that the two 'rest upon' clauses are about different things.

'As the LORD liveth' is the standard KJV oath formula, in some thirty verses, and the Book of Mormon uses it continuously. 2 Chronicles 18:13 is ranked only because 'even' happens to follow. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

A four-word run whose completion decides it: Romans 1:4 has 'the spirit of holiness' and Alma 10:12 has 'the spirit of prophecy', which is a KJV singleton at Revelation 19:10 and is where the link is filed. Romans 1:4 is a christological formula about the resurrection; the trap here is exactly the one ADJUDICATING §4 names, a window that closes one word early.

exclusions.sharedText: that they might be judged according to
exclusions.reason: The longest run in the chapter, seven words, and the top-ranked candidate for this verse. 1 Peter 4:6 is about the gospel preached to the dead, 'that they might be judged according to men in the flesh' — a statement about the scope of judgment, not about a prosecution. Alma 10:13's sentence is built from the Gospels' entrapment machinery (Mark 12:13, Mark 14:55, Luke 20:20, Matthew 5:25), where the link is filed. The shared string is the passive purpose-clause construction, which the KJV uses everywhere.

exclusions.sharedText: and now I say unto you
exclusions.reason: Six words, and worth a note only because Acts 5:38-39 is a genuine Book of Mormon source elsewhere in this catalogue (1 Nephi 16, 2 Nephi 25). Gamaliel's counsel to leave the apostles alone has no contact with Alma 10:20 beyond the discourse formula, and the verse's real borrowing is Matthew 3:2's whole clause, which the stream ranked below it.

A covenant conditional in the KJV's stock form, and tempting because Alma 10:23's protasis-apodosis shape genuinely is covenantal. But Exodus 19:5 promises a peculiar treasure for obedience and Alma threatens the sword for expelling the righteous; the shared words are the connective skeleton, and the conditional formula recurs in dozens of KJV verses.

Joshua 11:20 is God hardening the hearts of the Canaanite kings so that they will come out to battle and be destroyed; Alma 10:30 is the lawyers putting it into their own hearts to remember a grievance. The verb is different (harden / put into), the agent is different (the LORD / the lawyers), and the shared string spans a clause boundary. An artifact of English word order.

Considered, and declined for want of wording rather than for want of a case. Acts 6:13's false witnesses say of Stephen that 'this man ceaseth not to speak blasphemous words against this holy place, and the law', which is the accusation Ammonihah brings against Amulek at 10:26 and 10:28 and is answered the same way — by a speech that indicts the accusers' own custody of the law. But the KJV phrase is 'against this holy place, and the law', not 'against the law', and no distinctive string survives. The Acts 7 contact this chapter does have is verbal and is filed at 10:15 (Acts 7:22).

A five-word run of pure connective tissue. Deuteronomy 15:2's 'And this is the manner of the release' introduces the sabbatical remission of debts; Alma 13:3's 'And this is the manner after which they were ordained' introduces a priesthood. Nothing but the formula of introduction is shared, and it is covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

Ranked at both 13:3 and 13:5, and worth an entry because the string is exact and the sense is not merely different but of a different kind. Numbers 10:14's 'in the first place went the standard of the camp of the children of Judah' is SPATIAL and ordinal — Judah marched at the head of the column. Alma's 'in the first place being left to choose good or evil' and 'in the first place they were on the same standing with their brethren' are logical and temporal: originally, to begin with, before anything else was true of them. The two idioms are homonyms in English and share no situation. Alma 13:3 and 13:5 are adjudicated to 1 Peter 1:2 and its neighbours instead.

A genuine KJV phrase — it occurs in exactly two verses, John 1:18 and John 3:18 — but by Alma 13 it is one of the Book of Mormon's own standing titles for Christ and not a fresh borrowing at this verse; the machine will propose John 1:18 or 3:18 at every occurrence of it in the book. The chapter's real Johannine contact is at 13:9, where 'the only begotten of the Father, … full of grace, equity and truth' reproduces two singletons from John 1:14 in John's order, and that is where the link is filed.

The best near-miss in the chapter, and it deserves the space. Alma 13 says 'the order of his Son' or 'this holy order' fourteen times, and the KJV verse that comes closest to the string is Luke 1:8: Zacharias 'executed the priest's office before God in the order of his course.' Both verses are about priests and the word 'order' is in both, which is exactly what makes it a trap. Luke's 'order' is the rota — the twenty-four courses of 1 Chronicles 24, of which Zacharias belonged to the course of Abia, and 'the order of his course' means no more than 'when his shift came round'. Alma's 'order' is an eternal priesthood conferring a status, the sense the KJV carries only in 'after the order of Melchizedek'. The chapter's priesthood vocabulary comes from Psalm 110:4 through Hebrews 5-7, where the links at 13:14 and 13:15 are filed; Luke 1:8 contributes a duty roster.

Four words of relative-clause boilerplate; Psalm 65:9's river of God 'which is full of water' has nothing to do with a Son full of grace and truth. The verse's real source is John 1:14, where both of the phrases Alma completes are KJV singletons.
Narrative boilerplate; Acts 20:8's many lights in the upper chamber at Troas. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

exclusions.sharedText: had said these words unto them
exclusions.reason: The chapter's longest machine-ranked run and worth naming for that reason alone: six words in sequence, and worth nothing. 'When he had said these words unto them, he abode still in Galilee' is a scene-closing formula, and Alma 13:21's 'when Alma had said these words unto them, he stretched forth his hand' is the same formula opening a scene. Length is not evidence (ADJUDICATING §4). The link at this verse is 2 Corinthians 6:2, which shares four words and decides a mediation.

A real four-word phrase but far too widely distributed to point anywhere: it occurs in seven KJV verses, from Abraham taking the knife (Genesis 22:10) to Moses over the sea (Exodus 14:27) to Jesus catching Peter (Matthew 14:31). Nothing in Alma 13:21 selects among them.

The Babel formula, already covered at Mosiah 28:17 where the same run was ranked and sent to Genesis 11:9. Alma 13:22's use is the Book of Mormon's own dispersal idiom. The link at this verse is Luke 2:10 fused with Luke 1:19, on the phrase 'glad tidings of great joy', which is in no KJV verse and is made of two that are.
Four connective words. David executing judgment and justice over Israel has no contact with angels sounding glad tidings.
A four-word run that spans a clause boundary in both verses and is an artifact of the KJV's 'for to' infinitive. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

The right string and the wrong verse. Romans 1:4 completes as 'according to the spirit of HOLINESS'; Alma 13:26 completes as 'according to the spirit of PROPHECY which was in them', and both of those endings are KJV singletons elsewhere — 'the spirit of prophecy' at Revelation 19:10, and 'which was in them' at 1 Peter 1:11, where the subject is 'the Spirit of Christ which was in them' testifying beforehand of his sufferings. 1 Peter 1:10-12 supplies not only the clause but the whole situation of Alma 13:24-26: prophets who spoke beforehand, a later generation to whom they ministered, and angels. The link is filed there.
Connective narrative furniture. Absalom is sent to his own house under sentence; Alma returns to his to rest. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.
Cardinal-direction boilerplate in a geographical notice. 1 Chronicles 7:29, ranked at the same verse on 'by the borders of the', is the same case.
Connective. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5; Joshua 24:3, ranked here on 'throughout all the land', is the same.

'Three days' journey' occurs in seven KJV verses and by itself points nowhere; in this book it has already been adjudicated on Exodus 15:22 at 1 Nephi 2:6, where the wilderness march is the frame. Alma 8:6 is not a march but an arrival at a city, and the KJV's one verse measuring a CITY by three days' journey is Jonah 3:3, of Nineveh. The phrase is therefore treated here as supporting evidence for the Jonah type-scene, and the link is filed at Alma 8:16.
'The hearts of the people' occurs across the historical books and carries no signal. Joshua 7:5's hearts melt at Ai; Alma 8:9's are held by Satan.

exclusions.sharedText: behold an angel of the Lord
exclusions.reason: 'An angel of the Lord appeared' is the KJV's standard annunciation formula (Matthew 1:20, 2:13, 2:19, Luke 1:11, 2:9, Acts 5:19, 12:7 and more), and the Book of Mormon uses it throughout. Nothing distinguishes Matthew 2:19 from the rest. Deuteronomy 28:20 and Luke 1:8, also ranked at this verse, are pure boilerplate.

A tempting rarity that will not survive reading either context. 'Lift up thine head' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 40:13, and 'lift up thy head' in exactly one, Genesis 40:19 — the two halves of Joseph's prison interpretations, where the same idiom means restoration for the butler and decapitation for the baker. The angel's 'lift up thy head and rejoice' to Alma has no prison, no dream, no Joseph, and no pun; the idiom in his mouth is the ordinary one of Psalm 3:3 and Luke 21:28 ('lift up your heads'), neither of which Alma matches word for word either. Recorded because a KJV singleton in a four-word run is exactly the kind of match this register exists to talk a reader out of.

Ranked first at this verse. David sends Hushai back to Jerusalem to defeat Ahithophel's counsel; the angel sends Alma back to Ammonihah to preach destruction. Five words of ordinary commission and nothing else. The verse's link is filed at Alma 8:16 on Jonah 3:1-4.

'Statutes and judgments' is Deuteronomic boilerplate occurring in dozens of KJV verses; the triad with 'commandments' is nearly as common. Joshua 23:16, ranked at the same verse on 'which he hath given unto', is connective.

The string is a KJV singleton and the sense is inverted, which makes it the register's kind of entry rather than the catalogue's. Nathan's 'Thou art the man' identifies David as the guilty party in his own parable; Amulek's 'thou art the man which an angel saith in a vision, Thou shalt receive' identifies Alma as the man an angel promised him. One is an indictment sprung on a king, the other a recognition offered to a stranger, and outside the four words the two verses share nothing — no parable, no vision in Nathan, no accusation in Amulek. 1 Kings 21:2, ranked here by the machine on 'my house and I will', is Ahab bargaining for Naboth's vineyard and is pure connective tissue.

'Bread and meat' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 45:23, where it is part of an inventory of provisions Joseph sends his father on ten she-asses. Amulek 'brought forth bread and meat, and sat before Alma' — a meal set before a guest, not a consignment. The singleton is an accident of the KJV's translation choices ('corn and bread and meat'), and the verse's real background is 1 Kings 13's prophet fed in a house, filed at Alma 8:18. Judges 19:21 and Numbers 17:5, ranked here, are connective.

'Gave thanks to God' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 27:35, where Paul takes bread, gives thanks and breaks it before a shipful of men — a scene with obvious eucharistic shaping, and Alma 8:22's 'Alma ate bread and was filled … and he gave thanks unto God' invites the comparison. But the Book of Mormon reads 'unto God', which occurs in no KJV verse in this collocation, so the singleton is not actually matched; and 'gave thanks' with bread is common to every KJV meal formula (Matthew 15:36, 26:27, Luke 22:17, John 6:11, 1 Corinthians 11:24). Too little to adjudicate.
The same phrase excluded at Alma 7:5, and for the same reason: it is Alma's own formula of authorization, not a borrowing from Romans 1:4's 'spirit of holiness'.
Connective. Matthew 4:17, ranked at 8:32 on 'began to preach and to', is the same case — the phrase is the KJV's ordinary way of starting a ministry, and the Book of Mormon uses it continuously.

'Fierce anger' occurs in twenty KJV verses, mostly Jeremiah and Isaiah, and 'I will not turn away' in nine, seven of them the refrain of Amos 1-2. Alma 8:29's 'I will visit this people in mine anger; yea, and I will not turn my fierce anger away' is prophetic-threat diction assembled from the common stock; no single verse is in view, and the Amos refrain — 'I will not turn away the punishment thereof' — has a different object. The verse's real interest is structural and is argued at Alma 8:16, where 'the word came to Alma, saying, Go' answers Jonah 3:1-2.

A KJV singleton and a real contributor, retained as `composite` on the link at this verse rather than as a source in its own right. Alma 8:31's 'that the Lord might show forth his power in them' has Romans 9:17's syntax — purpose clause, shew, power, in, object pronoun — and Romans 9:17 is spoken of Pharaoh, which suits a chapter about hardened hearts. But the four-word narratorial formula that opens Alma's clause, 'this was done that', occurs in exactly three KJV verses and all three are Matthew's, and only Matthew 26:56 supplies the surrounding argument of power deliberately not exercised at an arrest. The link is filed on Matthew 26:56.

exclusions.sharedText: which the Lord had given them
exclusions.reason: Connective. Joshua 4:10, ranked at the same verse on 'unto the people according to', is the same. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

exclusions.sharedText: get gain … according to their employ
exclusions.reason: 'Now it was for the sole purpose for to get gain, because they recieved wages according to their employ' repeats Alma 10:32's 'the object of these Lawyers were to get gain; and they got gain according to their employ' almost word for word, twelve verses later and in the same narrator's voice. James 4:13's KJV singleton 'get gain' is adjudicated at Alma 10:32 (and first, for the whole corpus, at 2 Nephi 26:20). This is the formula recurring within one sitting, not a fresh borrowing, and CONVENTIONS §4 files it here rather than duplicating the row.

exclusions.sharedText: for behold the day cometh that
exclusions.reason: The chapter's highest-scoring n-gram, six words, and it is a prophetic discourse opener that the KJV uses in some form throughout Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos and Malachi. Malachi 4:1's day burns as an oven and leaves neither root nor branch; Alma 11:41's day raises the dead to be judged, which is Revelation 20:12-13's scene and where the link is filed. A clean instance of CONVENTIONS §9: the stream ranks a rare string, not a rare thought.

'Rise from the dead' is the standard KJV formula and appears in a dozen verses. Mark 12:25 is the Sadducees' question about marriage in the resurrection and shares nothing else with Alma 11:41. Worth a note only because Mark 12 has genuinely supplied this stretch of the Book of Mormon elsewhere — 12:13 at Alma 10:13 and 12:15 at Alma 11:23 — which makes a third contact look plausible until the wording is checked.

A five-word run of pure connective tissue. Hebrews 6:4's impossibility is that of renewing apostates to repentance; Alma 11:34's is that of God denying his word. Tempting only because both sentences are about a limit on what God will do, and the resemblance evaporates on reading either whole verse. The link at this verse is Matthew 1:21.

Isaiah 44:8's 'Is there a God beside me? yea, there is no God; I know not any' is God's own denial that other gods exist; Alma 11:24's 'thou knowest that there is a God' is an accusation that a man is denying the one God he knows of. The shared string is the interrogative-plus-existential skeleton, and the two verses are making opposite claims with it. Isaiah 44 is in view elsewhere in this chapter — 44:6's 'I am the first, and I am the last' stands behind the Revelation 22:13 quotation at 11:39 — which is what makes the false match worth recording.

exclusions.sharedText: to the judge and the judge
exclusions.reason: Luke 12:58 is the Lukan parallel of Matthew 5:25 and shares the same debt-court chain — adversary, magistrate, judge, officer, prison. It is composited into the link filed at Alma 11:2 against John 10:1 rather than given a row of its own, because Matthew's form is the one Alma 10:13 has already drawn on ('cast into prison') and the two Gospel versions cannot be separated here. Recorded so that a reader arriving at Luke 12:58 is sent to the right place.

exclusions.sharedText: the body … in its perfect form
exclusions.reason: Ranked on incidental burial vocabulary. Alma 11:43's subject is the reassembly of limb and joint at the resurrection; John 19:40's is the wrapping of Jesus's body in linen and spices. No shared content word carries any weight and the resemblance is entirely in the noun 'body'.

“A cunning man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and it is tempting to hang Amlici's characterisation on it. The verse is Huram of Tyre's letter to Solomon introducing the craftsman Huram-abi — 'a cunning man, endued with understanding', skilful in gold and silver and brass and fine linen — where 'cunning' means skilled and is a recommendation. Alma 2:1's cunning is deceit, and the sentence's real KJV source is the Pauline formula 'as to the wisdom of the world', adjudicated at this verse.

A four-word run, and the inversion is genuinely inviting — Acts 13:22 has God raising up David 'to be their king', Alma 2:9 has a faction consecrating Amlici to be theirs. But the run carries no distinctive vocabulary, Paul's speech at Antioch is about the succession from Saul to David rather than about kingmaking as such, and the chapter's kingmaking language is adjudicated at 2:7 from 1 Samuel 8:7, which is a KJV singleton and supplies the whole scene. Joshua 9:2's 'they gathered themselves together' is excluded with it as connective.
Four words of regnal boilerplate; Daniel 9:1 is a dating formula for Darius the Mede. Nothing else in the verse touches Daniel.

'The people of God' occurs in five KJV verses and is the Book of Mormon's ordinary term for the covenant community from Mosiah onward. 1 Peter 2:10's argument — that Gentiles who were not a people are now the people of God — has no purchase on a verse whose point is that one Nephite faction has taken a leader's name and the other has kept the old one.

A five-word run, and the KJV verse behind it is about migratory birds — the stork, the turtle, the crane and the swallow, which observe the season of their arrival while Israel does not know the LORD's judgment. Alma 2:13's 'the time of their coming' is an invading army's. The string is real and the sense has nothing in common; this is the trap ADJUDICATING §4 names as rare word, wrong sense.
Five words of military connective tissue with no content word shared beyond 'armies'. 2 Chronicles 16:4 is Benhadad's raid on the cities of Israel at Asa's request.

“Strengthen the hand” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the definition of the sin of Sodom: 'neither did she strengthen the hand of the poor and needy'. In Ezekiel the phrase names something *not* done, for the poor; in Alma 2:18 it is the Lord strengthening an army's hand in battle. The singleton is real and the sense is opposed, so the row is excluded here — but the same verse is a live source elsewhere in this book, adjudicated at Alma 1:32 for its pride, idleness, abundance and poor-and-needy, and a reader who arrives at 2:18 by way of the phrase should be sent there.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that on the morrow
exclusions.reason: The longest run in the chapter, nine words, and every one of them connective — the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1 covers this class. Aaron's rod budding has nothing to do with returning spies. Joshua 6:14 ('returned into the camp'), Acts 23:32 ('on the morrow they') and Genesis 21:32 ('they returned into the') are excluded with it. The verse's real intertext is the Numbers 13-14 spy report, adjudicated two verses later at 2:25.

Judah standing before the LORD with their wives and children before battle against a great multitude is a genuine thematic neighbour to Alma 2:25-28, and it is recorded here for a reader who reaches for it. It is displaced by Numbers 14:3, whose 'our wives and our children' is a KJV singleton in the Book of Mormon's own first-person form and which brings the spy-report scene of Numbers 13 with it. See the link at this verse.
A compass bearing. Alma 2:34 uses 'west of the river Sidon' twice and the run is an artifact of that repetition; Exodus 39:19's 'which was on the' is excluded with it.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that when they had
exclusions.reason: Nine words of connective tissue, scoring on length alone. Amos's locusts are not in view.
Standard battle narration; Joshua 7:4 is the rout at Ai. Exodus 16:35's 'the borders of the land' is excluded with it as a geographical formula.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass as I
exclusions.reason: The book's commonest narrative formula. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5. Acts 22:17 at 9:31 and Joshua 1:1 at 9:33 are the same string and the same non-finding.

'In one day' occurs in thirteen KJV verses and cannot identify a source; Isaiah 47:9's 'in a moment in one day' is the closest in tone, an oracle against Babylon's widowhood. The Ammonihahites' boast — 'if thou shouldst prophesy that this great city should be destroyed in one day' — is answered, in this catalogue's reading, by Isaiah 13:22's 'her days shall not be prolonged', which Alma quotes at 9:18 and which closes the KJV's principal Babylon oracle. The link is filed at Alma 9:18.

'Stiffnecked people' occurs in exactly six KJV verses — Exodus 32:9, 33:3, 33:5, 34:9, Deuteronomy 9:6 and 9:13 — all of Israel at or after the golden calf, and no one of them is distinguishable as the source. The Book of Mormon uses the epithet throughout (see the direct-address form adjudicated at 2 Nephi 25:28 on Exodus 33:5), and Alma 9:5 and 9:31 use it as settled vocabulary. The transfer of Israel's own epithet to a Nephite city is noted in the figural row at Alma 9:31 rather than catalogued as a borrowing here.

'Perverse generation' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 17:17 and Luke 9:41, and both read 'O faithless and perverse generation' — Jesus at the foot of the mount of transfiguration, exasperated with disciples who could not cast out a spirit. Alma 9:8's 'O ye wicked and perverse generation' substitutes the adjective that carries the sense, and what remains is one adjective and one noun. Deuteronomy 32:5's 'a perverse and crooked generation' and Philippians 2:15's 'crooked and perverse nation' are equally close and equally unprovable. Recorded because the vocative shape is genuinely arresting and a careful reader might accept it.

'Into the hands of their enemies' is the Deuteronomistic formula for defeat and occurs across Judges, Kings, Nehemiah and Psalms. Alma 9:10 inverts it — delivered OUT of the hands of their enemies — which is the same formula's other half. No single verse is in view.

A five-word run across a conditional and a promise, and the two promises are opposite in kind. John 15:10's 'If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love' is about union with Christ; Alma 9:13 is quoting the Lehite land-promise, 'inasmuch as ye shall keep my commandments, ye shall prosper in the land', which is the Book of Mormon's own covenant formula from 1 Nephi 2:20 and has no New Testament source. 1 Kings 9:6, ranked at the same verse, is closer in kind — Solomon warned that turning from the commandments will cut Israel off from the land — but shares only 'not keep my commandments', and the Book of Mormon formula is internal.
Connective covenant diction, distributed across the KJV. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

exclusions.sharedText: I say unto you that if ye
exclusions.reason: Six words of speech formula and a conditional. Luke 6:37, ranked at the same verse on 'and ye shall be', is the same. The verse's real borrowing is Isaiah 13:22's 'days shall not be prolonged', filed as the link at Alma 9:18.

exclusions.sharedText: which is and which is to come
exclusions.reason: Revelation's threefold formula is 'which is, and which was, and which is to come' (1:4, 1:8) or 'which was, and is, and is to come' (4:8, 11:17, 16:5). Alma 9:20 has 'of that which has been, and which is, and which is to come' — the same three tenses in a different order, attached to knowledge granted to a people rather than to a divine name, which is the point of Revelation's version. The Book of Mormon uses the tense-triad as its own idiom for prophetic knowledge (compare Words of Mormon 1:4, Mosiah 3:1). 'Highly favored' in the same verse is likewise a standing Book of Mormon formula from 1 Nephi 1:1; where it does carry a KJV link it is Luke 1:28's, adjudicated at Alma 13:23.

exclusions.sharedText: the gift of speaking with tongues
exclusions.reason: Alma 9:21's catalogue of gifts — the spirit of prophecy, the spirit of revelation, speaking with tongues, preaching, the Holy Ghost, translation — invites 1 Corinthians 12:8-10, and 'divers kinds of tongues' and 'the interpretation of tongues' stand there in a list of the same kind. But the KJV's phrase is never 'the gift of X' item by item, the nouns diverge at every point that could be tested ('translation' is not a KJV gift at all, and 'preaching' is not in Paul's list), and the shared material reduces to the word 'tongues'. A conceptual resemblance with too little verbal contact to adjudicate.

exclusions.sharedText: the Lord hath sent his angel
exclusions.reason: 'Hath sent his angel' occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Daniel 3:28, Daniel 6:22 and Acts 12:11 — and all three are rescues from a king's hand, which Alma 9:25 is not. Nothing distinguishes Acts from the two in Daniel. The verse's links are filed at Alma 9:25 on Jonah 3:8 ('cry mightily') and on Matthew 3:2 with Luke 21:31 ('the kingdom of Heaven is nigh at hand').

Isaiah 60:2's 'his glory shall be seen upon thee' shares a five-word run with Alma 9:26's 'and his glory shall be the glory of the only begotten of the Father', and the run stops one word before the phrase that matters. The verse's source is John 1:14, whose two KJV singletons Alma reproduces in order, with Matthew 25:31 supplying 'shall come in his glory'; the link is filed there.

exclusions.sharedText: prepare ye the way of the Lord
exclusions.reason: A verbatim six-word run of the KJV, and fuller than the form at Alma 7:9 — 9:28 restores the 'ye' that 7:9 dropped. It is registered here rather than catalogued again because it is the same speaker returning to the same borrowing inside one book: the argument, including the mediation test that decides for Matthew 3:3 over Isaiah 40:3 on 'his paths', is made at Alma 7:9, and 9:25's fusion of Matthew 3:2 with Luke 21:31 is filed separately. A reader arriving at 9:28 should be sent to both.

'Every man shall reap a reward of their works … if they have been righteous, they shall reap the salvation of their souls … if they have been evil, they shall reap the damnation of their souls' has the shape of Galatians 6:7-8's sowing and reaping to the flesh or to the Spirit, and Revelation 22:12's 'my reward is with me, to give every man according as his work shall be' supplies the reward. Neither is verbally present beyond the single verb, and the balanced righteous/evil antithesis is the Book of Mormon's own construction. Not enough to adjudicate at any confidence.

exclusions.sharedText: made an end of speaking unto the people
exclusions.reason: The chapter's longest machine run, eight words, and worth nothing. 'Made an end of speaking' occurs in nine KJV verses, from Moses to Samson to Jeremiah, and Deuteronomy 20:9's continuation is about appointing captains of the armies. The Book of Mormon uses the formula scores of times to close a discourse. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5; the link at this verse is John 5:39, on three words.
Narrative boilerplate. Nehemiah 8:16's people go forth to fetch olive branches for the booths; Alma 14:5's go forth to bear witness at a trial. No contact beyond the motion verb.

A five-word run spanning a clause boundary, and the direction is reversed: 2 Corinthians 6:17 is a command to the faithful to come out from among the unbelievers, while Alma 14:7 has the unbelievers casting the faithful out. Connective tissue in both.
A run that exists only because 'the word of God' ends a clause in both verses. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

A real five-word run and the best machine proposal in the chapter, so it gets an entry rather than silence. 'Cast them into the fire' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Jeremiah 22:7 and John 15:6, and John's continues 'and they are burned', which Alma 14:8's 'that they might be burned' appears to answer. But John 15:6 is a parable of fruitless branches gathered by unnamed men, with no agent, no victim and no book; the scene Alma 14:8 is enacting — an authority burning a prophetic record, with the phrase 'consumed in the fire' following at 14:9 and 14:14 — is Jeremiah 36:23, where the link is filed.

The KJV singleton is real and is adjudicated for this book at Alma 13:4, where it stands with the second half of the Book of Mormon's doublet, 'blindness of their minds' from Ephesians 4:18. Alma 14:11's use is the same narrator's formula fifteen verses later and is recorded there as a recurrence.

Ranked twice, from 1 Samuel 24:6 and 26:23, and the coincidence is closer than it looks — David twice refuses to 'stretch forth mine hand against the LORD's anointed' when he has the power and the provocation, and Alma refuses to stretch forth his hand when he has the power to stop a burning. But the refusals are of opposite acts. David declines to KILL a man he could kill; Alma declines to SAVE people he could save, and declines because the killing must be allowed to stand as evidence. Recorded because the string is exact and the situation is a genuine trap: a reader who accepted it would have Alma refusing to harm someone, which is the reverse of what the verse says.

2 Kings 6:18 is Elisha smiting the Syrian army with blindness at his prayer; Alma 14:14 is a judge hitting two bound prisoners in the face. Same five words, opposite agents. The verse's real Old Testament source is 1 Kings 22:24, where a prophet is struck on the cheek and jailed, and the link is filed there.
Four words of relative clause. Ezra 2:1 is the list of returning exiles. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that when they had
exclusions.reason: A nine-word run and the longest in the chapter's dossier — and pure boilerplate, the point ADJUDICATING §4 makes about length. Amos 7:2's locusts have made an end of eating the grass. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1.
A run created by a clause boundary in both verses; 1 Corinthians 14:34 is about women keeping silence in the churches. Alma 14:19's silence is Matthew 27:12's, and the row at 14:17 carries it.
Five words, and the sense is inverted: the LORD has HEARD the words of this people and approves them; Alma and Amulek refuse to ANSWER the words of this people. Connective in both.

The wrong nakedness, and worth an entry because the string is exact and Eden is the first place an English reader's mind goes. Genesis 3:7's nakedness is discovered — 'the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked' — and it is shame at a state that was always the case. Alma 14:22's is inflicted: 'they also did take from them their clothes, that they were naked', a deliberate humiliation of prisoners. The verse's source is 1 Corinthians 4:11, where hunger, thirst and nakedness are the three marks of an apostle's treatment, all three in Paul's order, and that is where the link is filed.

A regnal-year date formula. Both verses date an imprisonment by a ruler's tenth year, which is the sort of coincidence a date formula produces about once a chapter; Jeremiah 32:1 is Zedekiah's tenth year and Alma 14:23 is the tenth year of the reign of the judges. Nothing but the calendar is shared.
Four words. 1 Kings 6:15 is the cedar panelling of Solomon's temple. The links at this verse are Acts 16:26 and Matthew 27:51.

Connective, though the surrounding situation is closer than most — Jeremiah 38 is a prophet let down into a dungeon by the officials he warned, and drawn out again. The wording contributes nothing, and the prison-deliverance the chapter is actually following is Acts 16:22-29, filed at 14:27.

Recorded as a negative finding rather than a rejection of a machine proposal. Alma 14:29 closes the chapter with its most vivid image — the people fled 'even as a goat fleeth with her young from two lions' — and it has no KJV background at all. The KJV's lion similes are of the lion attacking, not of the prey; 'two lions' occurs in exactly two KJV verses and both are the carved beasts flanking Solomon's throne; and no KJV verse pairs a goat with a lion. Amos 3:12's shepherd rescuing scraps from a lion's mouth is the nearest thing and shares nothing. A catalogue of borrowings is more useful if it says where the borrowing stops, and in a chapter this saturated with the KJV the one original simile is worth marking.

Top-ranked on the verse at rarity 2.00 with a six-word run, and it is the wrong one of the KJV's two. 'Power and authority' occurs in exactly two verses, both Luke's: at 20:20 it is the Roman governor's, to whom spies hope to deliver Jesus up, and at 9:1 it is what Jesus gives the twelve when he sends them out. Alma 17:3 is about missionaries who 'taught with power and authority, even as with the power and authority of God' — a delegated commission, which is 9:1's sense and the opposite of 20:20's. The link is filed at Luke 9:1.

exclusions.sharedText: to the knowledge of the truth
exclusions.reason: Ranked here and again at 17:2. 'Knowledge of the truth' occurs in three KJV verses (1 Timothy 2:4, 2 Timothy 3:7, Hebrews 10:26) and is a fixed formula of the Pastorals rather than a quotable phrase; 2 Timothy 3:7's point is people 'ever learning, and never able to come' to it, which is the reverse of Alma 17:4's success in bringing many to it. Acts 18:11's 'teaching the word of God among them', also proposed here, is narrative boilerplate covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

The machine's only candidate on the verse, at rarity 2.00, and the sense is unrelated. 1 Corinthians 7:34's 'holy both in body and in spirit' distinguishes the unmarried woman's undivided attention from the married woman's; Alma 17:5's 'they did suffer much, both in body and in mind' is a hardship catalogue. The construction is an English merism and nothing else is shared. The verse's real sources are 2 Corinthians 11:26-27, where 'journeyings' and 'in hunger and thirst' come from consecutive verses.

A five-word run at rarity 2.00, and the two uses are opposed. Jeremiah 29:32 is a sentence of exclusion — Shemaiah 'shall not have a man to dwell among this people' — pronounced on a false prophet; Alma 17:23 is Ammon asking to be let in, 'I desire to dwell among this people for a time'. The KJV verse is a curse and the Book of Mormon's is a petition, and the shared words are the ones any such sentence would need.

exclusions.sharedText: in the service of the king
exclusions.reason: A six-word run of administrative English joining the Hebronite officers to Ammon's three days at Lamoni's court. Neither verse is doing anything the other is; covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

A tempting count with nothing behind it, and worth recording as a specimen of the trap. 'The edge of his sword' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 89:43 — but 'edge of the sword' occurs in thirty-four, and the possessive that makes the phrase a singleton is forced by the grammar of any sentence in which a named man uses his own weapon. The senses are also opposed: Psalm 89:43 is God turning back an anointed king's sword-edge so that he cannot stand in battle, and Alma 17:37 is a man's sword-edge doing exactly what he intends with it. The link at this verse is 'smote off', which the KJV has twice.

Raised because the chapter has already used Luke 9:1 at 17:3, so a second contact with the same sending would be a pattern. 'For a testimony' occurs in twelve KJV verses, and in Luke 9:5 and its Synoptic parallels it is dust shaken from the feet of a town that would not hear — a sign against, left behind. Alma 17:39's severed arms are carried in to the king as evidence of what happened, a sign for rather than against, and to the man being persuaded rather than the man refusing. The formula is too common and the direction too different to catalogue; it is noted here because the Luke 9 frame at 17:3 is real and a reader may want to weigh it.

exclusions.sharedText: What wilt thou that I shall do unto thee
exclusions.reason: Luke 18:41 is the same question in the same episode — blind Bartimaeus, told by Luke instead of Mark — and it reads 'What wilt thou that I shall do unto thee?' Alma 18:14 has 'should', which is Mark 10:51's auxiliary, and 'for thee', which is Mark 10:36's preposition; both of Alma's departures from Luke are Marcan, and both of its agreements are with Mark. The link is filed at Mark 10:51.

exclusions.sharedText: the thoughts and intents of the heart
exclusions.reason: 'He knows all the thoughts and intents of the heart' reproduces Hebrews 4:12's phrase, but it is by this point a standing Book of Mormon formula and not a fresh borrowing at Alma 18:32. The argument for it was made at Mosiah 5:13, where five words of the KJV singleton are reproduced exactly; within Alma the phrase enters earlier than this chapter and falls to be adjudicated there. Note that it is a different phrase from the Daniel 2:30 'thoughts of thy heart' catalogued twelve verses earlier at 18:20, and the two should not be collapsed: Hebrews' is about God's knowledge of anyone, Daniel's about an interpreter's knowledge of a particular king.

'All the journeyings of their fathers in the wilderness, and all their sufferings with hunger and thirst' repeats the pair adjudicated at Alma 17:5, where 'journeyings' (2 KJV verses, one of them 2 Corinthians 11:26) and 'in hunger and thirst' (a KJV singleton at 11:27) were taken from consecutive verses of Paul's hardship catalogue. Here the same two words are applied to Lehi's company rather than to the missionaries, inside Ammon's rehearsal of the record. A narrator reusing his own formula within one book is recorded as a recurrence, not a second borrowing (ADJUDICATING §4); see the recurrenceRefs on the link at 17:5.

exclusions.sharedText: from the foundation of the world
exclusions.reason: 'The plan of redemption, which was prepared from the foundation of the world' is close to Matthew 25:34's 'inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world', and the participle is shared. But 'from the foundation of the world' occurs in nine KJV verses across Matthew, Luke, Hebrews, 1 Peter and Revelation, and it is one of the Book of Mormon's own standing phrases; what is prepared differs in every case. Nothing here identifies Matthew's judgment scene in particular.

A clean example of a singleton that proves nothing. 'Fell unto the earth' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 6:13, and Alma 18:42 has the phrase word for word — but Revelation's subject is the stars of heaven falling at the sixth seal, 'even as a fig tree casteth her untimely figs', and Alma's is a king fainting. The three-word agreement is the ordinary English for a body going down and the KJV happens to spend it on a cosmic sign. The echo at this verse is filed at Revelation 1:17, on the situation rather than the string.

exclusions.sharedText: in the sixth year of the reign of
exclusions.reason: The regnal-year formula. Alma dates every paragraph of this chapter by the reign of the judges ('in the sixth year', 'in the seventh year', 'in the eighth year', 'in the commencement of the ninth year'), and the KJV dates Persian and Babylonian documents the same way, so a long run is guaranteed at 4:1, 4:5, 4:9 and 4:20 without any borrowing. Ezra 6:15 and Ezekiel 8:1 are the two highest-ranked and neither has a further word in common. One entry covers all four verses.

'Trodden under foot' occurs in five KJV verses and in Alma 4:2 it is literal: an army has trampled standing grain. Matthew 5:13's savourless salt and Hebrews 10:29's trampling of the Son of God are both figurative and neither shares another word with the verse. Isaiah 28:3's crown of pride 'trodden under feet' is closer to the chapter's theme and further from its wording; no source is identifiable.

The machine's top candidate at 4:4, 4:5 and 4:9 alike, on four words that Alma uses as the standing name of his institution throughout the book. 1 Corinthians 10:32 does bear on this chapter, but at 4:10, as the summary of the stumblingblock argument of 1 Corinthians 8-10; it is filed there as a composite. The bare phrase carries no signal at any of the three verses.

Connective tissue joining Alma's commodity list to its consequence. Hezekiah's 'in all these things is the life of my spirit' is a statement about recovery from illness and shares nothing else with the verse. Covered in kind by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5; entered here only because it was the sole candidate the machine offered at a verse that does have a source, Ezekiel 16:13.

Ezekiel 3:20 is the only KJV verse printing the word as 'stumbling-block', which is the form 1920 introduced into this verse against the 1830 text's two words — so it looks like the source and is not. In Ezekiel the stumblingblock is laid by God before a righteous man who has turned to iniquity; in Alma 4:10 it is laid inadvertently by the church before people outside it. The sense is Pauline and the link is filed at this verse to 1 Corinthians 8:9, with Romans 14:13 as a composite.

A rarity artifact worth naming, because it is the kind that will recur. Searched with both definite articles the string is a KJV singleton at Psalm 35:10, and the count looks decisive; searched as 'poor and needy' it is in seventeen verses, from Deuteronomy 24:14 to Ezekiel 16:49. The doubled article is Alma's own list-making habit ('to the poor and the needy; feeding the hungry'), not a fingerprint of the psalm, and Psalm 35 — a plea for rescue from false witnesses — has nothing else to do with the verse. The pairing that does bear on this chapter is Ezekiel 16:49's, cited in the provenance of the link at 4:6.

The machine's highest-scoring candidate at both 4:13 ('according to the spirit of prophecy') and 4:20 ('according to the spirit of revelation and prophecy'), on a four-word frame that is Alma's standard way of qualifying a claim. Romans 1:4's 'spirit of holiness' completes it differently and the verse is about the declaration of Christ's sonship; nothing else is shared.

Isaiah 52:2's bands are the bands of a captive's neck, to be loosed by the captive herself as Zion shakes off the dust; Alma 4:14's are the bands of death, from which Christ is delivered. Both are bonds and there the agreement stops — 'bands of death' occurs in no KJV verse and is the Book of Mormon's own idiom, running through the next chapter. The verse's real, and thin, contact is with 1 Peter 1:3, filed as a link with its own whyNot.

exclusions.sharedText: according to the voice of the people
exclusions.reason: A real link, adjudicated elsewhere. 'Voice of the people' against 1 Samuel 8:7 is written up at Mosiah 7:9 and again at Mosiah 29:2, where the second use is the argument because Mosiah abolishes the kingship that Israel's voice demanded. By Alma 4:16 the phrase is the constitutional formula of the government Mosiah 29 created and is used four times in Alma 2 before it reaches this verse; here it does no work the earlier adjudications have not done. A reader who arrives at 4:16 should be sent to Mosiah 29:2.

The window closes one word early, in the way the pilot warned about. Matthew 7:24's wise man is defined by what follows — 'which built his house upon a rock' — and is a figure for the hearer who does the sayings of Jesus; Alma 4:16's is a magistrate 'which was among the elders of the church', selected to enact and enforce laws. Nothing but the four words is shared, and the fifth word divides them.

Abraham sitting in the tent door in the heat of the day against Nephihah sitting in the judgment seat. The KJV does have a home for the second phrase — 'judgment seat' occurs in ten verses, eight of them a Roman tribunal (Pilate's, Gallio's, Festus's) and two the judgment seat of Christ — but the Book of Mormon's judgment seat is the office created at Mosiah 29 and used here as a piece of its own constitutional furniture, not as a borrowing. The eschatological sense is adjudicated at 2 Nephi 9:15 and 2 Nephi 33:7.

One of only three KJV verses with the infinitive, and tempting because it is a parable about riches in a chapter about riches: 'I will pull down my barns, and build greater.' But the rich fool pulls down his own storehouses in order to hold more goods, and Alma pulls down pride and contention in order to reclaim people — the verb has opposite objects and opposite motives. The wording goes to Jeremiah 1:10 (mediation-check decided the form against 2 Corinthians 10:4) and the sense to 2 Corinthians 10:4, both recorded at the link.

exclusions.sharedText: which was called the land of
exclusions.reason: Six words of place-naming boilerplate. Deuteronomy's 'all the region of Argob, with all Bashan, which was called the land of giants' shares nothing with Alma's land of Mormon but the naming formula, which the Book of Mormon uses constantly. Covered in kind by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

exclusions.sharedText: behold they were in the midst of
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run built entirely from 'behold', 'they were' and 'in the midst of'. Elisha's servants find themselves in the middle of Samaria; Alma's fathers are in the midst of darkness. The verse does have a source — Ephesians 5:14, filed as a link — and the run is an accident of two common phrases meeting.

A near miss worth recording because the count looks decisive and is not. 'Chains of hell' is the engine of Alma 5:7-10, repeated four times, and it occurs in no KJV verse; the KJV's nearest phrases are 2 Peter 2:4's 'chains of darkness' (a singleton) and Jude 1:6's 'everlasting chains under darkness'. But in both of those the chained are angels, the chaining is permanent, and the purpose is to reserve them unto judgment — whereas Alma's chains are on human beings and the whole point of the passage is that they were loosed. The Book of Mormon has coined its phrase against the KJV's, not from it; 'bands of death' likewise occurs in no KJV verse. No source identifiable.

Isaiah 63:1-3's treader of the winepress, whose 'blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments', and Revelation 19:13's 'vesture dipped in blood' are the KJV's two bloodstained garments, and both are tempting in a passage that has just washed garments in blood at 5:21. Neither will do: in both the blood is the blood of enemies and the stained one is a conqueror, whereas Alma 5:22-23's stains testify that the wearer is a murderer. The verse's real source is the same as 5:21's, Revelation 7:14, used in reverse.

Mis-ranked in the dossier and formulaic in any case: 'the holy spirit of God' is the Book of Mormon's standing designation, used at 5:46 and 5:54 among many, and Ephesians 4:30's 'grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption' shares no other word with any of them.

exclusions.sharedText: and now I say unto you
exclusions.reason: The single commonest connective in this chapter, which uses 'I say unto you' more than forty times as the hinge of a rhetorical question. Ranked at 5:47, 5:57 and 5:59 alike. Gamaliel's counsel to the Sanhedrin has nothing else in common with any of them. One entry covers every occurrence in the chapter.

Ranked at 5:52 and again at 5:53, and genuinely apt in theme — Isaiah 10:33's high ones of stature hewn down and the haughty humbled would suit a sermon against pride. But the chapter's tree, axe, fruit and fire are Matthew 3:10 and 3:12 entire, and the passive 'shall be hewn down and cast into the fire' is that sentence's, not Isaiah's, which has no fire and no fruit. The link is filed at 5:52 to Matthew 3:10; Matthew 7:19 is kept there as a composite because it supplies the relative pronoun.

exclusions.sharedText: setting your hearts upon the vain things of the world, upon your riches
exclusions.reason: Adjudicated at Alma 4:8, where the same clause — riches, vanity, and the setting of the heart — is argued against Psalm 62:9-10 and its KJV singleton 'set not your heart upon'. Alma 5:53 repeats it verbatim as part of the sermon's roll-call of the previous chapter's charges. The link at this verse is to Hebrews 10:29, for 'trample the holy one under your feet'; the riches clause belongs to 4:8.

exclusions.sharedText: turning your backs upon the poor, and the needy
exclusions.reason: The same charge, in almost the same words, as Alma 4:12 — 'turning their backs upon the needy, and the naked' — where it is adjudicated against Matthew 25:44's roll of the neglected. Alma 5:55 is Alma quoting his own indictment back at the congregation he made it about, which is the sermon's method throughout this section (compare 5:53's costly apparel against 4:6). A reader arriving at 5:55 should be sent to Alma 4:12; nothing is added here that the earlier row does not carry.

Five words of promissory syntax. Deuteronomy 1:39 gives the land to the children who had no knowledge of good and evil; Alma 5:58 grants an inheritance at the right hand. The inheritance-at-the-right-hand image is Matthew 25:33-34's and is recorded in the recurrence of the link at 5:16.

A good example of a string match whose sense is exactly inverted. Jeremiah 17:13's 'they that depart from me shall be written in the earth' is a curse — to be written in dust is to be erased — and Alma 5:58's 'the names of the righteous shall be written in the Book of Life' is the blessing. The two verses use the same four words to say opposite things about the same people. The link at 5:57-58 is to Psalm 69:28, which has both halves of the Book of Mormon's antithesis in one verse.

exclusions.sharedText: shepherds that do not feed the flock
exclusions.reason: Ezekiel 34 is the Old Testament's long arraignment of shepherds who feed themselves and not the flock, and it is the passage a reader expecting a source for Alma 5:59's rhetorical question will reach for first. It will not bear the weight: Ezekiel's shepherds are the rulers of Israel and his complaint is that they have not sought the strayed, whereas Alma's question is about a shepherd who does his job — 'what shepherd is there among you having many sheep, doth not watch over them?' — and the wolf that answers it is not in Ezekiel 34 at all but in Acts 20:29 and John 10:12, where the link is filed. Ezekiel 34:11-16 does stand behind the Book of Mormon's shepherd language generally and is worth a reader's attention; it is not the source here.

Four words. The kingdom established in the hand of Solomon after an execution has nothing to do with a church established in a city, and 'established' is one of this book's commonest verbs. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

Ranked at 6:1 and again at 6:7 on the Book of Mormon's standing way of locating a congregation ('the church which was established in the city of Zarahemla', 'the church which was in the city of Zarahemla'). Acts 11:22's 'the church which was in Jerusalem' is the same English construction and nothing more; the verse is about Barnabas being sent to Antioch and shares no other word.

exclusions.sharedText: their names were blotted out, that their names were not numbered among those of the righteous
exclusions.reason: Adjudicated one chapter earlier, at Alma 5:57, where the same two clauses are argued against Psalm 69:28's KJV singletons 'blotted out of the book' and 'written with the righteous'. Alma 6:3 is the narrative performing what Alma 5:57 commanded, in the sermon's own words, and the row is recorded there as a recurrence. A reader arriving at 6:3 should be sent to 5:57; the blotting out of names is the sermon's one instruction whose execution the record reports.

exclusions.sharedText: together to hear the word of God
exclusions.reason: Genuinely apt and still not a link. Acts 13:44's 'the next sabbath day came almost the whole city together to hear the word of God' is a congregation assembling to hear preaching, which is what Alma 6:5 describes, so the temptation is real. But every content word in the run is unavoidable for the sense, 'the word of God' is this book's constant phrase, and the two verses agree on nothing else — Acts 13:44 leads to the Jews' envy and Paul turning to the Gentiles. The verse's identifiable source is James 1:5, filed as a link on the much rarer 'liberal'.

Worth an entry because the reversal is attractive and the evidence will not support it. The KJV has 'them that know not God' at 2 Thessalonians 1:8, where they are the objects of vengeance in flaming fire, and 'the Gentiles which know not God' at 1 Thessalonians 4:5 — so Alma 6:6, in which the church fasts and prays 'in behalf of the welfare of the souls of those who knew not God', looks like a deliberate answer to Paul's sentence of judgment. But the Book of Mormon's tense is past, which matches instead 1 Corinthians 1:21 and Galatians 4:8, where the phrase describes the addressees' own former state and carries no threat at all. Four verses, two tenses, and no distinctive word beyond the three; no source is identifiable and the reversal cannot be claimed.

exclusions.sharedText: that they should gather themselves together
exclusions.reason: A six-word run of pure connective syntax; 'gather themselves together' is the KJV's ordinary phrase for an assembly and occurs across both testaments. Ezra 10:7's proclamation summoning the returned exiles to Jerusalem to put away foreign wives has no other contact with a church commanded to meet often for fasting and prayer. The fasting and prayer are Acts 14:23's and are recorded at the link at 6:1.

Topographical boilerplate in a verse that is doing nothing but naming a place — 'the valley that was called Gideon'. Judges 18:28's valley by Bethrehob is a different valley in a different narrative; the shared words are the only way English says the thing.

Alma 6:8 is built of four 'according to' clauses in a row, which is why Romans 16:25 and Romans 1:4 both score here and why neither is a source. 'According to the revelation of the mystery' and 'according to the revelation of the truth of the word' share only the frame. The verse's real borrowings are the two rare phrases inside those clauses — 'the spirit of prophecy' with 'the testimony of Jesus', and 'the Son of God which should come' — both filed as links.
The same candidate ranked at Alma 2:25 and is discharged there; here the phrase is simply a list of what men return home to. Ezra 2:1's 'those which had been' is excluded with it as connective.

A six-word run and worth nothing: 'flocks and herds' is the KJV's standing pair for livestock and occurs across the Pentateuch. Genesis 46:32 and 47:1 are Joseph presenting his brothers to Pharaoh as keepers of cattle, which has no bearing on an account of war damage. Recorded because six-word runs look decisive and this one is the trap ADJUDICATING §4 names.

Four words, and the Exodus verse is Marah: Moses casts a tree into the bitter waters and they are made sweet. Alma 3:3 casts bodies into the waters of Sidon. The sense is exactly opposed — a thing thrown in to purify against things thrown in to be got rid of — and the coincidence is the more inviting because Exodus 14-15 *is* a live source at this verse, adjudicated there from 14:30 and 15:5. It is the wrong verse of the right chapter-pair. Proverbs 9:18's 'in the depths of' is excluded with it as connective.

'Transgression' with a causal 'because of' is ordinary KJV moral vocabulary; Psalm 107:17's fools afflicted for their iniquities have no other contact. Ezra 3:3's 'upon them because of' is excluded with it.

A five-word run on a proper name, and it is a homonym. Genesis 25:16's sons of Ishmael are Abraham's grandsons by Hagar, twelve princes of twelve nations; Alma 3:7's are the descendants of the Ishmael of 1 Nephi 7, a Jerusalem man of Ephraim whose daughters married Lehi's sons. Nothing is shared but the name. Recorded because a rare-looking proper-noun run of this length is exactly what a reader would want checked, and because the neighbouring verses of Genesis 25 — the oracle of two peoples separated in the womb at 25:23, the red and hairy elder at 25:25 — *are* live sources for this chapter, adjudicated at 3:14 and 3:6. The chapter is using Genesis 25; it is not using this verse of it.

A four-word run split across a clause boundary in Ezekiel, where the Lord GOD sets on a pot for the parable of the seething cauldron. The verb 'set' in Alma 3:7 takes 'a mark' as its object, and the phrase 'set a mark upon' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 4:15 and Ezekiel 9:4 — both adjudicated at this verse. Isaiah 56:6's 'also the sons of' is excluded with it.

Four words of connective negation. 2 Kings 17:14's subject is Israel's refusal to hear the prophets; Alma 3:11's is which of two traditions a man accepted. Ezekiel 27:6's 'brought out of the' is excluded with it.

'Have mercy upon' is among the KJV's commonest petitions. Zechariah 10:6's promise to bring again the house of Joseph shares nothing else with a promise of separation conditioned on repentance. Genesis 17:7's 'thee and thy seed' — a real covenant formula, and closer than it looks — is excluded with it because Alma 3:14-17's seed language is adjudicated at 3:14 from Genesis 25:23, whose subject is the same covenant line divided rather than extended. Galatians 4:24's 'for these are the' is connective.
Five words of connective tissue from Jacob's remonstrance with Laban about searched baggage. The verse's substance — a mark set on him that mingleth his seed — is adjudicated at 3:9.

“Not many days after” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that verse is the departure of the prodigal son. This is the register's clearest specimen of CONVENTIONS §9's warning that the n-gram stream is a recall floor and not a ranking: an absolute singleton, five words long, scoring 2.00, and carrying no content at all — it is a date. Alma 3:20 uses it to say how soon a second Lamanite army arrived. John 11:6's 'the same place where' and Isaiah 34:5's 'upon the people of' are excluded with it.
Standard conquest phrasing; Caleb's request for Hebron shares no other element. Genesis 47:21's 'of the borders of' at 3:23 is excluded with it as geographical boilerplate.

'Amulek had caught him in his lying and deceiving' is close to Mark 12:13's KJV singleton 'to catch him in his words', which is adjudicated at Alma 10:13 for the lawyers' plot. Here the direction is reversed — the trappers are trapped — and the object has changed from words to lying, so no distinctive string survives. Recorded so a reader arriving at 12:1 is sent to 10:13, where the argument about this chapter's Gospel entrapment vocabulary is made.

exclusions.sharedText: both the just and the unjust
exclusions.reason: Genuinely tempting. Acts 24:15 — 'there shall be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust' — is the KJV's one verse joining a general resurrection to that pair, and Alma 12:8 asks about a resurrection 'both the just and the unjust'. It is declined here only because the phrase carries a second article in the Book of Mormon and because the whole of Zeezrom's question is a restatement of Alma 11:41-44, where the source is Revelation 20:12-13 and the link is filed. Note that Acts 24:25's Felix scene is adjudicated at Alma 11:46, ten verses earlier in the Book of Mormon and ten verses later in Acts; a reader who wants a case for Acts 24 in this stretch has one, and it is not built on this verse.

exclusions.sharedText: evil hath not been found in thee
exclusions.reason: Ranked on a five-word run of connective material. Abigail's plea for David has nothing to do with the astonishment of the people of Ammonihah, and the shared string spans a clause boundary in both verses.

exclusions.sharedText: should rise from the dead and
exclusions.reason: 'Rise from the dead' is the standard KJV resurrection formula. Acts 26:23's subject is that Christ should be the first to rise; Antionah's question is whether man rises at all, which is the opposite worry. The chapter's real Acts 26 contact, if there is one, is 26:3's 'expert in all customs and questions', composited into the link at Alma 11:21.

exclusions.sharedText: to do evil or to do good
exclusions.reason: The chapter's highest-scoring n-gram, a seven-word run, and a KJV singleton — 'to do evil, or to do good' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. It is nonetheless the wrong verse. Leviticus 5:4 is about a rash oath: a soul who swears 'pronouncing with his lips to do evil, or to do good' and then forgets it has incurred guilt, and the phrase is there a merism meaning 'anything at all'. Alma 12:31's is a statement of moral agency — men placed 'in a state to act, according to their wills and pleasures, whether to do evil or to do good' — where the two alternatives are genuinely alternatives and the whole point is that they are chosen between. Same six words, opposite grammatical work, and a model case for what CONVENTIONS §9 says about the n-gram stream: rarity of string is not rarity of thought.

Daniel 5:21 is Nebuchadnezzar's heart 'made like the beasts' in his madness; Alma 12:13's is a heart hardened against the word. The shared string is the copula. Worth recording only because Daniel 4-5 is a genuine source for Alma 10 (5:5 at 10:2, 4:17 at 10:17, 4:35 at 10:23), which makes a Daniel proposal in Alma 12 look more plausible than it is.

1 Corinthians 2:10's 'the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God' is the natural New Testament verse for revealed mysteries, and it was the machine's proposal for this stretch. The link at 12:9 is Matthew 13:11-12, which supplies not only the phrase 'to know the mysteries' but the graduated economy of more-to-those-who-have that Alma 12:10-11 spells out; Paul supplies neither. 1 Corinthians 4:1's 'stewards of the mysteries of God' is composited into that row for the noun phrase.

Ranked from both Matthew 10:14 and Luke 9:5, and worth an entry because the situation is so nearly right. Jesus tells the twelve that where they are not received they should 'depart out of that house or city' and shake off the dust of their feet — which is what a reader expects of Alma and Amulek leaving Ammonihah, and it would make a satisfying link. It is the wrong verb relation. In Matthew the missionaries choose to leave a city that would not hear them; in Alma 15:1 they 'were COMMANDED to depart out of that city', and the commander is God, who has just delivered them from its prison. The Book of Mormon does not have them shake off any dust, and Alma returns to the subject of Ammonihah at 15:15 rather than washing his hands of it.
Five words of narrative connective. Mordecai telling Hatach of Haman's bribe has no contact with Alma reporting the martyrdoms at Ammonihah. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

Four connective words. Luke 24:37's disciples 'supposed that they had seen a spirit'; Zeezrom supposed that Alma and Amulek had been slain. The verb of mistaken supposition is the only thing shared — though the coincidence is closer than the wording deserves, since in both cases the supposition is that a living man is dead, and in both it is corrected by the man's appearance. Recorded rather than passed over for that reason; the wording carries nothing.

A four-word run and a genuine contribution, but not the source. 'Burning heat' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 32:24 and James 1:11, and in both it is the sun or a plague acting from outside — James's is the sun withering grass, an image for the rich man fading away. Alma 15:3's heat is a fever produced by guilt, and the verb governing it, 'scorched', is the tell: of the KJV's three uses, the only one with a person as its object is Revelation 16:9, 'and men were scorched with great heat', whose next clause ('and they repented not') the Book of Mormon completes at Alma 15:15. The link is filed at 15:3 to Revelation 16:9 with James 1:11 recorded as the adjective's source.

The phrase occurs in seven KJV verses and is excluded at Alma 13:21 on those grounds, but this occurrence deserves its own entry because the gesture is genuinely at issue in the scene. In every KJV healing the hand that is stretched forth belongs to the HEALER — Matthew 8:3, 'Jesus put forth his hand, and touched him'; Matthew 12:49 toward his disciples; Matthew 14:31 to catch Peter. In Alma 15:5 it belongs to the PATIENT: 'when he saw them, he stretched forth his hand, and besought them that they would heal him.' The inversion is the verse's point and it makes the KJV verses inapplicable. The hand that heals arrives in the next verse, 'taking him by the hand', where the links to Mark 1:31 and Acts 3:7 are filed.

A real four-word phrase, and 2 Corinthians 12:9's 'that the power of Christ may rest upon me' is even about strength in weakness, which is Zeezrom's condition. But the phrase is ordinary Christian English by 1830 and nothing else of Paul's thorn-in-the-flesh passage is present. Alma 15:6's question — 'Believest thou in the power of Christ unto salvation?' — belongs to the catechetical healing of Matthew 9:28-29, where the link is filed.

Five words of relative clause; Isaiah 37:6 is Isaiah's message to Hezekiah about the words of the servants of Assyria. Alma 15:7's 'I believe all the words that thou hast taught' is the 'Yea' of Matthew 9:28, and that is where the row sits.

Four connective words, though the sense is close enough to be worth naming: Luke 7:17's rumour of the raising at Nain 'went forth throughout all Judaea', and Alma 15:11's knowledge of the healing 'went forth throughout all the land of Sidom'. Both report a healing becoming public. The phrase itself is boilerplate, and Luke 7:17's 'region round about' is adjudicated at Alma 15:14 to Matthew 3:5 instead, on the ground that only Matthew's has people coming in rather than a report going out.
Four words. Acts 11:10's 'and this was done three times' refers to Peter's sheet of unclean beasts. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.
