Five words that name the commonest activity in the Book of Mormon. Acts 10:42's 'he commanded us to preach unto the people' is Peter at Cornelius's house. No contact beyond the commission formula.

Ranked here from Revelation 16:9 and 16:11, and the proposal is right about the source and wrong about where it is adjudicated. 'And they repented not' occurs in exactly one KJV verse (16:9) and 'repented not of their' in exactly one (16:11), both in the fourth and fifth vials, and Alma 15:15's 'they repented not of their sins' is Revelation's clause. But the borrowing begins twelve verses earlier: Alma 15:3's 'scorched with a burning heat' takes its verb from Revelation 16:9's own 'men were scorched with great heat'. The link is filed at 15:3 with the split across the chapter set out there, and 15:15 carries it as a recurrence.

Five words of connective, and the sense diverges at the object: 2 Kings 17:14's northern Israelites 'hardened their necks … that did not believe in the LORD their God', while Alma 15:15's Ammonihahites 'did not believe in the repentance of their sins'. The hardened necks are a real coincidence and the verse's stiffneckedness is catalogued at 15:15 to Ezekiel 3:7 and Acts 7:51, where the wording is closer.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that … the word of God
exclusions.reason: Two separate pieces of boilerplate joined by the scorer, not by the text. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1. The verse's link is Matthew 19:27-29, on 'forsaken all', which the machine did not propose.

exclusions.sharedText: the tenth year of the reign of
exclusions.reason: A regnal-year date formula, ranked here as at Alma 14:23. Jeremiah 32:1 dates Jeremiah's imprisonment to the tenth year of Zedekiah and Alma 15:19 closes the tenth year of the reign of the judges; both chapters happen to involve a jailed prophet, which is what makes the coincidence look like something. It is a calendar.

Ranked alongside Luke 23:53 on the strength of a four-word run that is the KJV's only way of saying the thing. Both candidates are the burial of Jesus, and the pull toward a resurrection frame here is real — Lamoni lies as dead for two days and two nights and rises on the morrow. But 'they were about to take his body and lay it in a sepulchre' shares no distinctive word with either Gospel verse; the linen, the stone and the rock, which are what make Mark 15:46 recognisable, are all absent. The chapter's raising narrative is John 11's, and the sepulchre is discussed in the note at 19:5.

exclusions.sharedText: which they had made for the purpose
exclusions.reason: The top-ranked candidate in the chapter, and a genuine rarity: 'made for the purpose' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the seven-word run 'which they had made for the purpose' is reproduced word for word. It is still not a source. Nehemiah 8:4's object is Ezra's pulpit of wood, built so that a scribe can be seen and heard reading the law to a returned people; Alma 19:1's is a sepulchre, built so that the Lamanites can bury their dead. The two verses share a builder's idiom and nothing else — no person, no action, no theme — and the phrase is exactly the kind of rare boilerplate CONVENTIONS §9 warns the n-gram stream will rank first. The 19:1 burial does carry an intertextual charge, but it belongs to the John 11 raising the chapter is running from 19:5, and it is argued there.

Worth an entry because the temptation is strong and the wording will not bear it. John 4:19 is a foreign woman telling a Jewish stranger 'I perceive that thou art a prophet', after which she leaves and tells the men of her city, and they come out and believe — which is, beat for beat, what the queen and then Abish do in Alma 19. But the shared string is five words of unavoidable English, 'thou art a prophet' occurs across the KJV in that form, and the Book of Mormon's clause continues 'of a Holy God', which John has not. The verse's identifiable borrowing is Matthew 13:58's 'many mighty works', a KJV singleton, and the link is filed there. If the Samaritan woman is behind this chapter at all she is behind Abish at 19:17, where the register instead points at 2 Kings 5:3 on the strength of 'her mistress'.

'Stretched forth his hand' occurs in seven KJV verses spread from Abraham's knife to Moses at the sea to Jesus at the boat, which is a fair definition of a phrase that identifies nothing. Matthew 12:49 ranked here only because its next word is 'and said'. The borrowing in this verse is Daniel 2:20's 'Blessed be the name of God', a KJV singleton, filed as a link.

Ranked first at this verse and a real near-miss. Acts 26:14 is Paul before Agrippa recounting the Damascus road: 'when we were all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice.' Alma 19:16 has the king's servants calling on the Lord 'even until they had all fallen to the earth'. Both are involuntary prostrations under divine power in front of witnesses, so the parallel is not absurd. But the causes are opposite in the way that matters: Paul's company falls because a light strikes a persecutor down mid-journey, and the falling is the beginning of a rebuke; the Lamanites fall in the middle of their own prayer, and the falling is the answer to it. Nothing else in the two verses agrees, and 'fallen to the earth' is the KJV's ordinary phrase. The chapter's prostrations are its own.

Recorded because it is the one phrase in the Abish passage that looks like a borrowing and is not one. 'From house to house' occurs in four KJV verses. Acts 20:20 is the attractive one — Paul's own summary of his method, 'I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publickly, and from house to house' — and Abish is doing missionary work by that description. But the other three uses run from Luke 10:7's prohibition of the practice to 1 Timothy 5:13's idle gossips wandering from house to house, which is enough distribution to show that the phrase is simply how the KJV says it. Abish makes something known; she does not teach, and no other word of Acts 20:20 appears. The link at this verse is the type-scene from 2 Kings 5:2-3.

Checked because chapter 18 established Daniel as this narrative's frame and a third Daniel contact would have been worth having. 'A great evil' occurs in two KJV verses, Ecclesiastes 2:21 and Daniel 9:12, and Daniel's is 'bringing upon us a great evil', which is close to the Lamanites' 'a great evil that had come upon them'. But Daniel 9:12 is a confession of national judgment for sin in a penitential prayer, and Alma 19:19 is a crowd's superstitious guess about why their king is lying on the floor — a guess the chapter goes on to contradict twice over. Exodus 18:8's 'that had come upon them', which the machine also ranked here, is travel narrative. Neither is a source; the Daniel frame closes at 19:12 with the doxology.

A KJV singleton, and the wrong one. Psalm 125:3's 'lest the righteous put forth their hands unto iniquity' is a metaphor for committing sin under provocation; Alma 19:24's crowd 'durst not put forth their hands to touch him' is literal, and its subject is fear rather than restraint from wrongdoing. The singleton is a trap of the kind CONVENTIONS §9 describes — absolute rarity is the strongest evidence available and is worth nothing when the sense is opposed. The verse's link is to Acts 5:11-13, on the sequence rather than the string.

Four words of connective tissue straddling a clause boundary, with 'as' doing different work in each. Isaiah 51:23 is Jerusalem's tormentors telling her to lie down to be walked over; Alma 19:29 is a servant lifting her queen off the floor. The gesture in this verse is argued against Acts 9:41 and the KJV's small set of hand-raisings of women.

A five-word run of pure narrative dispatch. Zechariah 10:2's flock goes its way because there is no shepherd; the Lamanites who will not hear Lamoni go theirs because they will not hear him. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

exclusions.sharedText: believest thou that there is a God
exclusions.reason: 'Believest thou that there is a God?' invites James 2:19, 'Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble' — the KJV's one interrogation of bare theism. The sense is opposed and the wording is one word apart in the direction that matters: James has 'one God' and is arguing that the belief is worthless without works, while Aaron is treating the same belief as the ground on which everything else can be built. The exchange that follows (22:8-11) confirms the reading: assent is enough for Aaron to begin. No link.

Aaron's 'assuredly, as thou livest, O king, there is a God' looks like the KJV's oath by a king's life, and 1 Samuel 17:55 ('As thy soul liveth, O king, I cannot tell') is the closest fit — Abner swearing to Saul in the David-and-Goliath chapter this book draws on elsewhere. But 'as thy soul liveth' occurs in ten KJV verses across four books and cannot point to one of them, and the Book of Mormon's clause drops 'soul', which is the word that makes the KJV formula an oath at all. Recorded because the temptation is real: David's confession three verses earlier, 'that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel' (1 Samuel 17:46), is one of only two KJV verses containing 'there is a God', and the coincidence of both halves of Aaron's sentence with one page of 1 Samuel is the kind of thing that gets written up without checking.

'He created all things, both in Heaven and in earth' has two KJV backgrounds — 'created all things' at Ephesians 3:9 and Revelation 4:11, and the heaven-and-earth pairing at Colossians 1:16 ('all things ... that are in heaven, and that are in earth') — and no way to choose between them. 'Both in heaven and in earth' is in no KJV verse. The doctrine is a commonplace of every English creed and the phrasing is not any one verse's.

The chapter's top-ranked machine candidate, on a five-word run of pure narrative connective. 2 Chronicles 10:16 is Israel's revolt from Rehoboam; the shared words are 'saw that the king would' and nothing else. The verse's real source is Genesis 1-3, which the n-gram stream could not see because the Book of Mormon summarizes rather than quotes it.

exclusions.sharedText: that I may be filled with joy
exclusions.reason: The longest run in the chapter (seven words) and the highest-rarity machine score, and it is worth nothing. 2 Timothy 1:4 is Paul greeting Timothy — 'greatly desiring to see thee, being mindful of thy tears, that I may be filled with joy' — and the shared string is a purpose clause in a formula of affection. The verse's actual source is the rich young ruler pericope, which scored lower. A clean example of CONVENTIONS §9: rarity-weighted n-grams rank boilerplate above the real link.

'When he had said these words' is KJV narrative connective; the Book of Mormon uses it continuously. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1 and registered here only because the machine ranked it inside the chapter's top twenty-four.

Revelation 18:2's 'And he cried mightily with a strong voice, saying' is the only other KJV verse with the collocation, and the shape — 'cried mightily ... saying' followed by direct speech — matches Alma 22:17 more exactly than Jonah 3:8's infinitive does. It is nevertheless the wrong verse. Revelation 18:2 is an angel proclaiming the fall of Babylon; Alma 22:17 is a man on his face praying for the first time. The link is filed at Jonah 3:8, where the speaker is a heathen king and the whole surrounding sequence (throne abandoned, decree published through the land) recurs at Alma 22:27.

exclusions.sharedText: she came in unto the king
exclusions.reason: 'She came in unto the king' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the singleton is misleading in the worst way: Esther 2:14 is about the concubines going in to Ahasuerus by night, and the idiom there is sexual. Alma 22:19 is a queen entering the room where her husband lies unconscious. Esther 4:7 was proposed alongside it for 'all that had happened unto him', which is likewise narrative filler. A rare string with an opposed sense — the model case of the category, and exactly the row a careless pass would have promoted because the rarity tool said 'singleton'.

'Hardness of the hearts of the people' shares only 'the hearts of the people' with Joshua 7:5, where the hearts melt after the defeat at Ai. Hardness of heart in the Book of Mormon has its own KJV background (Mark 3:5, Matthew 19:8) adjudicated in 1 Nephi; nothing in Joshua 7 bears.

'His whole household were converted unto the Lord' is the Acts formula for a Gentile conversion — the jailer 'believing in God with all his house' (16:34), Crispus 'with all his house' (18:8), Lydia and her household (16:15) — and the chapter has already been read against Acts 14 and Acts 3. But 'whole household' and 'converted unto the Lord' are in no KJV verse, and 'all his house' is far too common to point anywhere. The resemblance is to a pattern in Acts rather than to a sentence in it, so it is registered here rather than catalogued as a link. Note that Alma 14:27 has already been adjudicated against the Philippian jailer's earthquake, so a reader who wants the Acts 16 frame has it at that verse.

Six words of narrative connective. Luke 19:7 is the crowd murmuring at Zacchaeus; the shared string is 'and when they saw it, they'. The murmuring parallel that does bear is filed at 22:24 against John 7:12.

exclusions.sharedText: sent a proclamation throughout all the land
exclusions.reason: The king's proclamation through all his land answers Jonah 3:7, where the king of Nineveh 'caused it to be proclaimed and published through Nineveh by the decree of the king and his nobles'. There is no rare string — 'proclamation' and 'throughout all the land' are both common KJV — and the element belongs to the Jonah sequence adjudicated at 22:17, where it is recorded as a composite and named in the significance. A reader arriving at 22:27 is sent there rather than shown a second thin row. The remainder of 22:27-34 is geography and carries no biblical wording at all.

Top-ranked at 25:2 on a six-word run of pure geography. 'The borders of the land of Zarahemla' and 'the borders of the land of Canaan' share a construction the KJV uses for any frontier; Exodus 16:35 is about the manna ceasing and has no other contact with a Lamanite army marching on Ammonihah. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

The plural phrase is a KJV singleton and it is Galatians 1:14's, but it was adjudicated at Mosiah 1:5 and again at Mosiah 26:1, and it has become one of the Book of Mormon's standing formulas — twelve occurrences, of which Alma's own first is 9:16, sixteen chapters before this one. Worth an entry rather than silence because 25:6 is the one place where the Book of Mormon's use comes closest to Paul's argument and not just his noun phrase: Galatians 1:14 is Paul saying what he was zealous for before God revealed his Son in him two verses later, and Alma 25:6 is a people who 'began to disbelieve the traditions of their fathers, and to believe in the Lord' after suffering loss. The sequence is Paul's; the wording is the Book of Mormon's own by this point. A reader arriving here should be sent to Mosiah 1:5.

exclusions.sharedText: commanded that they should be put to death
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run, the longest in the chapter, and worthless. 'Caused that they should be put to death' is the only way the KJV's English says a judicial killing ordered by an authority, and 'be put to death' alone occurs across the Pentateuch's penal code. Acts 12:19 is Herod executing the guards who lost Peter — no prophet, no belief, no fire, and a narrative running in the opposite direction, since Herod's victims are his own men. The verse's real content is the martyrdom it reports, and that is adjudicated at 25:12 against Luke 6:23.

exclusions.sharedText: a type of things to come
exclusions.reason: The KJV singleton is 'a shadow of things to come' and it was adjudicated at Mosiah 13:10, where Abinadi applies it to his own execution; 25:10 and 25:15 are the same speaker's formula reported at second hand, and 25:15 is filed as a link on other grounds. The entry is worth making for one fact that bears on every 'type' passage in the book: the KJV contains the word 'type' nowhere at all, in any sense. Where the Book of Mormon says type — 'a type of things to come', 'a type of his coming' — it is using a technical term of Christian exegesis that its purported source text does not supply, and the KJV word it stands in for is 'shadow' (Colossians 2:17, Hebrews 10:1) or 'figure' (Romans 5:14, Hebrews 9:9). That is a departure from the KJV's vocabulary rather than a borrowing of it, and it should not be catalogued as a link.

Ranked on a five-word window that closes one word early. 1 Peter 3:18's phrase is 'put to death in the FLESH, but quickened by the Spirit', a clause about the mode of Christ's death and resurrection; Alma 25:12's is 'put to death, in the like manner as he was', where 'in the' begins a new prepositional phrase and belongs to the singleton adjudicated at this verse against Luke 6:23. 2 Samuel 21:9's 'put to death in the days of harvest' is the same accident. The window is real and the phrase does not exist.

The most tempting rejection in the chapter. 1 Peter 2:10 — 'which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God: which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy' — is the New Testament's sentence for exactly what Alma 25:13 narrates, outsiders becoming God's people, and Peter is writing it about converts from the nations. But 'the people of God' occurs in five KJV verses and is the whole of the contact; nothing of Peter's antithesis, his 'in time past', or his mercy clause survives anywhere in Alma 25. The verse's identifiable borrowing is Isaiah 56:6's 'join themselves', filed as the link, and Isaiah 56 makes the same promise Peter is applying.

A genuine KJV singleton — 'it was expedient' occurs only at John 18:14, Caiaphas's counsel that one man should die for the people — and therefore a real trap, the same one already filed at Mosiah 13:29. The Book of Mormon uses 'expedient' as its ordinary modal for what is required or fitting, dozens of times and almost never with a death in view, and here it is doing so inside a sentence whose proximate model is demonstrably Mosiah 13:27, which reads 'it is expedient that ye should keep the law of Moses as yet'. The link at 25:15 records that route. Note for contrast that the catalogue does accept the Johannine calculus where the sense follows it: 1 Nephi 4:13 borrows John 11:50 to justify the killing of Laban.

'The spirit of prophecy' is a KJV singleton and was adjudicated for this book at Alma 6:8, where it arrives paired with 'the testimony of Jesus' in Revelation 19:10's own order — which is what identifies the source, since the KJV verse is a definition joining the two. At 25:16 the phrase stands alone and is doing different work: it is the faculty the converts rely on for knowledge of things to come, not a warrant for preaching. By this point in Alma it is the book's own term. A reader should be sent to 6:8.

exclusions.sharedText: in all the borders round about
exclusions.reason: A genuine six-word run and the highest-ranked candidate in the chapter, but the phrase is a surveyor's formula in both places and nothing else is shared. Genesis 23:17 is the conveyance of the field of Machpelah; Alma 28:1 is a description of Nephite troop dispositions round Zarahemla. 'In all the borders' recurs at Ezekiel 45:1 in the same neutral sense. The n-gram stream is doing what CONVENTIONS §9 says it does — scoring rare boilerplate.

'Tens of thousands of the Lamanites were slain' invites the women's song of Saul's thousands and David's ten thousands, and the Book of Mormon does use that arithmetic deliberately — it is adjudicated at 1 Nephi 4:1, where 'his tens of thousands' answers Laman's objection about Laban's fifty. Here it is not doing that work: the phrase is a casualty count in a battle report, 'ten thousands' occurs in eleven KJV verses, and 'tens of thousands' in none. The reader who wants the David allusion is sent to 1 Nephi 4:1.

Tempting, and worth recording as declined rather than passed over: Alma 28:6 repeats 'a time of' twice in one clause ('a time of solemnity, and a time of much fasting and prayer'), which is the anaphora of Ecclesiastes 3:1-8. But Ecclesiastes builds its catalogue out of paired opposites and runs to fourteen members; Alma 28:6 has two members and no antithesis between them, and it shares no content word with any verse of Ecclesiastes 3. The link at this verse goes to 1 Corinthians 7:5 instead, on the order of 'fasting and prayer'.

exclusions.sharedText: the fifteenth year of the reign
exclusions.reason: 'The fifteenth year of the reign' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Chronicles 15:10 (Asa) and Luke 3:1 (Tiberius), and the dossier ranked both at the head of this verse and of 28:9. The singleton-style rarity is an artifact of serial counting. The Book of Mormon dates by the year of the reign of the judges continuously from Alma 1:1 onward and must therefore produce every ordinal in turn; that the fifteenth happens to be one the KJV also uses twice is arithmetic, not borrowing. The regnal-dating formula itself is first used at Alma 1:1 and belongs there if it belongs anywhere.

exclusions.sharedText: the fifteenth year of the reign of
exclusions.reason: The same coincidence as at 28:7, where it is set out at length: a seven-word run produced by a serial year-count meeting the KJV's only two verses that name a fifteenth regnal year. Neither Asa's covenant assembly nor Tiberius's accession has any contact with this verse's summary of Nephite wars.

exclusions.sharedText: upon the face of the earth
exclusions.reason: Alma 28:11 contrasts bodies 'laid low in the earth' with bodies 'mouldering in heaps upon the face of the earth', which is the prophets' topos of the unburied dead after a slaughter — Ezekiel 39:11-16 detailing the burial of the multitude of Gog, and Jeremiah 8:2 and 16:4, where the slain 'shall not be gathered, nor be buried; they shall be for dung upon the face of the earth.' The topos is certainly in the background. The wording will not carry a link: 'upon the face of the earth' occurs in twelve KJV verses, 'in heaps' and 'mouldering' in none, and no candidate verse shares anything else.

exclusions.sharedText: snare / taken captive by him at his will
exclusions.reason: 'The cunning plans which he hath devised to ensnare the hearts of men' is the same borrowing already adjudicated in this book at Alma 12:6, where the snare of the devil of 2 Timothy 2:26 is drawn on three times in one discourse. This is the editor reusing a formula the book has already established, not a fresh contact with the source (ADJUDICATING §4), and the argument is at Alma 12:6.

The model case for why an exact-string singleton proves nothing on its own. 'In the vineyards of' occurs in exactly one KJV verse and it is Song of Solomon 1:14 — 'My beloved is unto me as a cluster of camphire in the vineyards of Engedi' — a lover's simile with no labour, no Lord and no vineyard-owner in it. The real sources at this verse share no exact run with it at all: Matthew 20:1's 'labourers into his vineyard' and Isaiah 5:7's 'the vineyard of the LORD of hosts', each a singleton in its own right, fused into 'labor in the vineyards of the Lord'.

Joshua's hearts melting as water at Ai has nothing to do with Zoram leading hearts astray; the five words are a KJV collocation used dozens of times. The real borrowing in this verse is 'dumb idols' with its verb of leading, filed as a link to 1 Corinthians 12:2.

A KJV singleton, and a worthless one. The four words are pure connective tissue — subject, verb, complementiser, subject — and John 16:30's completion is 'camest forth from God', which is the confession of Christ's origin that the Zoramite creed exists to deny. The singleton is an artifact of how rarely the KJV uses a first-person-plural 'we believe' at all.

David's thanksgiving at the temple offering. 'We thank thee, O God' as a formula belongs at 31:18 and 31:28, where the singleton 'God, I thank thee' pins it to Luke 18:11; 1 Chronicles 29:13 offers nothing beyond the three words and is a prayer of the right kind, which is the opposite of what this chapter needs.

'O how long, O Lord, wilt thou suffer' is Alma's own formula, adjudicated at its first use in this book at Alma 14:26 against the KJV singleton 'How long, O Lord' in the cry of the martyrs slain for the word of God. Alma 31:26 is the same speaker reusing his own cry, in a chapter where nobody has been killed; the borrowing was made and argued at 14:26 and is not made again here. See that entry.

Moses' plea to pardon the people scored highest of the chapter's petition candidates, but the shared words are the KJV's ordinary grammar of asking. Alma's petitions at 31:30-35 are a sustained prayer with no verbal contact with any single KJV prayer; the repeated 'wilt thou' is Book of Mormon idiom, not a citation.

exclusions.sharedText: hands upon … filled with the Holy Ghost
exclusions.reason: 'He clapped his hands upon all they which were with him … they were filled with the holy Spirit' is the New Testament's laying on of hands for the Spirit (Acts 8:17, 19:6) in substance, but not one distinctive word survives: the KJV never 'claps' hands upon a person — its 'clap' is always applause or derision — and it says 'Holy Ghost' where the Book of Mormon says 'holy Spirit'. A conceptual match with the wording pointing away from the source.

'Swallowed up in the joy of Christ' answers 'their hearts are swallowed up in their pride' at 31:27, and the chiasm is the writer's own. 'Swallowed up' occurs in fourteen KJV verses across both testaments; neither Paul's 'death is swallowed up in victory' nor 2 Corinthians 5:4 can be identified as the source of an idiom this widely distributed.

The dossier's top-ranked candidate for the chapter and worthless, exactly as CONVENTIONS §9 predicts: 'after the LORD had spoken these words unto Job' shares with 'after Alma had spoken these words unto them' only the KJV's ordinary way of ending one speech and beginning another. John 7:9 was ranked beside it on the same words. Covered in kind by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5, and registered here only because it heads the list.

'I would not have you ignorant, brethren' is a Pauline formula, used at Romans 1:13, 11:25, 1 Corinthians 10:1 and 12:1, 2 Corinthians 1:8 and 1 Thessalonians 4:13; no one of them can be the source of Amulek's 'I think that it is impossible that ye should be ignorant', and the sense is different in any case — Paul is about to tell his hearers something new, Amulek is refusing to.

A prophetic warrant-formula distributed across Isaiah 1:20, 25:8, 40:5, Amos 3:8 and dozens of Ezekiel verses. Amulek's 'for the Lord God hath spoken it' is the formula, not Amos; nothing else in Alma 34:8 touches Amos 3, whose subject is the compulsion to prophesy.

Ranked highest in two separate verses of this chapter (34:17 and 34:39) on the strength of an address and a conjunction. Amulek uses 'my brethren, that ye' as the standing hinge of every exhortation in the sermon; Paul's confidence in the Roman church's goodness has nothing else in common with either verse.

Tempting because prospering-in-the-land is a Deuteronomic promise the Book of Mormon uses heavily, but the verbal contact is five common words and the referents diverge: Deuteronomy's prospering follows from keeping the covenant, Alma's from crying to God over the crops of your fields. 'Prosper' appears in the Book of Mormon's land-promise formula from 1 Nephi 2:20 onward and needs no source here.

Five connective words. Jeremiah's 'because ye have done all these works' is an indictment; Alma's 'after ye have done all these things' introduces a further requirement. Hebrews 10:36's 'after ye have done the will of God' was ranked on the same run and fails the same way.
Four words of pure conditional syntax, ranked at 34:28 and 34:29 alike. One entry covers both.

'Come forth and bring fruit unto repentance' is the Baptist's 'bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance', but the phrase is already adjudicated in this book, at Alma 12:15 and again at Alma 13:13, and the occurrence here is Amulek reaching for a formula his companion has used twice in the same mission. A reader looking for the argument should go to those verses (ADJUDICATING §4).

exclusions.sharedText: now is the time, and the day of your salvation
exclusions.reason: Worth registering because the contact here is verbally CLOSER than at the verse where the link sits: Alma 13:21 has 'Now is the time to repent, for the day of salvation draweth nigh', whereas 34:31 puts both halves in one clause with the definite article, which is 2 Corinthians 6:2's own construction ('behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation'). It is still a recurrence within one book and the argument, including the control from 1 Nephi 21:8's Isaianic 'a day of salvation', is made at Alma 13:21. Note for a future pass that mediation-check.py finds no decisive word-level divergence between Isaiah 49:8 and 2 Corinthians 6:2 at any point Alma reproduces; the mediation is carried by the frame, not by a word.

Twice in this verse, and it is the same borrowing adjudicated at Alma 12:33 — where the mediation between Psalm 95:8 and Hebrews 3:8 was decided for Hebrews on the plural 'hearts', and where the surrounding verses supply the provocation and the rest that confirm it. Alma 34:31 has the phrase without any of that context, so it is the formula recurring, not a fresh borrowing.

'This life is the time for men to prepare to meet God' is the chapter's most quoted sentence and its source is the KJV singleton at Amos 4:12, adjudicated in this book at Alma 5:28 with its recurrences at 5:29 and 5:31. Amulek is completing his companion's sentence, not going back to Amos: Alma turned the imperative into a diagnosis ('ye are not prepared'), and Amulek supplies the deadline. The row belongs to the reader at 5:28.

exclusions.sharedText: he dwelleth not in unholy temples
exclusions.reason: The opening clause of the verse. Adjudicated at Alma 7:21, where the point is that Luke's God dwells in no temples made with hands while the Book of Mormon's declines only the unholy ones — the sentence-shape kept and the doctrine reversed. Amulek quotes the clause as scripture ('because the Lord hath said'), which is itself worth noticing, but the wording is his companion's from a sermon two chapters into the same mission and the argument for it stands at 7:21.

Hardy's apparatus cross-references Matthew 8:11 and Luke 13:28-29 at this verse, and it is pointing at a real borrowing — but the borrowing was adjudicated earlier in this same book, at Alma 5:24, where the full composite is argued: Luke supplies 'sit down in the kingdom' (a KJV singleton) and the prophets beside the patriarchs, Matthew 8:12 supplies the children of the kingdom, and Exodus 2:24 supplies the repeated preposition in 'with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob'. Alma 34:36 has the seating alone, without the patriarch list, without the casting out and without the prophets, so it is the shortest possible form of a saying already fully treated. A reader should be sent to 5:24; nothing at 34:36 adds to the case.

The other half of Hardy's cross-reference at this verse, discharged the same way. Alma 5:24 established that the Book of Mormon's form of this saying follows Luke rather than Matthew where the two differ — 'kingdom of God' not 'kingdom of heaven', and the prophets named beside the patriarchs — so Matthew 8:11 is not the proximate source even at 5:24, and at 34:36 there is not enough of the saying left to test.

exclusions.sharedText: their garments should be made white, through the blood of the Lamb
exclusions.reason: The closing clause of the verse, and a genuine borrowing — but the formula is adjudicated at Alma 5:21 and again at Alma 13:11, where the interesting feature is argued: Revelation washes robes IN the blood, and the Book of Mormon makes them white THROUGH it, converting an immersion into an instrument. Alma 34:36 has the same 'through' and adds nothing further, so it is registered here and argued at 13:11.

A near miss recorded because the thematic fit is nearly perfect and the wording will not carry it. Alma 34:40-41 asks the Zoramite poor to bear affliction patiently and 'not revile against those who do cast you out', which is 1 Peter 2:20-23's counsel exactly — take it patiently, and 'who, when he was reviled, reviled not again'. But 'reviled' occurs in five KJV verses and 'revile' in two, neither of them Peter's, and Alma shares no other word with the passage; Matthew 5:11's 'when men shall revile you' is an equally good and equally insufficient candidate. Conceptual agreement without verbal contact, so no link at any confidence.

Ranked at 35:1, 35:2 and 35:13 on the same four words, because this chapter is almost entirely about people going over into lands. Reuben and Gad's refusal to cross Jordan has nothing else in common with any of them. One entry covers all three.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that after the
exclusions.reason: The chapter's longest n-gram run, eight words, and pure connective tissue — ADJUDICATING §4's named trap. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1; registered here only because a reader who sees the number will wonder.

Tempting beyond its verbal weight: in both, a hostile people assembles its whole population to decide what to do about a holy thing that has come among them and is doing them damage, and in both the decision is to send it away. But the shared words are an assembly formula the KJV uses constantly (1 Samuel 5:8, 5:11, 7:5, 2 Chronicles 5:2), Alma's assembly is convened to canvass opinion rather than to resolve, and the ark and the preaching have no other point of contact. The verse's real interest is the Ephesus parallel filed as a link at 35:3.

The best trap in the chapter, and it is one word wide. Pharaoh's heart was hardened 'and he did not let the people go'; the Zoramite rulers 'did not let the people know concerning their desires'. Five identical words, a hard-hearted ruling class withholding something from a people, and an exodus of the persuaded poor three verses later — everything a typological reader wants. But the verb is different and the verb is the whole sense: Pharaoh withholds departure, the Zoramite rulers withhold information, and Alma's sentence is about a secret ballot, not a refused release. 'Let the people go' is Exodus's refrain thirteen times over and 'let the people know' is nowhere in the KJV, so the run is an accident of a negated auxiliary meeting a common noun.

A list of a nation's officials, which the KJV writes this way everywhere (Jeremiah 2:26, 4:9, 8:1, 32:32, Nehemiah 9:32). 'Their rulers, and their priests, and their teachers' is the Book of Mormon's own triad, used of the Zoramites at 31:1 and 32:1-2 before it appears here.

Registered because the narrative point is real and the verbal case is not. Amulek has just told the Zoramites at 34:28 that a man who turns away the needy and the naked prays in vain — a verse whose source is Matthew 25:43, filed as a link there — and the people of Ammon at 35:9 do the inventory in full: they receive the poor, nourish them, clothe them, give them lands, and administer to their wants. It reads as the sheep of Matthew 25:35-36 answering the goats of 34:28 across a chapter break. But the only shared word is 'clothe', Alma's list is not Matthew's and is not in Matthew's order, and 'nourish' occurs nowhere in the parable. The judgment scene is being enacted, not quoted, and a catalogue of dependence has to say so.

exclusions.sharedText: in the eighteenth year of the reign of
exclusions.reason: An eight-word run and worth nothing: regnal dating is a fixed KJV formula ('in the eighteenth year of the reign of Jeroboam', 1 Kings 15:1; 2 Kings 22:3; 2 Chronicles 34:8), and the Book of Mormon dates every year of the reign of the judges this way from Mosiah 29:44 onward. Josiah's passover and the Zoramite war share a calendar idiom and nothing else.

A KJV merism for a household under threat, distributed across Genesis 34:29, Numbers 14:3, Deuteronomy 3:19, 2 Chronicles 20:13 and many more. Jehoshaphat's assembly is a fast before a battle and Alma 35:14 is a note about land tenure and taking up arms; the phrase is the Book of Mormon's standing formula for what a Nephite army defends (see Alma 43:9, 46:12).

The machine's top candidate for the verse and the opposite of what the verse says. At Ai 'the hearts of the people melted, and became as water'; in Alma 'the hearts of the people began to wax hard'. Both are collective changes of heart reported by a narrator, which is why the run scores, but melting and hardening are the KJV's two contrary heart-metaphors and a catalogue that accepted this would have the sign reversed. The verse's real source is Matthew 13:21, filed as a link, and its hardening belongs to the Book of Mormon's own formula rather than to Joshua.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that when they had
exclusions.reason: A nine-word run and the highest-scoring candidate in the chapter, consisting entirely of the Book of Mormon's standing narrative opener plus 'when they had'. Amos 7:2 is the locusts finishing the grass; Alma 20:1 is a church established in a land. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5, and recorded here only because the run length is long enough to mislead a reader of the raw candidate file (CONVENTIONS §9).

exclusions.sharedText: when I made a feast unto my sons, and unto my people
exclusions.reason: 'Made a feast unto' occurs in three KJV verses — Genesis 40:20, Esther 1:3 and Esther 1:5 — and two of them are the Persian king's feast for his princes and then for all his people, which is close to 'a feast unto my sons, and unto my people'. Genesis 40:20 is closer still in function, since Pharaoh's birthday feast is where a prisoner is remembered and released, and this chapter is about releasing prisoners. But the great feast in this narrative has already been adjudicated: Alma 18:9's 'great feast appointed at the land of Nephi' by 'his father, who was king over all the land' is filed at Alma 18:12 against Daniel 5:1, on the strength of the changed countenance that follows. Alma 20:9 is the same feast referred to again, from the father's side, and the reader should be sent there. Esther is not absent from this chapter — see the link at 20:23 — but she is behind Mark 6:23 there, not here.

exclusions.sharedText: all the cause of his tarrying
exclusions.reason: Written because the temptation is a real one and the words are not there. Luke 14:16-24 is the KJV's one parable of a feast that the invited do not attend, and 'they all with one consent began to make excuse' is a KJV singleton; Alma 20:9-12 has a king demanding to know why his son missed his feast and a son giving 'all the cause of his tarrying'. The shape matches. But the Book of Mormon uses neither 'excuse' nor 'bidden' nor 'supper', its absentee gives his reason to the host's face rather than by messenger, and — decisively — Luke's excuses are refused while Lamoni's is heard and answered with a different quarrel altogether. No source is identifiable at this verse.

exclusions.sharedText: and he stretched forth his hand
exclusions.reason: Ranked first at this verse and rejected for the same reason as at Alma 19:12: 'stretched forth his hand' is one of the KJV's commonest gestures, spread over seven verses from Abraham's knife to Moses at the sea to Jesus pointing at his disciples. Matthew 12:49's hand is stretched toward disciples in affection. The verse's link is to Genesis 22:10, which is the only one of the seven where the hand is raised to kill — the qualifier 'to slay', not the run, is what selects it.

exclusions.sharedText: they were naked … they also had suffered hunger, thirst, and all kind of afflictions
exclusions.reason: The borrowing is real and it is adjudicated three chapters earlier. 2 Corinthians 11:26-27 stands behind Alma 17:5, where 'journeyings' and 'hunger, thirst' — a two-verse word and a KJV singleton — are taken from consecutive verses of the same passage, and it recurs at Alma 18:37. Alma 20:29 is the third use in the same book and by the same narrator: the same pair of nouns, plus the nakedness that closes 2 Corinthians 11:27 ('in cold and nakedness') and the imprisonment that opens the catalogue at 11:23 ('in prisons more frequent'). Under ADJUDICATING §4 a narrator reusing his own adopted phrase within one book is recorded rather than re-argued, so the reader arriving here should be sent to Alma 17:5. Worth noting for whoever revisits that row: 20:29 draws two further elements of Paul's catalogue that 17:5 does not, so the source is being read further down the page each time it is used.

exclusions.sharedText: had driven them from house to house, and from place to place
exclusions.reason: 'From house to house' occurs in four KJV verses and is discharged at Alma 19:17, where Abish runs house to house and the candidate was Acts 20:20. Here the machine offers 1 Timothy 5:13's idle young widows 'wandering about from house to house', which is a moral complaint about gossip and has nothing to do with missionaries driven out of one. The second half of the Book of Mormon's phrase, 'from place to place', is in no KJV verse at all. The nearest real parallel to what 20:30 describes is Matthew 23:34, 'persecute them from city to city', which shares the sense and not the words; it is not enough for a link.

exclusions.sharedText: they would not hearken unto their
exclusions.reason: Six words of the KJV's standard formula for a people refusing a prophet, which the Book of Mormon uses continuously. Judges 2:17's Israel would not hearken unto their judges; the people of Middoni would not hearken unto the missionaries' words. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

'Cast them into prison' is real verbal contact and Acts 16:23 is a plausible home for it — Paul and Silas at Philippi, which this book has already used at Alma 14:27. But the imprisonment in Alma 23:2 is one of seven items in a catalogue, and the item that governs the catalogue is the pair 'lay their hands on ... and put them in the common prison' at Acts 5:18, which sits inside the Acts 5 episode the chapter draws on again at 23:7. The link is filed at 23:2 against Matthew 10:17 with Acts 5:18 as a composite.
Four words of connective, and the object in Daniel is a burning fiery furnace. No contact beyond the infinitive.

exclusions.sharedText: that they should not ... but that they should
exclusions.reason: The chapter's top-scoring machine candidate, and it is entirely a correlative construction: 'that they should not kill them, but that they should be tormented'. Revelation 9:5 is the locusts of the fifth trumpet. The verse's real sources are Matthew 10:17 and its neighbours, which the n-gram stream reached only at rank four and only through the four-word run 'lay their hands on'.

exclusions.sharedText: that the word of God might have no obstruction
exclusions.reason: The King James Bible has two memorable expressions for the unhindered progress of preaching, and this verse matches the sense of both and the wording of neither. 2 Thessalonians 3:1 asks that the word of the Lord 'may have free course, and be glorified'; Acts 28:31 ends the book with Paul preaching 'no man forbidding him', a KJV singleton. Alma 23:3 says 'might have no obstruction', and 'obstruction' is not a King James word at all — it appears nowhere in the KJV. This is registered rather than catalogued because the temptation is strong (the chapter is otherwise steeped in Acts) and the verbal case is zero. The Acts frame that does bear is filed at 23:7.

'The wicked traditions of their fathers' is the Book of Mormon's standing description of Lamanite religion and appears scores of times across the book; the KJV's nearest phrases are Galatians 1:14, 'the traditions of my fathers', and 1 Peter 1:18, 'received by tradition from your fathers'. 'Traditions of their fathers' is in no KJV verse. Neither Pauline verse is doing what Alma 23:3 does — Paul's tradition is his own zeal for Judaism, Peter's is a vain manner of life — and the phrase is by Alma too thoroughly the book's own to be adjudicated as a borrowing here.

exclusions.sharedText: teaching the word of God among them
exclusions.reason: Six shared words, all of them the Book of Mormon's ordinary description of missionary work. Acts 18:11 is a note of how long Paul stayed in Corinth. 'The word of God' is used continuously in both corpora and carries no signal.

'Aaron and his brethren went forth from city to city' shares 'from city to city' with Matthew 23:34, one of only two KJV verses containing it (the other is 2 Chronicles 30:10, of Hezekiah's posts). The contact is genuine and the inversion is pointed — Matthew 23:34 is 'some of them shall ye scourge in your synagogues, and persecute them from city to city', and Alma 23:2-4 forbids the scourging and then sends the preachers city to city unharmed. But both halves belong to one argument, and that argument is made at 23:2, where Matthew 23:34 is recorded as a composite. A reader at 23:4 is sent there.

'Never did fall away' inverts Luke 8:13's parable of the seed on the rock, 'which for a while believe, and in time of temptation fall away' — the KJV's characteristic phrase for a conversion that does not hold. The link is already adjudicated in this book at Alma 16:17, where the sower parable is the governing figure; 23:6 is the same author using the same borrowed phrase for the opposite outcome, and is recorded there rather than given a second row.

'According to the spirit of revelation and of prophecy' shares only the frame 'according to the spirit of' with Romans 1:4's 'according to the spirit of holiness'. The genitive that follows is the content word in both and they do not match. Compare Revelation 19:10, 'the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy', which is closer in substance and has already been adjudicated in this book.

A list-heading formula. Revelation 14:4's 'These are they which were not defiled with women' introduces the hundred and forty-four thousand; Alma 23:8 introduces a list of Lamanite lands. The construction is common to both corpora and the content shares nothing.

'Weapons of war' occurs in nine KJV verses across six books and cannot point at one of them; Ezekiel 32:27's uncircumcised dead who go down to hell with their weapons have nothing else in common with converts laying theirs down. The laying-down and burial of weapons is developed at Alma 24:17-19, where 2 Samuel 1:27 and the wider KJV vocabulary of disarmament are adjudicated.

exclusions.sharedText: come to the knowledge of the truth
exclusions.reason: This is a genuine KJV singleton — 'come to the knowledge of the truth' occurs only at 2 Timothy 3:7, of women 'ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth', with 1 Timothy 2:4's 'come unto the knowledge of the truth' one preposition away. The Book of Mormon uses the phrase fifteen times, and the borrowing was argued at Jacob 7:24 and Mosiah 27:14, where the inversion of Paul's sense is the point. Within Alma its first use is 17:2, not here. Registered so that a reader at 23:15 is sent to Jacob 7:24 rather than shown nothing.

exclusions.sharedText: that they might have a name, that thereby they might be distinguished
exclusions.reason: Acts 11:26 — 'the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch' — is the King James Bible's only narrative of a body of converts acquiring a name that distinguishes them, and it is what a reader will reach for at Alma 23:16-17. It supplies no wording whatever: the shared idea is a name, and Acts 11:26 and Alma 23:16 have not one distinctive word in common. It is recorded as a composite on the Luke 1:61 echo at 23:17 and excluded here as a source in its own right.

exclusions.sharedText: brought into the fold of God
exclusions.reason: 'Thousands of them do rejoice, and have been brought into the fold of God' is tempting because John 10:16 — 'other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd' — is the New Testament verse about outsiders being brought into a fold, and the Book of Mormon elsewhere claims that verse for itself. But 'the fold' as a KJV noun occurs once, at Habakkuk 3:17, of livestock; John's phrase is 'this fold' and 'one fold', and Alma 26:4 has neither, nor 'other sheep', nor the shepherd. The chapter's shepherd language is at 25:12 and its harvest language at 26:5-7; the fold here is a single common noun.

exclusions.sharedText: they shall be gathered into the garners
exclusions.reason: The KJV singleton is 'into the garner' and it belongs to Matthew 3:12, John the Baptist's threshing-floor: 'he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.' The verse is a source at Mosiah 2:38 and stands as a composite behind Alma 5:52's Matthew 3:10, and the plural 'garners' is the Book of Mormon's own form. Registered here rather than passed over because 26:5-7 is a composite of three separate KJV harvests and a reader should be able to see all three: the sickle is Revelation 14:15's, the garner is Matthew 3:12's, the Lord of the harvest is Matthew 9:38's. The first and third are filed as links at 26:5 and 26:7. Note what the Book of Mormon does with the second — Matthew 3:12 puts the chaff in unquenchable fire immediately after the garner, and Alma 26:6-7 replaces the fire with a storm the gathered sheaves survive.

'Chains of hell' is not a KJV phrase at all — the KJV has 'chains of darkness' at 2 Peter 2:4 and 'everlasting chains under darkness' at Jude 6, both of angels and neither of hell — and it is one of Alma's own most characteristic formulas, at 5:7, 5:9, 5:10, 12:11, 13:30 and here. It is discharged at Alma 13:30, where 'bound down by the chains of hell, that ye may not suffer the second death' is adjudicated against Revelation 21:8 with 2 Peter 2:4 behind the chains. The row is registered because the phrase reads as biblical and is not, which is the kind of thing this register exists to record.

'Pray without ceasing' is 1 Thessalonians 5:17 entire, which makes the temptation strong, but 'without ceasing' occurs in six KJV verses and four of them attach it to prayer or remembrance (Romans 1:9, 1 Thessalonians 1:3, 2:13, 5:17, Acts 12:5). The Book of Mormon's phrase is doubled — 'prayeth continually without ceasing' — which is neither Paul's economy nor any KJV construction, and 'continually' comes from the Old Testament's 'continually before me'. No single verse can be identified. The verse's identifiable borrowing is 1 Corinthians 2:14 and 4:1 at 26:21, filed as a link.

The KJV singleton is Galatians 1:14's and was adjudicated at Mosiah 1:5. By Alma 26 it is one of the book's standing formulas — twelve occurrences, of which Alma's own first is 9:16 — and 26:24 is putting it in the mouths of scoffers rather than using it doctrinally. See also the entry at Alma 25:6, where the same phrase recurs three verses into a conversion narrative that follows Galatians 1:14-16's sequence.

'Believe on his name' is Johannine — John 1:12 and 2:23 — and the Book of Mormon uses it a dozen times, twice earlier in Alma at 19:36 and 22:13 where it is adjudicated against John 1:12, and twice before that in 2 Nephi 9:24 and 25:14. It is the book's settled formula by 26:35. Recorded here for one reason of provenance: Alma 26:35 is the single verse of these three chapters that appears in our index of Frederick's monograph, where John 1:12 and John 2:23 are discussed within 1,500 characters of it. That index records CO-OCCURRENCE and nothing more — Frederick's subject is the Gospel of John's presence in Restoration scripture generally and he proposes no source for this verse — so it must not be reported as his identification. The verse's own interest is the clause before the formula: 'he has all power, all wisdom, and all understanding', which returns to the wisdom-and-might pair of Jeremiah 9:23 that 26:11-12 refused for itself.

'In a strange land' occurs in four KJV verses and the choice among them was argued at Alma 13:23, where 'wanderers in a strange land' is adjudicated against Psalm 137:4 on situation rather than wording. Alma 26:36 repeats that exact phrase within the same book and the same author's speech-register, and it is the second of only two occurrences in the Book of Mormon. A reader should be sent to 13:23. Worth noting for that entry rather than this one: Psalm 137:4 asks how the LORD's song can be sung in a strange land, and Alma 26:8 has just answered by singing one.

exclusions.sharedText: a branch of the tree of Israel, and hath been lost from its body
exclusions.reason: The figure of Israel as a tree with branches broken off is Romans 11:17-24's and is the standing background of Jacob 5, so the temptation to key it here is real — and the branch that is 'lost from its body' is precisely Romans 11's grafted-out branch. But the wording is not Paul's at any point: Romans has 'the branches', 'broken off', 'the olive tree', 'the root', and Alma 26:36 has 'a branch of the tree of Israel' and 'lost from its body', neither of which is a KJV construction. The allegory this sentence is drawing on is Jacob 5's, which is the Book of Mormon's own, and the phrase belongs to that inheritance rather than to Romans directly.

The chapter's top-ranked candidate and pure connective tissue: 'the wish of mine heart, that I might go forth' against 'Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee'. No content word is shared. The real source at this verse is 1 Thessalonians 4:16.

exclusions.sharedText: scattered upon all the face of the earth
exclusions.reason: 'Upon all the face of the earth' is one of the Book of Mormon's standing formulas and covered by the boilerplate exclusion; Ezekiel 34:6's scattered flock has no other contact with a wish that sorrow might end.

A five-word run onto a KJV singleton, and worthless. 'As with the voice of' occurs in exactly one KJV verse and the voice in question is doves: Huzzab's maids lead her away captive 'as with the voice of doves, tabering upon their breasts'. Alma 29:2's simile is thunder. The construction is common English; the singleton is an accident of the KJV's vocabulary, not evidence of contact. Compare Revelation 14:2, 'as the voice of a great thunder', which shares the sense and not the run.

A six-word run onto a KJV singleton — 'whether it be unto death' occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and the sense is opposed. Ezra 7:26 is Artaxerxes' schedule of penalties for breaking the law of God and the king: death, banishment, confiscation, imprisonment. Alma 29:4 is about God granting men what they desire, 'whether it be unto death or unto life', which is the opposite kind of proposition — an allotment according to will, not a sentence imposed. The shared frame is the English construction 'whether it be unto X or Y', which needs no source.

Colossians 4:1's 'that which is just and equal' shares four words with Alma 29:8's 'that which is just and true', and the fifth word is where the evidence lives. 'Just and true' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 15:3, and that is where the link at this verse goes. The trap is ADJUDICATING §4's: the window closes one word early.

exclusions.sharedText: delivered them out of the hands of the Egyptians
exclusions.reason: 'Out of the hand of the Egyptians' occurs in exactly six KJV verses (Exodus 3:8, 14:30, 18:9, 18:10; Judges 6:9; 1 Samuel 10:18) and the phrase is too widely spread to fix a source. Worth registering for a detail that cuts against dependence: all six KJV verses read the singular 'hand', and Alma 29:12 reads 'out of the hands of the Egyptians'. The Exodus material this verse depends on is adjudicated at 29:11, where a thirteen-word run settles it.
Connective boilerplate. Gog's march on the land of unwalled villages has nothing to do with missionaries going up to the land of Nephi.

The machine ranked Ezekiel 14:11 first at this verse on 'may go no more astray'. The Book of Mormon reads 'go no more out', which is Revelation 3:12's phrase — the overcomer made a pillar in the temple who 'shall go no more out' — and that is where the link is filed. Ezekiel's idiom is about apostasy, Alma's about permanence.

Matthew 8:11's 'shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven' is the obvious candidate here, and would be attractive because Alma 29:11 has just named the same three patriarchs. It is not the source: Matthew reads 'kingdom of heaven' and Alma reads 'kingdom of God', which is Luke 13:29's wording, and 'sit down in the kingdom' as a contiguous phrase occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 13:29. The link is filed there.

'They shall put you out of the synagogues' is the Gospel of John's expulsion of confessors of Christ (9:22, 12:42, 16:2), and the machine ranked it first here. But the Zoramite poor are expelled for their clothes, not their confession, and the KJV passage that describes a congregation sorting worshippers by dress is James 2:1-6, where the link is filed. John's phrase would put the wrong charge on the wrong people; 'out of the synagogue' occurs in five KJV verses and cannot carry the row on its own.

'They were esteemed by their brethren as dross.' The KJV's dross is metallurgical and always describes the wicked being refined away (Psalm 119:119, Isaiah 1:22, Ezekiel 22:18-19). Alma's is a term of social contempt applied to the innocent, and the sense is inverted: the people called dross here are the ones the chapter vindicates. One word, and the wrong valuation attached to it.

Jesus stretching his hand toward his disciples to name his mother and brethren. The gesture is the KJV's ordinary notation for a speaker addressing a crowd and it carries nothing of Matthew's point, which is a redefinition of kinship. Alma 31:14's 'stretch forth his hands towards heaven' is a separate matter and is adjudicated there.

'It shall be unto every man according to his work.' The singular 'according to his work' occurs in two KJV verses (Psalm 62:12, Proverbs 24:29), and the same doctrine is stated again at Matthew 16:27 ('according to his works'), Revelation 20:12 ('according to their works') and Revelation 22:12 ('according as his work shall be'). No single verse can be identified behind a formula this widely repeated.

A KJV singleton, and already adjudicated in this book at its first use, Alma 19:36, with a second occurrence recorded at Alma 22:13. The phrase has become the book's own formula for conversion by this point in Alma and its third appearance is not a fresh borrowing. See Alma 19:36.

'Perfect knowledge' is a KJV singleton and the temptation is real, because it is the governing term of Alma 32 — it appears at 32:21, 32:26, 32:29, 32:34 and 32:35, more often than any other phrase in the chapter. But Acts 24:22's sense is procedural and secular: Felix, presiding at Paul's hearing, had 'more perfect knowledge of that way' and used it to adjourn. The KJV means he was better informed about the sect than he let on. Alma means a completed certainty that abolishes faith, which is not a sense the KJV verse contains at any strength. A singleton whose one occurrence is a Roman governor's grasp of the local religion cannot be the source of an epistemology, and the phrase is ordinary English of the period besides.

exclusions.sharedText: the fruit of the tree of life
exclusions.reason: 'Ye can never pluck of the fruit of the tree of life.' 'Tree of life' occurs in ten KJV verses across Genesis, Proverbs and Revelation, and none of them is closer to Alma than the Book of Mormon's own tree, which Lehi and Nephi see and eat from at 1 Nephi 8:10-12 and 11:8-25 and whose fruit is there described as white and sweet above all — the two adjectives Alma 32:42 uses. The proximate model is the earlier Book of Mormon vision, not the KJV, and the row is declined here rather than assigned to a biblical verse it does not follow.

'Ye shall reap the rewards of your faith, and your diligence, and patience, and long suffering.' Galatians 6:9's 'in due season we shall reap, if we faint not' is the nearest KJV sentence about reaping after endurance, but it shares only the verb, and Alma's four-term list (faith, diligence, patience, long suffering) matches no KJV series — 'long suffering' appears in Paul's virtue lists but never beside diligence. The harvest is the allegory's own conclusion, not a borrowing.

exclusions.sharedText: as we were the most lost of all mankind
exclusions.reason: The king's parenthesis invites Paul's 'Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief', the KJV's one first-person claim to superlative sinfulness, and the book has already used the next verse of that chapter at Alma 17:11. But 'most lost of all mankind' shares not a word with 1 Timothy 1:15, and 'lost' in the KJV is the sheep and the son of Luke 15, not a rank among sinners. The superlative is the Book of Mormon's own.

'Behold, I say unto you' is the Book of Mormon's standing formula of address and the KJV's; John 4:35 shares nothing else. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1 and noted here only because it was the chapter's only machine candidate at this verse, where a real link to Revelation 7:14 sits unseen — the borrowing is a figure with the object changed, and no n-gram window can find that.

exclusions.sharedText: in the earth that they may
exclusions.reason: Five words of connective spanning a clause boundary. Genesis 8:17 is the animals leaving the ark to breed abundantly; nothing else is shared.

exclusions.sharedText: hid thy talent in the earth
exclusions.reason: 'We will hide away our swords, yea, even we will bury them deep in the earth' is the KJV's gesture of burial for safekeeping, and the KJV has exactly one memorable instance of it: the servant of the parable who 'digged in the earth, and hid his lord's money' (Matthew 25:18) and pleads 'I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth' (25:25). The sense is opposed at the point that matters. Burial in the parable is the sin — the refusal to put something to use for which the servant is condemned — and burial here is the covenant, precisely a refusal to use, praised. Recorded because the verbal gesture is close enough that a reader could be tempted, and because getting the polarity backwards would misread the chapter's central act.

exclusions.sharedText: call on the name of the Lord
exclusions.reason: 'Began to call on the name of the Lord' is one of the KJV's most widely distributed phrases — Genesis 4:26, Joel 2:32, Acts 2:21, Romans 10:13 and many more — and cannot identify a source. The martyrdom scene's real biblical shape is in what surrounds it (the Deuteronomy 5:32 formula at 24:23), not here.
'Flee from the sword' is ordinary KJV battle diction and Isaiah 31:8 is the Assyrian falling by a sword not of man. Four common words, no further contact.

exclusions.sharedText: would not flee from the sword ... would lay down and perish
exclusions.reason: A people who go out to meet armed men, prostrate themselves and are killed without resisting is the most obvious invitation in the chapter to Isaiah 53:7 — 'he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth' — and a typological reading would put the link here without hesitation. There is no wording to support it: no lamb, no sheep, no silence, no shearer. Alma 24:23 has instead a ten-word run from Deuteronomy 5:32, which is where the link is filed, and the difference between the two candidates is the difference between what the scene means and what its sentences are made of. This is the register doing the job CONVENTIONS §5 describes for a typological expectation the wording will not bear.

'Their hearts had swollen in them' contains the KJV's only occurrence of 'swollen' — Acts 28:6, where the Melitans wait for Paul to swell up or drop dead from the viper's bite. A rarity check on the word alone returns a singleton and would tempt a careless row. The senses have nothing in common: Acts 28:6 is envenomed physical swelling and Alma 24:24 is compassion. The Book of Mormon's idiom is its own.

exclusions.sharedText: they were stung for the murders which they had committed
exclusions.reason: The KJV's picture of a crowd struck with remorse after witnessing a killing they took part in is Acts 2:37, 'when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart', with Acts 5:33's 'cut to the heart' beside it — and Alma 24:25 is that scene almost exactly. But 'stung' is not a KJV verb at all; the noun appears at 1 Corinthians 15:55-56, Proverbs 23:32 and Revelation 9:10 and never of conscience. With no shared word the resemblance cannot be adjudicated as dependence.

The same nine-verse phrase proposed at 23:13, and rejected for the same reason: 'weapons of war' is too widely distributed to point anywhere, and Ezekiel 32:27's uncircumcised dead share nothing else with converts throwing their arms down.

exclusions.sharedText: the people of God were joined that day by more than the number which had been slain
exclusions.reason: Acts 2:41 — 'the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls' — is the KJV's one mass conversion counted in a day, and Alma 24:26-27 counts one the same way. The link is already adjudicated in this corpus at Mosiah 18:16, where the addition of souls at a baptism is the point; here the numbering is arithmetic against the slain rather than a borrowing, and there is no shared wording ('joined' for 'added', no 'souls', no figure). Registered so a reader at 24:26 is sent to Mosiah 18:16.

'Fall away' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 8:13 and Hebrews 6:6, and Luke 8:13 is the one this book has used before, at Alma 16:17 and again in the background of 23:6. It is the wrong one here. Luke 8:13's seed on the rock falls away in time of temptation having no root — a failure of shallowness — while Alma 24:30 describes people who were once enlightened and had great knowledge, which is Hebrews 6:4's category and not Luke's. The link is filed at 24:30 against Hebrews 6:4 with 6:6 as a composite.

exclusions.sharedText: the borders of the land of
exclusions.reason: Topographical boilerplate at a verse doing nothing but locating a journey. Exodus 16:35 is the forty years of manna until Israel came to the borders of Canaan; Alma 21:1 is Aaron's road toward a Lamanite city named Jerusalem. The interesting thing in this verse is not a KJV borrowing at all but the Book of Mormon's own gloss — a city 'called by the Lamanites, Jerusalem; calling it after the land of their fathers' nativity' — which the record supplies because it knows the reader will hear the name.

exclusions.sharedText: to preach unto the people and
exclusions.reason: The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter and the emptiest: six words of which every one is required by the sense. Acts 10:42 is Peter at Cornelius's house on the commission to preach and testify that Christ is ordained judge of quick and dead; Alma 21:5 is a man entering a synagogue. The same run ranks again at 21:23. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5. The verse's link is to Acts 6:9, on 'there arose' and the synagogue together.

exclusions.sharedText: How knowest thou the thought and intent of our heart?
exclusions.reason: A KJV singleton — 'the thoughts and intents of the heart' occurs only at Hebrews 4:12 — and it is adjudicated in this book at Alma 12:7, where Alma and Amulek know the thoughts and intents of Zeezrom's heart and where the note shows the chapter working backwards through Hebrews 3:7-4:12 as a unit. It recurs at Alma 18:32. Alma 21:6 is the third use in Alma and the reader should be sent to 12:7 rather than shown a fresh row. Two things about this occurrence are worth recording for whoever revisits that link. First, the 1830 reads the singular, 'the thought and intent of our heart', where the later editions and the KJV have plurals. Second, and more interesting: every previous use in the book is an assertion that a servant of God does know the heart, and this one is a denial that he can — the Amalekite's question is Hebrews 4:12 turned into an objection, put to a preacher whose only instrument is the word of God, which is precisely the thing Hebrews 4:12 says is the discerner. Under ADJUDICATING §4 that is not quite a phrase returning to its source, since the passage being answered is not the passage first translated; it is the book's own adopted phrase used against the book's own missionaries, and it is registered here rather than argued as a new link.

'Sufferings of Christ' occurs in three KJV verses — 2 Corinthians 1:5, 1 Peter 1:11 and 1 Peter 5:1 — and nothing in Alma 21:9 chooses among them. The machine ranked 1 Peter 1:11 and 5:1 together, which is itself the sign that the phrase is distributed rather than owned. 1 Peter 1:11 is attractive because it is about prophets searching what the Spirit in them signified beforehand concerning Christ's sufferings, and Aaron is arguing at 21:8 that the fathers did know 'concerning the things which they spake, of that which is to come'. But the connection is thematic and the phrase is not decisive; the verse's link is to Acts 17:3, on the sequence Alma 21:9-11 runs.

exclusions.sharedText: and they would not hear the words which
exclusions.reason: Zechariah 7:11-13 is a real refusal-to-hear passage — 'they refused to hearken, and pulled away the shoulder' — and it scores here twice, at 7:7 and 7:13, on the KJV's ordinary phrase for it. But 'they would not hear the words which he spake' is how the Book of Mormon says this on every page, and no other element of Zechariah 7 appears. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5. What is happening at 21:10 is Acts 17:32's mocking, filed at 21:9.

exclusions.sharedText: they brought many to the knowledge of the truth
exclusions.reason: 'Come to the knowledge of the truth' is a KJV singleton at 2 Timothy 3:7 with 1 Timothy 2:4's 'come unto the knowledge of the truth' one preposition away, and the Book of Mormon uses the phrase fifteen times. It is adjudicated at Jacob 7:24 and Mosiah 27:14; within Alma its first use is 17:2, and Alma 23:15 already carries a register entry sending readers back. The row is repeated here for the same reason. One observation is worth adding, because it belongs to this chapter and not to the earlier ones: 1 Timothy 2:4 reads 'Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth', and Alma 21 splits that verse between the two sides of its dispute — the Amalekite claims the first half at 21:6, 'We do believe that God will save all men', and the missionaries are granted the second half at 21:17. Neither half is a fresh borrowing, and the pairing is not argued as a link; but a reader who has both halves of one Pauline verse eleven verses apart, in the mouths of opponents, should be told so.

Four words of consecutive-clause syntax. Acts 5:15's 'insomuch that they brought forth the sick into the streets' is Peter's shadow healing; Alma 21:17's 'insomuch that they brought many to the knowledge of the truth' is a conversion count. 'Insomuch that' is one of this book's commonest connectives. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

Four words that are not even a phrase — the run straddles 'the oppressions of the king, his father'. Proverbs 16:10's divine sentence in the lips of a king has no contact with Lamoni's declaration that his people are free. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

exclusions.sharedText: in the midst of the congregation
exclusions.reason: 'Thou hast been merciful unto me, and heard my cries in the midst of thy congregations.' Psalm 22:22, quoted at Hebrews 2:12, is the KJV's memorable use of the phrase — 'in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee' — and the temptation is that Zenos's prayer is otherwise built from KJV materials. But the phrase occurs in four KJV verses, the Psalm's action is praising and Alma's is being heard, and the Book of Mormon's plural 'congregations' matches none of them. Not enough to adjudicate.

'Thou art angry, O Lord, with this people.' 'Thou wast angry' is a KJV singleton and it is at Isaiah 12:1 — but the whole force of Isaiah's clause is concessive and past: 'though thou wast angry with me, thine anger is turned away, and thou comfortedst me.' Zenock's sentence is the reverse in both respects: the anger is present, and it is not turned away, it is the complaint. The singleton is real and the sense is opposed. Note that the neighbouring clause, 'thine anger is turned away', bears on Alma 33:11's 'thou hast turned thy judgments away from me', where the link is filed to Zephaniah 3:15 instead — Zephaniah has the judgments and the casting out that Alma 33:10-11 actually contains.

'Because the people would not understand his words, they stoned him to death.' 2 Chronicles 24:20-21 is the Old Testament's one narrative of a prophet stoned for a message the people would not receive — Zechariah son of Jehoiada, stoned in the court of the house of the LORD — and Matthew 23:35-37 makes that killing the type of all such killings ('thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee'). The resemblance of situation is exact and the verbal contact is one word: 'stoned' occurs in twenty-one KJV verses, mostly of judicial execution. Recorded here because a careful reader would reach for 2 Chronicles 24 and should know why the row was declined.

A KJV singleton, and already adjudicated in this book at its first use, Alma 13:4, where it is welded to Ephesians 4:18's 'blindness of their' to make a doublet neither verse has. Alma 33:20 uses the phrase alone and in its settled Book of Mormon sense; it is the formula recurring, not a fresh borrowing. See Alma 13:4.

exclusions.sharedText: would not look … therefore they perished
exclusions.reason: Hardy's apparatus cross-references Numbers 21:4-9 at this verse and the reference is sound, but the wording it points at is one verse earlier: 33:19's 'a type was raised up in the wilderness, that whosoever would look upon it might live' is where Numbers 21:8's looking and living stand, and the link is filed there with 33:20 and 33:21 in its recurrence list. Alma 33:20 itself adds no Numbers vocabulary — its content is the refusal to look and the hardness that causes it, which is the chapter's own analysis and has no counterpart in the Pentateuch narrative. See Alma 33:19 (CONVENTIONS §6a: where he keys a reference to a verse and the wording is elsewhere, the link goes where the wording is).

exclusions.sharedText: stand before him, to be judged … according to their works
exclusions.reason: 'All men shall stand before him, to be judged, at the last and judgment day, according to their works.' Revelation 20:12's dead 'stand before God' and are 'judged … according to their works', and the three elements arrive here in the source's order. But the judgment formula is already adjudicated in this book at Alma 11:41 against Revelation 20:12 and at Alma 3:26 against Revelation 20:13, and by chapter 33 it is Alma's own settled summary of the resurrection rather than a return to the text (ADJUDICATING §4). 'According to their works' occurs in three KJV verses besides. See Alma 11:41.

'It will become a tree, springing up in you unto everlasting life.' The same borrowing of John 4:14's KJV singleton that is adjudicated eleven verses earlier at Alma 32:41, in the same continuous sermon to the same congregation, with 'in you' added. A reader meets both in one sitting, which is exactly the case ADJUDICATING §4 reserves for the exclusion form. See Alma 32:41.

exclusions.sharedText: they suffered themselves to be slain according to the desires of their enemies
exclusions.reason: The scene is the KJV's chief image of unresisted death — 'he was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter' — and a reader who has just come from Alma 24's mass martyrdom will hear it. But Alma 27:3 has no lamb, no sheep, no silence and no shearers, and 'suffered themselves to be slain' is the Book of Mormon's own construction, used of this people four times in three chapters. Isaiah 53 is heavily worked elsewhere in the book (Mosiah 14 transcribes it) and this catalogue records dependence, not resemblance. The typology is real and the wording will not carry it.

exclusions.sharedText: as though they were angels sent from God
exclusions.reason: 'Sent from God' occurs in two KJV verses, John 1:6 ('there was a man sent from God, whose name was John') and Luke 1:26 ('the angel Gabriel was sent from God unto a city of Galilee'), and Luke 1:26 has the angel as well, which makes it look decisive. It is not: 'sent from God' is three ordinary words of which the Book of Mormon uses two dozen variants, and neither KJV verse has anyone treated AS THOUGH he were an angel, which is the whole content of the clause. The verse's identifiable borrowing is 'moved with compassion', filed as a link against Matthew 9:36.

exclusions.sharedText: desiring the voice of the people
exclusions.reason: 'The voice of the people' is adjudicated at Mosiah 7:9 against 1 Samuel 8:7 — Israel's demand for a king — and again at Mosiah 29:2 and Alma 2:7, where the phrase returns to the passage it first translated because the institution being described is the one Mosiah put in the king's place. Alma 27:21 is that institution running normally: the chief judge sends a proclamation and the voice of the people answers. Registered here rather than passed over because of what the answer is. 1 Samuel 8:7's voice of the people rejects the LORD from reigning over them; Alma 27:22's voice of the people gives away a province to a foreign people that has been trying to kill them, and pays for an army to defend it. That is the sharpest contrast the phrase has been put to in the book, and it is an argument for the institution rather than a fresh borrowing. A reader should be sent to Mosiah 7:9 and Alma 2:7.

exclusions.sharedText: they were perfectly honest and upright in all things
exclusions.reason: Tempting and just short. 'Perfect and upright' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 1:1 — 'that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil' — repeated by the LORD at 1:8 and 2:3, and it is the KJV's formal character-summary, which is the genre of Alma 27:27. But the Book of Mormon's words are 'perfectly honest and upright', with an adverb and an added noun, and 'honest' is not in Job's formula at any point. The pair 'perfect and upright' is not reproduced. The verse's two identifiable borrowings, Acts 22:3 and Hebrews 3:6, are filed as links; this clause between them is the one the KJV does not account for.

exclusions.sharedText: death was swallowed up to them by the victory of Christ over it
exclusions.reason: This is 1 Corinthians 15:54's 'Death is swallowed up in victory' and it is not in doubt; it is adjudicated at Alma 22:14, where Aaron's preaching to the Lamanite king brings four of Paul's terms together in one clause and the row stands at 'certain'.
