Alma 27:28 is the fruit of that sermon reported in the sermon's own words — the same people, five chapters later, no longer fearing death — so it is a recurrence rather than a fresh borrowing, and the register should send a reader to 22:14. Note that the chapter uses Paul's verb twice: at 27:17 it is joy that swallows a man up, which is filed as a link against 2 Corinthians 2:7, the KJV's one verse for a person swallowed up with a feeling.

exclusions.sharedText: a highly favored people of the Lord
exclusions.reason: 'Highly favoured' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Gabriel's salutation to Mary at Luke 1:28, and it was adjudicated for this book at Alma 13:23, with an earlier row at Mosiah 1:13. (The Book of Mormon's opening sentence, 1 Nephi 1:1's 'having been born of goodly parents … highly favored of the Lord', carries no row for the phrase in this catalogue; the pilot adjudicated that verse against Exodus 2:2 on 'goodly' alone.) By Alma 27:30 it is the book's standing epithet for a people under divine favour and no longer a fresh borrowing. Worth the entry for the trajectory: a phrase the KJV uses once, of one woman, at an annunciation, becomes in the Book of Mormon a collective political status, and 27:30 applies it to a people that six chapters ago was outside the covenant altogether.

exclusions.sharedText: the sixteenth year of the reign
exclusions.reason: The same serial-counting coincidence set out at Alma 28:7: the Book of Mormon dates continuously by the year of the reign of the judges and must produce every ordinal in turn, so a match with the KJV's regnal dates carries nothing. The formula itself is first used at Alma 1:1.

'Why do ye yoke yourselves with such foolish things' invites Acts 15:10's 'to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples' and Galatians 5:1's 'yoke of bondage' — Galatians 5:1 is already adjudicated at Mosiah 21:13 and 23:13 — and the invitation is strengthened by Korihor's bondage rhetoric at 30:24 and 30:27. It will not carry a link: only the noun is shared, the Book of Mormon reflexivises the verb in a way no KJV verse does, and the metaphor of a yoke for religious obligation is common to every English writer of the period. The verse's real dependence is on Hebrews 11:1, filed at 30:15.

Alma 30:18 and 30:23 both use 'lift up their heads', and the KJV's memorable instance is Luke 21:28, 'then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh' — an eschatological summons. The sense here is opposed twice over: at 30:18 the heads are lifted 'in their wickedness', and at 30:23 lifting them is what Korihor says the priests prevent. Psalm 24:7's lifted gates are further off still. The idiom is ordinary and the parallel is an artifact of it.

exclusions.sharedText: labour, working with our own hands
exclusions.reason: 'I have labored ... with mine own hands, for my support' is the phrase adjudicated in this book at Alma 1:3, where Nehor's denial of it is argued in full, and at Mosiah 18:24 and 27:5 before that. Within a book a repeat is recorded rather than relinked (ADJUDICATING §4), and the argument is at Alma 1:3. What is new at Alma 30:32 is not the phrase but the frame around it — the whole of 1 Thessalonians 2:5-9's defence against the charge of preaching for gain — and the link is filed there.

'What evidence have ye that there is no God' is the third of the chapter's three contacts with Hebrews 11:1, and the sharpest, since 'evidence' in the sense of grounds for belief occurs in exactly one KJV verse and this is Alma using it back at Korihor. It is adjudicated with the other two at 30:15, where the whole exchange across verses 13, 15 and 40 is set out; a reader arriving here is sent there.

exclusions.sharedText: the heavens declare the glory of God
exclusions.reason: Alma's argument from the motion of the planets — 'all things denote there is a God ... and also all the planets which move in their regular form, doth witness that there is a Supreme Creator' — is the classical argument from design, and Psalm 19:1 and Romans 1:20 are the KJV verses that state it. Neither is verbally present: no word beyond 'God' is shared with Psalm 19:1, and Romans 1:20's 'the invisible things of him ... are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made' is already adjudicated at 2 Nephi 6:3. The passage's actual source is Acts 17, where the same argument answers the same charge about an unknown God, and the link is filed at 30:28.

Matthew 12:39 and 16:4 ('an evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign') are the KJV's judgment on sign-seeking and stand behind this whole exchange; Matthew 16:4 is adjudicated at Mosiah 1:13. The verse that supplies the Book of Mormon's actual sentence is John 4:48, 'Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe', which Korihor reproduces in the first person at 30:48, and the link is filed there with Matthew 12:39 as a composite.

'Went about from house to house, a begging for his food' looks like the imprecation of Psalm 109:10, 'let his children be continually vagabonds, and beg', and 'from house to house' occurs in exactly four KJV verses (Luke 10:7, Acts 2:46, Acts 20:20, 1 Timothy 5:13). None of the four is about begging and none has any other contact here. The source of the detail is Acts 13:11, where the stricken Elymas 'went about seeking some to lead him by the hand' — a KJV singleton — and it is catalogued with the rest of the Elymas sequence at 30:22. Note that the 1830's 'a begging' is a dialect participle the 1920 edition removed; it is not KJV.

'Doth speedily drag them down to hell' is close in sense to 2 Peter 2:4's 'cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness', and 2 Peter 2 is genuinely behind this chapter's portrait of Korihor — the link at 30:31 says so. But the verb here is 'drag', which is in no KJV verse, and no run is shared. Registered rather than passed over because the epistle's presence elsewhere in the chapter makes the parallel tempting.

exclusions.sharedText: inasmuch as ye shall keep the commandments of God, ye shall prosper in the land
exclusions.reason: The land promise that opens and closes the chapter, and the outermost pair of its chiasm (36:1 and 36:30). It is the Book of Mormon's own covenant formula, given first at 1 Nephi 2:20 and repeated by nearly every Nephite prophet; its biblical background is the Deuteronomic prosperity clause (Deuteronomy 29:9, 30:16, Joshua 1:7-8) but no KJV verse supplies the sentence, and 'inasmuch as' is not the KJV's conjunction here. Adjudicate at the formula's first use, not on its four-hundredth. Registered so that a reader of Alma 36:1 is not left supposing the catalogue overlooked its most repeated line.

exclusions.sharedText: that ye should do as I have done
exclusions.reason: The chapter's second-highest-scoring candidate and a false one: 'I would that ye should do as I have done, in remembering the captivity of our fathers' shares with the footwashing only a subjunctive of imitation. The n-gram window closes before the words that matter in each — 'to you' in John, 'in remembering the captivity' in Alma — and the two sentences have no other contact. A textbook instance of ADJUDICATING §4's window-closes-early trap.

exclusions.sharedText: by the mouth of his holy
exclusions.reason: 'By the mouth of his holy prophets' is a KJV formula (Luke 1:70, Acts 3:21) and 'by the mouth of' alone occurs dozens of times. Alma 36:5 has 'by the mouth of his holy angel', which is the formula with the noun changed, and the change is the whole content — Zacharias's prophets speak across the ages, Alma's angel spoke to him once. No verse of Luke 1 is in view.

Registered because the wish in 36:15 — 'that I could be banished and become extinct both soul and body, that I might not be brought to stand in the presence of my God, to be judged of my deeds' — reads like a deliberate inversion of Revelation 20:11-13, where earth and heaven flee from the face of him on the throne and the dead stand before God and are judged 'according to their works'. The elements line up: fleeing the presence, standing to be judged, judgment by deeds. But the shared wording is 'the presence of' and 'judged', both far too common to point at a verse; Matthew 10:28's 'able to destroy both soul and body in hell' is a better candidate for the middle clause and is itself only a two-word contact. Conceptual, not verbal.

exclusions.sharedText: I say unto you my son that
exclusions.reason: 'Again I say unto you' is the KJV's commonest emphatic connective and the Book of Mormon's; the camel and the needle's eye have nothing else in common with Alma's contrast of exquisite pain and exquisite joy. Luke 12:4 was ranked beside it on the same words.

'I have labored without ceasing, that I might bring souls unto repentance' is close to 1 Thessalonians 1:3's 'remembering without ceasing your work of faith, and labour of love' and to Paul's habit generally, but 'without ceasing' occurs in six KJV verses and five of them are about prayer or remembrance rather than labour. No one verse is identifiable, and the phrase had long since passed into ordinary devotional English.
Five words of temporal connective. Sheshbazzar's unfinished temple and Alma's unceasing labour share a way of saying 'ever since'. Covered in kind by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

The same Ahab-and-Naboth verse that was the runner-up at Alma 35:15, ranked again here on the same five words, and wrong in the opposite direction. At 35:15 the phrase belongs to Matthew 13:21 and describes hearers who take offence; here — 'because of the word which he hath imparted unto me, behold, many hath been born of God' — it describes a word that converts. Ahab is heavy and displeased because of the word Naboth spoke; the collocation is a bare causal formula and carries no sense in either place.

A KJV singleton, which is why it deserves an entry rather than silence — 'I will put my trust in him' occurs only at Hebrews 2:13. But Hebrews is there quoting Isaiah 8:17 to prove Christ's solidarity with his brethren, there is no deliverance in the context, and the singleton cannot account for what makes Alma 36:27 distinctive: the three tenses of deliverance surrounding the trust. That is 2 Corinthians 1:10's construction, filed as the link at this verse, and 2 Corinthians 1:9 supplies the raising of the dead that Alma 36:28 then states.

Hezekiah's account of the wrath that came upon Judah, 'and he hath delivered them to trouble' — the same five words with the opposite object and the opposite sense. Alma 36:28's deliverance is out of bondage; 2 Chronicles 29:8's is into it. The run is an accident of a very common verb.

exclusions.sharedText: our fathers out of the land of
exclusions.reason: A real seven-word run and still not decidable. Joshua 24:17's 'brought us up and our fathers out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage' is one of some dozen KJV recitals with this shape — Exodus 13:3, 20:2, Deuteronomy 5:6, 6:12, Judges 6:8, 1 Kings 8:21 — and 'house of bondage' alone occurs in ten verses. Alma 36:28-29 recites the exodus twice, once for Egypt and once for Jerusalem, in the formula's ordinary words. The one word in the recital that is a choice rather than a formula is 'swallowed', and the link at 36:28 is placed there.

The negative half of the land promise, and the closing words of the chapter. Cain's 'from thy face shall I be hid' and the KJV's various 'cut off from before me' (Jeremiah 7:15) and 'cast out of my sight' (2 Kings 17:20) stand in the general background, but 'cut off from his presence' is the Book of Mormon's own formula, coined at 1 Nephi 2:21 as the counterpart to the prosperity clause and repeated with it throughout. Adjudicate at 1 Nephi 2:21; registered here because a reader who has just been shown the promise will look for its threat.

exclusions.sharedText: the Egyptians in the red sea
exclusions.reason: Hardy's apparatus cross-references Exodus 14:26-28 at this verse and it points at the right event, but the wording Alma uses is not in that chapter. Exodus 14:27-28 has the LORD overthrowing the Egyptians in the midst of the sea and the waters returning and covering them; nothing there is swallowed and the Red sea is not named. The verb and the name both come from the Song of the Sea in the chapter following — “the earth swallowed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 15:12, of these same Egyptians, and “drowned in the Red sea” occurs in exactly one, Exodus 15:4 — so the link is filed at Exodus 15:12 with 14:28 in its composite (CONVENTIONS §6a: put the link where the wording is, and record where the apparatus points). The choice of the poem over the prose is itself the finding, since Alma 36:28 introduces the recital with a vow of praise.

'Hands of their enemies' is a KJV singleton at Judges 2:14 and the machine ranked it first here, but the Book of Mormon uses the phrase seventeen times and the Judges-cycle argument for it is already made in this book at Alma 2:28, where it is adjudicated against Judges 2:18 ('the Lord raised them up judges … and delivered them out of the hand of their enemies'), the verse that completes the cycle Judges 2:14 begins. Alma 43:9 is Mormon's own formula recurring, not a fresh borrowing. See Alma 2:28.

exclusions.sharedText: the true and the living God
exclusions.reason: The KJV singleton is 'the living and true God' (1 Thessalonians 1:9); the Book of Mormon's inverted 'the true and the living God' occurs in no KJV verse at all. The inversion and its Thessalonian source are adjudicated at Alma 7:6, with a further row at Alma 11:27. This is the same formula recurring inside the same book. See Alma 7:6.

exclusions.sharedText: fall into the hands … the living God
exclusions.reason: The machine ranked this at 43:10 and 43:11 on a six-word run, and it is the most tempting candidate in the chapter because Hebrews 10:31 is the only KJV verse that holds 'fall into the hands' and 'the living God' together — both of which stand in Alma 43:10, eleven words apart. The sense is exactly inverted. In Hebrews the hands are God's and falling into them is the fearful thing; in Alma the hands are the Lamanites' and the living God is the one whose worshippers those hands would destroy. Hebrews makes God the danger; Alma makes God the reason for the danger. The coincidence is an artifact of a single verse holding two ordinary phrases the Book of Mormon happens to use in one sentence for unrelated reasons.

'In spirit and in truth' belongs to John 4 and to no other KJV chapter, and it is adjudicated in this book at Alma 34:38, where Amulek gives it in full ('Worship God in whatsoever place ye may be in, in spirit and in truth'). Here it is Mormon quoting the formula the book has already established. Worth recording that 43:10 is the one verse in the Book of Mormon that fuses it with the Thessalonians formula — 'worship God, in spirit and in truth, the true and the living God' — so a reader arriving at 43:10 should be sent to both Alma 34:38 and Alma 7:6.

The sequence is arresting — an army under threat, a commander who enquires of the Lord about where to go, an oracle that answers with a route rather than a promise, and a flanking attack from the rear — and 2 Samuel 5:22-25 is the KJV's one instance of it ('fetch a compass behind them, and come upon them over against the mulberry trees'). But the verbal contact is nil: the Book of Mormon writes 'inquire', where every one of the KJV's ten instances reads 'enquire', and shares no other word. Recorded here because a careful reader might accept it, and because Joshua 8 (adjudicated at 43:30) accounts for the ambush without needing it.
A five-word introduction formula the KJV uses whenever a new character enters. Nothing connects Lehi's flanking column to the annunciation but the syntax of naming somebody.

'They did fight like dragons' is one of the chapter's few genuinely vivid phrases and 'like dragons' is a KJV singleton, which makes it look adjudicable. Read Jeremiah 14:6 and the simile evaporates: 'the wild asses did stand in the high places, they snuffed up the wind like dragons; their eyes did fail, because there was no grass.' The tenor is drought, the vehicle is a panting animal, and the point of comparison is gasping for air — the opposite of ferocity in battle. The KJV's dragons elsewhere (Jeremiah 51:37, Isaiah 34:13, Malachi 1:3) are desolation-markers haunting ruined cities, never fighters. The Book of Mormon's dragon is the fighting dragon of Revelation 12:7 in everything but its name, and no wording connects them.

43:46-47 quotes a divine word licensing defensive killing — 'inasmuch as ye are not guilty of the first offence, neither the second, ye shall not suffer yourselves to be slain by the hands of your enemies' — and attributes it to what the Lord said to 'their fathers'. The Bible has exactly one law of that kind, Exodus 22:2, whose 'there shall no blood be shed for him' is a KJV singleton and which Alma 43:54 comes near ('he commanded his men that they should stop shedding their blood'). But no wording is shared, the Exodus case is a householder and a burglar rather than a nation and an army, and the two-offences condition has no biblical counterpart at all. Recorded because the verse invites a source-hunt and does not reward one; the quoted law appears to be the Book of Mormon's own.
A quotation formula. Solomon's dedication of the temple and Moroni's law of defensive war share nothing but the way English introduces reported divine speech.

exclusions.sharedText: this is the thing which I have
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and a genuine formal parallel — both sentences are a revealer telling a hearer that what follows is the disclosed thing — and still not a link. Joseph's 'This is the thing which I have spoken unto Pharaoh' and Alma's 'this is the thing of which I do know' diverge at the verb, which is where all the meaning is: Joseph has spoken a dream's interpretation, Alma has inquired and been told. The frame 'this is the thing which' is KJV disclosure boilerplate (Exodus 16:16, 16:32, 35:4, Leviticus 8:5, 9:6, Numbers 30:1), and nothing in Genesis 41 bears on souls, death, or the interval Alma is describing.

exclusions.sharedText: they shall rise from the dead
exclusions.reason: The stream's top candidate for both 40:5 and 40:9, on a six-word run, and it is the wrong chapter of the right subject. Mark 12:18-27 is the Sadducees' riddle about the woman with seven husbands, and Jesus' answer is about marriage, not about an interval between death and resurrection; nothing else in the verse or its context surfaces in Alma 40. 'Rise from the dead' is distributed across some twenty KJV verses. Where Alma 40 does touch the Sadducees it is at 40:2, and the phrase there is 'there is no resurrection', which the register sends to 1 Corinthians 15:12 with the Sadducee verses named.

exclusions.sharedText: led captive by the will of the Devil
exclusions.reason: The verse's closing clause is the fourth appearance in Alma of the snare-and-captivity sentence of 2 Timothy 2:26 ('who are taken captive by him at his will', a KJV singleton). It is adjudicated at Alma 12:6, with 12:11 and 12:17 recorded there as recurrences; 40:13 is a fifth instance of the same speaker's settled formula rather than a fresh borrowing, and it adds nothing the earlier verses do not have. Registered here because a reader meeting 'led captive by the will of the Devil' at the climax of Alma 40 will want to be told where the argument for it is made.

Four shared words in the same order and an opposed sense. Deuteronomy's 'no part nor inheritance' is a statement about the priestly tribe's landlessness and it is a privilege, not a punishment — Levi has no allotment because the LORD is his inheritance. Five KJV verses say it (Deuteronomy 10:9, 12:12, 14:27, 14:29, 18:1) and all five are that same provision. Alma 40:13 is denying the wicked dead a share in the Spirit as the consequence of their own choice. The only KJV verse in which the frame denies a man a part in the Spirit is Acts 8:21, to Simon Magus, and that is filed as a link at this verse at low confidence with its own whyNot.

The devils of Gadara begging to enter the swine is the machine's proposal for 'the spirit of the Devil did enter into them', and it is a real thematic neighbour — the KJV's other scene of spirits entering a body at their own request. But the four shared words are ordinary, Luke 8 supplies no 'house' and no 'possession', and what Alma 40:13 actually reproduces is the figure of the possessed person as a house, which belongs to Matthew 12:43-45 and Luke 11:24-26. The link is filed there.

'Both soul and body' occurs in exactly two KJV verses and this is one of them, so the rarity is real; the sense is not. Isaiah 10:18 is the burning of Assyria's forest and fruitful field, where 'both soul and body' is a totalizing idiom for utter consumption and the standard-bearer faints. Alma 40:21 has soul and body reunited and standing before God. The other KJV occurrence, Matthew 10:28, is nearer the subject — God able to destroy both soul and body in hell — but its sense is destruction where Alma's is restoration, and the phrase is doing no work in Alma beyond naming the two halves he has spent the chapter separating. The link at this verse is Revelation 20:12-13.

exclusions.sharedText: no unclean thing can inherit the Kingdom of God
exclusions.reason: The sentence is adjudicated at Alma 11:37, where Amulek offers it as a divine quotation and the note shows it has two KJV parents and no KJV existence — Ephesians 5:5's 'no whoremonger, nor unclean person' having 'any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God', and 1 Corinthians 6:9-10's list who 'shall not inherit the kingdom of God'. Alma 40:26 is the same formula in the same book, with one change worth recording here: Amulek said 'Kingdom of Heaven', a phrase confined in the KJV to Matthew, and Alma says 'Kingdom of God', which is the form 1 Corinthians 6:9-10 and Galatians 5:21 actually use. The formula has drifted toward its Pauline source rather than away from it.

A five-word run and the machine's best candidate for the chapter's last verse, matching a regulation about ovens and pot-ranges defiled by a carcase falling on them, which are to be broken down. The Book of Mormon's 'they are unclean' is a verdict on persons at the judgment. The one genuine point of contact is that Alma's uncleanness is cultic rather than moral vocabulary, which is a Levitical inheritance in general and not a borrowing from this verse.

A genuine curiosity that resolves to boilerplate. “to reign in his stead” does occur in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 1:8, because the infinitive is rare; the finite form 'reigned in his stead' occurs in sixty-three, from Genesis 36 through 2 Kings, and that formula is plainly what stands behind 'thus king Ammoron, the brother of king Amalickiah, was appointed to reign in his stead'. The singleton cannot be the source on sense either: 2 Chronicles 1:8 is Solomon thanking God for having 'made me to reign in his stead' after David, a lawful and divinely granted succession, whereas Ammoron is a usurper's brother taking the throne of a man murdered in his tent. The same candidate was declined on the same grounds at Jacob 1:11 and, in its finite form, at Mosiah 10:6.

Four words of relative-clause tissue. Numbers 13:32 is the spies' evil report of 'the land which they had searched'; Alma 52:5 has 'those parts of the land which they had obtained possession of'. The shared run stops exactly where the content would begin.

Worth registering because the rarity looks promising and the sense is opposed. Lamentations 3:34, 'To crush under his feet all the prisoners of the earth', is one clause in a list of things the Lord does not approve; Alma 52:8 is Moroni's order that Teancum 'retain all the prisoners of the Lamanites, as a ransom' — an instruction to keep captives alive and exchange them, which is the chapter's distinguishing humane policy and the opposite of crushing them. Five shared words, none of them doing the same work.

exclusions.sharedText: the cities which he had taken
exclusions.reason: The run is real but it belongs to a link filed three verses earlier. Alma 52:10's programme of retaking lost cities is adjudicated against 2 Kings 13:25, the KJV's one verse about a king recovering cities an enemy took from his predecessor, and 2 Kings 13:25 carries the same six words as 2 Chronicles 15:8 plus the two singletons ('taken out of the hand', 'recovered the cities') that decide it. Asa's captured cities in 2 Chronicles 15:8 are the setting for smashing idols, not for a war of recovery. See Alma 52:10.

exclusions.sharedText: in the twenty and seventh year of
exclusions.reason: The regnal-dating formula, which Alma uses as its chapter furniture and which the n-gram stream ranks highly in every chapter of the book. 1 Kings 16:15, 2 Kings 15:1 and 1 Kings 16:10 were all offered on the same seven words for this verse, and 1 Kings 16:8 twice for 'the twenty and sixth year' at 52:1 and 52:14; the fact that three unrelated verses tie for first place is itself the demonstration that no one of them is a source. 'In the Nth year of the reign of the judges' is the Book of Mormon's own dating system wearing the KJV's regnal syntax. Covered in kind by the standing exclusions at Alma 4:1, Alma 15:19, Alma 28:9 and Alma 35:13.

Not a rejection: a cross-reference. The Lukan formula 'sent unto him, desiring him that he would' is adjudicated at Alma 52:10, where the Book of Mormon reproduces eight consecutive words of Acts 19:31. Alma 52:20's 'desiring him that he would come out with his armies to meet them upon the plains' is the same borrowing used a second time in the same chapter, and it is the more interesting of the two — Acts 19:31's message asks its recipient NOT to venture into the public arena, and Jacob, declining Moroni's invitation to the open plain, does what Paul's friends asked Paul to do. The argument is made at 52:10; a reader arriving here should go there.

The five-word run is exact and the situations do not touch. 1 Kings 21:16 is Ahab going down to Naboth's vineyard 'to take possession of it' after Jezebel has had Naboth judicially murdered — the KJV's paradigm of unlawful seizure. Alma 52:24 is Moroni's detachment entering a city its own people lost in war. 'Take possession of' is the ordinary English for occupying, and the machine's high score here is an artifact of the phrase being short and complete.

exclusions.sharedText: leading away the Lamanites which were pursuing them in vain
exclusions.reason: A cross-reference rather than a rejection. Joshua 8:16's 'they pursued after Joshua, and were drawn away from the city' is the source of this verse's action — the garrison drawn out and away by a feigned flight — but the whole Ai sequence is adjudicated at Alma 52:22 on Joshua 8:13's singleton 'on the west of the city', with Joshua 8:16 recorded there as a composite. A reader who wants the argument for the decoy should go to 52:22; the recurrence references there return to this verse, 52:31 and 52:36.

'Weapons of war' occurs in nine KJV verses and is the Book of Mormon's standing phrase for arms; Alma 52 alone uses it at 25, 32, 36, 38 and 39. No single KJV verse can be its source. Ezekiel 32:27's uncircumcised mighty gone down to hell with their weapons of war, swords laid under their heads, is a burial image with nothing to do with a surrender in the field.

Five words of relative-clause tissue, and the 1830's 'which' where 1920 reads 'who' is what lengthens the run. Ezra 2:1's returning exiles have no bearing on a count of prisoners against dead. Covered in kind by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

'Keep all these things sacred which I have kept, even as I have kept them.' A five-word run, and the machine's best offer for the verse. The verb decides against it. John 15:10's keeping is obedience — 'even as I have kept my Father's commandments, and abide in his love' — and Alma's is custody: the object of the verb is a set of plates, and the whole paragraph is about who physically holds them and hands them on. The same run has already been declined at 1 Nephi 2:20 and 2 Nephi 4:4, where it attached to the prosperity conditional; here it attaches to an inventory. The register keeps the row because 'keep the commandments' is genuinely a live idiom two verses later at 37:13, and a reader who saw the run at 37:2 could reasonably think John was in the room.

exclusions.sharedText: his paths are straight; and his course is one eternal round
exclusions.reason: The Book of Mormon's formula for divine immutability, and it has one adjudication in this book, at Alma 7:20, where the same speaker sets 'he cannot walk in crooked paths', 'neither doth he vary from that which he hath said', and 'his course is one eternal round' against James 1:17's 'no variableness, neither shadow of turning'. Alma 37:12 is the compressed form of that same sentence — straight paths, one eternal round — thirty chapters later in Alma's own mouth, and it is his formula recurring rather than a fresh borrowing (ADJUDICATING §4). Its first statement in the corpus is 1 Nephi 10:19. A reader tempted by Isaiah 40:3 or Matthew 3:3 ('make his paths straight') should note that the straightness there is a road to be prepared by men, not a property of God's own course.

exclusions.sharedText: if ye will keep my commandments, ye shall prosper in the land
exclusions.reason: The land covenant in its fullest Book of Mormon form, given here as direct divine speech with both halves intact — 'if ye will keep my commandments, ye shall prosper in the land; but if ye keep not his commandments, ye shall be cut off from his presence.' Its adjudication is at 1 Nephi 2:20, to 1 Kings 2:3, where the promise is first stated; within Alma the recurrence is registered at Alma 36:1, whose chiasm turns on it. Nothing at 37:13 departs from the established formula, so the row here is a cross-reference rather than a link. Note that the negative clause reads 'cut off from HIS presence' where 1 Nephi 2:21 has 'the presence of the Lord' and 2 Nephi 4:4 has 'my presence' — the drift in the possessive is catalogued at 2 Nephi 4:4.

exclusions.sharedText: the blood of those which they murdered, did cry unto the Lord
exclusions.reason: 'They murdered all the prophets of the Lord which came among them … and the blood of those which they murdered, did cry unto the Lord their God, for vengeance upon those which were their murderers.' Both halves of the sentence are already adjudicated in this book and within twenty-three chapters of each other: crying blood to Genesis 4:10 at Alma 14:11 ('blood crieth' is a KJV singleton), and the martyrs' demand for vengeance to Revelation 6:10 at Alma 14:26 ('avenge our blood' is a KJV singleton). Alma 37:30 fuses them, which is worth a reader's notice, but it is Alma reusing two figures the book has already given him rather than reaching for the Bible again (ADJUDICATING §4). Two further candidates were considered and declined: Luke 11:50, 'the blood of all the prophets, which was shed from the foundation of the world, may be required of this generation', which is closest in situation and shares no distinctive wording, and Matthew 23:35, which supplies neither the crying nor the vengeance.

exclusions.sharedText: never be weary of good works
exclusions.reason: 'Teach them to never be weary of good works.' The New Testament says this twice — Galatians 6:9, 'let us not be weary in well doing', and 2 Thessalonians 3:13, 'be not weary in well doing' — and the sense is identical to Alma's. But 'weary in well doing' is the fixed KJV form of the idiom, occurring in those two verses and nowhere else, and Alma has neither the preposition nor the noun: 'weary OF GOOD WORKS' matches no KJV verse. Since the second half of the same clause reproduces Matthew 11:29 word for word (see the link at this verse), the failure to reproduce Paul is evidence rather than noise — the chapter can quote when it is quoting, and here it is not.

'Yea, let all thy doings be unto the Lord.' 'All thy doings' is a KJV singleton and the temptation is real, since this catalogue has already put Zephaniah 3 in Alma's hands four chapters earlier — Zephaniah 3:15 stands behind Alma 33:11. But the singleton's sense is opposed at the only point that matters. Zephaniah 3:11 reads 'In that day shalt thou not be ashamed for all thy doings, wherein thou hast transgressed against me': the doings are sins, named as such in the same clause, and the verse is a promise that they will no longer shame the sinner. Alma's doings are the whole of a righteous young man's conduct, offered to God. The phrase in Alma is better explained as the substituted noun in the Proverbs 3:6 borrowing at 37:37 — 'in all thy doings' for Proverbs' 'in all thy ways' — where it is set up a verse in advance.

exclusions.sharedText: if they would look, they might live
exclusions.reason: Hardy's apparatus cross-references Numbers 21:7-9 here and the reference is sound; the link is filed four chapters earlier, at Alma 33:19, where the brazen serpent is described rather than merely alluded to — 'a type was raised up in the wilderness, that whosoever would look upon it might live' — and where Numbers 21:8's own words, looking and living, actually stand. Alma 33:20 and 33:21 are already in that link's recurrence list, and Alma 37:46 belongs with them: it is the same speaker returning to his own figure at the end of the same sermon-cycle, and it supplies no Numbers vocabulary that 33:19 does not already have. What 37:46 does add is a shift of tense and party, 'so was it with our fathers … even so it is with us. The way is prepared, and if we will look, we may live forever', which extends the type from the wilderness generation to Alma's own and from living to living forever. That extension is the verse's contribution and it is Alma's, not Moses'. See Alma 33:19 (CONVENTIONS §6a). The recurrence list at Alma 33:19 should be extended to include Alma 37:46 and Alma 37:47 when that chapter file is next touched.

exclusions.sharedText: that as many as would not
exclusions.reason: The chapter's highest-scoring machine candidate, and a false one. 'As many as would not' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 13:15, where the beast's image kills as many as would not worship it; Alma 46:1 has 'as many as would not hearken to the words of Helaman' gathering against their brethren. The two agree in a five-word relative construction and in nothing else: Revelation's clause names victims of a tyrant, Alma's names the tyrant's own faction. Where the Book of Mormon does pick up a covenant enforced by death it is Asa's, not the beast's, and that link is written at 46:35.

'The flattering words of Amalickiah' (46:7), and again 'a man of many flattering words' (46:10), use a phrase that occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Thessalonians 2:5. The borrowing is real and the argument for it — that Paul's disavowal of flattery and of 'a cloke of covetousness' is the exact anti-type of a demagogue seeking power — is made in this catalogue at Alma 30:47, with the earlier Nephite instance at Mosiah 11:7. Within one book a narrator reusing his own formula is not a fresh borrowing (ADJUDICATING §4), so the reader of 46:7 is sent to Alma 30:47 rather than given the row twice.

'The hearts of many people' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the absolute rarity is why this needs an entry rather than silence. Ezekiel 32:9 is God vexing the hearts of many people by destroying Egypt; Alma 46:10 is Amalickiah leading away the hearts of many people to do wickedly. The shared four words are a quantifier plus a body part, the verbs are opposed in agent and in effect, and nothing else in either verse touches the other. A KJV singleton that carries no sense with it is exactly the trap CONVENTIONS §9 warns the n-gram stream will set.

'Our wives and our children' with exactly these pronouns occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Numbers 14:3, and it is tempting because the title of liberty ends on those five words. But Numbers 14:3 is the wilderness generation's argument for going back to Egypt — 'that our wives and our children should be a prey? were it not better for us to return' — the classic KJV speech of a people refusing to fight. Moroni's banner exists to make them fight. The register keeps the row because the rarity is real and a careful reader would stop at it; the link at this verse goes instead to Nehemiah 4:14, whose 'fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives' is the same list on the right side of the argument.

Scored at the top of its verse, and proposed again at 46:28. 'These words he went forth' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 18:1 — Jesus crossing the Kedron to Gethsemane — but the run is produced entirely by the Book of Mormon's own transition formula, 'when [X] had said these words, he went forth', which recurs across the whole book. The window closes before the words that would matter in either text: 'with his disciples over the brook Cedron' in John, 'among the people, waving the rent of his garment' in Alma. A narrative hinge shared by two writers of English narrative, not a borrowing.

exclusions.sharedText: the words of Jacob, before his death
exclusions.reason: Moroni quotes a prophecy of Jacob about a preserved remnant of Joseph's coat, introduced as 'the words of Jacob, before his death'. Genesis 49:22-26 is the King James Bible's only speech of Jacob before his death concerning Joseph, and a reader will go there. It is not the source: Genesis 49 says nothing about the coat, nothing about a remnant preserved from decay, and shares no wording with Alma 46:24-26 beyond the name Joseph. The quoted prophecy has no KJV background at all — it belongs to the Book of Mormon's own tradition of Joseph material (compare 2 Nephi 3) — and is registered here so the catalogue is not read as having missed the chapter's longest quotation. The Genesis contact in this passage is at 46:23, where 'rent in pieces' is Genesis 37:33.

'If we do not stand fast in the faith of Christ' reproduces a KJV singleton, 1 Corinthians 16:13, and it is a genuine borrowing. It is adjudicated in this catalogue at Alma 1:25, where the phrase stands beside 15:58's 'steadfast and immoveable' in the same sentence and the argument can be made properly; that row records earlier instances at 1 Nephi 2:10 and Mosiah 5:15. Within a single book a repeated formula is adjudicated at first use (ADJUDICATING §4), so 46:27 is cross-referenced rather than duplicated.

'Appointed by the Chief Judges and the voice of the people' uses the phrase that occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 8:7, God's concession to Samuel when Israel demands a king. The catalogue adjudicates it at Mosiah 7:9, again at Mosiah 29:2 where the kingship it first authorized is abolished, and within Alma at 2:3 and 10:19. Its appearance here is pointed — Moroni's authority rests on the voice of the people in the same chapter in which Amalickiah tries to become king by flattering it — but the borrowing itself has been argued, and a fifth full row would be the narrator's formula, not a new dependence.

'Thus Moroni planted the standard of liberty among the Nephites' is the chapter's closing image and the phrase every reader of Isaiah expects to be a borrowing: 'the Spirit of the LORD shall lift up a standard against him' (59:19), 'he shall set up an ensign for the nations' (11:12), 'set up a standard' (Jeremiah 50:2). It will not bear a link. 'Standard' occurs in nineteen KJV verses and 'ensign' in eight, most of them Numbers' tribal standards; 'planted the standard' occurs in none; and Isaiah's standard is raised by God against an enemy, not hoisted on towers by an army. The verse's real intertext is the one this catalogue writes at 46:12, where the object raised on the pole is a rent garment, and that figure is Samuel's and Ahijah's rather than Isaiah's.

The chapter's last verse — 'there were many who died with old age; and those who died in the faith of Christ, are happy in him' — invites Genesis 25:8's 'Abraham gave up the ghost, and died in a good old age', the KJV's formula for a peaceful death. The Book of Mormon's preposition is different ('with' for 'in'), the KJV's qualifying adjective 'good' is absent, and 'old age' is spread across fifteen KJV verses. There is nothing here to identify a source; the sentence is a demographic note, not an allusion.

exclusions.sharedText: in the eleventh month … day of the month
exclusions.reason: A rarity count that looks decisive and is not, and worth the register for that reason. 'In the eleventh month' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 1:3, so the n-gram stream ranks it first for Alma 49:1 — but the singleton is an artifact of the biblical calendar's coverage rather than of a distinctive phrase. The frame around it, 'in the Nth month … on the Nth day of the month', occurs in 52 KJV verses, and the eleventh month simply has almost nothing dated to it. Deuteronomy 1:3 dates Moses's farewell address; Alma 49:1 dates the approach of a Lamanite army on Ammonihah, and shares no word with it that the other 51 dating formulas do not also supply. An absolute rarity is the strongest evidence this project has (ADJUDICATING §3.1) precisely when the phrase is a choice; here the writer chose a month, not a phrase.

A genuine KJV singleton — 'yoke of bondage' occurs only at Galatians 5:1 — and a real borrowing, but not one to adjudicate here. It is already carried in the corpus at Mosiah 21:13 and Mosiah 23:13, where the Limhi and Alma bondage narratives use it of an actual servitude, and within the book of Alma its first appearance is at 44:2, five chapters earlier, in Moroni's speech to Zerahemnah. Alma 49:7 and 49:26 are the phrase recurring as the narrator's own formula for what Amalickiah wants and does not get (ADJUDICATING §4), and the whole verse of Galatians 5:1 — liberty, being made free, the yoke — supplies the political vocabulary of Alma 46-51 rather than of any one verse in it. Registered here because a reader meeting the phrase twice in this chapter should be sent to where the argument is made.

exclusions.sharedText: there lacketh not one man of us
exclusions.reason: 'There was not a single soul of the Nephites which were slain' against more than a thousand Lamanite dead is the KJV's one-sided muster report, and Numbers 31:49 is the KJV's one instance of it in words — 'thy servants have taken the sum of the men of war which are under our charge, and there lacketh not one man of us', a singleton. It is tempting and it is the wrong home. No word is shared; the Book of Mormon's phrasing ('not a single soul') is in no KJV verse; and the chapter has a better account of the asymmetry in the Sennacherib oracle already adjudicated at 49:2, where 185,000 of the besieging host fall and Jerusalem loses nobody. Alma 49:24's fifty wounded also breaks the Numbers 31 claim, which is absolute. Sent to 49:2.

A four-word run and the senses are opposed. In Revelation 12:6 the woman flees into the wilderness to a place prepared of God, where she is fed for 1,260 days: flight as divine preservation, and the wilderness as sanctuary. In Alma 49:25 a defeated Lamanite army flees into the wilderness because its captains are all dead, and the wilderness is where beaten armies go in this book from Alma 2:37 onward. The Book of Mormon's wilderness is a route and a refuge for the righteous elsewhere; here it is a rout. The candidate is the n-gram stream matching a phrase that any narrative of a defeat in KJV English would produce.

exclusions.sharedText: will not keep my commandments … cut off
exclusions.reason: The verse is a quotation, and the text says so: 'his words … which he spake unto Lehi, saying: Blessed art thou, and thy children …' What is quoted is 1 Nephi 2:20-21, the conditional promise of prosperity and of being cut off from the presence of the Lord, and that is where its biblical sources are adjudicated — 1 Kings 2:3 and Ezekiel 20:6 at 1 Nephi 2:20, Genesis 4:16 at 1 Nephi 2:21. The n-gram stream's proposal of 1 Kings 9:6 ('will not keep my commandments … then will I cut off Israel out of the land') is not wrong about the family: 1 Kings 8-9 is the Solomonic covenant text, and the link filed at Alma 50:19 argues that this whole passage is running on it. But the promise itself is quoted from earlier in the Book of Mormon, not from Kings, and a reader should be sent to 1 Nephi 2:20 for the words and to Alma 50:19 for the frame.

exclusions.sharedText: (no shared wording — a beaten maidservant who flees)
exclusions.reason: A typological expectation the wording will not bear, and worth recording because the expectation is strong. Morianton 'was angry with one of his maidservants, and he fell upon her, and beat her much', and she flees to Moroni's camp and tells him everything — which is the Bible's one scene of a beaten maidservant in flight, Hagar at Genesis 16:6, 'when Sarai dealt hardly with her, she fled from her face'. Judges 19 offers the other candidate, the Levite's concubine, whose flight ends in civil war. Neither will do. Not one word is shared with either; 'maidservant' in the KJV occurs only in law codes and lists of property (Exodus 20:17, Deuteronomy 5:21, Jeremiah 34:9); and the two biblical flights run the other way from this one — Hagar's flight is reversed by an angel who sends her back, the concubine's precipitates a war, while this woman's flight prevents one. The inversion is the interesting thing about the episode, but an inversion of a scene that shares no language is a reading, not a link.

A KJV singleton — 'flattering words' occurs only at 1 Thessalonians 2:5, where Paul denies using them — and the Book of Mormon's standing term for demagoguery, eight times from Mosiah 11:7 onward. It is adjudicated at Mosiah 11:7, of Noah and his priests, and already registered as a recurrence at Alma 46:7 for Amalickiah. Alma 50:35's use is the narrator's own, in a parenthesis explaining why Morianton's people fought ('being inspired by his wickedness and his flattering words'), and it is the same formula a third time. Sent to Mosiah 11:7.

Checked because the phrase is rare and the verse is memorable, and rejected on sense. “bury their dead” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 8:22 and Luke 9:60, and both are the same saying: 'Let the dead bury their dead' — a refusal of a burial duty in favour of following Jesus. Alma 53:1 is the imposition of a burial duty on prisoners of war, under guard. The Book of Mormon's clause is the plain English for the action and shares nothing with the Gospel logion but three words in the same order.

A tempting one, and worth the register because of what sits beside it. “the more part” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 19:32 and Acts 27:12, both Lukan and both meaning 'the majority' — and this catalogue has just adjudicated a KJV singleton from Acts 19:31 at Alma 52:10, one verse from the first of them. So the coincidence looks like recurrence. It is declined anyway: 'the more part' is standard Early Modern and early-nineteenth-century English for a majority, not a King James coinage, and Alma 53:2's 'in the more part of all his battles' uses it in a quantitative sense ('most of') that neither Acts verse has — both of theirs are the greater number of persons in an assembly. A shared archaism is not a borrowing.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that after the
exclusions.reason: The dossier's longest run in the chapter, eight words, and worth nothing: 'and it came to pass that after the' is the Book of Mormon's commonest sentence opening and the KJV's. That 1 Chronicles 20:1 goes on to a siege of Rabbah while Alma 53:3 goes on to a ditch dug round Bountiful is the sort of thematic near-miss that makes a long run look meaningful. Covered in kind by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1.

Four words, and the senses face opposite ways. Amos 3:11's adversary 'round about the land' is an enemy encircling Israel for destruction; Alma 53:3's ditch is dug 'round about the land, or the city Bountiful' as a defence built by the enemy's own prisoners. The KJV's siege idiom that would matter here is 'cast up a bank against the city' (2 Samuel 20:15, and compare 2 Kings 19:32), and Alma 53:4's 'they cast up dirt out of the ditch against the breastwork' inverts it — earth thrown up by besiegers in the KJV, earth thrown up by the besieged here — but 'cast up' is too widely used (seven KJV verses) to carry a link on its own.

exclusions.sharedText: and they entered into a covenant to
exclusions.reason: A cross-reference, not a rejection, and the highest-ranked candidate in the chapter. “entered into a covenant” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Chronicles 15:12 and Ezekiel 16:8, and only 2 Chronicles 15:12 has the Book of Mormon's construction with an infinitive of purpose — 'entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers' / 'entered into a covenant, to fight for the liberty of the Nephites'. That borrowing is adjudicated in this book at Alma 46:35, where Moroni's covenant of freedom carries the second half of Asa's passage as well ('whosoever would not' and the death penalty of 2 Chronicles 15:13). Alma 53:17 is the same formula in the same hand seven chapters later, so it is registered here rather than relinked; a reader should go to 46:35. The Johannine 'laying down of their lives' in the same verse is a separate borrowing and is filed as a link.

'Weapons of war' occurs in nine KJV verses and is the Book of Mormon's own standing phrase for arms, used four times in this chapter alone (53:14, 16, 18, 19). Ezekiel 32:27's uncircumcised warriors gone down to hell with their weapons of war have nothing to do with two thousand young men taking theirs up. The same candidate was registered on the same words at Alma 52:36.

'Keep the commandments' is one of the most widely distributed phrases in the King James Bible and one of the Book of Mormon's most frequent; Deuteronomy 10:13 has no better claim on Alma 53:21 than a dozen other verses. The clause that matters in this verse is 'men of truth and soberness', which is adjudicated as a link on two KJV singletons.

Geographical boilerplate. 'The borders of the land' is the Book of Mormon war narrative's standing phrase for a frontier and appears three times in the two preceding chapters; Exodus 16:35's borders of Canaan are where the manna stopped. The same candidate was offered on the same words at Alma 52:11. The word in this verse that carries a link is 'stripling'.

The machine's top candidate for the verse, on a five-word run that breaks at the decisive word: Paul's is 'ye are in our hearts', Moroni's is 'ye are in our hands'. The real source of the clause is 1 Samuel 24:10, adjudicated at this verse.

'We do not desire to be men of blood' is a Book of Mormon hapax — the phrase occurs in this verse and nowhere else in the book — and it sounds biblical. It is not: 'men of blood' occurs in no KJV verse. The KJV's equivalent is 'bloody men' (Psalm 26:9, 59:2, 139:19), always an imprecation against enemies and never a self-description a speaker declines. 2 Samuel 16:7-8's 'thou bloody man' is the nearest situational fit and is likewise not the Book of Mormon's word order. Recorded because the phrase reads like a quotation and is not one.

A stock list-item. Numbers 14:3 is the murmuring at Kadesh, adjudicated in this book at Alma 2:25 for a genuine reason; nothing here recalls it. The list at 44:5 is the continuation of the Nehemiah 4:14 list adjudicated at Alma 43:45.

exclusions.sharedText: had made an end of speaking these words
exclusions.reason: The chapter's longest machine run — eight words reproducing a KJV singleton — and it is a genuine borrowing, but it is a borrowing the catalogue has already adjudicated twice: at Jacob 3:14, where the argument is made, and again at Alma 12:19 across the book boundary. Here it is the Book of Mormon's own speech-closing formula recurring. The 1 Samuel 24 material that is fresh at this scene is 24:10's sparing of the enemy in hand, and that row sits at Alma 44:1.
An oath formula in twenty-seven KJV verses, twelve of them in 1 Samuel alone. Nothing selects 26:16 over any of the others.

The phrase is adjudicated one verse earlier, at Alma 44:14, where the three KJV owners of it are weighed and Numbers 25:12 is preferred to the two Ezekiel verses. 44:15 is the same covenant being entered rather than offered. See Alma 44:14.

'Cried mightily' is a KJV singleton and Zerahemnah's 'he cried mightily unto Moroni' looks like a quotation of it. It is not. Revelation 18:2 is an angel's proclamation of Babylon's fall 'with a strong voice' — an announcement made from a position of total authority — whereas Alma 44:19 is a beaten commander begging for the lives of his men. The KJV's petitionary form is Jonah 3:8's 'cry mightily unto God', which the Book of Mormon does not use here either; and 'cried mightily' occurs five times in the Book of Mormon, so it is the book's own idiom for urgent speech rather than a borrowing.

exclusions.sharedText: could not be told nor numbered
exclusions.reason: 'The number of their dead were not numbered, because of the greatness of the number' is the KJV's uncountable-multitude idiom, which runs through eleven verses in the 'for multitude' family (Genesis 16:10, 1 Kings 3:8, 1 Kings 8:5 and others) and is a figure rather than a source. The Book of Mormon's version also inverts the usual application: in the KJV the uncountable thing is always a blessing — seed, a congregation, a people — and here it is a body count.

'They did cast their dead into the waters of Sidon; and they have gone forth, and are buried in the depths of the sea' invites Exodus 15:4-5, the drowned Egyptian army whose 'depths have covered them', and Micah 7:19, whose 'depths of the sea' receive what is disposed of for good. Both are adjudicated in this book at Alma 3:3 ('their bones are in the depths of the sea, and they are many'), which is the same author disposing of the same kind of dead in the same water. Fourteen Book of Mormon verses use the phrase; this is the formula recurring. See Alma 3:3.

The stream's top-ranked candidate for the chapter and pure connective boilerplate: Asa in a rage with the seer. 'Because of this thing' is KJV narrative filler (Genesis 19:21, Deuteronomy 15:10, 1 Samuel 24:6 and elsewhere) and Alma uses 'this thing' twice in one verse as a pronoun for the doctrine of restoration. Nothing in 2 Chronicles 16 is in view. A model instance of CONVENTIONS §9's warning that the n-gram score is a recall floor and not a ranking.

A five-word run matching a two-verse KJV phrase, which is rare enough to look like evidence, and it is not. 'I have somewhat to say unto thee' is the KJV's polite formula for opening a difficult subject and it occurs twice, at 1 Kings 2:14 (Adonijah to Bathsheba) and Luke 7:40 (Jesus to Simon the Pharisee); both are followed by 'Say on', and Alma is followed by 'But behold, I will explain it unto thee'. Alma 40:1 opens the previous chapter with the same formula in a different inflection ('here is somewhat more I would say unto thee'), which shows it is the letter's own way of starting a section rather than a borrowing. Registered because the Luke context — a man about to be taught the arithmetic of debt and forgiveness — is close enough to Alma 41's subject to tempt a reader.

exclusions.sharedText: mortality raised to immortality; corruption to incorruption
exclusions.reason: The clause is the fourth appearance in Alma of 1 Corinthians 15:53-54's paired antitheses, and the closest of them to Paul's own wording is Alma 40:2, one chapter earlier, where the verb 'put on' survives and the argument is made. Here the verb is gone and the pairs are reduced to a two-item list inside a longer catalogue of restorations, which is Alma using a formula he has already established rather than reaching for Paul again. Adjudicate at Alma 40:2, with Alma 5:15 and 11:45 recorded there as the earlier paraphrases.

'The night cometh' is a KJV singleton (John 9:4, 'the night cometh, when no man can work') and Alma 41:5 ends its day/night antithesis with it: 'as he has desired to do evil all the day long, even so shall he have his reward of evil, when the night cometh'. The link is adjudicated at Alma 34:33, where Amulek builds the whole day-of-this-life argument on John 9:4 across two verses and keeps John's order. Alma 41:5 and 41:7 ('that endless night of darkness') are the same book's later reuse of that antithesis, five chapters on; 'all the day long' is separately distributed across thirteen KJV verses and identifies nothing.

A five-word run in the wrong argument entirely. Isaiah 41:23 is the LORD's taunt to the idols — show us what is coming, do something, anything, good or bad, so that we may know you are gods — and 'do good, or do evil' there means 'act at all'. Alma 41:7 uses the pair as a genuine moral alternative offered to a free agent. Luke 6:9's 'is it lawful on the sabbath days to do good, or to do evil' is nearer the moral sense and further from the wording. The real borrowings in this verse are Romans 14:4 and Isaiah 44:9, and both are filed as a link.

exclusions.sharedText: these are they that are redeemed of the Lord
exclusions.reason: 'The redeemed of the LORD' occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Psalm 107:2, Isaiah 51:11 and Isaiah 62:12 — and none of them can be shown here. The Psalm has the redeemed telling of it, Isaiah 51:11 has them returning to Zion with singing, Isaiah 62:12 has it as a name given to a people; Alma has it as a class-label for those who pass the judgment. Worth registering rather than passing over because Isaiah 51:11 is itself transcribed in the Book of Mormon at 2 Nephi 8:11, so a reader might reasonably ask whether the phrase reached Alma through the earlier book — but nothing in Alma 41:7 follows 2 Nephi 8 beyond the three words shared with all three KJV verses, so there is no evidence either way and no link.

'Now the decrees of God are unalterable' looks for a KJV parent and has none: 'unalterable' occurs in no KJV verse, and the KJV's one idiom for a decree that cannot be revoked is Persian royal law — 'the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not' (Daniel 6:8, 6:12; compare Esther 1:19, 8:8). That is a real and suggestive background, since the point of the Persian formula is that the king himself cannot undo what he has signed, which is exactly the constraint Alma needs God to be under in order for restoration to be inevitable rather than arbitrary. But there is no shared wording at all, the association is available from general English usage of 'decree', and building a figural link on it would be manufacturing a case. Recorded so that the absence is on the record.

exclusions.sharedText: that they should gather themselves together
exclusions.reason: The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter, on a six-word run: the Lamanite king's proclamation that his people 'should gather themselves together again, to go to battle' against Ezra's proclamation that the children of the captivity 'should gather themselves together unto Jerusalem'. Both are proclamations and both use the KJV's reflexive of assembly, which the Book of Mormon uses hundreds of times. The window closes exactly where the two texts part — 'unto Jerusalem' against 'to go to battle against the Nephites' — and there is no other contact. The chapter's genuine Ezra-shaped material, a covenant enforced by penalty, is in the preceding chapter and is adjudicated at Alma 46:35 against 2 Chronicles 15.

exclusions.sharedText: they would not obey the commandments of the king … the king was wroth
exclusions.reason: Alma 47:2-3 stages the scene Esther 1 opens with: subjects refuse the king's command, and the king is angry at the disobedience. Esther 1:12 — 'the queen Vashti refused to come at the king's commandment … therefore was the king very wroth' — is the King James Bible's one such scene, and a reader who knows Esther will stop here. It will not carry a link. 'The king was wroth' as the Book of Mormon has it occurs in no KJV verse; 'was wroth' is spread over twenty-four; nothing else in the two passages agrees; and the Book of Mormon's refusers are an army afraid of dying, not a queen refusing to be displayed. Registered so the resemblance is on record as considered and declined.

exclusions.sharedText: come down / four times after this sort
exclusions.reason: The closest situational analogue in the King James Bible to Alma 47:10-13, and the one a reader is most likely to propose. Nehemiah's enemies invite him repeatedly to come down from his work to a meeting in the plain — 'but they thought to do me mischief' — he answers 'I cannot come down' twice in one verse, and Nehemiah 6:4 counts the sendings: 'yet they sent unto me four times after this sort'. Amalickiah likewise sends four times, likewise means mischief, and likewise cannot get his man to come down. The reason it is not the source is that the wording belongs to another passage: 'sent again the second time' is a KJV singleton at 2 Samuel 14:29, where Absalom is the sender and the refusal is verbatim, and the chapter's other borrowings (47:4, 47:30) come from the same three chapters of 2 Samuel. The link is written at 47:11 and a reader of Nehemiah 6 is sent there. Nehemiah's fourfold count remains the better explanation of why Amalickiah sends four times rather than Absalom's two, and it is recorded on that link.

A six-word run of pure connective tissue. The nobleman of Capernaum besought Jesus 'that he would come down, and heal his son'; Amalickiah sends a message 'desiring that he would come down, and that he would bring his guards with him'. Two indirect requests in the same English construction, sharing no content word but the verb of descent, which both texts need because both have a person higher up than another. 'Come down to' alone stands in eleven KJV verses. Nothing about Alma 47 touches the Capernaum healing.

exclusions.sharedText: that he would suffer them to
exclusions.reason: Tied for the chapter's top n-gram score, and worthless. Amalickiah's surrounded men 'plead with Amalickiah that he would suffer them to fall in with their brethren'; the Gadarene demons 'besought him that he would suffer them to enter into' the swine. The six shared words are the KJV's ordinary formula for a granted petition and the two petitions have nothing else in common. A clean instance of the trap at ADJUDICATING §4: a long run that means nothing on its own.

exclusions.sharedText: the king assassinated by his own servants, who then flee
exclusions.reason: Alma 47:24-30 turns on a story the Book of Mormon has Amalickiah fabricate — that the king's own servants stabbed him and fled — and the King James Bible tells that story three times: Rechab and Baanah kill Ishbosheth and escape (2 Samuel 4:5-7), Joash's servants make a conspiracy and slay him (2 Kings 12:20), Amon's servants conspire and slay the king in his own house (2 Kings 21:23). The Book of Mormon supplies no wording from any of them and, more tellingly, refuses the only idiom they share: the KJV kills kings by smiting them 'under the fifth rib', in four verses and always politically, while Alma 47:24 says 'stabbed the king to the heart' — a verb that appears in no KJV verse at all, in a sentence whose 'lying in his gore' uses a noun the KJV never uses. The scene is biblical and its language is not. The type-scene that does carry a link is the treacherous greeting of 2 Samuel 20:9-10, written at this verse.

exclusions.sharedText: Whosoever loved the king, let him go forth
exclusions.reason: 'Whosoever loved the king, let him go forth and pursue his servants' is a loyalty muster, and the KJV has two famous ones: Moses in the gate — 'Who is on the LORD's side? let him come unto me' (Exodus 32:26) — and Jehu at Jezreel's window, 'Who is on my side? who?' (2 Kings 9:32). Both are interrogatives answered by a gathering; Alma 47:27 is a relative clause followed by a jussive, shares no wording with either, and is a fraud rather than a test of allegiance. The resemblance is generic to the situation. Recorded because the cry is the kind of sentence a reader assumes must be quoted from somewhere.

The machine's proposal at the verse where the true source is 2 Samuel 15:6. Joshua 7:5 is the rout at Ai: 'wherefore the hearts of the people melted, and became as water' — courage failing. Alma 47:30 is 'Amalickiah, by his fraud, gained the hearts of the people' — allegiance transferred. Same four words, opposite organ-metaphor; and the KJV's own phrase for what Amalickiah does, 'stole the hearts of the men of Israel', is a singleton one book later.

'Took her unto him to wife' reproduces a phrase that occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 20:30 — 'and the second took her to wife, and he died childless' — the second of seven brothers in the Sadducees' levirate riddle about the resurrection. The rarity is real and the sense is unrelated: Luke's phrase is a legal obligation discharged in a hypothetical, Alma's is a usurper securing a crown. The figural link at this verse is written to 1 Kings 2:22, where the King James Bible states the convention Amalickiah is exploiting.

A KJV singleton, the n-gram stream's top candidate for this verse, and adjudicated three times already — at Mosiah 7:9 for the phrase's first substantial use, at Mosiah 29:2 where it returns to its source as Mosiah abolishes the kingship, and at Alma 2:7 where the voice of the people first decides a question the other way by refusing to make Amlici king. Alma 51:7 is that same decision a second time, and the narrator's formula rather than a fresh borrowing: 'the voice of the people came in the favor of the freemen', against a party whose object was 'to establish a king over the land' (51:5). Registered rather than linked because a reader of this chapter should be sent to Alma 2:7, where the argument about a people voting down a king is made, and to Mosiah 29:2 for Samuel's own verse. The Alma 46:34 row does the same for Moroni's oath.

exclusions.sharedText: the standard of liberty … the title of liberty
exclusions.reason: The title of liberty is Alma 46's, not this chapter's: Moroni's rent coat, the writing on it, and the biblical language behind them are adjudicated at Alma 46:12 (Nehemiah 4:14 and Ahijah's rent garment at 1 Kings 11:30), 46:13 and 46:22. Alma 51:20's 'yielded to the standard of liberty, and were compelled to hoist the title of liberty upon their towers' is the ensign five chapters later, doing the work the earlier chapter set up — the coerced hoisting is the narrative point, and it has no new biblical contact. Registered so that a reader meeting the title here is sent to where it was raised.

A four-word run against a KJV singleton, and the association is apt enough to be worth refusing in writing. 'Take possession of the' occurs only at 1 Kings 21:15, Jezebel's instruction to Ahab to go down and take Naboth's vineyard now that Naboth has been judicially murdered — the Bible's paradigm of seizing land by killing for it. Amalickiah is taking cities by killing for them. But 'take possession' in its other inflections is ordinary KJV and ordinary English (Joshua 22:19, 1 Kings 21:16), the object here is a province and not a vineyard, and there is no second point of contact anywhere in the chapter: no false witness, no fasting proclaimed, no dogs, no prophet sent afterward. The rarity is a fact about the KJV's inflections, not about this sentence.

exclusions.sharedText: inasmuch as ye shall keep the commandments of God, ye shall prosper in the land
exclusions.reason: The land covenant, quoted here in the same breath as the Psalm 5:1 exordium and flagged by the text itself as a repetition of what was said to Helaman at Alma 37:13. Its adjudication is at 1 Nephi 2:20, to 1 Kings 2:3. Worth one observation the register can hold: 38:1 reads 'ye shall be CAST off from his presence' where Alma 37:13, seventeen verses earlier, reads 'CUT off from his presence'. Neither wording is the KJV's — 1 Kings 9:7 has 'cut off' of Israel and the land, not of a presence — so the variation is internal drift in a formula the book has repeated for five hundred years of its own chronology, and it is evidence about the Book of Mormon rather than about its source.

'My son, give ear to my words.' The KJV singleton is real and the catalogue records it — at Alma 36:1, the opening of the blessing to Helaman, which Alma 38:1 deliberately repeats to the second son ('even as I said unto Helaman'). Adjudicating it twice would double-count a formula the chapter itself marks as a repetition. The corpus's other use is at 2 Nephi 9:40. See Alma 36:1.

'For blessed is he that endureth to the end.' 'Endureth to the end' is a KJV singleton at Matthew 10:22 and the machine ranks it first in the chapter, but the phrase has already been adjudicated in this book at Alma 32:13, where seven continuous words are reproduced ('he that findeth mercy and endureth to the end, the same shall be saved') and where the fusion with Matthew 24:13's apodosis is the finding. Alma 38:2 has three of those words and replaces the apodosis with a beatitude formula, which is the standing Book of Mormon form (2 Nephi 31:15-20, 3 Nephi 15:9). Alma reusing his own compressed version six chapters later is not a fresh borrowing (ADJUDICATING §4). See Alma 32:13.

exclusions.sharedText: his voice was as thunder, and it shook the whole earth
exclusions.reason: Alma's conversion is told three times in the Book of Mormon and twice by Alma himself in consecutive chapters. The biblical wording of the angelic voice is adjudicated at Alma 36:7, where the fuller telling supports links to both Acts 26:14 (the Damascus-road pattern) and Revelation 19:6 ('as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of mighty thunderings'). Alma 38:7 is the two-clause abridgement of that same sentence, delivered to a different son in the same week, and it introduces no biblical vocabulary the fuller telling lacks. See Alma 36:7.

The longest exact run the machine finds in this chapter — eight words — and it is the same run already adjudicated at Alma 36:10, in the parallel account, where the argument is that the Book of Mormon's third telling of the episode (Mosiah 27:23) lacks the nights and Alma's two first-person tellings supply them from Matthew's Jonah formula. Alma 38:8 is that second telling. The one thing it adds is 'the most bitter pain and anguish of soul', which is not Matthew's and whose nearest KJV neighbours ('anguish of spirit', Exodus 6:9; 'bitterness of soul', Job 7:11, 10:1) are too scattered to adjudicate. See Alma 36:10.

exclusions.sharedText: he is the life and the light of the world
exclusions.reason: 'Behold, he is the life and the light of the world.' The joining of light to life is adjudicated at Alma 28:14, where the catalogue notes that the KJV puts the two nouns together in one verse only. Alma 38:9 states the same title more fully, adding 'of the world' from John 8:12's 'I am the light of the world' and inverting John 1:4's order ('in him was life; and the life was the light of men') so that life comes first. The inversion is worth a reader's notice and is not enough to re-adjudicate. Note that the verse's other clause, 'no other way nor means whereby man can be saved', carries a link of its own at this verse to Acts 4:12. See Alma 28:14.

exclusions.sharedText: receive you at the last day into his kingdom, to sit down in peace
exclusions.reason: 'And may the Lord bless your soul, and receive you at the last day into his kingdom, to sit down in peace.' Sitting down in the kingdom is adjudicated at Alma 7:25, which reproduces two KJV singletons of Matthew 8:11 ('sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob', 'in the kingdom of heaven'). Alma 38:15 has the eschatological sitting without the patriarchs and without the KJV's phrase for the kingdom, and adds 'in peace', which is not Matthew's. Recorded so that a reader who arrives at the last verse of the farewell is sent to where the borrowing is argued. See Alma 7:25.

exclusions.sharedText: sent unto Moroni, desiring that he would
exclusions.reason: A cross-reference, not a rejection. 'Ammoron sent unto Moroni, desiring that he would exchange prisoners' is the third use in three chapters of the construction adjudicated at Alma 52:10, where the Book of Mormon reproduces eight consecutive words of Acts 19:31 — the KJV's one verse containing 'sent unto him, desiring him that he would'. This occurrence is the interesting one for a different reason: at 52:10 and 52:20 the formula carries Nephite messages, and here it carries the enemy king's, so the whole negotiation of Alma 52-54 runs in both directions on one borrowed frame. Registered here so that a reader arriving at 54:1 is sent to 52:10 rather than shown nothing.

The same candidate the machine offered at Alma 52:8, on the same words, and declined for the same reason. Lamentations 3:34's 'To crush under his feet all the prisoners of the earth' is one item in a list of things the Lord does not approve; Alma 54:3 is an inventory of who is held by whom before an exchange. The Book of Mormon uses 'the prisoners of' whenever it counts captives, which in these three chapters is constantly.

Five words of pure address-formula, and the senses run opposite: the Gibeonites' 'and now, behold, we are in thine hand' is a surrender, Moroni's 'and now behold, we are prepared to receive you' is a threat. Covered in kind by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

Registered because the collocation is genuinely close and still will not carry a link. 'Maintain the cause' occurs in two KJV verses (1 Kings 8:59, Psalm 140:12) and 'maintain their cause' in four more, all of them in Solomon's temple prayer or its Chronicles double, and all of them petitions that God will maintain a cause. Alma 54:10's 'we will maintain our religion and the cause of our God' reverses the direction — men undertaking to maintain God's cause rather than asking him to maintain theirs — and 'the cause of' is in any case the Book of Mormon war narrative's own idiom, running from 'the cause of freedom' at Alma 46 onward.

'As the LORD liveth' occurs in twenty-seven KJV verses and is the Bible's standard oath; no one of them can be a source. That the n-gram stream picked Gehazi's oath in 2 Kings 5:20 is an artifact of the preceding 'but', which Alma 54:10 also has. The Book of Mormon uses the formula throughout.

The chapter's top-ranked candidate by the n-gram score and worthless. Five words made entirely of auxiliaries and pronouns, straddling a clause boundary in both texts; Ezekiel 24:14's 'I will do it; I will not go back' is the Lord's oath of irrevocable judgement, Alma 54:11's 'if this be the case that ye will do it, I will exchange' is the terms of a prisoner swap. CONVENTIONS §9's warning about the n-gram stream in one row.

Four ordinary words. Zechariah 12:9's 'I will seek to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem' is a divine promise of protection; Alma 54:13 is a man's threat of reprisal in kind ('if ye seek to destroy us more, we will seek to destroy you'), and the doubling within the verse is what the sentence is for. Nothing else in the verse touches Zechariah.

Worth a line because the collision is instructive. Ephesians 1:6's 'he hath made us accepted in the beloved' is about election and grace; Alma 54:21's 'we know not but that he hath made us as well as you' is about creation, and is offered by a man denying that he knows whether there is anyone to have made him. Four shared words, opposite theological work. The link at this verse is filed on 'as well as you' (Job 12:3) and 'as concerning that' (Acts 13:34), both KJV singletons.

The same machine proposal discharged at Alma 43:9. 'Hands of their enemies' is a KJV singleton at Judges 2:14, but the Book of Mormon uses it seventeen times and the Judges-cycle reading is adjudicated in this book at Alma 2:28 against Judges 2:18, the verse that supplies the deliverance rather than the selling. See Alma 2:28.
A four-word run of intensifiers. The magi seeing the star and a nation giving thanks after a war share the KJV's stock superlative for gladness and nothing else.

exclusions.sharedText: the words which I spake unto
exclusions.reason: A six-word run of pure reported-speech tissue, and the chapter's longest. Luke 24:44 is the risen Christ opening the scriptures; Alma 45:2 is a father asking his son whether he believed what he was told about the records. The shared string is the English for referring back to something one has said.

The catechetical exchange at 45:2-7 — 'Believest thou in Jesus Christ, which shall come?' / 'Yea, I believe … with all my heart' — reaches for the KJV's baptismal confession at Acts 8:37 ('If thou believest with all thine heart … I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God') and for John 11:26-27's 'Believest thou this? … Yea, Lord: I believe'. Both are already adjudicated in this book: Acts 8:37 at Alma 6:8 and Alma 15:6, John 11:26-27 at Alma 19:9. 'Believest thou' occurs in seventeen Book of Mormon verses, thirteen of them in Alma, so by chapter 45 it is the book's own interrogative and not a fresh borrowing. What is fresh at this scene is what follows the confession, and that row sits at Alma 45:8.

A five-word run of dialogue tags, scoring 2.00 on a string that is three function words and a pronoun. Worth recording only for the coincidence: the verse the machine reached is from 2 Kings 2, the chapter in which Elijah is taken up, eleven verses before Alma 45:18-19 says its own prophet was taken up. The coincidence is the ranker's, not the text's — 2 Kings 2:3 is the sons of the prophets telling Elisha the Lord will take his master away, and nothing of that reaches Helaman's promise to keep his father's commandments. 2 Kings 2:11 does bear on 45:19 and is recorded in that row's composite.

A four-word run whose sense is opposed. 2 Kings 10:30 is a reward — Jehu is told his children to the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel — while Alma 45:12 is a deadline: 'even the fourth generation shall not all pass away, before this great iniquity shall come.' The fourth generation is a blessing in the source and a term of destruction here. The generation-count Alma 45 is actually working from is Matthew 24:34's 'this generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled', which belongs to the Olivet material adjudicated at 45:11.

'Works of darkness' occurs in two KJV verses, Romans 13:12 and Ephesians 5:11, and neither is selected by anything at 45:12. Paul's is a metaphor of night and dawn with armour attached; Alma's is one item in a list of vices ('the works of darkness and lasciviousness, and all manner of iniquities') where the phrase is doing no metaphorical work at all.

'He also blessed the earth, for the righteous' sake' is a striking half-line and 'for the righteous' sake' occurs in no KJV verse at all. The idea — a land spared or preserved on account of the righteous who are in it — has one biblical home, Abraham's bargaining over Sodom ('If I find in Sodom fifty righteous within the city, then I will spare all the place for their sakes'), and the pairing of 45:15's blessing with 45:16's curse on the same land is Genesis 18's logic applied in both directions. But there is no wording to test, and the Book of Mormon's own land-blessing-and-cursing doctrine is established from 2 Nephi 1:7 onward without it.
